Being is not one, but one and many, and is not one kind: its kinds are also its principles, and they are found by taking soul as a way in, as one would take a stone to learn what body is. In soul there are substance and life; life is motion, and motion calls for rest; thought, setting the three apart and bringing them together, sees otherness and sameness. So there are five first kinds, being, motion, rest, sameness and otherness, the greatest kinds of Plato's Sophist (254d-255e). The one is not a kind, nor are quantity, quality, relation and the rest, nor the good, the beautiful, knowledge, intellect and the virtues: they are beyond being, or come after the first kinds, or are made of them. Last Plotinus begins to show how the species come from the kinds: the universal intellect holds the particular intellects potentially, as knowledge holds its theorems; number, magnitude, quality, shape and life come forth in it, and it is the complete living being of Plato's Timaeus, whose image is soul and this world. How the kinds of the perceptible stand is left to VI.3.

@ch VI.2.1 | Our own kinds of being
After the ten kinds of Aristotle's school and the Stoics' one, we must say what we think, bringing it back to Plato. If being were one, there would be no questions about kinds and principles; but it is not. First we must mark off what we call being, what always is, from what others take for being but we say comes to be: not as two species of one kind, but as being from its image.

@p
Since we have examined the ten kinds, as they are called, and have also spoken about those who bring all things into one kind and set four under the one as if they were its species, it would follow to say what appears to us about these matters, as we try to bring our views back to Plato's opinion.
!note The ten kinds are the categories of Aristotle's school, examined in VI.1.1-24; the one kind with four under it is the Stoics' "something" (τί), with substrate, qualified, disposed and relatively disposed, examined in VI.1.25-30.

@p
@greek εἰ μὲν οὖν ἓν ἔδει
If we had to posit being as one, there would be no need to inquire whether there is one kind over all things, or kinds not under one; whether there are principles; whether the principles and the kinds must be posited as the same, or the kinds and the principles the same; or whether all the principles are also kinds, but the kinds are not principles, or the other way round; or whether on each side some principles are also kinds and some kinds also principles; or whether on one side all are also the other, while on the other side only some are.
!flag And do both the sets of categories we have been examining imply | The Greek has only "on the one side ... on the other" (ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν ἑτέρων ... ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἑτέρων), the principles and the kinds; nothing here of the two sets of categories examined in VI.1.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ δὲ οὐχ ἕν φαμεν
But since we say that being is not one (why, Plato and others have said), it becomes necessary, perhaps, to look into these questions too, first setting out before us what number we speak of, and how.
!flag these questions become imperative, once we are satisfied as to the number of genera | The Greek says we must look into these questions "first setting out" (πρότερον εἰς μέσον θέντας) what number of kinds we speak of, and how: the number is the first task, not a condition already met.
!note Plato argues against those who say that being is one in the Sophist (244b-245e); among the "others" is Aristotle (Physics I.2-3, 185a20-187a10).

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ οὖν περὶ τοῦ ὄντος
Since, then, we are inquiring about being, or the things that are, we must first distinguish these among ourselves: what we call being, about which our inquiry may rightly be now, and what others think is being, but we say comes to be and never really is.
!note Plato's Timaeus (27d-28a): "What is that which always is and has no coming to be, and what is that which always comes to be and never is?"

@p
@greek δεῖ δὲ νοεῖν ταῦτα
These must be thought of as divided from each other, not as if a kind, "something", were divided into them; nor must we suppose that Plato did so. For it would be ridiculous to put being under one kind with not-being, as if one were to put Socrates under the same kind as his portrait. Dividing here is marking off and setting apart, and saying that what seemed to be being is not being, showing them that what truly is being is something else. And by adding "always" to being he showed that being must be such as never to belie the nature of being. It is of this being, then, that we shall speak, and we shall examine it as not being one; later, if it seems good, we shall say something about coming to be, what comes to be, and the perceptible world.
!flag implying that the nature of True Being has been quite misapprehended | The Greek says Plato showed "them" (αὐτοῖς) that what truly is is something else; nothing here of a misapprehension.
!note "Something" (τί) is the Stoics' highest kind, over bodies and bodiless things alike (VI.1.25); Plotinus will not put being and what comes to be under any such kind. The perceptible world is the subject of VI.3.

@ch VI.2.2 | Kinds that are also principles
Being is one and many, a varied one. Either it is one kind with the beings as its species, or many kinds under one, or many kinds under none, each with its own species, all making up the intelligible world: then they are kinds and principles at once. How the kinds mix and stay pure is for later. They cannot all be species of one being, for one does not become many of itself; nor is being or substance said of each thing as its kind.

@p
Since, then, we say it is not one, is it some number? Or unlimited? For what do we mean by "not one"? Surely that it is one and many at once, a varied one holding the many in one. This one, then, must be either one in kind, with the things that are as its species, by which they are many and one; or there are more kinds than one, but all under one; or there are more kinds, none under another, but each embracing what is under it, whether these too are lesser kinds, or species with individuals under them; and all contribute to one nature, and from all of them the intelligible world, which we call being, has its constitution.
!flag the number may well be infinite | The Greek asks "is it some number? Or unlimited?" (ἆρα ἀριθμόν τινα; ἢ ἄπειρον), and leaves it a question; Page answers it.

@p
@greek εἰ δὴ τοῦτο, οὐ μόνον
If so, these are not only kinds but at the same time principles of being: kinds, because under them are other, lesser kinds, and species after these, and individuals; principles, if being is in this way from many, and the whole is from these. But if there were more things from which it comes, and they came together as wholes and made the all, without having anything under them, they would be principles, but not kinds: as if someone made the perceptible world from the four, fire and the rest; these would be principles, but not kinds, unless "kind" is said by a shared name only.
!note Empedocles' four roots, fire, air, water and earth, are the four elements of the perceptible world (Aristotle, Metaphysics A.3, 984a8-11). Principles that have nothing under them are not kinds: a kind is said of what falls under it.

@p
@greek λέγοντες τοίνυν καὶ γένη
Saying, then, that there are certain kinds, and that the same are principles, do we mix the kinds with each other, each together with what is under it, to complete the whole, and make a blend of them all? But then each would be potentially, not actually, and none would be pure itself. Shall we, then, leave the kinds alone and mix the individuals? What, then, will the kinds be by themselves? They too will be by themselves and pure, and the things mixed will not destroy them. And how? That is for later.
!note In a blend, Aristotle says, the ingredients are no longer actually, but only potentially (On generation and corruption I.10, 327b22-31). How the kinds mix and yet stay pure comes back in chapter 19.

@p
@greek νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ συγκεχωρήκαμεν
For now, since we have agreed that there are kinds, and moreover that they are principles of substance, and in another way principles and compounds, we must first say in relation to what we call them kinds, and how we keep them apart from each other and do not bring them under one, as though they had come together by chance and made some one thing; and yet it would be much more reasonable to bring them under one.
!flag that there are genera as distinct from principles of Being | The Greek agrees that there are kinds "and moreover" (καὶ προσέτι) principles of substance: the same things are kinds and principles, as the chapter has argued, not kinds distinct from principles.
!flag it would be more plausible to dispense with their separate existence | The Greek says it would be much more reasonable "to bring them under one" (ὑφ’ ἕν): the objection is that one kind over them would be the likelier view.

@p
@greek ἤ, εἰ μὲν εἴδη οἷόν
Or rather: if all of them could be species of being, with the individuals next under them and nothing outside these, perhaps one could do so. But such a position does away with them. The species will not be species, nor will there be many under one at all, but all will be one, with no other thing or things outside that one. For how could the one have become many, so as to generate species, unless there were something else besides it? It is not many of itself, unless someone chops it up like a magnitude; but even so, what chops it is something else. And if it chops itself up, or divides itself in any way, it will be divided before it is divided.
!note "Chopped up" (κερματίζειν) is Plato's word for being divided among all the things that are (Parmenides 144b-e), taken up again in chapter 22.

@p
@greek ταύτῃ μὲν οὖν καὶ δἰ
For this reason, then, and for many others, we must keep away from a single kind; and also because it is not possible to call each thing taken, whatever it is, being or substance. If someone does call it being, he will say so by accident, as if he called a substance white: for he does not say that it is what white is.
!flag we are not predicating the Absolute Whiteness | The Greek says only that he does not call it "just what white is" (ὅπερ λευκόν), white in its essence; Page's capitals make it a Platonic form. Being said of each thing would be said by accident, not as its kind.
!note "Just what a thing is" (ὅπερ) is Aristotle's way of saying what is said of a thing in its essence (Posterior Analytics I.22, 83a24-30). Aristotle too denies that being is a kind, because a kind is not said of its own differences, and the differences of being are beings (Metaphysics B.3, 998b22-27).

@ch VI.2.3 | The One beyond the kinds
The kinds are many, and not by chance, so they come from one; but the One they come from is beyond, not counted among them, for we are seeking the things that are. If what is counted with them were their cause, they would still be kinds of their own. Perhaps they are rather parts of one nature, which our thinking divides and puts together again. How many kinds there are must be shown by thought, not by denials.

@p
We say, then, that there are more than one, and more not by chance. So they are from one. Or rather, even if they are from one, but from one not predicated of them in what they are, nothing prevents each, not being of the same species as another, from being a kind apart by itself.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν ἔξωθεν τοῦτο
Is this one, then, outside the kinds that have come to be, their cause, but not predicated of the others in what they are? Yes, it is outside: for the One is beyond, so as not to be counted with the kinds, if the others, which are equal to one another in being kinds, are through it. And how is it not counted with them? Because we are seeking the things that are, not what is beyond. So much for that.
!note "Beyond" (ἐπέκεινα): the good is "beyond substance" in Plato's Republic (VI 509b), and the One beyond being in Plotinus (V.1.8-10, V.4.1-2).

@p
@greek τί δὲ τὸ συναριθμούμενον
But what of what is counted with them? Here one might wonder how it is counted along with the things it causes. If it and the others are under one kind, that is strange. But if it is counted in with those it causes as being itself the kind, with the others next after it, and these differ from it, and it is not predicated of them as a kind, nor is anything else, then they too must be kinds, having things under them. For if you produced walking, walking would not be under you as under its kind; and if there were nothing else before walking as its kind, but there were things after it, walking would be a kind among the things that are.

@p
@greek ὅλως δὲ ἴσως οὐδὲ
Perhaps, in general, we should not even say that the one is the cause of the others, but that they are as it were its parts and its elements, and all are one nature, divided by our ways of thinking; while it, by a wonderful power, is one in all, appearing many and becoming many, as when it is moved; and the abundance of its nature makes the one not one. And we, bringing out as it were its portions, set each of them down as one and call it a kind, not knowing that we did not see the whole at once. Bringing them out part by part, we join them again, since we cannot hold them apart for long, as they hasten to one another. So we let them go again into the whole and let them become one, or rather be one.
!note "Our ways of thinking" (ἐπίνοιαι): the kinds are distinguished in thought, as chapter 7 says of motion and being, though in being they are one.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ ἴσως σαφέστερα
But perhaps this will be clearer when those other things are known too, if we grasp how many the kinds are: for so we shall also grasp how. But since one who speaks must not speak only in denials, but must go on to a notion and a thought of what he says, we must proceed as follows.
!flag for thus we shall also discover their causes | The Greek says "so too the how" (οὕτω γὰρ καὶ τὸ πῶς): knowing how many the kinds are will show how they are one and many; nothing here of their causes.

@ch VI.2.4 | Soul as the way in
To learn what body is, we would take a stone and find in it substrate, quantity and quality, three in thought but one body. In the same way, to find the kinds of intelligible substance, we must take away what belongs to body and take something that truly is and is more one. The wonder is how it is many: soul seemed simple, but let us take soul, which comes from the intelligible, and see how its one nature is many.

@p
If we wanted to see the nature of body, what the nature of body itself is in this all, would we not learn it from one of its parts, say a stone: that one thing in it is like its substrate, another its how much, its magnitude, and another its what sort, as its colour? And we would say of every other body that in the nature of body one thing is something like substance, another is quantity, another quality: all together, but divided by account into three, and body would be the three as one. And if motion too were in it, grown into its make-up, we would count this too, and the four would be one, and the one body would be completed, for its unity and its own nature, by them all.
!flag the pseudosubstance, the quantity, the quality | The Greek says "something like substance" (οἷον οὐσία): the substrate of a body is called substance only loosely, since perceptible substance is not substance in the proper sense (VI.3.2-8); Page's "pseudo" makes it false.
!note "Divided by account" (τῷ λόγῳ διαιρεθέντα): here λόγος is the account, in thought, not the forming principle.

@p
@greek τὸν αὐτὸν δὴ τρόπον
In the same way, since our account is of intelligible substance and of the kinds and principles there, we must take away the coming to be found in bodies, and the knowing through perception, and the magnitudes (for these are what make things apart and standing away from one another), and grasp some intelligible reality, what truly is, and is more one.

@p
@greek ἐν ᾧ καὶ τὸ θαῦμα
And here is the wonder: how what is one in this way is many and one. For in bodies it is agreed that the same thing is one and many: the same body can be divided without limit, and its colour is one thing and its shape another, for they are separated. But if one takes soul, one, without extension, without magnitude, most simple, as it will seem at the first glance of thought, how could one hope to find it many after all? And yet one who thought he had come to an end when the living being was divided into body and soul, the body many-formed, composite and varied, was confident that he had found the soul simple, and could rest from his journey, having come to a principle.
!flag single, continuous, without extension | The Greek's words are "one, without extension, without magnitude, most simple" (μίαν, ἀδιάστατον, ἀμεγέθη, ἁπλούστατον); "continuous" is Page's, and a word for bodies.

@p
@greek ταύτην τοίνυν τὴν ψυχήν
Let us take this soul, then, since it has been put before us from the intelligible place, as body was, in the other case, from the perceptible, and see how this one is many and how the many are one: not a composite one from many, but one nature that is many. For when this has been grasped and made clear, the truth about the kinds in being, we said, will be clear too.
!note "The intelligible place" (νοητὸς τόπος): Plato's Republic (VI 508c, VII 517b). Soul is the intelligible nearest to us, as a stone is the nearest body.

@ch VI.2.5 | Soul, a one that is many
Bodies are many and come from one, and what is more one is more being. Since they do not come from what is simply one, they come from a one that is many: soul, which makes them. Soul is many as the sum of the forming principles, its act; and even the part of it that does not make has many powers. Its being is not bare being, as a stone's is being a stone, but being soul, a substance that has nothing from outside.

@p
First we must keep this in mind. Bodies, those of animals and plants for example, are each many, in colours, shapes and magnitudes, and in the forms of their parts, one here and another there; yet all of them come from one. They come either from what is altogether one, or from something more one than what comes from it, and so too more being than what comes to be from it: for the further from one, the further from being.
!note The Greek of the second case is uncertain (ἢ ἕξει πάντη παντὸς ἑνός); the modern version gives its sense.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ οὖν ἐξ ἑνὸς μέν
Since, then, they come from one, but not from one in such a way as to be wholly one, or the one itself (for that would not have made a plurality standing apart), it remains that they come from a one that is many. What made them was soul: so soul is a one that is many.

@p
@greek τί οὖν; τὸ πλῆθος
What, then? Is the plurality the forming principles of the things that come to be? Is soul itself one thing, and the forming principles another? Or is soul too a forming principle, the sum of the forming principles, and the forming principles are its act, as it acts by its substance, while its substance is the power of the forming principles? This one, then, is shown in this way to be many, from what it makes in other things.
!flag the Reason-Principles of the things of process | VI.1 and VI.2 keep λόγος as "the forming principle", the principle in soul that forms what comes to be; "Reason-Principle" is Page's word for it, after MacKenna.
!note Soul as holding all the forming principles: III.2.2, IV.3.10; the forming principles as the act of soul and its substance as their power, as act and power are paired in II.5.

@p
@greek τί δ’ εἰ μὴ ποιοῖ
But what if it did not make, and someone took it as not making, going up to the part of it that does not make? Will he not find many powers here too? Everyone would grant that it is. But is it the same as if he said that a stone is? No, not the same. And yet even there, in the stone, being for the stone was not simply being, but being a stone; so here too soul's being has, with being, being soul.
!note "Being for a stone" (τὸ λίθῳ εἶναι) is Aristotle's way of naming what it is to be something, as "water" and "being for water" (On the soul III.4, 429b10-22; Metaphysics Z.4-6).

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν ἄλλο τὸ εἶναι
Is its being, then, one thing, and the rest, which completes soul's substance, another? Is it being, while a difference makes it soul? Or is soul a certain being, yet not as a man is white, but as some substance only? And this is the same as not having from outside its substance what it has.

@ch VI.2.6 | Being and life, one and many
If soul were substance by being and soul by a character from outside, only part of it would be substance. Its being must be a source, all that it is: being and life are one. Yet soul is one and many: in a kind of motion, trying to see itself, it becomes many, because it cannot bear to be one when it can be all; it appears many so that it may think.

@p
But does it not, then, have something from outside its own substance, so that it is in one respect by being and in another by being of such a kind? But if it is soul by being of such a kind, and the such-kind comes from outside, then soul will not be substance as a whole, as soul, but in some respect; a part of it will be substance, but not the whole. Then, what will its being be without the rest? A stone's? No: this being of it must be in its being like a source and principle, or rather all that it is: so it is life too, and both are one.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν οὕτως ἕν
Is it one, then, as one forming principle is? No: the substrate is one, but one in such a way as to be two or more, as many as are the first things that soul is. Either, then, it is substance and life, or it has life. But if it has it, what has it is not, by itself, in life, and life is not in substance. But if the one does not have the other, both must be called one.
!flag One, in the sense of being one Reason-Principle | λόγος here too is the forming principle; "Reason-Principle" is Page's.

@p
@greek ἢ ἓν καὶ πολλὰ καὶ τοσαῦτα
Or rather it is one and many, as many as appear in the one; one in itself, but many in relation to the others; being one, it makes itself many in a kind of motion, and it is one whole, but many when it tries, as it were, to contemplate itself. For it is as if being could not bear to be one when it is able to be all that it is. Contemplation is the cause of its appearing many, so that it may think: for if it appeared one, it would not have thought, but would already be that.
!flag its purpose is the Act of the Intellect | The Greek says only "so that it may think" (ἵνα νοήσῃ): thinking needs the many; nothing here of the act of intellect as a purpose.
!note Thinking needs a duality of thinker and thought, which is why the One does not think (V.3.10-11, V.6.1-2). The subject has passed from soul to being itself, which soul shows.

@ch VI.2.7 | Being, motion and rest
In soul we found substance and life; life is common to soul and intellect, and what is common to all life is motion. So substance and motion, the first life, are two kinds, one in being but set apart by thought, as in the perceptible, a shadow of being, being is apart from life. Motion is with being as its act. And since being stays always the same, rest must be a kind too, other than motion and other than being; otherwise motion and rest would be one.

@p
What, then, and how many are the things seen in it? Since we found in soul substance and life together, and substance is common to all soul, and life too is common, and there is life in intellect as well, bringing in intellect too and its life, we shall set down what is common to all life, motion, as one kind; and substance, and motion, which is the first life, we shall set down as two kinds. For even if they are one, thought separates them, finding the one not one; otherwise it could not separate them.
!note Plato's Sophist (248e-249a): what wholly is cannot be without motion, life, soul and intelligence. The five greatest kinds, being, motion, rest, the same and the other, are set out there (254d-255e).

@p
@greek ὅρα δὲ καὶ ἐν ἄλλοις
Look too in other things, how clearly motion or life is separated from being, if not in true being, at least in the shadow of being, which bears its name. For as in a man's portrait much is lacking, and above all the chief thing, life, so in perceptible things being is a shadow of being, taken away from what most is, which in the archetype was life. From here, then, we have been able to separate being from living and living from being.

@p
@greek ὄντος μὲν δὴ εἴδη
Of being, then, there are many species, and it is one kind. Motion is to be ranked neither under being nor over being, but with being, found in it not as in a substrate: for it is its act, and neither is without the other except in thought, and the two natures are one; for being is in act, not in potential. And yet if you took each apart, motion would appear in being and being in motion, as in "the one being" each part had the other apart; but thought still says they are two, and each form a double one.
!flag Being, then, containing many species, has but one genus | The Greek says being "has many species and is one kind" (εἴδη πολλὰ καὶ ἓν γένος): being is itself the kind, not something that has one.
!flag in the individual they may be mutually exclusive | The Greek speaks of "the one being" (ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς ὄντος) of Plato's Parmenides, where each part "had the other" (εἶχε θάτερον); Page makes it the individual, and the having exclusion.
!note In the Parmenides' second hypothesis (142d-143a), each part of "the one that is", its one and its being, has the other in it, so that it is endlessly many. Motion is "not in being as in a substrate": an accident is in a subject (Aristotle, Categories 2, 1a24-25), but motion is being's own act.

@p
@greek κινήσεως δὲ περὶ τὸ ὂν
Since motion has appeared about being without displacing its nature, but rather making it, as it were, complete in being, and such a nature always stays in moving in this way, anyone who did not bring in rest would be more absurd than one who did not grant motion. For the notion and thought of rest about being is readier to hand than that of motion: what is there is "in the same respects and in the same way", and keeps one account.
!flag single Reason-Principle—these are characteristics of the higher sphere | Here λόγος is the account a thing keeps, as what is always the same keeps one, not the forming principle; "Reason-Principle" is Page's.
!note "In the same respects and in the same way" (κατὰ ταὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως) is Plato's phrase for what always is (Phaedo 78c-d; Sophist 248a, 249b-c, where the Stranger shows that without rest there would be no intellect).

@p
@greek ἔστω δὴ καὶ στάσις
Let rest too, then, be one kind, other than motion, where it might even appear its contrary. That it is other than being too would be clear in many ways, and because, if it were the same as being, it would be no more the same as being than motion is. For why should rest be the same as being, and motion not, when motion is a kind of life of being, and the act both of its substance and of its very being?
!note Plato's Sophist (250a-c, 254d-255b): motion and rest are "most contrary" to each other, and neither is being, though both are.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ἐχωρίζομεν
But just as we separated motion from being, as both the same as it and not the same, and said that both were two and again one, in the same way we shall separate rest from it and again not separate it, separating it by intellect only so far as to set down another kind among the things that are. Otherwise, if we brought rest and being wholly into one, saying they differ in no way at all, and being and motion likewise, we shall bring rest and motion, through being as a middle, into the same, and motion and rest will be one for us.

@ch VI.2.8 | Five kinds: sameness and otherness
Intellect thinks the three apart, and for what is without matter, being thought is being. Look at pure intellect: the hearth of substance, a light that does not sleep, a life that stays, a thinking always present. Its thinking is motion, its object being, and being is the seat of rest. Seeing the three, apart and each one, we see otherness; gathering them into one, sameness: so there are five kinds. None is said of the others in what they are: they are first kinds.

@p
But we must set down these three, if intellect thinks each apart. And it thinks and posits them at once, if it thinks them, and they are, if they have been thought. For things whose being is with matter, their being is not in intellect; but these are immaterial, and for things that are immaterial, being thought is their being.
!note In things without matter, Aristotle says, what thinks and what is thought are the same (On the soul III.4, 430a2-5; Metaphysics Λ.9, 1075a3-5).

@p
@greek ἴδε δὴ νοῦν καθαρὸν
Look, then, at intellect pure, and gaze at it intently, not seeing with these eyes. You see the hearth of substance, and a sleepless light in it, and how it stands in itself, and how it stands apart while being together, and a life that stays, and a thinking that acts not toward what is to come but toward what is already, or rather what is always already and always present; and how it thinks in itself and not outside.
!flag how it puts apart things that were together | The Greek says "how it stands apart, being together" (ὡς διέστηκεν ὁμοῦ ὄντα): the things in intellect are distinct while together; Page makes intellect part what was together. "Stands in itself" and "stands apart" (ἕστηκεν, διέστηκεν) are one word, as rest and otherness will be found in it.
!note "Hearth" (ἑστία): Hestia, who stays at home when the gods go out (Plato, Phaedrus 247a). Plato's Cratylus (401c-d) ties her name to οὐσία, substance; the hearth that "stands" (ἕστηκεν) points to rest.

@p
@greek ἐν μὲν οὖν τῷ νοεῖν
In its thinking, then, is act and motion; in its thinking itself, substance and being. For being, it thinks, and thinks itself as being, and that on which it is as it were supported, as being. For the act directed to itself is not substance, but being is that to which it is directed and from which it comes: for being is what is seen, not the seeing. Yet the seeing too has being, because what it is from and what it is toward is being. And being in act, not in potential, it joins the two again and does not separate them, but makes itself that, and that itself.
!flag Now in the Act of Intellect there are energy and motion | The Greek says "in its thinking" (ἐν τῷ νοεῖν) are the act (ἐνέργεια) and the motion; Page puts "Act" for the thinking and "energy" for the act.
!flag Intellect bridges the dualism (of agent and patient) | The two that are joined are the seeing and what is seen, the act and being; "agent and patient" is Page's.

@p
@greek ὂν δὲ τὸ πάντων ἑδραιότατον
And being is the most firmly seated of all things, that about which the others have their rest, and it has rest not brought in, but from itself and in itself. It is also that in which thinking ends, a rest that did not begin, and that from which it started, a rest that did not start: for motion is not from motion, nor into motion. Further, the form, at rest, is the limit of intellect, and intellect is its motion; so that all are one, both motion and rest, and they are kinds that run through all things, and each of the later things is a certain being, a certain rest and a certain motion.
!flag the Form-Idea has Stability, since it is the goal of Intellect | The Greek says the form, at rest, is "the limit" (πέρας) of intellect, its boundary, not its goal.
!note Kinds that "run through all" (διὰ πάντων): Plato's Sophist (254b-c, 259a-b) has being and the other pervade all the kinds.

@p
@greek τρία δὴ ταῦτα ἰδών
Someone who has seen these three, having come into contact with the nature of being, and who has seen being by the being in himself, and the others by the others, motion in it by the motion in himself, and rest by his rest, and has fitted these to those, mixing them as they come together and run together as it were, not distinguishing them, but then setting them a little apart, as it were, holding them back and distinguishing them, and looking at being, rest and motion, three, and each one: has he not called them other than one another, and set them apart in otherness, and seen the otherness in being, positing three, and each one? And again, bringing them back into one, and in one, and all one, gathering them into the same, and looking, has he not seen sameness, come to be and being?
!flag We have caught the radiance of Being | The Greek says "having come into contact" (ἐν προσβολῇ) with the nature of being: a touch or approach of thought; "radiance" is Page's.
!flag found Being to contain Difference | The kind is ἑτερότης, "otherness", Plato's "the other" (θάτερον) of the Sophist; the modern version keeps "otherness" and "the other" for it, and "difference" for διαφορά, the difference that divides a kind into species.
!flag do we not see in this amalgamation Identity emerging | ταυτότης is "sameness", Plato's "the same" (ταὐτόν); Page's "Identity".

@p
@greek οὐκοῦν πρὸς τρισὶν ἐκείνοις
So to those three we must add these two, the same and the other, so that all the kinds come to five in all; and these give the things after them their being others and the same: for each of them is a certain same and a certain other; but the same and the other simply, without the "certain", would be in the kind.
!flag the thing of Sense has, it is clear, a particular identity | The Greek says only that "each" (ἕκαστον) of the later things is a certain same and a certain other; "the thing of Sense" is Page's, and the later things are first the intelligible species.
!note Plato's Sophist (254e-255e): the same and the other are the fourth and fifth of the greatest kinds, after being, motion and rest.

@p
@greek καὶ πρῶτα δὲ γένη
And they are first kinds, because you will predicate none of them of the others in what they are. You will predicate being of them, for they are; but not as a kind, for they are not just what a being is. Nor is it the kind of motion and rest, for these are not species of being: of things that are, some are as its species, others as sharing in it. Nor again does being share in these as its kinds: for they do not stand above it, nor are they prior to being.
!flag they do not even attain to its level | The Greek says they "do not stand above it" (οὐδὲ ἐπαναβέβηκεν αὐτῷ), nor are prior to being, as a kind would be over its species; Page reverses it, as if they fell short of being.

@ch VI.2.9 | Why the one is not a kind
These five are first kinds; but why only these? Why not the one, or quantity, quality and relation? The One wholly one is said of nothing; the one with being is not one first. The one has no differences, so it cannot make species: divided, it would be many. Nor is it common to all the kinds, any more than being is. It cannot come after being, nor at once with it, nor before it, as a kind. The one in being is close to the One and stays one, refusing to be divided.

@p
That these are first kinds one might confirm from this, and perhaps from other things too. But that they are the only ones, and no others besides, how could one be sure? Why not the one as well? Why not quantity, and quality, and relation, and the others that others have already counted?
!note Quantity, quality and relation are Aristotle's categories, examined in VI.1.4-12; they are taken up here in chapters 13 to 16.

@p
@greek τὸ μὲν οὖν ἕν, εἰ μὲν
As for the one: if it is what is altogether one, to which nothing else is added, not soul, not intellect, not anything, it would be predicated of nothing, and so it is not a kind. But if it is the one added to being, as when we say "one being", this is not one in the first sense. Further, being without difference in itself, how could it make species? And if it does not, it is not a kind. For how will you divide it? Dividing it, you will make many, so that the one itself will be many and will destroy itself, if it wants to be a kind.

@p
@greek ἔπειτά τι προσθήσεις
Then, you will add something in dividing it into species: for there would be no differences in the one, as there are differences of substance. Intellect accepts that there are differences of being; but of the one, how? Then, each time you set down two, with the difference, you do away with the one, since everywhere the addition of a unit destroys the quantity before it.
!flag The mind accepts: differences of Being | The Greek says "intellect" (ὁ νοῦς) accepts it; the modern version keeps "intellect" for νοῦς throughout.

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις λέγοι τὸ ἐπὶ τῷ ὄντι
If someone says that the one in being, and the one in motion and in the others, is common, and so brings being and the one into the same, then by the argument by which being did not make a kind of the others, because they were not just what being is, but beings in another way, in the same way the one will not be common to them either, but one first, and the others otherwise.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ μὴ πάντων λέγοι
If he says that it does not make a kind of all things, but is one thing by itself, like the others: if being and the one are the same for him, then, since being has already been counted among the kinds, he is bringing in a name; but if each of the two is one, he is speaking of some nature, and if he adds something to it, he speaks of a one, and if nothing, he speaks again of that which is predicated of nothing. If it is the one that goes with being, we have said that he is not speaking of what is one in the first sense.
!flag Admitted that not everything suffices to produce a genus | The Greek's objector says the one is not the kind "of all things, but one thing by itself, like the others" (μὴ πάντων ... ἀλλὰ ἕν τι ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῦ, ὥσπερ τὰ ἄλλα): a sixth kind beside the five.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ τί κωλύει
But what prevents this from being one in the first sense, once that which is wholly one is set apart? For we call the being after that one being, and being in the first sense. Because what was before being was not being, or, if it were, being would not be being in the first sense; but what is before this one is the One. Then, separated in thought from being, it has no differences.

@p
@greek ἔπειτα ἐν τῷ ὄντι
Then, in being: if it follows on being, it follows on all things, and is later, but the kind is prior; if it is at once with being, it is at once with all things, but the kind is not at once with its species; if it is prior, it is a principle, and of being only; and if it is the principle of being, it is not its kind; and if it is not the kind of being, it is not of the others either: or else being too would have to be the kind of all the others.

@p
@greek ὅλως γὰρ ἔοικε τὸ ἓν
For in general the one in being seems to be near the One, and as it were to fall in with being. Being is, on the side toward that, one; on the side after that, being, which can also be many; and the one stays one itself, not willing to be divided, nor wishing to be a kind.
!note "The one in being" (τὸ ἓν ἐν τῷ ὄντι) is the "one that is" of the Parmenides' second hypothesis (142b-c), which Plotinus reads as intellect, below the One that only is one (V.1.8).

@ch VI.2.10 | The one is said of all, as no kind is
Each species is one only by a shared name, as an army is one. A kind is not said where its opposites are; but one and many are said of every being, so the one is no kind of the first kinds or the later. As the one is in numbers without being their kind, and the simple is the principle of the composite, not its kind, so with the one. What is common is not always a kind: a kind needs differences of its own and makes species, and the one has neither.

@p
How, then, is each part of being one? Because the "some one" is not one: "some one" is already many. Each of the species is one only by a shared name: for the species is a multitude, so that it is one here as an army or a chorus is. So the one there is not in these, so that the one is not common, nor would the same be seen in being and in the beings that are "some". So the one is not a kind.
!note An army or a chorus is one by its order (Aristotle, Metaphysics Λ.10, 1075a11-15; Politics III.3, 1276b1-6).

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ πᾶν γένος
For every kind is such that, of what it is truly said, its opposites are no longer truly said; but the one cannot be truly said, as a kind, of what the one and its opposites are both truly said of, as they are of every being. So it will not be truly said, as a kind, of the first kinds, since being that is one is no more one than many, nor is any of the other kinds one in such a way as not to be many; nor of the later things, which are altogether many. And no kind as a whole is one; so that if the one is a kind, it will lose its being one. For the one is not a number; but it will be a number once it has become a kind.
!flag The unit is prior to number; yet number it must be | The Greek says "the one is not a number" (οὐ γὰρ ἀριθμὸς τὸ ἕν); nothing here of its being prior.
!note For the Greeks one is the principle of number, its measure, not itself a number (Aristotle, Metaphysics Δ.6, 1016b17-21; N.1, 1088a4-8).

@p
@greek ἔτι τὸ ἓν ἀριθμῷ ἕν
Further, the one is one in number: if it were one in kind, it would not be one in the proper sense. Further, as in numbers the one is not predicated of them as a kind, but is said to be present in them, not to be their kind, so too, even if the one is in the things that are, it would not be the kind of being, nor of the others, nor of all things.
!note One in number, one in species, one in kind: Aristotle, Metaphysics Δ.6, 1016b31-1017a3.

@p
@greek ἔτι ὥσπερ τὸ ἁπλοῦν
Further, as the simple would be the principle of what is not simple, but not its kind (for then the not simple would be simple too), so with the one: if the one is a principle, it will not be the kind of what comes after it. So it will be the kind neither of being nor of the others. But if it is to be a kind, it will be the kind of the things that are each one, as if someone thought fit to separate the one from substance. Then it will be the kind of some things only. For as being is not the kind of all things, but of the species that are beings, so the one is the kind of the species that are each one. What, then, is the difference of one from another, in respect of its being one, as there is a difference of one being from another?

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ συμμερίζεται
But if the one is divided along with being and substance, and being, by its division and by being seen in many, is the same kind, why should not the one too, appearing as many as substance does, and divided into as many, be a kind?

@p
@greek ἢ πρῶτον οὐκ ἀνάγκη
First, it is not necessary, if something is present in many, that it be a kind, either of those it is in or of others; nor in general, if something is common, that it be a kind at all. The point, at any rate, is present in lines, and is not a kind, either of them or at all; nor, as was said, is the one in numbers the kind either of numbers or of other things. For what is common and in many must also use differences of its own, and make species, and be in what they are. But what differences would the one have? Or what species does it generate? If it makes the same species as there are about being, it would be the same as being, and the other would be a name only; and being is enough.
!note A kind is divided into its species by differences of its own, as animal by footed and two-footed (Aristotle, Metaphysics Z.12, 1038a9-35).

@ch VI.2.11 | The one looks to the good
The one is not the same in all things: not in perceptible and intelligible, nor in a chorus, a camp, a ship, a house and a continuous body; it is truer in soul, more in intellect and in being. A thing is one as far as it attains the good, for each wants to be with the good: so things hasten to become one, from the one and toward it. Being, nearest, is most one. The one in being has a prior and later, and no differences: it is no kind.

@p
We must examine how the one is in being, and how the division is made, as it is called, and in general the division of the kinds, and whether each is the same or different. First, then, how each thing, whatever it is, is said to be one and is one; then whether we say it in like manner of the one being, and as it is said there.
!flag especially the dividing of the genera Being and unity | The Greek asks about the division "and in general that of the kinds" (καὶ ὅλως ὁ τῶν γενῶν), and whether each division is the same; Page narrows it to being and unity.

@p
@greek τὸ μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ πάντων ἓν
The one in all things is not the same. It is not in like manner in perceptibles and intelligibles (nor, indeed, is being), nor among perceptibles in relation to one another: it is not the same in a chorus, a camp, a ship and a house, nor again in these and in what is continuous. And yet all imitate the same one, some attaining it from far off, others more; and it is already truer in intellect: for soul is one, and intellect still more one, and being one.
!note A chorus, a camp, a ship and a house: bodies made of separate parts, or of joined parts, as against bodies that are continuous, in the Stoics' division of bodies (Sextus Empiricus, Against the mathematicians IX.78-80; Seneca, Letters 102.6).

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν ἐν ἑκάστῳ
When in each thing we speak of its being, do we then speak of its one, and as it has being, so too the one? It happens so, but it is not in so far as it is being that it is one: it can be no less being and yet less one. An army or a chorus is no less than a house, but still less one.

@p
@greek ἔοικεν οὖν τὸ ἐν ἑκάστῳ
It seems, then, that the one in each thing looks rather to the good, and as far as it attains the good, so far it is one, and the more and less of the one lies in this: for each thing wants to be, not simply, but with the good. That is why things that are not one hasten, as far as they can, to become one: natural things, by nature itself, coming together into the same, wanting to be united with themselves; for each thing does not hasten away from the others, but toward one another and toward itself; and all souls would want to go into one, after their own substance.
!flag related not so much to Being as to a standard of perfection | The Greek says the one in each thing "looks to the good" (πρὸς ἀγαθὸν βλέπειν); "a standard of perfection" and "perfection" are Page's for the good, here and in what follows.

@p
@greek καὶ ἀμφοτέρωθεν δὲ
And the one is on both sides: it is both what they come from and what they go to; for they begin from the one and hasten to the one. So it is with the good too: for nothing among the things that are came to be, nor, once come to be, could endure, without having its striving toward the one. So it is with natural things; and in the arts, each art makes each of its works toward this, as far as it can, and as they can be made. And being attains this most of all: for it is near.
!flag Unity is thus identical with Goodness | The Greek says only "so it is with the good too" (οὕτω γὰρ καὶ τὸ ἀγαθόν): the good, like the one, is origin and goal; Page makes them identical.

@p
@greek ὅθεν τὰ μὲν ἄλλα
So the other things are called only what they are called, "man", for example: for if we ever say "one man", we say it in relation to two; and if we say "one" of him in some other way, we say it by adding it. But of being we say that the whole of it is one being, and we think it right to call it one, showing its close union with the good.

@p
@greek γίγνεται οὖν τὸ ἓν
The one, then, is in it too as principle and end, but not in the same way, but otherwise, so that there is a prior and a later in the one too.
!flag not however in the same sense as for things of the physical order | The Greek says "not in the same way, but otherwise" (οὐχ ὡσαύτως δέ, ἀλλὰ ἄλλως), and names no physical order.

@p
@greek τί οὖν τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ ἕν
What, then, is the one in it? Is it not seen in like manner in all its parts, and common? First, in lines too the point is common, and not the kind of lines; and in numbers the one, perhaps this one, is common, and not a kind: for the one in the One itself is not the same as that in the unit and the two and the other numbers. Then, in being too nothing prevents some things from being first and others later, some simple and others composite. And even if the one is the same in all the things of being, having no difference it makes no species; and if no species, it cannot be a kind.

@ch VI.2.12 | The good of soulless things; the kinds whole in each
How is there good for numbers, which have no soul, in being one? As for other soulless things; and a point in a circle has the circle's good, and strives toward it through the circle. The kinds are not chopped up into what is under them: each is whole in each, one as a whole in many, and by itself too.

@p
So much for this. But how is there good for numbers, which are without soul, in each being one? This question is common to the other soulless things too. If someone says they do not exist at all, we were speaking of the things that are, in so far as each is one. If they ask how the point shares in the good: if they say it exists by itself, and call it soulless, they are asking the same as about the other such things; but if it is in other things, as in a circle, the good of the circle is its good, and its desire is toward this, and it hastens, as far as it can, through the circle to there.
!flag Just as all other inanimates find their perfection in their unity | The Greek says only that the question "is common to the other soulless things too" (κοινὸν τοῦτο), and gives no answer here.
!flag but perfection does exist in such things, for example in a circle | The Greek's second case is the point "in other things, as in a circle" (εἰ δ’ ἐν ἄλλοις, οἷον ἐν κύκλῳ), the point that is not by itself; Page joins it to the first.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ πῶς τὰ γένη ταῦτα
But how are these kinds? Are they chopped up, each into the things under it? No: the kind is whole in each of the things whose kind it is. And how is it still one? What is one in kind is one as a whole in many. Is it, then, only in the things that share in it? No: it is both by itself and in the things that share in it. But perhaps this will be clearer later.
!note How one and the same is whole everywhere is the subject of VI.4 and VI.5.

@ch VI.2.13 | Why quantity is not a first kind
The first kinds are together with being; number is later than they are, and has a prior and a later in itself, so it is not a first kind, if it is a kind at all. Magnitude is later still, number in something. Quantity, if common to both, is a later kind. Perhaps number is a mixture of motion and rest, magnitude a motion; but this is for later.

@p
Now, how is quantity not among the first kinds, and quality too? Quantity is not first with the others because those are together with being. For motion is with being, which is in act, since it is its life; and rest came in with substance itself; or rather, being was together with these, being others and the same, so that these too are seen together with it. But number is later than those and than itself: the later comes from the earlier, and they follow one another, and the later are present in the earlier. So it would not be counted among the first kinds; and we must ask whether it is a kind at all.
!flag in number the posterior is divided from the prior | The Greek says "the later comes from the earlier" (τὸ ὕστερον παρὰ τοῦ προτέρου); nothing here of a division.
!note Where there is a prior and a later there is no common kind over them (Aristotle, Metaphysics B.3, 999a6-13), the rule that VI.1.1 turned on its authors.

@p
@greek τὸ μέντοι μέγεθος
Magnitude is still more later, and composite: for it is number in this, the line a sort of two, and the plane three. If, then, continuous magnitude too has its quantity from number, how could it have it, when number is not a kind? And there are prior and later in magnitudes too. If being quantities is common to both, we must find what this is, and when we have found it set it down as a later kind, not among the first; and if it is a kind not among the first, we must lead it back to one of the first, or of those that lead to the first.
!flag for it contains within itself number, line and surface | The Greek says magnitude is "number in this" (ἀριθμὸς ἐν τῷδε), and the line "a sort of two", the plane "three": magnitude is number in something, the line and the plane numbered two and three.
!note The line as two and the plane as three are the Platonists' derivation of magnitudes from numbers (Aristotle, Metaphysics A.9, 992a10-24; On the soul I.2, 404b18-24).

@p
@greek δῆλον τοίνυν ἴσως
It is clear, then, perhaps, that the nature of quantity shows a how much, and measures the how much of each thing, and is itself a how much. But if the how much is common to number and magnitude, either number is first and magnitude from it, or in general number is in a mixture of motion and rest, and magnitude is a motion, or from motion: motion going forth into the unlimited, and rest, in holding back what goes forth, making the unit.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ περὶ γενέσεως
But the coming to be of number and magnitude, or rather their reality and how they are thought, must be looked at later. For perhaps number is among the first kinds, and magnitude later, in composition; and number belongs to what stands still, and magnitude is in motion. But this, as we say, is for later.
!flag or that number belongs to the genus Stability | The Greek says number belongs to "what stands still" (ἑστώτων), not to the kind rest; and it joins the two thoughts ("and number ...") rather than setting them against each other.
!note Numbers are the subject of VI.6.

@ch VI.2.14 | Why quality is not a first kind
Quality too comes after substance: the first substance has quantity and quality following it, not making it up. In composite substances qualities differ and have something common; but the first kinds are divided into simples and what completes substance, not a certain substance. What makes a man this man does not add substance to him: he is substance already, higher up, as he is already a living being before he is rational.

@p
As for quality, why is it not among the first? Because it too is later, and comes after substance. The first substance must have these following on it, and not have its constitution from them, nor be completed through them; or it would be later than quality and quantity.

@p
@greek ἐν μὲν οὖν ταῖς συνθέτοις
In composite substances, made of many, in which numbers and qualities have made the differences between them, there might be qualities, and something common will be seen in them. But in the first kinds the division must be made not between simple and composite, but between simple and what completes substance, not a certain substance. For that a certain substance should be completed by quality too is perhaps not strange, since it has its substance before the quality, and its such-kind from outside; but substance itself must have what it has as belonging to substance.
!flag the qualities may be detached from the common core around which they are found to group themselves | The Greek says "a certain commonness will be seen in them" (κοινότης τις ἐν αὐταῖς): something common among the qualities themselves, which would make quality a kind; Page makes it a core they gather round.

@p
@greek καίτοι ἐν ἄλλοις
And yet elsewhere we held that what completes substance is called qualities by a shared name only, while what comes from outside, after substance, is qualities; and that what is in substances is their acts, while what comes after them is already affections. Now we say that what belongs to a certain substance does not complete substance at all: for no addition of substance comes to man, in so far as he is man, toward substance; but he is substance from above, before coming to the difference, as he is already a living being before reaching the rational.
!flag are only by analogy called qualities | The Greek says "by a shared name only" (ὁμωνύμως), not by analogy.
!flag he is, on the contrary, Substance in a higher degree before he arrives at differentiation | The Greek says he is substance "from above" (ἄνωθεν), already, before coming to the difference: higher up the division, from the kind down, not in a higher degree.
!note "Elsewhere": II.6 (On substance, or on quality), chapters 1 to 3. Rational is the difference that divides living being and makes man (Aristotle, Metaphysics Z.12, 1037b11-14).

@ch VI.2.15 | The kinds complete substance, not a qualified one
The four kinds complete substance without making it of a kind. Motion is being's act, so no accident but substance itself, ranked with being, not after it. Being does not first exist and then move or stand still; and the same and the other are not later, for being was from the start one many. These are enough for substance; the kinds that make qualified and quantified substance come lower, and are not first.

@p
How, then, do the four kinds complete substance without yet making it a qualified substance? For they do not make it a certain substance either. That being is first has been said; and that motion could not be anything other, nor rest, nor the other, nor the same, is clear. And that this motion does not work quality into it is perhaps evident, but saying it will make it clearer.
!note "The four kinds" are the four beside being (motion, rest, the same, the other), which with it complete substance; chapter 19 counts them otherwise.

@p
@greek εἰ γὰρ ἡ κίνησις ἐνέργειά
For if motion is its act, and being, and the first things in general, are act, motion would not be an accident; but being act, the act of what is in act, it could no longer be called something that completes, but substance itself. So it has not entered into something later, nor into quality, but is ranked with what is at once. For it is not that being is, and then is moved, nor that it is, and then stands still; nor is rest an affection. And the same and the other are not later, because being did not become many later, but was what it was, one many; and if many, there is otherness too, and if one many, sameness too.
!flag If Motion is the Act of Substance, and Being and the Primaries in general are its Act | The Greek says being and the first things "are act" (ἐνέργεια δὲ τὸ ὂν), not the act of substance: motion is the act of being, and being is itself act.

@p
@greek καὶ ταῦτα εἰς τὴν οὐσίαν
And these are enough for substance. But when it is to go forward to what is below, then there are others, which no longer make substance, but qualified substance and quantified substance; and let these be kinds, but not first.

@ch VI.2.16 | Relation and the rest are not first kinds
Relation is an offshoot, one thing toward another. Where and when are further off: place is two, and there is no place there; time is probably not there, and as a measure of motion it is composite and later. Acting and being acted on are in motion and twofold; having is two, lying three.

@p
Relation, which is like an offshoot, how could it be among the first? For the relation is of one thing toward another, and not toward itself, and toward something else. Where and when are still further off. For "where" is one thing in another, so it is two; but the kind must be one, not a composition. And there is no place there; and our account now is about the things that truly are. Whether time is there, we must consider; more likely, perhaps, not. And if it is a measure, and not simply a measure, but of motion, it is two, and the whole is composite and later than motion, so that it is not where motion is, in the same division.
!flag Apparently it has less claim than even Place | The Greek says "more likely, perhaps, not" (μᾶλλον δὲ ἴσως οὔ): time is probably not there at all; Page compares it with place.
!note Relation "is like an offshoot and accident of being" (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.6, 1096a21-22). Time as the measure of motion: Aristotle, Physics IV.12, 220b32-221a1, which III.7.9 examines.

@p
@greek τὸ δὲ ποιεῖν καὶ τὸ πάσχειν
Acting and being acted on are in motion. If, then, being acted on and acting are there, acting is two, and being acted on likewise: so neither is simple. And having is two, and lying is one thing in another in such a way that it is three.
!note Acting, being acted on, having and lying are the last of Aristotle's categories, examined in VI.1.15-24.

@ch VI.2.17 | Why the good is not a first kind
The good, if it is the first, is said of nothing and is before substance; if it is a quality, quality is not first. Being is good in another way, in itself; but the good is not the same in all its parts, but first, second and later, so it is no first kind; set down as a kind, it is later than substance. The good in being is its act toward the One, its life: that is motion, already a kind.

@p
But why are the beautiful and the good and the virtues not among the first, and knowledge, and intellect? The good, if it is the first, which we call the nature of the good, of which nothing is predicated, but we call it so because we have no other way to signify it, would be the kind of nothing. For it is not said of other things; or each of the things it was said of would be that, being called so. And that is before substance, not in substance. But if the good is meant as a quality, quality in general is not among the first.
!note The good "beyond substance": Plato's Republic (VI 509b). That nothing can be said of it, and its name only points to it: V.3.13-14, VI.9.5.

@p
@greek τί οὖν; ἡ τοῦ ὄντος
What, then? Is the nature of being not good? It is, first, in another way, and not in that way, as the first is; and it is good not as a quality, but in itself. But we said that the other kinds too were in it, and that each was a kind because it was something common, seen in many. If, then, the good too is seen in each part of substance or being, or in most, why is it not a kind, and among the first? Because it is not the same in all the parts, but first, second and later: either because one comes from another, the later from the earlier, or because all come from the one beyond, and different things share in it differently, according to their own nature.
!flag but as a constituent | The Greek says being is good "in itself" (ἐν αὐτῷ), not as a quality; "constituent" is Page's.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ δὴ καὶ γένος
If someone wants to set it down as a kind too, it is a later one: for its very being good is later than substance and the what-it-is, even if it is always with it; while those were of being as being, and went to make substance. That is why there is also what is beyond being, since being and substance cannot but be many, but must have these kinds that have been counted and be one many.
!flag If however we must make goodness a genus as well (as a transcendent source) | Page's parenthesis is not in the Greek: the good set down as a kind would be the good in being, later than substance, not the good beyond.

@p
@greek εἰ μέντοι τὸ ἀγαθὸν τὸ ἐν τῷ ὄντι
If, however, we do not shrink from calling the good in being its act according to nature toward the One, and from saying that this is its good, so that from there it is good in form, then this good will be act toward the good; and this is its life; and this is motion, which is already one of the kinds.
!note "Good in form" (ἀγαθοειδής): Plato's Republic (VI 509a) calls knowledge and truth "good-like", but not the good itself.

@ch VI.2.18 | Beauty, knowledge, intellect and the virtues
Beauty is treated as the good is, or is substance itself, or, as it affects us, is act and so motion. Knowledge, the sight of being, is an act, under motion or rest or both, and so later. Intellect is being with all the kinds, all the things that are, and not one kind; bare being is its element. Justice, self-control and every virtue are acts of intellect, later than a kind: species.

@p
As for the beautiful: if that is the first beauty, the same or nearly the same might be said as in the arguments about the good; and if it is what shines, as it were, on the form, then because it is not the same in all, and because shining on is later. If the beautiful is nothing other than substance itself, it has been dealt with under substance. If it is in relation to us who see, by making an affection of such a kind in us, this acting is motion; and if the act is toward that, it is motion.
!flag none the less Motion by being directed towards Absolute Beauty | The Greek says "if the act is toward that" (πρὸς ἐκεῖνο), the beautiful thing seen, which moves us; "Absolute Beauty" is Page's.
!note The beauty that shines on the form: I.6.2-3 and VI.7.22, where grace comes to the form from the good.

@p
@greek ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐπιστήμη
Knowledge too is self-motion, being sight of being and act, not a state; so it too falls under motion, or, if you like, under rest, or under both; and if under both, as a mixture; and if so, the mixture is later.
!flag or perhaps more suitably under Stability | The Greek says "if you like" (εἰ δὲ βούλει), not "more suitably": either will do.
!note Knowledge as a state (ἕξις) is Aristotle's (Categories 8, 8b26-35); for Plotinus the knowledge that sees being is act.

@p
@greek ὁ δὲ νοῦς ὂν νοοῦν
Intellect, being that thinks and composite of all, is not one of the kinds; and the true intellect is being with all the others, and already all the things that are; while being alone, bare, taken as a kind, is an element of it. Justice and self-control, and virtue in general, are all acts of intellect: so they are not among the first, and are later than a kind, and species.
!flag Intelligence, since it connotes intelligent Being and comprises the total of existence | The Greek's νοῦς is "intellect", as Page himself has it in the same sentence ("the true Intelligence (or Intellect)"), and it is "being that thinks" (ὂν νοοῦν), composite of all the kinds.
!note Justice and self-control in intellect: I.2.6-7, V.8.4, where justice is seen beside intellect.

@ch VI.2.19 | How the kinds make species
Can each kind make species by itself? Being cannot, for differences come from outside a kind, and from beings: from the other kinds, coupled with it. But coming together, the kinds made intellect, what is from all; how, then, are there others after it, and how do the kinds make species while staying whole and pure? Since the intellect from all is later, let us take it as a pattern.

@p
These four, then, being kinds and first, does each make species by itself? Could being, for example, be divided by itself, without the others? No: since the differences must be taken from outside the kind, and they are differences of being as being, but are not being itself. Where, then, will it get them? Not from things that are not. If from things that are, and the remaining kinds were the three, clearly from these, and with these added and coupled with it and coming to be together.
!note Here the Greek counts four kinds, and three left besides being, though chapter 8 set down five; perhaps the same and the other are taken as one pair, or being apart from the four, as in chapter 15. The modern version keeps the Greek's numbers.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ ἅμα γινόμενα
But coming to be together, they made this which is from all. How, then, are the others after what is from all? And how, all being kinds, do they make species? How does motion make species of motion? And rest, and the others? For this too must be watched: that each is not lost in its species, nor is the kind only predicated, as seen in them; but that it is both in them and in itself at once, and mixed and again pure, and is there unmixed too, and does not destroy itself by contributing with the others to substance. These things, then, must be examined.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ δὲ ἔφαμεν
But since we said that what is from all the things that are is each intellect, and we set down being and substance, before all of them as species and parts, as intellect, we say that intellect already formed is later. Let us make this difficulty useful for what we are seeking, and, using it as a kind of pattern, lead ourselves into knowledge of what is said.
!flag the particular intellect, Intellect as such being found identical with Being | The Greek says "each intellect" (νοῦν ... ἕκαστον) is what is from all the beings, and that being and substance, set down as intellect, are before all of them as their species and parts; "Intellect as such" is Page's.

@ch VI.2.20 | The universal intellect and the particular ones
Take intellect touching nothing particular, as knowledge is before its theorems: the whole is none of them, but their power, each is itself in act and the whole potentially. So the universal intellect is before the particular intellects, which are filled from all; it supplies them and holds them, and they hold it, each in itself and in the other. As kind it is potentially all, at rest; its act must cause them to be in act.

@p
Let us take, then, the intellect that touches none of the particular things and acts on nothing, so that it does not become a certain intellect; as knowledge is before its particular species, and the knowledge in a species before its parts. The whole is none of the particular things, but the power of all; each is that thing in act, and potentially all; and with universal knowledge likewise. The knowledges in species, which lie potentially in the whole, taking what is in the species, are potentially the whole (for the whole is predicated of them, not a part of the whole); and yet the whole must be intact by itself.
!note Knowledge as a whole and its theorems, each holding the whole potentially: IV.9.5, III.9.2, V.9.8.

@p
@greek οὕτω δὴ ἄλλως μὲν νοῦν
So then we must say that in one way the whole intellect is, before the particular intellects which are in act, and in another way the particular intellects are, filled from all; and that the intellect over all is the supplier of the particular ones, and their power, and holds them in its universality, while they in turn, being particular, hold the universal, as a certain knowledge holds knowledge.
!flag we find that what subsists in the particulars must be maintained from the totality | The Greek says the particular intellects are "filled from all" (ἐκ πάντων πληρωθέντας): completed from all the kinds.
!note The "supplier" (χορηγός) is the man who paid for a chorus and fitted it out at Athens.

@p
@greek καὶ εἶναι καὶ καθ̓ αὑτὸν
And the great intellect is by itself, and the particular ones in themselves; and the particular are contained in the whole, and the whole in the particular; each is by itself and in another, and that one by itself and in those; and in that one, which is by itself, all are potentially, it being in act all things together, and potentially each apart; and they in turn are in act what they are, and potentially the whole. For in so far as they are what they are called, they are in act that which they are called; but as in that kind, they are that potentially. And it, in so far as it is a kind, is the power of all the species under it, and in act none of them, but all are at rest in it; but in so far as it is what it is before the species, it is in act, not of particular things. If, then, they are to be in act, as in a species, the act from it must become the cause.
!flag all are latent in it | The Greek says all are "at rest" (ἥσυχα) in it: still, not hidden.

@ch VI.2.21 | What comes forth in intellect
How does intellect, staying one, make the particular things from the four kinds? Look in this great intellect: it has number, one and many, and powers without limit, and the great; with the beauty and light of substance, quality blooms, magnitude shows itself, then shape; the other divides them, sameness makes equality and otherness inequality. It is one great forming principle, which has gone forth always; all that reasoning finds in nature is there without reasoning, as being wills; and with life all things are living beings, held in eternity. The weaving of all in one is intellect, the complete living being.

@p
How, then, does it, staying itself one in its forming principle, make the particular things? This is the same as asking how the things said to come next come from those four. Look, then, in this great intellect, beyond all contriving, not of many words but of much intellect, the intellect that is all, whole, and not a part nor a certain intellect, how all things are in it, from it.
!flag while, in virtue of its Reason-Principle, remaining a unity | The modern version keeps λόγος as "forming principle"; "Reason-Principle" is Page's.
!note "Not of many words but of much intellect" (οὐ πολυλάλῳ ἀλλὰ πολύνῳ): a play on words in the Greek.

@p
@greek ἀριθμὸν δὴ πάντως ἔχει
It has number, at any rate, in these things it sees; and it is one and many, and these are powers, and wonderful powers, not weak, but, being pure, they are the greatest, and as it were swelling with vigour, and truly powers, not having a limit to where they reach: unlimited, then, and unlimitedness, and the great.
!flag so that they are infinite, infinity, Magnitude-Absolute | The Greek says "the great" (τὸ μέγα); Page's capitals make it a form. The great is the first of the things Plotinus will see coming forth, as magnitude.

@p
@greek τοῦτο τοίνυν τὸ μέγα
Seeing this great, then, with the beauty of substance in it and the splendour and light about it, as being in intellect, you see quality too already blooming on it, and, with the continuity of its act, magnitude showing itself to your gaze, lying in stillness. And with one and two and three there, magnitude is threefold, and so is all quantity. With quantity seen in it, and quality, and both coming into one and as it were becoming one, see shape too. When the other falls in and divides both quantity and quality, there are differences of shapes and other qualities; and sameness, present with them, makes equality be, and otherness inequality in quantity, both in number and in magnitude; and from these come circles and squares and figures of unequal sides, and like and unlike numbers, odd and even.
!flag Identity; coming in with Difference, creates equality | The Greek says sameness, "being present" (συνοῦσα), makes equality; Page has it come in "with Difference", the kind that makes inequality.
!note Three dimensions from one, two and three: chapter 13. "Like" numbers are plane or solid numbers whose sides are in proportion (Euclid, Elements VII, definition 21; Plato, Theaetetus 147e-148b, for square and oblong numbers).

@p
@greek οὖσα γὰρ ἔννους ζωὴ
For being a life full of intellect, and an act that is not incomplete, it leaves out nothing of what we now find to be an intellectual work, but has all things in its own power, having them as they are, and as intellect would have them. And intellect has them as in thinking, but not in thinking that goes through step by step. Nothing that forming principles are is left out, but it is as it were one forming principle, great, complete, embracing them all, going forth from its own first things, or rather having always gone forth, so that its going forth is never true.
!flag may itself be regarded as one great and perfect Reason-Principle | λόγος is "forming principle" here too; "Reason-Principle" is Page's, for the forming principles and for the one great one alike.

@p
@greek ὅλως γὰρ πανταχοῦ
For in general, whatever things anyone finds by reasoning to be in nature, he will find these in intellect without reasoning, so that one would think that being, an intellect that had reasoned, had made them so; as with the forming principles that make living things: for as the most exact reasoning would reason for the best, so all things are in the forming principles, which are before reasoning.
!flag we conclude that Being has so created Intellect | The Greek says one would think "being, an intellect that had reasoned" (τὸ ὂν νοῦν λελογισμένον), had made things so: being is the intellect that seems to have reasoned, not the maker of intellect.
!note The forming principles in nature work without reasoning, as reasoning would if it worked best: III.2.14, IV.4.12, V.8.7.

@p
@greek τί οὖν χρὴ προσδοκᾶν
What, then, must we expect in the things before nature and the forming principles in it, which are higher? In those where substance is nothing other than intellect, and neither being nor intellect is brought in from outside, it would be best without toil, if it lies in accord with intellect, and is this, what intellect wants and is: that is why it is true and first: for if it were from another, that other would be intellect.
!flag it is obvious that Being is best served by the domination of Intellect | The Greek says it would be at its best "without toil" (ἀμογητί), lying in accord with intellect; nothing here of domination.

@p
@greek σχημάτων δὴ πάντων
So, all shapes having been seen in being, and all quality (for it was not a certain one: there could not be only one, with the nature of the other in it, but one and many; for sameness was there too; one and many, and such from the beginning, so that in all the forms there are one and many; and so there are different magnitudes, different shapes and different qualities: for it was not even lawful for anything to be left out, since the all there is complete, or it would not be all), and with life running over it, or rather present everywhere with it, all things of necessity became living beings; and there were bodies too, since there were matter and quality.
!note The intelligible living being lacks nothing, and the world made after it is complete (Plato, Timaeus 30c-31b, 39e). Matter is there too, the intelligible matter of II.4.2-5.

@p
@greek γενομένων δὲ πάντων ἀεὶ
And all things having come to be always, and staying, and held in their being by eternity, each apart being what it is and again together in one, the weaving together, as it were, and composition of all in one is intellect. And holding the things that are in itself, it is a complete living being and what living being is; and to what comes from it, giving itself to be seen, having become intelligible to it, it gives the right to be called so.
!note "The complete living being" (τὸ παντελὲς ζῷον) and "what living being is" (ὃ ἔστι ζῷον) are Plato's names for the pattern of the world (Timaeus 31b, 39e); the world is called a living being because it is its image (Timaeus 30b-d, 92c).

@ch VI.2.22 | The many intellects, soul, and the image
Plato's riddling words that intellect sees the forms in the complete living being fit soul and our intellect too, which see better in what is before them. Intellect, having the other with it, becomes one many and makes the many intellects. Substance chopped up goes into the unlimited only at the last species; held by the one, it comes into number. Soul is the act of intellect going out of itself, and its last part an image, like a reflection in a mirror. So the intelligible world is complete, and this world, its image, is a living being too.

@p
And this is what Plato said in a riddle: "in the way that intellect sees the forms present in the complete living being, what they are and how many". For soul too, after intellect, in so far as it is soul, having them in itself, sees them better in what is before it; and our intellect, having them in itself, sees them better in what is before it: for in itself it only sees, but in what is before it, it also sees that it sees.
