!note The motions of intellect and the otherness in them are those of VI.2.7-8; that intellect knows simply, by direct grasp (ἐπιβολή), without reasoning: V.8.6.

@p
@greek αἱ τοίνυν ποιότητες πότερα
Are all qualities, then, differences, or not? Whiteness, and colours in general, and the qualities of touch and taste, might be differences of other things while being species themselves; but grammar and music, how? Or by making one soul grammatical and another musical, and above all if they are so by nature, so that they become differences that make species.
!note A man is called grammatical after grammar, as the qualified is named after its quality (Aristotle, Categories 8, 10a27-b11).

@p
@greek καὶ εἰ εἴη τις διαφορὰ
And we must ask whether there might be a difference from this kind, or from another too; and if from this kind, it would be of things from the same kind, qualities of qualities, for instance. For virtue and vice are, the one a state of such a sort, the other of such a sort; so that, the states being qualities, their differences are qualities: unless someone were to say that the state without the difference is not a quality, and that the difference makes the quality.
!flag Virtue and vice are two states differing in quality | The Greek says that virtue is "a state of such a sort" and vice "of such a sort" (ἡ μὲν ἕξις τοιάδε, ἡ δὲ τοιάδε): the "such" is the difference that would be a quality.
!note Virtue and vice are states (ἕξεις), the first species of quality: Categories 8 (8b27-35); Nicomachean Ethics II.5 (1105b19-1106a13).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ τὸ γλυκὺ ὠφέλιμον
But if the sweet is beneficial and the bitter harmful, this divides by relation, not by quality. And what if the sweet is thick and the astringent thin? "Thick" perhaps does not say what the sweet is, but what the sweetness is in; and the same account holds of the astringent. So we must consider whether a quality is never a difference of a quality, as substance is not of substance, nor quantity of quantity. Or five differs from three by two. Or rather it exceeds it by two, but is not said to differ: for how could it differ by two in the three? Nor would a motion differ from a motion by a motion, nor would one find it in the other kinds.
!flag hardly reveals the essence but merely the cause of sweetness | The Greek says that "thick" names not what the sweet is (τὸ τί ἦν) but "that in which the sweetness is" (ᾧ ἡ γλυκύτης), its subject; "cause" is Page's.
!note Explaining tastes by the thick and thin, the shapes and sizes of what makes them, is the atomists' way (Theophrastus, On the senses 65-67, on Democritus); "what it was to be" (τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι) is Aristotle's phrase for the essence (Metaphysics Z.4).

@p
@greek ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς ἀρετῆς καὶ κακίας
With virtue and vice, whole must be taken against whole, and in this way they will differ by themselves. And as for the difference from the same kind, quality, and not from another: if someone divides by one virtue's being about pleasures and another about angers, and one about getting in the harvest and another about spending, and accepts that they are well defined in this way, it is clear that there can be differences that are not qualities.
!flag if we proceed on the principle that virtue is bound up with pleasure, vice with lust | The Greek divides the virtues among themselves, "one about pleasures, another about angers, one about getting in the harvest, another about spending" (τὴν μὲν περὶ ἡδονάς, τὴν δὲ περὶ ὀργάς); no vice is named.
!note Temperance is about pleasures, gentleness about anger, liberality about getting and spending (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.10, IV.5, IV.1); such virtues are divided by what they are about, which is not a quality.

@ch VI.3.19 | The qualified, negations, privations and affections
The qualified are ranked with quality, by going up to what they are named after. "Not white" is a quality if it means another colour; a negation is a sound or a relative, and negations, like affirmations, are better not counted. Privations of qualities are qualities; naked and clothed are ways of being in relation. An affection while one is being affected is a motion, and a quality when it stays; reddening is a motion, being red a quality, unless only states are qualities and not dispositions.

@p
With quality, as was decided, we must rank also the qualified things that are so by qualities, in so far as quality is about them, not bringing in the things themselves, so that there are not two categories, but going up from them to that from which they are named.
!note Quality is "that by which things are called qualified" (Aristotle, Categories 8, 8b25); the qualified are named from it, as the just from justice (10a27-b11). The qualified as against the substrates: VI.1.29.

@p
@greek τὸ δὲ οὐ λευκόν
"Not white", if it signifies another colour, is a quality. But if it were only a negation, or a counting out of things, it would be nothing, unless a sound, or a name, or an account, which is itself a thing that comes about: and if a sound, a sort of motion; if a name or an account, a relative, in so far as they signify. But if the counting by kinds is not only of things, but must also take in what is said and what signifies, and of what kind each is significant, we shall say that some of them only make plain the things set down, and others do away with them. Yet it is perhaps better not to count the negations with the things, as we do not count the affirmations either, because they are compound.
!flag if a name or definition, it is a relative | The Greek's λόγος here is an account, spoken words that signify, beside the sound and the name; "definition" is Page's.
!flag it would be better, in view of their composite nature, not to include the negations in the same genus as the affirmations | The Greek says it is better not to count the negations, "as we do not count the affirmations either" (τάς τε καταφάσεις μὴ συναριθμοῦντας), both being compound; Page sets the one against the other.
!note Words said without combination, such as "man" or "runs", signify one of the categories; affirmation and negation come about only by combination (Aristotle, Categories 4, 2a4-10, and On interpretation 1, 16a9-18).

@p
@greek τὰς δὲ στερήσεις πῶς
And the privations, how? If the things of which they are privations are qualities, they too are qualities, as toothless or blind. But the naked man and the clothed man are neither of them qualified, but rather in some way disposed: in a relation, then, to something else.
!flag on the other hand, are neither of them qualities but states | The Greek says they are "rather in some way disposed" (μᾶλλόν πως ἔχων), in relation to another; "states" is Page's word, which he gives to the ἕξεις at the end of the chapter.
!note Privation and having, as blindness and sight, toothlessness and teeth: Categories 10 (12a26-34); having clothes is one of the ways of having (Categories 15, 15b17-24). "In some way disposed" is the Stoics' third kind (πως ἔχον), weighed in VI.1.30.

@p
@greek πάθος δὲ τὸ μὲν ἐν τῷ πάσχειν
As for affection: the affection that is in being affected still is not a quality, but a sort of motion; that in having been affected, and keeping the affection now that it remains, is a quality; and if a thing no longer has the affection, but is said to have been affected, it has been moved. And this is the same as "was in motion". But we must think only of the motion, taking away the time; for it is not fitting to bring in even the now. "Well" and words of that sort must be brought back to the one notion of the kind.
!flag Such is the theory | No such words are in the Greek: Plotinus' own conclusion follows at once, that only the motion must be thought of, without the time.
!note Affections that pass quickly are not qualities but affections (Categories 8, 9b28-10a10); whatever has been moved, and the "has moved" of the perfect, Physics VI.6 (236b32-237a17). Time is set aside here as in VI.1.16, where the motion is thought of apart from its "how long".

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ τὸ μὲν ἐρυθριᾶν
We must look into whether blushing is to be brought back to the qualified, and the red man not. Becoming red is rightly not brought back to it: for the one becoming red is affected, or in general moved. But if he is no longer becoming red, but is already red, why is he not qualified? For one is not qualified by time. Or by what is it to be defined? By being such: and in calling him red we call him qualified. Or else, in this way, we shall call only the states qualities, and no longer the dispositions. And so the hot is not what is being heated, and the sick is not what is being brought into sickness.
!flag We shall accordingly maintain that states alone, and not dispositions, constitute qualities | The Greek offers this as a consequence to be weighed: "or else, in this way, we shall call only the states qualities" (ἢ οὕτως τὰς ἕξεις μόνας ποιότητας ἐροῦμεν); Plotinus does not assert it.
!note Those who blush from shame are not called red, while those who are red by nature are qualified: Categories 8 (9b19-33); states, which last, and dispositions, which are easily moved: Categories 8 (8b26-9a13).

@ch VI.3.20 | Contraries, and the more and less
Has every quality a contrary? The mean is contrary to the extremes among the virtues, but the colours between are not so. Contraries are not those that differ most, since that already takes in the intermediates, and health and sickness have none; perhaps they are what have nothing the same in form, within quality. The more is in the things that share in qualities; there each quality is whole.

@p
We must see whether there is not, for every quality, some other quality contrary to it. For in virtue and vice even the mean seems to be contrary to the extremes; but with the colours, those between are not so.
!note Not every quality has a contrary: there is none to red or yellow (Aristotle, Categories 8, 10b12-25); the mean is opposed to both extremes (Nicomachean Ethics II.8, 1108b11-1109a19).

@p
@greek εἰ μὲν οὖν, ὅτι μίξεις
If, then, it is because the intermediates are mixtures of the extremes, we should not have set them against one another, but only white and black, and the others are compositions. Or we set them against one another because in each of the intermediates we see some one other colour, even if it is to be seen as coming from a composition. Or because contraries not only differ, but differ most. But differing most seems to be taken from having already set down these intermediates: for if one took this arrangement away, by what would one define the most? Or because grey is nearer to white than black is: and this is reported by sight; and with the tastes likewise; hot, cold, and between them what is neither.
!flag Contrariety however demands that there be some one distinct quality in the intermediates | The Greek gives a reason for setting the intermediates against one another, "because we see some one other colour in each" (τῷ μίαν τινὰ ἄλλην... ἀντιτίθεμεν); contrariety makes no demand.
!flag taste may be our judge when we have hot, cold and no intermediate | The Greek has "what is neither, between them" (τὸ μηδέτερον μεταξύ): the lukewarm is the intermediate.
!note Contraries are what differ most within the same kind: Aristotle, Categories 6 (6a17-18) and Metaphysics Ι.4 (1055a3-33); the colours between white and black are mixtures of these (On sense and the sensibles 3).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ὅτι μὲν οὕτως
That we are used to suppose so is clear; but perhaps someone might grant us this, and yet say that white and yellow, and anything against anything, are all wholly other than one another in like manner, and, being other qualities, are contraries. For it is not by there being others between them that they are contraries: health and sickness, at any rate, have nothing that has fallen between them, and are contraries. Or it is because the things that come from each have the greatest divergence. And how can one say "greatest" when there are no lesser ones in the means? So with health and sickness one cannot say "greatest". The contrary, then, must be defined by something else, not by the greatest.
!flag White and yellow are entirely different from each other | The Greek gives this as what someone might say against the usual view, "perhaps someone might grant us this, and yet say" (τάχα δ’ ἄν τις ἡμῖν συγχωροῖ ταῦτα); Page makes it the argument's own conclusion.
!note Health and sickness have no intermediate, white and black have: Aristotle, Categories 10 (11b38-12a25).

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ τῷ πολλῷ
If by "much": if "much" stands for "more" against "less", the immediate contraries will again escape; and if simply much, once it is granted that each stands far off by nature, we must not measure the distance by the more.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ἐπισκεπτέον, πῶς τὸ ἐναντίον
But we must look into how the contrary is. Are things that have some likeness (I mean not by kind, nor at all by being mixed with other things, their shapes, so to speak, more or less) not contraries, while those that have nothing the same in their form are contraries? And we must add: in the kind quality. For from this come the immediate contraries, which have nothing that makes for likeness, there being no others that, as it were, play both sides and have likeness to one another, while some alone do not have it. If so, the colours that have something in common would not be contraries. But nothing will prevent, not every colour from being contrary to every other in this way, but one to another; and likewise with the tastes. So much for working through these difficulties.
!flag they differ in degree but are not contraries | The Greek's "more or less" (ἢ πλείονα ἢ ἐλάττονα) belongs to the mixing that is ruled out, "by being mixed with other things, their shapes, so to speak, more or less"; Page makes such things differ in degree.

@p
@greek περὶ δὲ τοῦ μᾶλλον
About the more: it seemed that it is in the things that share in qualities, but health itself and justice were in doubt. If each of these has a latitude, we must give the more to the states themselves too; but there each is the whole, and does not have the more.
!flag If indeed these qualities possess an extension quite apart from their participants | The Greek says "if each of them has a latitude" (πλάτος), a range within which it can be more or less; "quite apart from their participants" is Page's.
!note Whether justice and health themselves admit the more and the less is disputed: Aristotle, Categories 8 (10b26-11a5). The latitude of health was a physicians' word.

@ch VI.3.21 | Motion: a kind of its own
Is motion a kind? It goes into no other kind: not substance or quality, not acting or being acted on, which go into it, nor relation, since, though it is of something, it is something first. Is change before it? Then coming to be would be a change and not a motion; but coming to be is a species of its own, as when an animal takes a form. Or change may rather be a species, and alteration a motion that displaces.

@p
About motion, whether it must be set down as a kind, one might consider it this way: first, whether it is not right to bring it back into another kind; then, whether nothing above it is predicated of it in what it is; then, whether, taking many differences, it will make species. Into what kind could one bring it? For it is neither the substance nor the quality of the things that have it. Nor, again, into acting, for there are many motions in being acted on too; nor into being acted on, because many motions are actings: rather, actings and beings-acted-on go into it.
!flag These conditions satisfied, we may consider the nature of the genus to which we shall refer it | The Greek's question "into what kind could one bring it?" (εἰς ποῖόν τις γένος αὐτὴν ἀνάξει;) belongs to the first test, whether motion goes back into another kind; Page makes it a further step.
!note A kind is predicated "in what it is" and is divided by differences into species (Aristotle, Topics I.5, 102a31-35; IV.2, 122b12-17). Acting and being acted on were brought back to motion in VI.1.17-22.

@p
@greek οὐδ’ αὖ εἰς τὸ πρός τι
Nor, again, would it rightly go into relation because motion is of something and not by itself: for in that way quality too would be in relation, for quality is of something and in something; and quantity likewise. If it is said that those are something, even if they are of something, and are called the one quality and the other quantity by what each is, then in the same way, since motion too, even if it is of something, is something before being of something, we would have to take what it is by itself. For in general we must set down as relative not what is something and then is of another, but what the relation begets, there being nothing else besides the relation by which it is so called: the double, for instance, in so far as it is called double, which took its coming to be and its existence in being compared with the cubit's length, and, nothing being thought of before this, had its being called double, and its being double, in being compared with another.
!flag takes birth and actuality in juxtaposition with a yard | The Greek has "the cubit's length" (τὸ πηχυαῖον), Aristotle's example of a quantity; Page makes it a yard.
!note "Two cubits long" is Aristotle's example of quantity, "double" and "half" of the relative (Categories 4, 1b28-29; 7, 6a39-b2); what the relation begets is the relative of VI.1.6-9.

@p
@greek τί οὖν ἐστι τοῦτο
What, then, is this thing that, being of another, is something, so that it can also be of another, as quality, quantity and substance are? Or first we must establish that nothing before it is predicated of it as its kind.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ τὴν μεταβολὴν
But if someone were to say that change is before motion: first, either he is saying the same thing, or, by calling that a kind, he will make another kind besides those named before; then it is clear that he will set motion down as a species, and set something else against motion, coming to be perhaps, calling that a change too, but not a motion. Why, then, is coming to be not a motion? If it is because what is coming to be is not yet, and motion is not about what is not, then plainly coming to be would not be a change either. If it is because coming to be is nothing but a sort of alteration and growth, since coming to be is of things that are being altered and are growing, he is taking what comes before the coming to be. But we must take coming to be in these as another species: for coming to be, and becoming, is not in being altered in the way of being affected, as being heated or whitened; for when these have come about, coming to be simply may not yet have come about, but only this itself, the having been altered; but it is when an animal or a plant comes to be, when it takes some form.
!flag the antecedents of becoming are being confused with becoming itself | The Greek says he "takes what comes before the coming to be" (τὰ πρὸ τῆς γενέσεως λαμβάνει), the alteration and growth before it; Page's words agree, but "confused" is his.
!note Coming to be and passing away are changes but not motions, since what is not cannot be moved: Aristotle, Physics V.1 (225a20-b9); Categories 14 counts six kinds of motion, coming to be and passing away among them (15a13-14). "Coming to be simply" (ἁπλῶς γένεσις) is Aristotle's, for the coming to be of a substance (On generation and corruption I.3, 317a32-b5).

@p
@greek εἴποι δ’ ἄν τις τὴν μεταβολὴν
One might say that it fits better to set change down as a species than motion, because the word "change" means one thing in place of another, while "motion" has also the moving away from one's own, as change of place has; and if someone does not want this, then learning and playing the lyre, or in general motion from a state. So alteration would rather be a species of motion, being a motion that displaces.
!flag we must accept as types of Motion knowledge and musical performance | The Greek has "learning and playing the lyre" (ἡ μάθησις καὶ ἡ κιθάρισις), motions from a state (ἀφ’ ἕξεως); knowledge is the state, not the motion.
!note "Every motion displaces what is moved" (Aristotle, Physics IV.12, 221b3; On the soul I.3, 406b12-13); change (μεταβολή) as the wider word, of which motion is a part: Physics V.1 (225a34-b3).

@ch VI.3.22 | What motion is
Motion, in outline, is the way from potency into what a thing is said to be able for: the statue, the walking, the dance. Some motions leave a form behind, others none; motion is a waking form among forms that stand, and may be called the life of bodies, sharing only a name with the motions of intellect and soul. What is common to all motions is a thing's never staying in the same, always otherness, and so time is always other; and the going forward from potency into act.

@p
But let what is meant by alteration be the same as motion, in that something other follows upon motion. What, then, must we call motion? Let motion be, to speak in outline, the way from potency into that which a thing is said to be able for. For one thing is potentially because it could come into some form, as a potential statue, and another because it could come into act, as what can walk: when the one goes forward into a statue, the going forward is motion; and when the other is walking, the walking itself is motion; and dancing, in what can dance, when it dances.
!flag on the ground that Motion itself results in difference | The Greek says that "something other" (τὸ ἄλλο) follows on motion; "difference" is kept in the modern version for διαφορά.
!note Motion is the act of the potential, as such: Aristotle, Physics III.1 (201a10-11), with the bronze that is potentially a statue (201a29-b5); Plotinus took up "incomplete act" in VI.1.16.

@p
@greek καὶ ἐπὶ μέν τινι κινήσει
Upon one kind of motion another form follows, which the motion has worked; the other, being as it were the simple form of the potency, has nothing after it once the motion has stopped. So if someone were to call motion a waking form, set against the other forms, which stand, in that they stay and it does not, and a cause to the other forms when something comes to be after it, he would not be absurd. And if someone were to call this motion, the one we are now speaking of, the life of bodies, he would not be absurd either: for this motion must be called homonymous with the motions of intellect and soul.
!flag regarded Motion as a dynamic Form in opposition to the other Forms which are static | The Greek calls motion "a waking form" (εἶδος ἐγρηγορός), set against forms that "stand" (ἑστηκόσιν), in that they stay and it does not; "dynamic" and "static" are Page's.
!flag To proceed to identify this bodily motion with life would however be unwarrantable | The Greek says the reverse: if one were to call this motion "the life of bodies", "he would not be absurd either" (οὐκ ἂν ἄτοπος εἴη); the next words, that it shares only a name with the motions of intellect and soul, give the reason.
!note Motion is "like a sort of life for all the things that are put together by nature" (Aristotle, Physics VIII.1, 250b14-15). The motion of intellect, one of the five kinds of the intelligible: VI.2.7-8.

@p
@greek ὅτι δὲ γένος ἐστίν
That it is a kind one might be convinced no less by its not being easy, or even possible, to grasp by a definition. But how is it a form, when the motion is towards the worse, or when the motion is one of being affected? Or it is alike: as if the heating from the sun made some things grow and led others into the contrary; and in so far as motion is something common, it is the same in both, and has its apparent difference from its subjects. Is healing, then, the same as falling sick? Or in so far as it is motion, it is the same; but by what will they differ? By their subjects, or by something else too? But this later, when we look into alteration; now we must consider what is the same in every motion. For so it would be a kind. Or it would be said in many ways, and so it will be like being.
!note Motion is hard to grasp, since it is neither potency nor act simply: Aristotle, Physics III.2 (201b24-202a3). What is said in many ways is not a kind, as being is not (Metaphysics Γ.2; VI.1.1-3).

@p
@greek πρὸς δὲ τὴν ἀπορίαν
To the difficulty, perhaps this: those motions that lead into what is according to nature, or are at work in the things that are according to nature, are to be as it were forms, as has been said; while the leadings into what is against nature are to be set down by analogy with what they lead to.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ τί τὸ κοινὸν ἐπί τε ἀλλοιώσεως
But what is common to alteration, growth and coming to be, and to their contraries, and to change of place too, by which these are all motions? Or it is each thing's not being in the same in which it was before, nor keeping still, nor being in complete quiet, but, so long as motion is there, always having its leading towards another; and the other, by its not staying in the same: for motion perishes when there is no other. So otherness too is not in having come to be in the other and staying there, but is always otherness. Whence time too is always other, because motion makes it: for it is motion measured, not staying; so it runs along with it, as if riding on something carried along.
!flag never acquiescing in Identity but always courting Difference | The Greek has "the other, by not staying in the same" (τὸ ἕτερον τῷ οὐκ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ μένειν); "Identity" and "Difference" are Page's names for the same and the other.
!flag in the sense of being itself perpetual difference | The Greek has "always otherness" (ἀεὶ ἑτερότης), the kind of VI.2; the modern version keeps "difference" for διαφορά.
!flag Time is the measure of unceasing Motion | The Greek says that time "is motion measured, not staying" (μεμετρημένη γὰρ κίνησις οὐ μένουσα); Page makes it Aristotle's measure of motion, which Plotinus rejects in III.7.
!note Aristotle: time is the number of motion (Physics IV.11, 219b1-2); Plotinus argues in III.7.8-13 that time is not the measure of motion but the life of soul in a motion of passage. Motion is other than the same and the other, and shares in both: Plato's Sophist (256a-b).

@p
@greek κοινὸν δὲ πᾶσι τὸ ἐκ δυνάμεως
Common to all is that each is a going forward and a leading from potency and the potential into act: for everything that is moved with any motion whatever was there before, able to do or undergo this, and comes to do it in being moved.

@ch VI.3.23 | Where motion is, and its kinds
Motion here comes into things from another and shakes them awake, so that they hold together by an image of life. It is not the things moved: walking is the act about the feet, unseen, seen only in the feet's changing places. It is neither cut off from the agent nor in it, but goes from it into the other like a breath. The powers that walk, heat, build, take away, beget, destroy and heal make the kinds of motion, which take their character from what they are from and through, and what they are in.

@p
And the motion about perceptible things is sent into them from another, shaking, driving, waking and pushing the things that have taken a share in it, so that they do not sleep or stay in sameness, so that by this unquiet and, as it were, busyness they may be held together by an image of life.
!flag that they may neither rest nor preserve their identity | The Greek says "that they do not sleep, nor be in sameness" (μὴ εὕδειν μηδ’ ἐν ταυτότητι εἶναι); "identity" is Page's word for ταυτότης.
!note The busyness (πολυπραγμοσύνη) is the word for meddling in Republic IV (433a-434c). The image of life is the life of bodies of chapter 22.

@p
@greek δεῖ δὲ οὐ τὰ κινούμενα
We must not think that the things moved are the motion: for the feet are not the walking, but the act about the feet, coming from a potency. Since the potency is invisible, one can only see the feet acting: not feet simply, as if they were still, but now with something else, which is invisible, but which, because it is with something else, is seen incidentally, in our seeing the feet having now one place and now another, and not being still. And alteration we see from what is altered, because the quality is not the same.

@p
@greek ἐν τίνι οὖν ἡ κίνησις
In what, then, is the motion, when one thing moves another, and when a thing goes from the potency within it into act? In the mover? Then how will what is moved and affected share in it? In what is moved? Why, then, does it not stay, once it has come? Or it must be neither cut off from the agent nor in it, but from it and into the other, not cut off in the other, but from the one into the other, like a breath into something else.
!flag when there is one thing that moves and another that passes from an inherent potentiality to actuality | The Greek asks about two cases, "when another moves it, and when it goes from the potency within it into act" (ὅταν ἄλλο κινῇ, καὶ ὅταν δὲ ἐκ τῆς ἐνούσης δυνάμεως εἰς ἐνέργειαν ἴῃ); Page makes them two parties to one motion.
!note Motion is in what is moved, the act of the mover in the moved: Aristotle, Physics III.3 (202a13-b22). Plotinus weighed this in VI.1.22.

@p
@greek ὅταν μὲν οὖν ἡ δύναμις
When, then, the power of moving is a power of walking, it pushes, as it were, and has made the other change its place continually; when it is a power of heating, it has heated; and when the power takes matter and builds it into a nature, there is growth; and when another power takes away, there is diminution of what can undergo taking away, as it diminishes. When the begetting nature is at work, there is coming to be; when this is powerless, and the power that can destroy prevails, there is destruction, not the destruction in what has already come about, but that in what is under way. And healing in the same way, when the power that can make health is at work and prevails, and falling sick when the contrary power makes the contraries. So it turns out that motion is so not only by the things it is in, but also by those from which and through which it is; and that the property of motion is to be a motion qualified, and such, in such things.
!flag when another potentiality demolishes the structure, the result is decay | The Greek has "diminution" (μείωσις), the contrary of growth (αὔξησις), "of what can undergo taking away"; not decay.
!flag not the destruction of what already exists, but that which intervenes upon the road to existence | The Greek has destruction "not that in what has already come about, but that in what is under way" (οὐχ ἡ ἐν τῷ ἤδη γεγονότι, ἀλλ’ ἡ ἐν τῷ πορευομένῳ): the motion is the destroying, still going on.
!note Growth and diminution, coming to be and destruction, alteration and change of place: the six motions of Aristotle, Categories 14 (15a13-14).

@ch VI.3.24 | Change of place
How do motion up and down, in a circle and in a straight line differ? The power that pushes is one, unless up and down are lightness and heaviness; but moving to one's own place is common to all, so the difference comes from outside. The circle differs from the straight line by the figure of the course, unless it is mixed; change of place is one, taking its differences from outside.

@p
About motion in place: if moving upwards is contrary to moving downwards, and motion in a circle will differ from motion in a straight line, how is the difference to be found, as between throwing over one's head and under one's feet? For the pushing power is one: unless someone were to say that the power pushing upwards is one and that pushing downwards another, and that the downward course is otherwise than the upward, above all if things move by nature, if the one is lightness and the other heaviness.
!flag in which case the up-motion constitutes lightness, the down-motion heaviness | The Greek says "if the one is lightness and the other heaviness" (εἰ ἡ μὲν κουφότης εἴη, ἡ δὲ βαρύτης): the powers that move are lightness and heaviness, not the motions.
!note The light moves up and the heavy down, each to its own place: Aristotle, On the heavens IV.3-4 (310a16-311a29).

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ κοινὸν καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ
But moving into its own place is common and the same, so that here the difference is perhaps from outside things. As for the circle and the straight line, if they ran round in a circle just as they run on a straight line, how is it other? Or by the figure of the course: unless someone were to call motion in a circle mixed, as not being wholly motion, nor displacing altogether. But it seems that change of place is wholly some one motion, taking its differences from outside.
!flag in this tendency we seem to have the differentia which separates locomotion from the other species | The Greek says that moving to its own place is common to these motions, "so that here the difference perhaps comes from outside things" (ὥστε ἐνταῦθα κινδυνεύειν παρὰ τὰ ἔξω τὴν διαφορὰν γίνεσθαι); Page makes it the difference of change of place.
!flag not involving a complete surrender of identity | The Greek says "nor displacing altogether" (οὐδὲ πάντη ἐξισταμένην), the displacing of chapter 21; nothing of sameness is named.
!note The simple motions are in a straight line and in a circle, the rest mixed of these (Aristotle, On the heavens I.2, 268b17-26); the circle turns in one place, as if at rest (Plato's Laws X 893c-d); Plotinus on the heaven's circling in II.2.1.

@ch VI.3.25 | Combination and separation
Are combination and separation motions of their own? As coming near and withdrawing, they are motions in place; but blending and mixing, and the coming together into one, follow on change of place without following of necessity, as growth does. Nor is alteration to be brought back to them, as if dense and rare, and wine mixed with water, were only combined and separated: that would need a void, and would do away with colours and qualities, and learning is not a combining.

@p
How combination and separation stand must be looked into. Are they motions other than those named, coming to be and destruction, growth and wasting, change of place, alteration? Or must they be brought back to these? Or must some of these be set down as combinations and separations? If, then, combination has this, the approach of one thing to another and its coming near, and separation again a withdrawing backwards, one would call them motions in place, speaking of two things moving towards one, or withdrawing from one another.
!flag The nature of integration and disintegration calls for scrutiny | The Greek has "combination and separation" (σύγκρισις, διάκρισις), the gathering and parting of the elements; "integration" and "disintegration" are Page's.
!note Those who made coming to be and passing away combination and separation, Empedocles, Anaxagoras and the atomists: Aristotle, On generation and corruption I.1-2 (314a1-317a31) and Metaphysics A.3-4 (984a8-16, 985b4-20).

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ σύγκρασίν τινα
But if they mean a sort of blending, mixture and fusion, and a coming together into one, the one that happens in the coming together, not in having already come together, to which of the motions named would one bring these back? Change of place will begin it, but what comes about upon it would be something other: as one would find with growth too, that change of place begins it and the motion in quantity comes upon it. So here too being moved in place leads, but being combined, or again separated, does not follow of necessity: when there is an intertwining of the things that met, they are combined, and when they are split by the meeting, they are separated.

@p
@greek πολλαχοῦ δ’ ἂν καὶ διακρινομένων
And often, too, when things are separated, change of place would follow, or come about at the same time, while another affection is thought of about the things separated, not in their being moved in place; and in combination too another affection, a standing together, follows, other than the change of place.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν ταύτας μὲν
Are we, then, to take these by themselves, and bring alteration back to them? For what has become dense has been altered, and this is the same as "has been combined"; and what has become rare, again, has been altered, and this is the same as "has been separated"; and when wine and water are mixed, each has become other than it was before, and this is combination, which has made the alteration.
!flag Are we then to posit a new species for these two motions, adding to them, perhaps, alteration | The Greek asks whether we are to take these by themselves "and bring alteration back to them" (τὴν δὲ ἀλλοίωσιν εἰς ταύτας ἀνακτέον), making alteration a combining or separating; not adding it to them.
!note A drop of wine in much water is not mixed but changes into water (Aristotle, On generation and corruption I.10, 328a23-28); here the mixture of the two makes each other than it was.

@p
@greek ἢ φατέον καὶ ἐνταῦθα
Or we must say that here too combinations and separations lead some alterations, but that these are other than combinations or separations: for neither are the other alterations of this sort, nor are rarefaction and condensation combination and separation, or made of these at all; for in that way one would accept a void too. And with blackness or whiteness, how? If someone disputes over these, first he does away with the colours, and perhaps with the qualities, or most of them, or rather all of them: for if he were to call every alteration, which we call change in quality, combination and separation, what comes about is nothing, only things lying near together and standing apart. Then learning and being taught, how are they combinations?
!note The rare and the dense explained by the void between bodies: Aristotle, Physics IV.9 (216b22-217b20); colours as arrangement and position, Democritus' account (On generation and corruption I.2, 315b33-316a14). On learning as a change, not a combining: VI.1.20.

@ch VI.3.26 | The species of motion
Change of place may be divided by up and down, straight and circle, by the motions of the ensouled and the soulless, and these by walking, swimming and flight; or by according to nature and against nature, which are not differences from outside; or into motions by nature, by art and by choice.

@p
About these we must look, and inquire again now into the motions said by species, change of place for instance: whether they are not to be divided by up and down, straight and circle, as has been asked, or by the motion of the ensouled and of the soulless (for their motion is not alike), and these again by walking, swimming and flight.
!flag whether the organic motion should be distinguished from the inorganic | The Greek has the motion "of the ensouled and the soulless" (ἐμψύχων καὶ ἀψύχων); "organic" is Page's.

@p
@greek ἢ καὶ τῷ φύσει γε
Or one might perhaps divide each species by its being according to nature and against nature; but these are not differences of motions from outside. Or these differences produce them, and they could not be without them; and nature seems to be their principle. Or some are by nature, some by art, some by choice: by nature growths and wastings; by art building houses and building ships; by choice inquiring, learning, taking part in the city's life, in general speaking and acting. And again about growth, alteration and coming to be: by nature or against nature, or in general by their subjects.
!flag It may indeed be the case that motions create these differences | The Greek has it the other way: "these produce them" (ποιητικαὶ τούτων αὗται), the differences, according to nature and against it, produce the motions, which could not be without them.
!note Nature is a principle of motion in what it is in (Aristotle, Physics II.1, 192b13-23); things come to be by nature, by art or of themselves (Metaphysics Z.7, 1032a12-13); choice (προαίρεσις): Nicomachean Ethics III.2.

@ch VI.3.27 | Rest and stillness
Rest is better given to the intelligible, and stillness looked for here. Here nothing stands, but moves more slowly; stillness is only the negation of a motion, of place for instance, and so no kind, while motion brings something and works on its subject. There rest is no negation of motion, for it is while motion is, and what stands there stands by rest; here a thing is still by an absence. Nor is health or sickness a rest.

@p
About rest, which is set against motion, or stillness, what must we say? Is it too to be set down as one kind, or to be brought back into one of the kinds named? Perhaps it is better to give rest to the things there, and to look for stillness here.
!flag whether it be Stability or Rest | The Greek has "rest" (στάσις), the kind of VI.2, and "stillness" (ἠρεμία); "Stability" is Page's name for rest, and his "Rest" is the stillness.
!note Rest is one of the five kinds of the intelligible, after Plato's Sophist (254d-255e): VI.2.7-8. Aristotle calls stillness (ἠρεμία) the privation of motion in what is of a nature to be moved (Physics V.2, 226b12-16).

@p
@greek τὴν οὖν ἠρεμίαν ταύτην
This stillness, then, we must first ask what it is. If it appeared to be the same as rest, one would not rightly look for it here, where nothing stands, but what seems to stand is moving with a slower motion. But if we were to say that stillness is other than rest, in that rest is about what is wholly unmoved, and stillness about what stands, but is of a nature to be moved, when it is not moved: if one meant by being still coming to be still, it is a motion not yet stopped, but present; and if he means the stillness that is no longer about what is moved, we must first ask whether there is anything here that is not moved.
!flag the apparently stable has merely a less strenuous motion | The Greek says that what seems to stand is moving with "a slower motion" (σχολαιοτέρᾳ τῇ κινήσει); "less strenuous" is Page's.
!note That everything here is always moving is the flux of the Theaetetus (152d-e, 181c-183b).

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ μὴ πάσας
But if it is not possible for a thing to be moved with all the motions, but there must be some motions it is not moved with, so that one can say that this is the thing being moved, what else must we call what is not moved in place, but is still with respect to this motion, than that it is not moved? Stillness, then, will be a negation of being moved; and this is not in a kind. And it is still with respect to nothing other than this motion, change of place for instance: so what it means is the taking away of this.

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις λέγοι: διὰ τί
If someone were to say: why shall we not call motion a negation of rest? Because, we shall say, motion comes bringing something, and is something else, at work and pushing the subject as it were, working countless things in it and destroying it; while each thing's stillness is nothing besides the thing, but signifies only that it has no motion.
!flag why not regard Motion as the negation of Stability | The Greek has "a negation of rest" (ἀπόφασιν τῆς στάσεως); "Stability" is Page's name for rest.
!flag giving it a thousand forms and destroying them all | The Greek says that motion is "working countless things in it and destroying it" (μυρία ἐργαζόμενον αὐτὸ καὶ φθεῖρον), the subject; "forms" is Page's.

@p
@greek τί οὖν οὐ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν νοητῶν
Why, then, did we not call rest among the intelligibles too a negation of motion? Because one cannot call rest there a doing away with motion, since it is not when motion has stopped, but while that is, this is too; and what stands there is not a thing of a nature to be moved that stands in so far as it is not moved, but in so far as rest has taken hold of it, it stands, and in so far as it is moving, it will always move: so it both stands by rest and moves by motion. But here a thing is moved by motion, and is still by an absence, deprived of the motion owed to it.
!flag what is of a nature to move is not stationary because the Stability of that realm is motionless | The Greek says that what stands there is not "a thing of a nature to be moved, standing in so far as it is not moved", but stands "in so far as rest has taken hold of it" (καθ’ ὃ στάσις κατείληφεν); Page has rest itself motionless, and calls it "Stability".
!note The real is both at rest and in motion, and rest and motion are both, and are each other than the other: Plato's Sophist (249c-d, 250a-c, 255e); VI.2.7.

@p
@greek ἔπειτα δὲ ὁρᾶν δεῖ
Then we must see what this rest itself is that is called rest here: in sickness and health, for instance. The one being healed is moved, and so, when he goes from sickness into health, he is being healed. What form of stillness, then, shall we set against this healing? If what it is from, that is sickness, but not rest; if what it is into, that is health, which is not the same as rest. If someone were to say that health or sickness is a sort of rest, he will say that health and sickness are species of rest; which is absurd. And if he says that rest is an accident of health, health before the rest will not be health. But about these, let each think as seems good to him.
!flag What we have to observe is the essential character of this Sensible counterpart of Stability | The Greek has "the rest itself that is called rest here" (ἡ στάσις αὐτὴ ἡ ἐνταῦθα λεγομένη): Plotinus uses the word "rest" here himself; "Sensible counterpart" and "Stability" are Page's.
!flag It may be declared that health or sickness is indeed some form of Stability | The Greek has "a sort of rest" (τινὰ στάσιν); "Stability" is Page's, here and in the next sentence.
!note Motion from sickness to health and the rest opposed to it: Aristotle, Physics V.6 (229b23-230a18).

@ch VI.3.28 | Acting and being acted on, and the relatives
Acting and being acted on are motions, and some motions are absolute; the other so-called kinds go back into these. The relative is a relation of one to another, both together at once; substance is relative only as a part, a cause, a principle or an element. The relatives may be divided as the ancients divided them. So much for these kinds.

@p
It has been said that acting and being acted on are to be called motions, and that one can call some of the motions absolute, others actings and others beings-acted-on. And about the other so-called kinds, that they go into these; and about the relative, that it is a relation of one thing to another, and that both are together at once; and that the relative, when a relation of substance makes it, will not be relative as substance, but either as a part, such as a hand or a head, or as a cause, a principle or an element.
!note Acting and being acted on: chapter 21 and VI.1.17-22; the other kinds, "when", "where", position and having, were brought back to these in chapter 3 and VI.1.13-14 and 23-24. Relatives are together by nature (Aristotle, Categories 7, 7b15-22); whether a hand or a head is a relative: Categories 7 (8a13-b21).

@p
@greek ἔστι δὲ καὶ τὰ πρός τι διαιρεῖν
The relatives can also be divided, as the ancients divided them: some as productive, some as measures, some in excess and defect, and some as in general separating by likenesses and differences. And about these kinds, so much.
!flag We may also adopt the ancient division of relatives into creative principles | The Greek has "as productive" (ὡς ποιητικά), the agent relative to what it acts on; "creative principles" is Page's.
!flag Our investigation into the kinds of Being is now complete | The Greek says only "and about these kinds, so much" (καὶ περὶ μὲν τούτων τῶν γενῶν ταῦτα), the kinds of the perceptible; Page closes the whole of the three treatises.
!note Aristotle divides relatives into those of number, excess and defect, those of acting and being acted on, and the measurable to the measure, with the same, the like and the equal among them (Metaphysics Δ.15, 1020b26-1021b11). Plotinus weighed the relatives in VI.1.6-9.

# VI.4 (milestone E27): MacKenna's own English (vol. V, 1930, pp. 106-124); Page translated only VI.1 to VI.3.

@treatise VI.4 | That being, one and the same, is everywhere whole, first part
The twenty-second treatise in the order of writing, and the first of the two On that being, one and the same, is everywhere whole; VI.5, the twenty-third, is its second part. Porphyry says they were the first Plotinus wrote in the six years Porphyry was with him, when Amelius and Porphyry asked him to write (Life 5). How can soul, which has no parts and no size, be in every part of the body of the All? Plotinus asks first about what is before body. The true All, being, is in nothing and needs no place; the visible world, its image, finds it everywhere and circles within it. It is not present by powers sent out and cut off, for powers cannot be apart from their source, nor images from what they are images of: whatever shares in it shares in the whole, as far as it is fit, as the transparent takes the light and the clouded takes less. The images are a hand that holds a long beam, a light inside a sphere, the sun, and a voice heard whole by every ear. The many souls and intellects are many by otherness, not by place, as the sciences are many in one soul. Then: who are we? Men who were there before our birth, to whom another man has added himself, so that we are double, and the body's uproar is like a crowd shouting in an assembly. Last, the descents, judgements and Hades of the ancients are read as the body's coming to soul and soul's giving more or less of itself. The argument goes on in VI.5.

@ch VI.4.1 | Is soul everywhere because of body?
Is soul everywhere in the All because the body of the All is so large, or is it everywhere by itself, before body? If it fills all that extent, how is it without magnitude? It is not spread as a quality is: the white on two parts is the same in form, not in number, but the soul in foot and hand is the same in number. So begin from the start: how can what is bodiless go so far, before bodies or in them?

@p
Is it because the body of the All is of such a size that soul is present everywhere in the All, since it has a nature to be divided about bodies? Or is it everywhere of itself? Then it is not brought wherever body brings it, but body finds it already everywhere before body itself, so that wherever body is set, it finds soul there before it was set in a part of the All, and the whole body of the All was set in a soul that already was. But if soul reaches so far before a body of that size has come, filling the whole extent, how will it not have magnitude? Or what way could it have of being in the All before the All came to be, when the All did not exist? And how could anyone accept that what is called without parts and without magnitude is everywhere, though it has no magnitude? And if it were said to be stretched out along with the body, though it is not body, not even so does one escape the difficulty by giving it magnitude by accident: for one could likewise reasonably ask here too how it comes to have magnitude by accident.
!flag coupled with some native tendency in soul to distribute itself over material mass | The Greek says soul has "a nature to be divided about bodies" (περὶ τὰ σώματα φύσιν ἔχουσα μερίζεσθαι), the Timaeus' phrase, not a tendency to spread itself.
!flag We may perhaps be told that, though extended over the corporeal, it does not itself become so | The Greek says soul is "stretched out along with the body, not being body" (συνεκτείνεσθαι μὴ σῶμα οὖσα); the magnitude would be soul's by accident, which is what the next words weigh.
!note The question is the Timaeus' soul, mixed from the undivided being and "the being that becomes divided about bodies" (Timaeus 35a), which Plotinus reads in IV.2.1-2: soul is undivided in itself, and divided only in that it is in every part of a body. The treatise's title is the question of the Parmenides (131a-c), whether one form can be whole in many things.

@p
@greek οὐ γὰρ δή, ὥσπερ ἡ ποιότης
For soul is not through the whole body in the way a quality is, sweetness, say, or colour. Those are affections of bodies, so that the whole of what is affected has the affection, and it is nothing on its own, being something of the body and known only then; and so it is necessarily of that size, and the white of one part is not affected along with that of another. With the white, what is on one part is the same in form as what is on another, but not the same in number; with soul, what is in the foot and in the hand is the same in number, as our perceptions show. And yet in qualities the same thing is seen divided, while in soul the same thing is not divided, but is said to be divided in this sense, that it is everywhere.
!flag no doubt the Form, White, is the same all over, but there is not arithmetical identity | The Greek says the white on one part is "the same in form" (τὸ αὐτὸ μὲν εἴδει) as that on another, "but not the same in number" (οὐ μὴν ταὐτὸν ἀριθμῷ): two whites of one kind, not the Form White itself.
!note The same in form and the same in number: Aristotle, Topics I.7 (103a6-14) and Metaphysics Δ.6 (1016b31-1017a3). That one soul perceives in foot and hand at once is argued in IV.2.2 and IV.7.6-7.

@p
@greek λέγωμεν οὖν ἐξ ἀρχῆς
Let us, then, speak about these things from the beginning, to see whether something clear and easy to accept may come to us: how soul, being bodiless and without magnitude, can go out over the greatest extent, whether before bodies or in bodies. Perhaps, if it appeared that it can do this before bodies too, it would be easy to accept the same thing in bodies.
!flag whether before material masses exist or as enveloping them | The Greek has "before bodies or in bodies" (εἴτε πρὸ τῶν σωμάτων εἴτ᾽ ἐν τοῖς σώμασι); "enveloping" is MacKenna's.

@ch VI.4.2 | The true All and its image
There is the true All, and its imitation, this visible world. The true All is in nothing and needs no place; what comes after it is in it, as resting on it. The All cannot fall short of itself: whatever is set in it finds it whole in itself, for being cannot be in non-being. We think the perceptible great and wonder how being stretches over it, but this great is small: the world, unable to take hold of it or go outside it, circles in it, finding it everywhere, and it is present whole to whatever can receive it.

@p
There is, then, the true All, and there is the imitation of the All, the nature of this visible world. What is really the All is in nothing, for nothing is before it. Whatever is after it must then be in the All, if it is to be at all, and above all hang from it, unable without it either to stay or to move. For even if one does not set such a thing in it as in a place, taking place to be the limit of the surrounding body, by which it surrounds, or some extension which was before of the nature of the void and still is, but as resting, as it were, upon it and reposing on it, since that is everywhere and holds it together, one should drop the predication of the name and take what is said with one's thought. This has been said for the sake of something else: that that All, which is first and is being, does not look for place, and is not in anything at all.
!flag Side by side exist the Authentic All and its counterpart, the visible universe | The Greek says there is the true All and "the imitation of the All" (τοῦ παντὸς μίμημα), this visible nature: an image after its original, not two side by side.
!flag the boundaries of some surrounding extension considered as an envelope | The Greek has "the limit of the surrounding body, by which it surrounds" (πέρας σώματος τοῦ περιέχοντος καθ᾽ ὃ περιέχει), Aristotle's definition of place; the "extension" is the other view, named next.
!flag but this objection is merely verbal and will disappear if our meaning is grasped | The Greek raises no objection: whoever says the world is "in" the true All should "drop the predication of the name" (τὴν τοῦ ὀνόματος ἀφεὶς κατηγορίαν) and take the meaning with his thought.
!note Place as the first unmoved limit of the surrounding body, and against place as an extension of its own: Aristotle, Physics IV.4 (211b14-212a21). The world as an image of the intelligible living being: Plato's Timaeus (30c-31b, 92c).

@p
@greek πᾶν δὴ τὸ πᾶν οὐκ ἔστιν
The All, then, being all, cannot fall short of itself in any way: it has filled itself and is equal to itself, and where the All is, there it is itself, for it is itself the All. In general, if something other than it were settled in the All, it shares in it, meets with it and is strengthened by it, not dividing it, but finding it in itself, having itself come to it, while it has not come to be outside itself. For being cannot be in non-being, but, if anything, non-being in being. It meets being, then, as a whole, for being could not be torn away from itself; and that it is said to be everywhere shows that it is in being, and so in itself. And it is no wonder if what is everywhere is in being and in itself, for then the everywhere comes to be in one.
!flag the omnipresence should be at once self-abiding and universal | The Greek says it is no wonder if "the everywhere" is "in being and in itself" (ἐν τῷ ὄντι καὶ ἐν αὑτῷ): the everywhere is in being, not being in the everywhere.

@p
@greek ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸ ὂν ἐν
But we, setting being in the perceptible, set the everywhere there too; and thinking the perceptible great, we are at a loss how that nature stretches out in something so great and so large. But this which is called great is small, and what is thought small, that is great, if indeed it reaches whole to every part of this; or rather this, coming to it from every side with its parts, finds it everywhere all, and greater than itself.
!flag meets it everywhere as the omnipresent All ever stretching beyond | The Greek says the world finds it "everywhere all, and greater than itself" (πανταχοῦ πᾶν καὶ μεῖζον ἑαυτοῦ), greater than the world, not stretching beyond it.

@p
@greek ὅθεν ὡς οὐκ ἐν τῇ ἐκτάσει
So, since it would take nothing more by stretching out (for it would come to be outside the All too), it wished to run round it; and as it could neither take hold of it round about nor, again, come to be inside it, it was content to have a place and an order where it would be kept safe, as its neighbour, that being present to it and again not present; for that is by itself, even if something wishes to be present to it. So the body of the All, coming together, finds the All wherever it is, so that it needs nothing further, but turns in the same place, as if this were all, of which it enjoys the whole with every part of itself.
!flag it is content to accept place and subordination | The Greek has "a place and an order" (τόπον καὶ τάξιν), a rank where the world is kept safe as the All's neighbour; "subordination" is MacKenna's.
!flag in that movement its every part embraces the All | The Greek says that with every part of itself the world "enjoys the whole of that" (ἀπολαύει ὅλου ἐκείνου); it cannot embrace it, as the paragraph has just said.
!note The circling of the heaven as soul's going round what it cannot go out to: II.2.1-2 (On the motion of the heaven).

@p
@greek εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἐν τόπῳ ἦν
If that itself were in place, the body would have to go up to it there and take a straight path, and touch one part of it with one part of itself, and there would be far and near. But if there is neither far nor near, it must be present whole, if it is present at all. And it is present wholly to each of those for whom it is neither far nor near, but who are able to receive it.

@ch VI.4.3 | Present itself, or by its powers?
Is being itself present everywhere, or does it stay by itself and send powers out, as some say souls are sent out like darts? Where a thing cannot take the whole, a power of it is present, but even then it is not cut off from its power; where all the powers are, it is itself present, though separate, since it is no one thing's. It is no wonder that what is in no place is present to all in place, and whole to each; for it cannot be divided: not its life, its intellect or its being, and even body is divided only as a body of a certain size.

@p
Shall we say, then, that it is itself present? Or that it is by itself, while powers go out from it to all things, and in this way it is said to be everywhere? For in this way they say that souls are like darts thrown out, so that it is settled in itself, while the souls sent out come to be in one living being after another. Or rather: in things in which the one is present without keeping the whole of the nature that is in that itself, a power of it is present there, to whatever it is present to; yet not even so is that not wholly present, since even then it is not cut off from its power, which it gave to that thing; but the one receiving could take only so much, though all of it was present.
!flag any presence is presence of an emanant power | The Greek says "a power of it" (δύναμιν αὐτοῦ) is present; "emanant" is MacKenna's.
!note Who "they" are is not said. That the source stays in itself while what comes from it goes out is Plotinus' own image too (V.1.6, the sun and its light), but here he argues that what goes out is not cut off.

@p
@greek οὗ δὲ πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις
But where all the powers are, it is itself clearly present, though it is still separate. For had it become the form of this thing, it would have stood away from being all and from being everywhere in itself, and would be, by accident, of another too. But being of none, though the thing wishes to be its, it draws near to whatever it wishes, as it can, not becoming that thing's, but with that thing longing for it, nor, again, another's. It is no wonder, then, that it is in all things in this way, because, again, it is in none of them in such a way as to be theirs. So it is perhaps not out of place to say that soul too shares the body's affections in this way, by accident, if it is said to be by itself, not become matter's or body's, while the whole body is lit up, as it were, in every part of itself.
!flag becoming the informing principle of some definite thing | The Greek has "becoming the form of this" (τοῦδε εἶδος): the form of one body, which would then belong to it.
!flag in the same accidental way, we may reasonably put it, soul concurs with body | The Greek says soul "shares the body's affections" (συμπαθεῖν τῷ σώματι) by accident; "concurs" loses the affections.

@p
@greek θαυμάζειν δὲ οὐ δεῖ
One should not wonder that, though it is not itself in place, it is present to everything in place. The opposite would be wonderful, and impossible on top of wonderful, if, having a place of its own, it were present to another thing in place, or were present at all, and present in the way we say. But now the argument says that, since it has been allotted no place, it must be present whole to whatever it is present to, and, being present to all, present whole to each. Otherwise one part of it will be here and another elsewhere, so that it will be divisible and will be body.

@p
@greek πῶς γὰρ δὴ καὶ μεριεῖς
For how will you divide it? Will you divide its life? But if the whole was life, the part will not be life. Its intellect, then, so that one is in one thing and another in another? But neither of them will be intellect. Its being? But the part will not be being, if the whole was being. What, then, if someone said that body too is divided and its parts are bodies? Rather, the division was not of body but of a body of a certain size, and each part was called body by the form by which it is body; and this had no size, not any size at all.
!flag do we not thus sunder Intelligence, one intelligence in this man, another in that | The Greek says only "so that one is in one, another in another" (ἵν᾽ ὁ μὲν ᾖ ἐν ἄλλῳ, ὁ δὲ ἐν ἄλλῳ); "this man" is MacKenna's, and the modern version keeps "intellect" for νοῦς.
!note Being, life and intellect together are the Sophist's (248e-249a), which Plotinus reads as the intelligible itself (VI.2.7-8). The form of body, which is not a quantity: II.4.8-9 and II.7.3.

@ch VI.4.4 | Many souls and intellects, and one
How then are there many beings, intellects and souls, if being is one everywhere? It seems better to say the whole generates parts and stays by itself; but then souls could not be whole in whole bodies either, and the things that go forth, numbers and not magnitudes, raise the same difficulty. Being is many by otherness, not by place: being draws near to being. So are souls: soul seems divided only because bodies are. The one soul and the many do not hinder each other, as the many sciences are in one soul.

@p
How, then, are there being and the beings, and many intellects and many souls, if being is one everywhere, and not one as one in kind, and intellect is one and soul one? And yet there is the soul of the All, and the other souls. These things seem to bear witness against it, and what has been said, even if it has some necessity, does not persuade, since the soul thinks it unbelievable that the one should be the same everywhere in this way.
!note The beings (τὰ ὄντα) are the forms, which are in intellect and are intellects (V.9.6-8, VI.2.20-22). One in kind (ὁμοειδές) as against one in number, as in chapter 1.

@p
@greek βέλτιον γὰρ ἴσως
For perhaps it is better to divide the whole so that what the division came from is not lessened, or rather to say it generated from itself, to use better words, and so to let it be by itself, while what came from it, as parts, at once fill up all things. But if that being stays by itself because it seems strange that something should be present whole everywhere at once, the same argument will hold of the souls. For in the bodies in which they are said to be whole in wholes, they will not be so: they will either be divided, or, staying whole somewhere in the body, will give a power of themselves to the rest. And about the powers the same difficulty will arise, whether the whole is everywhere. And further, one part of the body will have soul, another only a power.
!flag would come into being to produce the multiple total of the universe | The Greek says only that what came from it, "as it were parts" (οἷον μέρη), "fill up all things" (συμπληροῦν ἤδη τὰ πάντα); MacKenna's "the separate souls" before it is his gloss.
!note Soul whole in the whole body and whole in each part of it: IV.2.1 and IV.3.3.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ πῶς ψυχαὶ πολλαὶ
But how are there many souls and many intellects, and being and the beings? And indeed the things that go forth from the prior, being numbers and not magnitudes, will raise a like difficulty, how they fill the All. So nothing has been found by us from the multitude going forth in this way to get us out of the difficulty.
!flag No doubt the beings proceed from the Priors in the mode only of numerical distinction and not as concrete masses | The Greek says the things that go forth "are numbers, not magnitudes" (ἀριθμοὶ ὄντα, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ μεγέθη), and so raise the same difficulty; "numerical distinction" is MacKenna's.
!note The beings as numbers: VI.6.9-15 (On numbers), the next treatise in Porphyry's order after VI.5.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ ὂν πολλὰ
For we grant that being too is many by otherness, not by place. All being is together, even if it is many in this way: "being draws near to being", and all is together; and intellect is many by otherness, not by place, but all together. Are souls so too, then? Souls too. For what is divided about bodies is said to be without parts in its nature; but bodies have magnitude, and when this nature of soul is present to them, or rather when the bodies come to be there, the soul was thought to be divisible about bodies in this way, because that nature images itself in every part of them in so far as they are divided. For that it is not divided along with the parts, but is whole everywhere, makes plain that its nature is one and really without parts.
!flag diversity within the Authentic depends not upon spatial separation but sheerly upon differentiation | The Greek says being is many "by otherness, not by place" (ἑτερότητι, οὐ τόπῳ). The modern version keeps "otherness" for ἑτερότης, one of the five kinds of VI.2.
!flag thus the Intellectual-Principle (which is Being and the Beings) remains an integral, multiple by differentiation | The parenthesis is MacKenna's; the Greek says "intellect is many by otherness, not by place, but all together" (νοῦς πολὺς ἑτερότητι, οὐ τόπῳ, ὁμοῦ δὲ πᾶς).
!note "Being draws near to being" is Parmenides (B8.25): being is continuous, not parted. "The being divided about bodies" is the Timaeus' (35a), as in chapter 1. Being many by otherness: VI.2.8 and Plato's Sophist (255e-256e).

@p
@greek οὔτ’ οὖν τὸ μίαν
So the one soul does not do away with the many, as being does not do away with the beings; nor does the multitude there fight with the one; nor must the bodies be filled with life by the multitude; nor must we think that the multitude of souls comes about because of the body's size: before bodies, they are both many and one. For in the whole the many are there already, each not potentially but actually: the one whole soul does not prevent the many from being in it, nor do the many prevent the one. They stand apart without standing apart, and are present to one another without being made strangers; for they are not marked off by limits, as the many sciences in one soul are not, and the one is such as to have them all in itself. In this way such a nature is unlimited.
!flag present each to all as never having been set in opposition | The Greek says the souls are present to one another "without being made strangers" (οὐκ ἀλλοτριωθεῖσαι), not without opposition.
!flag the nature of such a principle must be utterly free of boundary | The Greek says "in this way such a nature is unlimited" (οὕτως ἐστὶν ἄπειρος): it is unlimited because it holds all in itself, not by a demand of the argument.
!note The sciences in one soul, each whole and the whole in each: IV.9.5 and V.9.8. That the souls are one and many: IV.9 (Whether all souls are one).

@ch VI.4.5 | The greatness of soul
Soul's greatness is not in bulk, which goes to nothing if you take from it. It cannot fail or flow away; it has taken hold of the All. It gives the All as much as the All can bear, and is not smaller than the body, for bulk is not to be measured against what has none: as well call medicine smaller than the doctor's body. The same soul reaches over a body as it grows.

@p
And its greatness must be taken in this way, not in bulk: for bulk is small, going to nothing if one takes away from it. There one cannot take away, and even if you take away, it will not run short. And if it will not run short, why need one fear that it stands away from anything? For how does it stand away, when it does not run short, but is an ever-flowing nature that does not flow? If it flowed, it would go as far as it could flow; but it does not flow, for it would not even have anywhere to flow: it has taken hold of the All, or rather it is itself the All, and something greater than the nature of body.
!flag it lies spread over the universe | The Greek says "it has taken hold of the All" (τὸ πᾶν κατείληφε), "or rather it is itself the All"; it is not spread.
!note "Ever-flowing" (ἀέναος) is said of springs and rivers, and so of what never fails; Plotinus says the nature is ever-flowing and yet does not flow.

@p
@greek ὀλίγον γὰρ ἂν εἰκότως
So it would reasonably be thought to give little to the All, as much of itself as the All can bear. But one must not call that smaller, nor, setting it down as smaller in bulk, then disbelieve that the smaller can go over what is greater than it. For one must not predicate "smaller" of it at all, nor set bulk beside what has no bulk in measuring: it would be as if someone said the art of medicine was smaller than the doctor's body. Nor, again, must it be thought greater in this way, by a measuring of quantity, since not even with soul are its being great and greater than the body so. The soul's greatness is witnessed too by this: when the bulk grows greater, the same soul that was in the smaller bulk reaches over all of it. It would be absurd in many ways to add bulk to the soul too.
!flag too great to be held by body, giving, therefore, to the material universe but little of itself | The Greek says it is "greater than the nature of body" and so would reasonably be thought (νομίζοιτο) to give little; "too great to be held by body" is MacKenna's.
!note Medicine in the soul of the doctor, with no size: the soul's sciences, as in chapter 4. The soul growing with no growth of its own: IV.7.5.

@ch VI.4.6 | One soul in many bodies?
Why does the soul not go into another body? Because the other body must come to it, if it can. Does that other have the same soul? Why not, but for the additions; the same soul is in foot and hand. Perceptions differ because the affections judged differ, not what judges, as one of us judges a pleasure in the finger and a pain in the head. One soul does not perceive another's judgement because a judgement is not an affection, as sight does not speak to hearing.

@p
Why, then, does it not go to another body? Because that body must come to it, if it can, while the one that has come and received it has it. What then? Does the other body, having itself too the soul it has, have the same soul? For what difference is there? Only the additions. Then how is it the same in foot and hand, while the soul in this part of the All is not the same as that in that part? And if the perceptions are different, the affections that befall them must also be said to be different.
!flag Are we to think that this second body, in keeping its soul with a like care | The Greek asks only whether the other body, "having itself too the soul it has" (ἔχον καὶ αὐτὸ τὴν ἣν ἔχει ψυχήν), has the same soul; "with a like care" is MacKenna's.
!flag Merely some additions (from the experiences of life, none in the soul itself) | The Greek says only "by the additions" (ταῖς προσθήκαις); the parenthesis is MacKenna's.
!note The additions are what a soul takes on in coming to a body, the other man of chapter 14; compare IV.3.15.

@p
@greek ἄλλα οὖν ἐστι τὰ κρινόμενα
So what is judged is different, not what judges. The one judging is the same judge, coming to be in different affections, and yet it is not he who is affected but the nature of a body of a certain kind. It is as if the same one of us were to judge both a pleasure in the finger and a pain in the head.
!flag it is only as a man pronounces simultaneously upon a pleasant sensation in his finger and a pain in his head | The Greek has no "simultaneously": it is as if "the same one of us" (ὁ αὐτὸς ἡμῶν) judged both.

@p
@greek διὰ τί οὖν οὐ συναισθάνεται
Why, then, does the one soul not perceive along with the other the other's judgement? Because it is a judgement, not an affection. Then too, the soul that judged does not say "I have judged", but only judged; since not even in us does sight speak to hearing, though both judged, but reasoning is over both, and this is other than both. Often, too, reasoning has seen the judgement in another and come to understand another's affection. But this has been spoken of elsewhere too.
!flag Often, as it happens, reason does become aware of a verdict formed in another reason | The Greek says reasoning sees "the judgement in another" (τὸ ἐν ἑτέρῳ κρίμα), another person, and understands his affection; not a verdict in another reason.
!note That sight cannot judge sweet and white, but one power over both: Plato's Theaetetus (184b-186a) and Aristotle, On the soul III.2 (426b8-427a14). Why one soul does not feel another's experience is asked in IV.9.2-3.

@ch VI.4.7 | The hand, the light and the sun
How is the same over all things? Not by dividing it among the many, but by bringing the many back to it; we think it divided because they are scattered. A hand holds a long beam with a power not parted out over it; take away the hand's bulk and the power is whole in all of it. A small light inside a transparent sphere lights all of it; take away the body, and the light is everywhere and nowhere in particular. So the sun, if it were only a power, would light from no one place.

@p
But let us say again how the same is over all things. This is the same as asking how each of the many perceptible things, lying in many places, is not without a share in the same. For by what has been said it is not right to divide that among the many, but rather to bring the divided many back up to the one; and that has not come to these, but these, because they are scattered, have given us the opinion that that too is parted out among them, as if someone were to divide what masters and holds together into parts equal to what is mastered.
!note Bringing the many back to the one: VI.5.1-3 and VI.9.1.

@p
@greek καίτοι κρατοίη ἂν
And yet a hand could master a whole body, a beam many cubits long, or something else; and what masters reaches over all of it, yet it is not parted out in the hand into parts equal to what is mastered, the power being bounded, as it seems, as far as it touches; but the hand is still bounded by its own quantity, not by that of the body lifted and mastered. And if you added another length to the body mastered, and the hand could carry it, the power masters that too, not parted out into as many parts as the body has. What, then, if one supposed the hand's bodily bulk taken away, but left the same power that held the body up before, the power that was before in the hand? Would it not be the same, without parts, in all of it alike, in every part?
!flag though the hand is only hand-long, not taking the extension of the mass it wields | The Greek says the power seems bounded "as far as it touches" (καθ᾽ ὅσον ἐφάπτεται), while the hand is bounded "by its own quantity" (τῷ αὑτῆς ποσῷ); "hand-long" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ δὴ φωτεινὸν
And if you made a small luminous bulk a centre, as it were, and set round it a larger spherical transparent body, so that the light within shone in all that surrounds it, the outer bulk having no brightness from elsewhere, shall we not say that the inner one is itself not affected at all, but, staying, has gone over the whole outer bulk, and that the light seen in the small bulk has taken hold of what is outside? Since, then, the light was not from that small bodily bulk (for it did not have the light as body, but as luminous body, by another power, which is not bodily), come, if someone took away the body's bulk but kept the power of the light, would you still say the light was somewhere, or would it be equally within and through the whole outer sphere? You will no longer rest your thought on where it lay before, and will no longer say from where, or how; but you will be at a loss about it and wonder, as you gaze at the light here in the spherical body and here at once.
!flag which illuminates not as body but as body lit | The Greek says it had the light "as luminous body" (ᾗ φωτεινὸν σῶμα), a body that gives light, "by another power, which is not bodily"; not a body lit.
!note The transparent sphere imagined with all things in it: V.8.9. Light as an act of the luminous body, not a body: IV.5.6-7 and II.1.7.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἡλίου
So with the sun too: you can say from where the light shines through all the air, looking at the body of the sun, and yet you see the same light everywhere, and this is not divided either. What cuts it off shows this: it does not let the light be on the other side from where it came, but it does not divide it either.
