And so, if the sun were only a power, being without body, and gave light, the light would not begin from there, nor would you say from where; but the light would be everywhere one and the same, not beginning nor having a beginning anywhere.
!flag Consider too the refraction of light by which it is thrown away from the line of incidence | The Greek has "the cuttings-off" (αἱ ἀποτομαί), the bodies that block the light, which keep it from the far side and yet do not divide it; there is no refraction.

@ch VI.4.8 | What has no body has no parts
The sun's light has a source because it is of a body; but what is immaterial, prior to all body and settled in itself, has no starting place, and so no part here and part there: whatever shares in it shares in all of it. To be divided is an affection of body as body. One in many is not one become many: we fasten the many's affection on the one. Without size there is no where, and so no division; the many long for it whole, and must have it as though they had not taken it, as not their own.

@p
Light, then, since it is of a body, you can say where it came from, since you can say where the body is. But if something is immaterial and needs no body, being prior in nature to all body, settled in itself, or rather not even needing any such settling, then this, which has such a nature, having no beginning from which to set out, neither from some place nor being of some body: how will you say that this of it is here and that here? For then it would already have both where it set out from and being something's. It remains, then, to say that, if anything shares in it, it shares in all of it by the power of the whole; nothing else, then, and nothing divided.

@p
@greek τῷ μὲν γὰρ σῶμα ἔχοντι
For what has a body could be affected, if only by accident, and in this way could be called affectable and divisible, since it is something of body, like an affection or a form. But what is of no body, but body wishes to be its, must not be affected at all by the other affections of body, and cannot be divided: for this too is an affection of body, and first of all, and of body as body. If, then, the divisible is so as body, the undivided is so as not body. For how will you divide what has no magnitude? If, then, what has magnitude somehow shares in what has none, it would share in it without its being divided, or else it will have magnitude again.
!flag passive and partible in view of its close relationship with the body | The Greek says such a thing is "something of body, like an affection or a form" (σώματός ἐστί τι οἷον πάθος ἢ εἶδος); "close relationship" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ὅταν οὖν ἓν ἐν πολλοῖς
When you say one in many, then, you are not saying that it has itself become many; you are fastening the affection of the many on that one, as you see it in the many at once. And the one in them must be taken in this way: not as having become each one's, nor the whole's, but that is its own and is itself, and being itself it does not fall short of itself. Nor, again, is it as large as the whole perceptible All, nor as some part of the All: for it is not a quantity at all. How, then, could it be so large? "So large" belongs to body; to what is not body, but of another nature, "so large" must in no way be fastened.
!flag we link the variety in the multiples with the unity which we discern | The Greek says we "fasten the affection of the many on that one" (τῶν πολλῶν τὸ πάθος περιάπτεις τῷ ἑνί): the many-ness is the many's affection, laid on the one.
!flag cannot fail within its own scope (and therefore does reach over the multiple) | The parenthesis is MacKenna's; the Greek says only that, being itself, it "does not fall short of itself" (οὐκ ἀπολείπεσθαι ἑαυτοῦ).
!note The form whole in each of many things, like a day, or divided, like a sail: Plato's Parmenides (131a-c), the question this treatise and VI.5 answer.

@p
@greek ὅπου δὲ μὴ τὸ τοσοῦτον
And where there is no "so large", there is no "where" either; and so no "here and here", for then it would be in many places. If, then, division goes with places, when one part of it is here and another here, how could what has no "here" be divided? It must, then, be undivided, with itself, even if the many happen to long for it. If the many long for it, plainly they long for the whole of it; so that if they can share in it, they would share in the whole of it, as far as they can. Those that share in it, then, must have it as if they had not shared in it, since it is not their own: for in this way it would stay whole by itself, and whole in the things in which it is seen. For if it is not whole, it will not be itself, nor will the sharing be in what is longed for, but in something else, for which there was no longing.
!note Having it as though they had not shared in it: what is shared in stays apart. The later Neoplatonists make this the unparticipated before the participated (Proclus, Elements of Theology 23-24).

@ch VI.4.9 | If each share were a first
If each share were whole, there would be many firsts, and nothing to keep them from being one. If the shares are powers, how were they cut off, and where did they go? If they are not still in the source, the source is lessened; if they are, either the same is everywhere undivided, or each power is whole and with only one substance, but there is no power without substance. Weaker powers, like a dim light, are still all of one kind; divided they would be powerless; and an image cut off from what it images cannot be. So the source is with them, whole, everywhere.

@p
For if the part that came to be in each were whole, and each itself were like the first, then, with each always cut off, the firsts would be many, and each a first. Then what would keep these many firsts apart, so that they are not all one together? Not their bodies: for they could not be forms of the bodies, if they too are like that first from which they came. And if what are called the parts in the many are its powers, first, each is no longer whole; then, how did they come, cut off, and leaving it behind? For if they left it, plainly they left it to go somewhere.
!flag those firsts cannot be present in the material masses as their Forms if they are to remain identical with the First | The Greek says "if they too are like that first" (εἴπερ ὅμοια καὶ ταῦτα ἐκείνῳ τῷ πρώτῳ): like it, not identical.
!flag they certainly have not moved away with no purpose in their movement | The Greek says "if they left it, plainly they left it going somewhere" (κατέλιπόν ποι ἰοῦσαι): leaving is going to a place, which powers of what has no place cannot do; there is no purpose in it.

@p
@greek εἶτα πότερα ἔτι
Then, are the powers that have come to be here in the perceptible still in it, or not? If they are not, it is absurd that it should have been lessened and become powerless, deprived of the powers it had before; and how could the powers be apart from their own substances, cut off? If they are both in it and elsewhere, either they will be here whole, or parts of them. If parts, the remaining parts are there. If whole, either those which are there are here too, undivided, and again the same will be everywhere undivided; or each power, become many, is whole, and they are like one another, so that with each substance there will be only the one power that is with it, and the others will be only powers. Yet as there cannot be substance without power, so neither can there be power without substance. For power there is reality and substance, or greater than substance.
!flag for There power is Being or something greater than Being | The Greek has "reality and substance, or greater than substance" (ὑπόστασις καὶ οὐσία ἢ μεῖζον οὐσίας); the modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία.
!note "Greater than substance" recalls the Good, "beyond substance" (Republic VI 509b); compare III.8.10, where the first is the power of all things.

@p
@greek εἰ δ’ ἕτεραι ὡς ἐλάττους
And if the powers from it are other, as lesser and dim, like a dim light from a brighter, and substances go with these powers, so that there is no power without substance: first, with such powers too, which are all of one kind with one another, it must be granted either that the same is everywhere, or, if not everywhere, at least that the same is whole in every part at once, undivided, as in one and the same body. And if so, why not in the whole All? And if each is divided to infinity, it will no longer be whole itself, but by the division there will be powerlessness.
!flag such secondary powers would be perfectly uniform | The Greek says the powers are "of one kind with one another" (ὁμοειδῶν πρὸς ἀλλήλας), not uniform in themselves.

@p
@greek ἔπειτα ἄλλη κατ’ ἄλλο
Then, being one in one part and another in another, it will leave no perceiving together. And then, as the image of something, like the weaker light, would no longer be when cut off from what it is from, and in general whatever has its reality from another, being an image of it, cannot be cut off and made to be in reality, so neither would these powers that came from it be, cut off from it. And if so, that whose powers they are, from which they came, will be there with them at once, so that again it will itself be everywhere at once, undivided, whole.
!flag the conditions of consciousness cease | The Greek has "perceiving together" (συναίσθησις), the one body's feeling of itself as one; "consciousness" is MacKenna's.
!flag for example, a reflected light | The Greek has "the image of something, like the weaker light" (τὸ ἴνδαλμά τινος, οἷον καὶ τὸ ἀσθενέστερον φῶς), the dim light of the paragraph before; there is no reflection.
!note Perceiving together across the parts of a body: IV.2.2 and IV.7.7.

@ch VI.4.10 | Images and warmth
It may be said that an image need not hang on its archetype, as a painting outlasts its sitter, and warmth stays when the fire goes. But a painting is the painter's work, and the placing of the colours; images in water and mirrors and shadows are properly from what they image and cannot be cut off from it. Warmth is not an image of fire, and it fades. If the powers were quenched, the souls and intellect would perish; but the sun gives the same light while it stays, and souls and intellect are immortal.

@p
But suppose someone says that the image of something need not be attached to its archetype, for there can be a likeness when the archetype from which the likeness comes is absent, and when the fire has gone away the warmth can be in what was warmed. First, about the archetype and the likeness: if one means the likeness made by the painter, we shall say that it was not the archetype that made the likeness but the painter, and it is not a likeness of him, not even if someone paints himself; for what painted was not the painter's body, nor the form imitated; and one must say that not the painter, but the placing of the colours just so, makes such a likeness.
!note The portrait made from memory: Life 1, where Plotinus will not sit for one. The painter's likeness third from the truth: Republic X (596e-598b).

@p
@greek οὐδὲ κυρίως ἡ τῆς
Nor is this properly the making of a likeness and an image, as in water and mirrors or in shadows. There the image has its reality, properly, from the prior, and comes to be from it, and what has come to be cannot be cut off from it. And it is in this way that they will hold that the weaker powers come to be from the prior.
!flag Nor is there strictly any such making of image as we see in water or in mirrors or in a shadow | The Greek says the painting is not properly the making of an image "as in water and mirrors or in shadows" (οἷον ἐν ὕδασι καὶ κατόπτροις ἢ ἐν σκιαῖς): those are the images made properly, which hang on their originals; MacKenna's "Nor is there" denies them.
!flag it is in this sense that we are to understand the weaker powers to be images of the Priors | The Greek says this is how "they will claim" (ἀξιώσουσι) that the weaker powers come from the prior: those who hold the powers are cut off must grant it.

@p
@greek τὸ δ’ ἐπὶ τοῦ πυρὸς
As for what is said about fire, the warmth must not be called an image of the fire, unless one says there is fire in the warmth too: for if so, one will make the warmth apart from fire. Then, even if not at once, the warmed body does stop and grows cold when the fire has gone away.
!flag unless we think of warmth as containing fire so that the two are separate things | The Greek says that if there were fire in the warmth, one "will make the warmth apart from fire" (χωρὶς πυρὸς ποιήσει τὴν θερμότητα), which is absurd; the separate things are MacKenna's.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ καὶ οὗτοι
And if these people too were to quench these powers, first, they will say that only the one is imperishable, and will make the souls and intellect perishable; then they will make what comes from a flowing substance flowing too. And yet, if the sun stayed settled wherever it is, it would give the same light to the same places; and if someone said it was not the same, he would be using this to prove that the sun's body flows. But that what comes from that is not perishable, and that the souls and all intellect are immortal, has been said at more length elsewhere too.
!flag then since Being (identical with the Intellectual-Principle) becomes transitory, so also must the Beings, its productions | The Greek says they "will make what comes from a flowing substance flowing" (ἐκ ῥεούσης οὐσίας ῥέοντα τὰ ἐξ αὐτῆς); the parenthesis and "the Beings" are MacKenna's.
!note The soul's immortality: IV.7 (On the immortality of the soul). Whether the sun's body flows and is fed: II.1.3-5.

@ch VI.4.11 | First, second, third: not by place
If it is whole everywhere, why do not all things share in all of the intelligible, and why are some first and others second? It is present by the fitness of what receives it, as light to the transparent, and otherwise to the clouded; first, second and third are by order, power and differences, not place, as soul and intellect and the sciences are together. It is varied and many, yet one: one forming principle, and its otherness is its own. Presence is of many kinds.

@p
But why, if it is whole everywhere, do not all things share in the whole of the intelligible? And how is one thing first after it, another second, and others after that? Rather, one must think that what is present is present by the fitness of what will receive it, and that being is everywhere in being, not falling short of itself, and that what can be present to it is present, and as far as it can, so far it is present to it, not by place: as the transparent is to the light. To the clouded the sharing is otherwise.
!flag why do not all things participate in the Intellectual Order in its entirety | The Greek has "the intelligible" (τοῦ νοητοῦ); the modern version keeps "intelligible" for νοητός.
!flag the transparent object and the opaque answer very differently to the light | The Greek has "the clouded" (τῷ τεθολωμένῳ), the troubled or muddied, which takes the light otherwise, not the opaque, which takes none.

@p
@greek καὶ δὴ τὰ πρῶτα
And the firsts, seconds and thirds are so by order, by power and by differences, not by places. For nothing prevents different things from being together, as soul and intellect and all the sciences, the greater and the lower. Since from the same thing the eye sees the colour, smell the fragrance, and another sense another thing, all being together, not apart.
!note The ranks of what receives: VI.5.11. That from one thing each sense takes its own: Aristotle, On the soul II.6 (418a7-25).

@p
@greek οὔκουν ἐκεῖνο ποικίλον
Is that not, then, varied and many? Rather, the varied is simple again, and the many one. For the forming principle is one and many, and all being is one. For the other is in it, and the otherness is its own: it is surely not of non-being. And being belongs to the one, which is not separated from it, and wherever being is, its one is present to it too, and the one, being, is again by itself. For it is possible to be present while being separate. The perceptibles are present to the intelligibles in one way, those of them that are present, and to those they are present to; the intelligibles are present to themselves in another; since body is present to soul in one way, and science to soul in another, and science to science, each being in the same, in another; and body to body otherwise again, besides these.
!flag for it is a Reason-Principle, which is to say a unity in variety | The Greek says "the forming principle (λόγος) is one and many" (λόγος γὰρ εἷς καὶ πολύς); "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's name, and "which is to say a unity in variety" his gloss.
!flag the differentiation is within Being, obviously not within non-Being | The Greek says "the other is in it and the otherness is its own" (τὸ ἕτερον ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ ἡ ἑτερότης αὐτοῦ). The modern version keeps "otherness" for ἑτερότης.
!flag for presence in the sensible does not abrogate independence | The Greek says "it is possible to be present while being separate" (ἔστι γὰρ καὶ παρεῖναι χωρὶς ὄν), nothing of the sensible.
!note The other is, and is not non-being, but otherness of being: Plato's Sophist (256d-259b) and VI.2.8. The one never apart from being: VI.2.9-11.

@ch VI.4.12 | The voice in the air
A voice in the air, and the word in it, is received whole by every ear that is present, and many eyes see the same thing: so what can have soul has it, from the same. The voice is whole everywhere in the air, not stretched along it part for part: why disbelieve that soul is whole wherever it is present? Before bodies soul is like the speaker; in bodies, like the voice spoken, and still the speaker. What newly takes soul does not receive a part sent to it: it comes to soul, into the world of life, and shares in the whole.

@p
As when there is a voice in the air, and a word in the voice, the ear that is present has received and perceived it, and if you set another between, in the empty space, the word and the voice came to it too, or rather the ear came to the word; and many eyes have seen the same thing, and all were filled with the sight, though what is seen lies in a bounded place, because one was an eye and the other an ear: so too what can have soul will have it, and another again, and another, from the same.
!flag from a great distance many eyes look to the one object and all take it fully | The Greek has no great distance: many eyes saw the same, "though what is seen lies in a bounded place" (ἐν ἀφωρισμένῳ τοῦ θεάματος κειμένου).
!flag while from the one identical presence another will derive something else | The Greek says "another again, and another, from the same" (καὶ ἄλλο αὖ καὶ ἕτερον ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ) will have soul; not something else.
!note The word (λόγος) is the meaning carried in the voice, as in VI.3.18-19.

@p
@greek ἦν δὲ ἡ φωνὴ πανταχοῦ
The voice was everywhere in the air, not one voice divided, but one, whole everywhere. And so with sight: if the air, affected, has the shape, it has it undivided, for wherever sight is set, it has the shape there. Not every opinion grants this, but let it be said for this reason, that the sharing is from the same one.
!note That the air between is affected and passes on the shape is Aristotle's account of sight (On the soul II.7, 419a9-21); Plotinus doubts it in IV.5.1-4.

@p
@greek τὸ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς φωνῆς
The case of the voice is clearer, that the whole form is in all the air: for not everyone would have heard the same unless the spoken word were whole everywhere, and each hearing had taken in all of it, like every other. If not even here is the whole voice stretched along through the whole air, so that this part of it is yoked to this part of the air, and that part divided along with that, why should one disbelieve that soul is not stretched along and divided with the body, but is present wherever it is present, and is everywhere in the All, undivided?

@p
@greek καὶ γενομένη μὲν ἐν σώμασιν
And when it has come to be in bodies, in whichever it comes to be in, it will be analogous to the voice already uttered in the air, and before the bodies, to the one uttering and about to utter. And yet even when it has come to be in a body, it has not even so ceased to be as in the one uttering, who in uttering both has the voice and gives it. What belongs to the voice, then, does not have sameness with what it is taken to show, but it has a likeness in some respect; what belongs to soul, which is of the other nature, must be taken not as though one part of it were in bodies and another by itself, but as whole in itself and again appearing in many.
!flag though even embodied it remains at once the speaker and the silent | The Greek says it remains as in "the one uttering, who in uttering both has the voice and gives it" (ὅστις φωνῶν καὶ ἔχει τὴν φωνὴν καὶ δίδωσι); there is no silent one.
!flag the soul belongs to that other Kind | The Greek has "the other nature" (φύσεως τῆς ἑτέρας), here the intelligible over against body; MacKenna's "Kind" suggests the kinds of VI.2.
!note The image has "no sameness" (ταυτότης) with what it shows, only "a likeness in some respect". In VI.3.1 "the other nature" was the perceptible; here, from the side of body, it is soul's.

@p
@greek καὶ αὖ εἰ ἦλθεν ἄλλο
And again, if another thing has come to take soul, this too has, again from the invisible, the same that was in the others too. For it was not so prepared that a part of soul, lying here, should come to this; what is said to come was in the All, in itself, and is in itself, though it seems to have come here. For how could it have come? If, then, it did not come, but is seen now present, and present not by waiting for what will share in it, plainly, being by itself, it is present to this too. And if, being by itself, it is present to this, this has come to it.
!flag receives mysteriously that same principle | The Greek says the newcomer has it "from the invisible" (ἐξ ἀφανοῦς): from what cannot be seen, not by a mystery.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ τοῦτο ἔξω ὂν
And if this, being outside what really is, came to what really is, and came to be in the world of life, and the world of life was by itself, and all of it was by itself, not parted out into its own bulk, for it was not bulk, then what came did not come into bulk either. It shared in it, then, not in a part but in the whole. And if another comes into such a world, it will share in the whole of it. Likewise, then, if that is said to be whole in these things, it will be whole in each. And so everywhere it will be the same, one in number, not divided, but whole.
!note The world of life (ὁ κόσμος ὁ τῆς ζωῆς) is the intelligible, where being is life: V.8.3-4 and VI.7.12.

@ch VI.4.13 | Nothing stretched out
How then does soul stretch over the whole heaven? It does not. Perception says "here and here", but the argument says the stretched-out shares in what is unextended. Nothing shares in itself: body shares in what is not body, magnitude in what is not magnitude, as two cubits do not become three. So what is shared in must be no quantity at all: not small, for the small is divisible and cannot fit the whole, and not a point, for the bulk has infinitely many points. It is whole in every part of the bulk.

@p
Where, then, does the stretching out over the whole heaven and the living beings come from? Rather, it was not stretched out. Perception, which we heed when we disbelieve what is said, says "here and here"; but the argument says that the "here and here" came about not by its being stretched out here and here, but that what is stretched out has shared in all of it, while it is itself without extension.
!flag the extended has participated in that kosmos of life which itself has no extension | The Greek says the extended "has shared in all of it" (πᾶν αὐτοῦ μετειληφέναι), the soul's, "which is without extension"; the world of life was chapter 12's.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν τι μεταλήψεταί
If, then, something will share in something, plainly it will not share in itself, or it will not be a sharer but itself. So body, sharing in something, must share in what is not body, for body it has already. Body, then, will not share in body. Nor, then, will magnitude share in magnitude, for it has it already. Not even if it took an addition will that magnitude which it was before share in magnitude: for the two-cubit does not become three-cubit, but the underlying thing, which had one quantity, has come to have another; since in that way the two themselves will be three.
!flag the actual two cubits must themselves become the new three (which cannot occur) | The parenthesis is MacKenna's; the Greek says only "since in that way the two themselves will be three" (ἐπεὶ οὕτω γε αὐτὰ τὰ δύο τρία ἔσται).
!note What becomes larger by addition is the underlying thing, not the quantity: Plato's Phaedo (96d-97b, 100e-101c).

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν τὸ διειλημμένον
If, then, what is parted out and stretched to so much is to share in another kind, or in general one thing in another, what it shares in must be neither parted out nor stretched out, nor any quantity at all.

@p
@greek ὅλον ἄρα δεῖ
So what is to be present must be present itself, whole, everywhere, being without parts: not without parts in the way the small is, for in that way it will be no less divisible, will not fit all of the body, and will not stay with it the same as it grows; nor as a point is, for the bulk is not one point, but has infinitely many in it, so that this too would be infinitely many points, if it is at all, and not continuous; so not even so will it fit. If, then, the whole bulk is to have it whole, it will have it in every part of itself.
!flag the universe must hold that one soul present at its every point | The Greek says "the whole bulk will have it in every part of itself" (ἕξει αὐτὸ κατὰ πᾶν ἑαυτοῦ): it is the bulk, not the universe, and the Greek does not name soul.
!note The continuous is not made of points: Aristotle, Physics VI.1 (231a21-b18).

@ch VI.4.14 | Who are we?
If the same soul is everywhere, how is each one's own, and one good, another bad? It suffices for each and holds all souls and intellects, one and unlimited, each distinct and not apart; nothing comes to be there, and it seems divided only to what receives it. Who are we? Before our birth we were there, pure souls and intellect, parts of the intelligible not cut off, and are not cut off now. But another man has added himself to the man each of us was, as an ear comes to a voice, and we have become the pair.

@p
But if the same soul is everywhere, how is each one's own? And how is one good, another bad? Rather, it suffices for each, and has all souls and all intellects. For it is one and again unlimited, and it has all things together, and each distinct, and again not distinguished apart: for how else would it be unlimited? Or rather, it may be said in this way, that it has all things together, all life, all soul and every intellect, but each of them is not marked off by limits; and for this reason it is one again. For it had to have not one life but an unlimited one, and again one, and the one one in this way: because all are together, not heaped together into one, but beginning from one and staying where they began, or rather not even beginning, but always being so. For nothing comes to be there; nor, then, is anything divided there, but it seems divided to what receives it. What is there is the ancient and from the beginning; what comes to be draws near, and seems to be joined, and hangs from that.
!flag It was to hold life not single but infinite and yet one life, one in the sense not of an aggregate built up | The Greek says all the lives are together "not heaped together into one" (οὐ συμφορηθείσας εἰς ἕν), but beginning from one; "aggregate built up" is MacKenna's.
!note The unlimited (ἄπειρον) here is the inexhaustible fullness of the intelligible, not the unlimited of matter: VI.6.18.

@p
@greek ἡμεῖς δέ
But we: who are we? Are we that, or what draws near and comes to be in time? Rather, even before this becoming came about, we were there, other men, some of us even gods: pure souls, and intellect joined to the whole of substance, parts of the intelligible, not marked off nor cut away, but being of the whole; for not even now are we cut away.
!flag Intelligence inbound with the entire of reality | The Greek has "intellect joined to the whole of substance" (νοῦς συνημμένος τῇ ἁπάσῃ οὐσίᾳ); the modern version keeps "intellect" for νοῦς and "substance" for οὐσία.
!note That not all of the soul came down, but something of it is always in the intelligible: IV.8.8. "Who are we?": I.1.7-10, and the man of Alcibiades I (129e-130c).

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ γὰρ νῦν ἐκείνῳ
But now to that man another man has come, wishing to be, and finding us, for we were not outside the All. He has put himself round us and added himself to that man who each of us was then (as if, when there is one voice and one word, one man here and another there set his ear to it, and heard and received it, and came to be a hearing in act, having what acts on it present to it); and we have become the pair, and not the one we were before, and sometimes the other, the one we added afterwards, when that prior one is idle and in another way not present.
!flag now we have lost that first simplicity | The Greek has no loss here: the voice and its hearers are an image of how the second man adds himself to the first, and "we have become the pair" (γεγενήμεθα τὸ συνάμφω); MacKenna makes the image our first state.
!note The pair (τὸ συνάμφω), soul and body together, is the living being of I.1.7 and IV.4.18; the three men, VI.7.5-6.

@ch VI.4.15 | The newcomer and the crowd
What came had a fitness for soul and got what it was fit for; what is less fit, like animals and plants, takes what it can, as some hear only the sound and not the word. The living body, not empty of soul, takes a trace of soul, like warmth or light, and with it desires, pleasures and pains. Soul from the divine was quiet, but what is weak and struck from outside cried out and troubled the whole, like a hungry crowd in an assembly of elders; when it is quiet and a wise word comes from above, there is order. One who masters the crowd goes back up to the man he was; another lives a mixed life.

@p
But how did what came come? Because it had a fitness, it got what it was fit for. It had come to be such as to receive soul. But what comes to be such as not to receive all of it, though all of it is present, yet not for it, as with the other living beings and the plants, has as much as it can take: as, when a voice signifies a word, some share in the word too, with the sound of the voice, and others only in the voice and its blow.
!note The voice as a blow of air: Plato's Timaeus (67b) and Aristotle, On the soul II.8 (420b5-421a6). Animals and plants hear the sound without the meaning.

@p
@greek γενομένου δὴ ζῴου
So, when a living being has come to be, which has soul present to it from being, by which it hangs on all being, and a body is present too, not empty, nor without a share of soul, which did not lie even before in the soulless, and still more came near, as it were, by its fitness, and came to be no longer only body but living body, and by the neighbourhood, as it were, reaped some trace of soul, not a part of that, but like a sort of warmth or illumination that came: then the becoming of desires and pleasures and pains grew up in it. So the body of the living being that had come to be was not foreign to it.
!flag but that it is warmed and lit by soul entire | The Greek says the body takes "some trace of soul" (τι ἴχνος ψυχῆς), "not a part of that, but like a sort of warmth or illumination that came"; not soul entire.
!note The trace of soul in the body, the seat of desire and pain: IV.4.18-20 and I.1.7.

@p
@greek ἡ μὲν δὴ ἐκ τοῦ θείου
The soul from the divine was quiet, in keeping with its own character, standing on itself; but what was in uproar from weakness, and flowing, and struck by blows from outside, cried out, first to itself, then into what is common to the living being, and gave its own disturbance to the whole: as, in an assembly, with the elders sitting in quiet thought, a disorderly people wanting food, and blaming the other things it suffers, might throw the whole assembly into an unseemly uproar. When such people keep quiet, and a word comes to them from someone with sense, the crowd settles into a moderate order, and the worse has not mastered; if not, the worse masters while the better keeps quiet, because what is in uproar could not receive the word from above. And this is the vice of a city and of an assembly.
!flag This is the evil of state and of council | The Greek has "the vice (κακία) of a city and an assembly" (πόλεως καὶ ἐκκλησίας κακία), the city's badness; "council" is MacKenna's for the assembly.
!note The city and the soul, and the many-headed beast of desires within: Republic IV (439c-442d), VIII (557a-562a) and IX (588c-589b).

@p
@greek τοῦτο δὲ καὶ ἀνθρώπου κακία
This is the vice of a man too, who has in himself a people of pleasures, desires and fears, which have mastered him when such a man gives himself over to such a people. But one who enslaves this mob and runs back up to that man he once was lives by that one, and is that one, giving to the body what he gives as to something other than himself. Another lives now in this way, now in another, a sort of mixture, come to be from a good self and a bad other.
!flag and these become masters when the man, the manifold, gives them play | The Greek says they master him when "such a man gives himself over to such a people" (συνδόντος ἑαυτὸν τοῦ τοιούτου ἀνθρώπου δήμῳ τῷ τοιούτῳ); "the manifold" is MacKenna's.

@ch VI.4.16 | Descents, judgements and Hades
If soul cannot become bad and is present to body in this way, what are the ancients' descents and ascents, judgements and entries into animals? Coming is the body's coming to soul; descent is soul's giving something of itself, not becoming the body's, and departure is the end of that communion. The communion is bad because soul becomes partial, acting by a part as a knower by one theorem; it leaps from the whole into a part. Hades is the unseen, or a worse place where the image goes; but the soul set free by philosophy is in the intelligible.

@p
But if that nature could not become bad, and this is the way soul goes into body and is present to it, what is the descent in periods, and again the ascent, and the judgements, and the entries into the bodies of other living beings? For we have received these from those of old who did philosophy best about soul, and it is fitting to try to show that the present argument is in harmony with them, or at least not out of tune.
!flag the banishment into animal forms | The Greek has "the entries into the bodies of other living beings" (αἱ εἰς ἄλλων ζῴων σώματα εἰσκρίσεις); "banishment" is MacKenna's.
!note The periods, judgements and entries into animals: Plato's Phaedrus (248c-249b), Republic X (614b-621b), Timaeus (42b-d) and Phaedo (81d-82b); in Plotinus, IV.8.1 and III.4.2.

@p
@greek ἐπειδὴ τοίνυν τὸ μεταλαμβάνειν
Since, then, sharing in that nature was not its coming into things here, standing away from itself, but this coming to be in it and sharing in it, plainly what those men call coming must be said to be the nature of body coming to be there and sharing in life and soul; and the coming is not by place at all, but whatever the way of such a communion is. So descending and coming to be in a body, as we say soul comes to be in a body, is giving something of itself to it, not becoming its; and departing is the body's having no communion with it at all. And there is an order of such communion for the parts of this All; and soul, being as it were at the last place of the intelligible, gives of itself more often, since it is near in power, and at shorter intervals, by the law of such a nature.
!flag will give forth freely to body | The Greek says soul at the last place of the intelligible gives of itself "more often" (πλεονάκις), "at shorter intervals" (ἐν βραχυτέροις διαστήμασι), not freely.
!note Soul as the last of the intelligible, at its border with the perceptible: IV.8.7. The law of descents in their times: IV.3.12-13.

@p
@greek κακὸν δὲ εἶναι
And such communion is bad, and the release good. Why? Because, even if it is not this body's, still, called the soul of this, it becomes in some way partial, out of the whole. For its act is no longer toward the whole, though it is of the whole: as if, when the science is whole, the knower were to act by some one theorem; whereas his good was not in some part of the science, but in all of it that he has.
!flag a soul in any way to be described as attached to this universe | The Greek says "a soul called this one's" (ψυχὴ τοῦδε λεγομένη), the soul of one body; not of this universe, whose soul does not become partial.
!note The release (ἀπαλλαγή) of soul from body: Plato's Phaedo (64c, 67a-d). The theorem and the whole science: IV.9.5.

@p
@greek καὶ τοίνυν αὕτη τοῦ παντὸς
And so this soul, being of the whole intelligible world, and hiding its part in the whole, has, as it were, leapt out of the whole into a part, into which it shuts itself, being a part: as if a fire that could burn everything were made to burn some small thing, though it has all its power. For soul, when it is wholly apart, is each and not each; but when it is set apart, not by place but by act, and becomes the individual, it is a portion, not all, though even so it is all in another way. And when it presides over nothing, it is wholly all, being a part then as it were potentially.
!flag it is perfectly the All-Soul, the partial in it latent | The Greek says it is "wholly all" (πάντη πᾶσα), "being a part then as it were potentially"; "All-Soul" is MacKenna's, and the soul of the All is not what is meant.
!note Souls leap from the whole into a part, and are kept there: IV.8.4.

@p
@greek τὸ δὲ εἰς ᾅδου
As for coming to be in Hades: if it means in the unseen, it is its being apart that is meant; if some worse place, what is surprising? Since even now, where our body is and in what place it is, soul too is said to be there. But when the body no longer is? Rather, if the image is not torn away, how is soul not there where the image is? But if philosophy has set it wholly free, the image might go off alone to the worse place, while soul itself is purely in the intelligible, with nothing of it taken out.
!flag the authentic passing uncontaminated into the Intellectual | The Greek says soul is "purely in the intelligible" (καθαρῶς ἐν τῷ νοητῷ); the modern version keeps "intelligible" for νοητός.
!note Hades (ᾅδης) and the unseen (ἀιδής): Plato's Phaedo (80d), Gorgias (493b) and Cratylus (403a). Heracles' image in Hades while he is with the gods: Odyssey XI (601-604), read in I.1.12 and IV.3.27.

@p
@greek τὸ μὲν οὖν ἐκ τοῦ τοιοῦδε
So much for the image that has come to be from such a thing. But when soul itself shines, as it were, toward itself, the image, by the inclination to the other side, is drawn together toward the whole, and is not in act, nor yet has it perished. But so much about these things; let us take up again the argument from the beginning, and speak.
!flag chooses the higher and by that choice blends into the All | The Greek has "inclination" (νεῦσις) "to the other side", and the image is "drawn together toward the whole" (πρὸς τὸ ὅλον συνέσταλται); there is no choice.
!note The argument taken up again from the beginning is VI.5, the treatise's second part.

# VI.5 (milestone E28): MacKenna's own English (vol. V, 1930, pp. 125-137).

@treatise VI.5 | That being, one and the same, is everywhere whole, second part
The twenty-third treatise in the order of writing, and the second of the two On that being, one and the same, is everywhere whole; VI.4, the twenty-second, is its first part, and ends by saying that the argument must be "taken up again from the beginning". Porphyry counts both among the first Plotinus wrote in the six years Porphyry was with him (Life 5). Plotinus starts from a common notion: all men, moved by nature, speak of the god in each of us as one and the same, and this is the surest principle of all, older even than that all things desire the good. Reasoning that borrows its principles from bodies divides being; the argument about being must take principles proper to being, which stays in itself, in no place, and in which the other things share as far as they can. The god present everywhere, the unlimited that never fails, the firsts, seconds and thirds of the intelligible as one sphere hung from one centre, and the centres with their lines show the one in many: the lines do not make the many centres but show them. Man in matter is stamped from one Man like a seal; matter shares in the form of fire without the form leaving itself; one life holds the sphere of the elements, so that all souls are one. Being stays in itself in its right mind, and the other things hang from it, like Love who sleeps at the door; wisdom is common, as in an assembly, and we touch the same good, not streams from it. Time beside eternity, a line circling a point, shows how what is extended runs beside a power that has no extent. Last, the All is present to whoever lets go of the "so much" he added to himself: it did not come; we went away, and turned to the contrary, while the cities, earth and heaven turn to it.

@ch VI.5.1 | The god in each of us is one
A common notion says that what is one and the same is everywhere whole: all men speak of the god in each of us as one and the same. This is the surest principle, older even than that all things desire the good, for that is true only if all things hasten to one. The good of each is to be its own, to be one; so it is not to be sought outside being. We are in being, and it is not apart from us: all beings are one.

@p
That what is one and the same in number is everywhere at once whole, a common notion says, when all men, moved by their nature, speak of the god in each of us as one and the same. And if no one asked them how, and no one wished to examine their opinion by reasoning, they would lay it down so, and, active in their thought in this way, would come to rest, leaning together on what is one and the same, and they would not wish to be split off from this oneness. And this is the surest principle of all, which our souls, as it were, cry out: not summed up from the particulars, but come before all the particulars, and before that principle which lays down and says that all things desire the good. For that would be true if all things hasten to one, and are one, and the desire is for this one.
!flag It would be taken as certain if no one asked How | The Greek says that if no one demanded the how of them (τὸν τρόπον), they would lay it down so and rest in it: what is in question is how they hold it, not whether it would be certain.
!flag for this universal quest of good depends on the fact that all aim at unity | The Greek says the principle that all things desire the good "would be true if" (οὕτω γὰρ ἂν αὕτη ἀληθὴς εἴη, εἰ) all things hasten to one: a condition of its truth, not a fact it depends on.
!note A "common notion" (κοινὴ ἔννοια) is a notion all men have by nature, the Stoics' word for the starting points of knowledge. The god in each of us: Plato's Timaeus (90a), where the highest kind of soul is the daemon god gave each of us.
!note That all things desire the good is the first sentence of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (I.1, 1094a2-3), and Plato's Philebus (20d): everything that knows the good hunts it and wants to take hold of it.

@p
@greek τὸ γὰρ ἓν τοῦτο προιὸν
For this one, going forth to the other side, as far as it can go forth, would appear many, and in a way would be many; but the ancient nature, and the desire of the good, which is itself, leads to what is really one, and every nature hastens to this, to itself. For this is the good for this one nature: to be its own and to be itself; and this is to be one.
!flag towards the Other Order must become manifest as multiplicity | The Greek has "to the other side" (ἐπὶ θάτερα), toward what is other; "the Other Order" is MacKenna's.
!flag to this every form of Being is urged in a movement towards its own reality | The Greek says "every nature hastens to this, to itself" (ἐφ' ἑαυτήν): the good of each nature is itself, and "form of Being" and "reality" are MacKenna's.

@p
@greek οὕτω δὲ καὶ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ὀρθῶς
And in this way the good too would rightly be called one's own; so one must not look for it outside. For where would it be, fallen outside being? Or how could anyone find it in non-being? Plainly it is in being, since it is not itself non-being. And if it is being, and in being, it would be in itself, in each. We have not, then, stood away from being, but we are in it; nor, again, has it stood away from us. All beings, then, are one.
!flag In virtue of that unity the Good may be regarded as truly inherent | The Greek says the good would rightly be called "one's own" (οἰκεῖον): what belongs to each, not what is inherent in it.
!flag yet that Good is not exclusively ours | The Greek says "nor again has it [stood away] from us" (οὐδ' αὖ ἐκεῖνο ἡμῶν): we are not apart from being, and it is not apart from us; nothing is said of its not being ours alone.
!note "In being, since it is not itself non-being": the good as being, and being as one, is the theme of the whole treatise; the Good beyond being (Republic VI 509b) is not yet in view. The same argument from being and non-being opens VI.4.2.

@ch VI.5.2 | Principles proper to being
Reasoning that brings in the nature of bodies divides being, and does not believe in its oneness. The argument about being must take principles proper to it, intelligible ones. Becoming is borne about and parcelled out in place; being always is, stays in itself and is in no place. Of becoming we reason from likely things; of being, from its own nature, since the what-it-is is the principle, and with being everything is in its what-it-is.

@p
But reasoning, setting out to examine what is said, being not one thing but something divided, and bringing the nature of bodies into the inquiry and taking its principles from there, divided substance, thinking it to be such, and did not believe in its oneness, since it had not made the start of its search from the principles proper to it. But we must take, for the argument about what is one and wholly being, principles proper to persuading of it: that is, intelligible principles of intelligibles, which hold to the true substance.
!flag thus it thinks of the Essential Existence as corporeal and as a thing of parts | The Greek says reasoning "divided substance" (ἐμέρισε τὴν οὐσίαν), thinking it such as bodies are; "Essential Existence" is MacKenna's for οὐσία, and the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag we must hold to the Intellectual principles which alone apply to the Intellectual Order | The Greek has "intelligible principles of intelligibles" (νοητὰς νοητῶν); the modern version keeps "intelligible" for νοητός, and "which alone apply" is MacKenna's.
!note Reasoning (λόγος, in the sense of discursive thought, διάνοια) is "divided", because it goes from one thing to another; the error of borrowing principles from bodies is the one VI.4.2 opened with, setting being in the perceptible.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ γὰρ τὸ μέν ἐστι πεφορημένον
For there is, on the one hand, what is borne about, taking changes of every kind and parcelled out into every place, which it would be fitting to call becoming, not substance; and there is, on the other, being that always is, not parcelled out, holding the same way in the same respects, neither coming to be nor perishing, having no room or place or seat, neither going out from anywhere nor going into anything, but staying in itself. Speaking about the first, one would reason fittingly from that nature and what is thought of it, making likely reasonings through likely things.
!flag On the one hand there is the unstable | The Greek has "what is borne about" (πεφορημένον), carried this way and that, the world of becoming in motion.
!flag not so much Being as Becoming | The Greek says it would be fitting to call it "becoming, not substance" (γένεσιν ... ἀλλ' οὐκ οὐσίαν): not a matter of degree.
!note What always is and has no becoming, and what becomes and never is: Plato's Timaeus (27d-28a). "Having no room" (χώρα) recalls the Timaeus' receptacle (52a-b), in which becoming comes to be. Of becoming only a "likely account" can be given (Timaeus 29b-d), and here "likely reasonings through likely things" (εἰκότως δι' εἰκότων εἰκότας).

@p
@greek ὅταν δ’ αὖ τοὺς περὶ τὼν νοητῶν
But when someone makes arguments about the intelligibles, he would justly take the nature of the substance he is dealing with and make it the principle of his arguments, not straying aside, as if forgetful, to another nature, but making his study of it from it itself; since everywhere the what-it-is is the principle, and those who define well are said to know most of the accidents too. And with things in whose what-it-is everything belongs, one must all the more hold to this, look to this, and bring everything back to this.
!flag In every entity the essential nature is the governing principle | The Greek says "the what-it-is (τὸ τί ἐστιν) is the principle" (ἀρχή), the starting point of the argument; "governing" is MacKenna's.
!flag where the essential nature is the entire being | The Greek says "those in whose what-it-is everything belongs" (οἷς πάντα ἐν τῷ τί ἐστιν ὑπάρχει): things that have no accidents, whose all is their essence.
!note That a good definition makes known most of the accidents: Aristotle, On the soul I.1 (402b16-403a2), and the what-it-is as the principle of demonstration, Posterior Analytics II.3 (90b24-27) and Metaphysics Z.9 (1034a30-32).

@ch VI.5.3 | What stays in itself is in many
If being stays the same, does not go out of itself and is in no place, it must always be with itself, not part here and part there, nothing going out of it; for in another it would be affected. So it is in nothing, and the others share in it, as far as they can be present to it. Either we do away with such a nature, or we accept that the one and the same is whole, apart from nothing, with nothing poured or sent out of it; this argument is drawn from the thing itself.

@p
If, then, this real being holds the same way, and does not stand outside itself, and there is no becoming about it, and it was said not to be in place, it must, being so, always be with itself, and not stand apart from itself, nor have one part of it here and another there, nor anything go out from it: for then it would be in this and in that, and in general in something, and not by itself, nor unaffected; for it would be affected if it were in another, and if it is to be unaffected, it is not in another. If, then, without standing away from itself, without being divided, without undergoing any change at all, it were in many at once, being one whole together with itself, it would have, being the same everywhere with itself, its being in many: and this is to be by itself and again not to be by itself. It remains, then, to say that it is itself in nothing, but the other things share in it, as many as can be present to it, and as far as it is possible for them to be present to it.
!flag then it must be always self-gathered, never in separation | The Greek says it must "always be with itself" (σὺν αὑτῷ) and "not stand apart from itself" (μὴ διεστάναι ἀφ' αὑτοῦ).
!flag all that are apt and in the measure of their aptitude | The Greek says the other things share in it, "as many as can be present to it, and as far as it is possible for them to be present to it" (ὅσα δύναται αὐτῷ παρεῖναι): they are present to it, not it to them.
!note That the one is not in another, nor in itself, so as to be in nothing at all: Plato's Parmenides (138a-b); that a whole in many would be apart from itself is the difficulty of the Parmenides (131a-c), which VI.4.1 names.

@p
@greek ἀνάγκη τοίνυν ἢ τὰς ὑποθέσεις
So one must either do away with those hypotheses and principles, saying there is no such nature, or, if this is impossible and there is by necessity such a nature and substance, accept what was said at the start: that what is one and the same in number, not divided but whole, stands away from none of the other things beside it, needing neither to be poured out, nor for some portions to come from it, nor again for it to stay whole in itself while something else that has come from it, leaving it behind, comes to the other things in many places.
!flag something produced and projected from it enter at various points into that other order | The Greek says "something else that has come from it, leaving it behind" (γεγονὸς καταλελοιπὸς αὐτὸ), comes to "the other things" (εἰς τὰ ἄλλα); "projected" and "that other order" are MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἔσται τε γὰρ οὕτως τὸ μὲν ἄλλοθι
For so the one will be in one place and what has come from it in another, and it will have place, standing apart from what came from it. And again with those, whether each is whole or a part: if a part, it will not keep the nature of the whole, as has been said; if each is whole, either we shall divide each into parts equal to that in which it is, or we shall grant that the same can be whole everywhere. This argument, then, is drawn from the thing itself and its substance, dragging in nothing foreign, nothing from the other nature.
!flag Either would imply something of it remaining there while the emanant is elsewhere | The Greek has "what is from it" (τὸ ἀπ' αὐτοῦ) elsewhere; "emanant" is MacKenna's, a word Plotinus does not use here.
!flag anything belonging to the Other Order | The Greek has "from the other nature" (ἐκ τῆς ἑτέρας φύσεως), the nature of bodies of chapter 2.
!note The dilemma of whole and part, the one in many either divided or whole in each, is the Parmenides' (131a-e); VI.4.8 and VI.4.13 meet it with powers and with the two-cubit thing.

@ch VI.5.4 | The god everywhere, and the firsts, seconds and thirds
All who have a notion of gods say they are everywhere, and reason agrees. Divided, a god would no longer be one, nor everywhere, and would be a body; so every man, in believing in god, already holds that the same is everywhere whole. And the unlimited is what never fails, present to each. What comes after the one is with it and about it, so that whatever shares in what comes after shares in it: the firsts, seconds and thirds of the intelligible are like one sphere hung from one centre.

@p
See too, if you like, this god: we do not say that he is here and not there. For all who have a notion of gods think it right to say, not only of him but of all the gods, that they are present everywhere, and reason says that it must be laid down so.
!flag Then consider this god (in man) | The words "in man" are MacKenna's: the Greek has only "this god" (τόνδε τὸν θεόν), which may be the god in each of us of chapter 1, or the god of this visible world.
!flag All that have insight into the nature of the divine beings | The Greek says "all who have a notion (ἔννοιαν) of gods": the common notion of chapter 1 again, not an insight into their nature.
!note The gods present everywhere: Plato's Laws X (899b), "all things are full of gods", the saying of Thales (Aristotle, On the soul I.5, 411a8).

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν πανταχοῦ, οὐχ οἷόν τε
If, then, he is everywhere, he cannot be divided; for then he would no longer himself be everywhere, but each part of him would be here or there, and he himself would no longer be one: as if a magnitude were cut into many, it will perish, and its parts will all no longer be that whole. And besides, he will be a body.
!flag just as a mass cut up ceases to be a mass | The Greek says a magnitude cut into many "will perish" (ἀπολλύμενον), and its parts are "no longer that whole": what is lost is the whole, not the mass.

@p
@greek εἰ δὴ ταῦτα ἀδύνατα
If this is impossible, then again what is disbelieved has shown itself in every human nature, together with thinking there is a god: that the same is everywhere at once whole. Again, if we call that nature unlimited, for surely it is not limited, what else would this mean but that it will not fail? And if it will not fail, it is because it is present to each. For if it cannot be present, it will fail, and there will be somewhere where it is not.
!flag holding the god to pervade the Being of man, we hold the omnipresence of an integral identity | The Greek says the disbelieved doctrine "has shown itself in every human nature, together with thinking there is a god" (ἐν πάσῃ φύσει ἀνθρώπου ὁμοῦ τῷ θεὸν νομίζειν): every man who believes in a god already holds it; nothing is said of the god pervading man's being.
!note The unlimited (ἄπειρον) here is not the indefinite of matter but what never fails, as in VI.4.4 and VI.5.9: the one "unlimited by having no magnitude" of chapter 12.

@p
@greek καὶ γὰρ εἰ λέγοιμεν ἄλλο
For even if we were to speak of something else after the one itself, what comes after it is again together with it, about it and toward it, and as it were its offspring, joined to it, so that whatever shares in what comes after it has shared in it too. For since there are many things in the intelligible, firsts and seconds and thirds, hung, as it were, from one centre of one sphere, not parted by intervals but all together with one another, wherever the thirds are present, the seconds and firsts are present too.
!flag any third will be about that second and move towards it | The Greek speaks of the second only: what comes after the one is "about it and toward it" (περὶ ἐκεῖνο καὶ εἰς ἐκεῖνο), and is like its offspring; the thirds come only in the next sentence.
!flag where, therefore, the Intellectual tertiaries are present | The Greek has "wherever the thirds are present" (τὰ τρίτα), the thirds of the intelligible; the modern version keeps "intelligible", and "tertiaries" is MacKenna's.
!note The firsts, seconds and thirds: Plato's Second Letter (312e), "about the king of all are all things ... second about the second, and third about the third", which Plotinus reads as the One, intellect and soul (V.1.8).

@ch VI.5.5 | The centre and the lines
For clearness the account draws many lines from one centre, to show the many that have come to be; but they must be kept together. Where there is no extension, all are centres united in one centre, as if the lines were let go. Add the lines, and each centre is joined to its line yet not cut off from the first centre; the centres seem as many as the lines. The lines do not make the centres but show them: they stand for the things that the intelligible touches and so appears many.

@p
For clearness' sake, the account often draws many lines as if from one centre, wishing to lead us to a notion of the multitude that has come to be. But we must say that the things called many have come to be while keeping them all together, as there too, in the circle, one cannot take the lines as marked off, for the plane is one. And where there is not even one extension, as on a plane, but powers and substances without extension, all things might fittingly be said to be centres, united together in one centre, as if they had let go of their lines, the ends of them that lie at the centre; and then all are one.
!flag but while we provide for individualisation we must carefully preserve mutual presence | The Greek says that, "keeping them all together" (τηροῦντας ὁμοῦ πάντα), we must say that the things called many "have come to be"; "individualisation" and "mutual presence" are MacKenna's.
!flag all is power and reality undifferentiated | The Greek has "powers and substances without extension" (ἀδιάστατοι δυνάμεις καὶ οὐσίαι): what they lack is extension, not difference.
!note The centre and the circle as an image of the intelligible: VI.8.18, VI.9.8 and IV.2.1. A centre, being without parts, is one even when many lines meet in it.

@p
@greek πάλιν δέ, εἰ προσθείης τὰς γραμμάς
Again, if you were to add the lines, they will each fasten on the centres that each left behind, yet each centre will be none the less not cut off from the one first centre, but each will be together with it, and they will be as many as the lines to which they gave themselves as ends; so that they appear as many as the lines they touch, but all of them are one together.
!flag once more we have lines, each touching a generating centre of its own | The Greek says the lines "will fasten on the centres that each left" (ἐξάψονται τῶν κέντρων αὑτῶν ἃ κατέλιπον ἑκάστη); "generating" is MacKenna's, and the next paragraph denies that the lines generate the centres.

@p
@greek εἰ δ’ οὖν κέντροις πολλοῖς
If, then, we have likened all the intelligibles to many centres brought back to one centre and united, but appearing many because of the lines, the lines not begetting them but showing them, let the lines serve us for the present as analogous to the things which the intelligible nature touches, and so appears to be many and present in many places.
!flag The radii, thus, afford a serviceable illustration for the mode of contact by which the Intellectual Unity manifests itself | The Greek says the lines are analogous to "the things which the intelligible nature touches" (ὧν ἐφαπτομένη ἡ νοητὴ φύσις): the lines stand for the bodies that receive it, not for a mode of contact.

@ch VI.5.6 | Man in many, and the many in Man
The intelligibles are many and one, and act toward whole and part with the whole. The part takes the act first as a part, and the whole follows, as Man coming into some man becomes some man while still Man. The man in matter is one Man stamped in many like a seal; but Man itself, and the All, are not in the many: the many are in it, or about it, as soul is the same in every part of the body.

@p
For the intelligibles, being many, are one, and, being one, are many by their unlimited nature: many in one and one over many, and all together; and it acts toward the whole with the whole, and toward the part again with the whole. The part takes into itself the first act, as of a part, but the whole follows: as if Man, coming into some man, were to become some man while being still Man.
!flag Thus, when Man enters into human form there exists a particular man | The Greek says Man comes "into some man" (εἰς τόν τινα ἄνθρωπον), the particular man, and becomes some man (τὶς ἄνθρωπος): there is no human form for it to enter.
!note "One over many" (ἓν ἐπὶ πολλοῖς) is the old phrase for the form, set over the many things named after it: Plato's Republic X (596a) and Aristotle's Metaphysics A.9 (990b7-8).

@p
@greek ὁ μὲν οὖν ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ
The man in matter, then, from the one Man of the idea, has made many men who are the same; and one same thing is in many in this way, that it is one thing, as it were stamped like a seal in many.
!flag material man has come to constitute many individual men | The Greek says the man in matter, from the one Man of the idea, "made many men the same" (πολλοὺς ἐποίησε τοὺς αὐτοὺς ἀνθρώπους): the form in matter makes them the same, it does not compose them.
!note The seal and the wax: Plato's Theaetetus (191c-d) and Timaeus (50c), where the things that come into the receptacle are "impressions" (τυπωθέντα) of what always is; Aristotle's On the soul II.12 (424a17-21).

@p
@greek αὐτὸ δὲ ἄνθρωπος καὶ αὐτὸ ἕκαστον
But Man itself, and each thing itself, and the whole All, are not in many in this way; rather the many are in it, or rather about it. For the white is everywhere in one way, and the soul of each is the same in every part of the body in another; and it is in this way that being too is everywhere.
!flag This does not mean that Man Absolute, or any Absolute, or the Universe in the sense of a Whole, is absorbed by multiplicity | The Greek says they are "not in many in this way" (οὐχ οὕτως ἐν πολλοῖς), but the many are "in it, or rather about it" (περὶ αὐτό); nothing is absorbed.
!flag There is a difference between the mode in which a colour may be absorbed by a substance entire | The Greek has "the white is everywhere" (τὸ λευκὸν πανταχοῦ) in one way: the white in each part is the same in form, as in VI.4.1, not absorbed.
!note The white the same in form but not in number, and soul the same in number in foot and hand: VI.4.1.

@ch VI.5.7 | We are those things; the many faces
What is ours and we ourselves go up to being and think the intelligibles without images; sharing in true knowledge, we are those things, being in them. Since the others are too, all of us are one. Looking outside, we do not know it, like many faces with one crown turned inward. Whoever could turn round, by himself or pulled by Athena, would see God, himself and the All, and, ceasing to mark himself off, would come to the All without going anywhere.

@p
For what is ours, and we ourselves, are brought back to being, and we go up to it and to what first comes from it, and we think those things, having not images or impressions of them; and if not this, it is because we are those things. If, then, we share in true knowledge, we are those things, not taking them into ourselves, but being ourselves in them. And since the others too, not only we, are those things, we all are those things. So, being together with all, we are those things: we are all, then, one.
!flag to that we return as from that we came | The Greek says "we go up to it, and to what first comes from it" (τὸ πρῶτον ἀπ' ἐκείνου): nothing is said here of whence we came.
!flag and to know without image is to be | The Greek says only "and if not this, being those things" (εἰ δὲ μὴ τοῦτο, ὄντες ἐκεῖνα): if we think them without images, it is because we are them.
!note That intellect does not have images or impressions (τύποι) of the intelligibles, but is them: V.5.1-2 and V.3.5. True knowledge is of what really is: Plato's Republic V (477a-478a).

@p
@greek ἔξω μὲν οὖν ὁρῶντες
Looking outside, then, or away from where we are fastened, we do not know that we are one: like many faces that face outward, with one crown of the head turned inward. But if someone could turn round, either by himself or having the luck of being pulled by Athena herself, he will see God and himself and the All. He will not see them at first as the All, but then, having nowhere to set himself and mark off how far he himself goes, he will stop drawing a line round himself to part himself from all being, and will come to the whole All, going forward nowhere, but staying there where the All is founded.
!flag looking outward we see many faces ; look inward and all is the one head | The Greek says we are "like many faces" (οἷον πρόσωπα πολλά), outward, "having one crown inward": the faces are ours, a head with many faces, not what we see.
!flag we cease to rule ourselves out from the total of reality | The Greek says he will stop "drawing a line round himself" (περιγράφειν αὑτόν) to part himself "from all being" (ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄντος ἅπαντος).
!note Athena pulls Achilles back by his hair, seen by him alone (Iliad I 194-200), the same scene that VI.5.12 recalls; the turn (ἐπιστροφή) is the soul's turning back to what it comes from.

@ch VI.5.8 | How matter shares in the form of fire
Looking at how matter shares in the forms makes the doctrine easier to believe: the forms do not lie apart with matter far off, or sharing would not be the hardest thing to tell. Illumination is said only because the things in matter are images of archetypes. Matter touches the idea everywhere and takes what it can, the idea staying in itself; the idea of fire, not coming into matter, gives the shape of fire to all of it. One idea shapes all fire, not one part this and another that; many ideas of fire would be absurd.

@p
For my part I think that if anyone were to look into matter's sharing in the forms, he would come more to believe what is said, and would no longer disbelieve it as impossible, or be at a loss again. For it is reasonable, I think, and necessary, that the illumination has come into matter, as if from somewhere far off and above, without the forms lying apart and matter far away; let what is said not be empty. For what would the far and the apart be in these things?
!flag a meaningless conception, for what have distance and separation to do here | The Greek says it is reasonable and necessary that the illumination has come into matter, "the forms not lying apart" (μὴ κειμένων τῶν εἰδῶν χωρίς), lest the word be said emptily: the illumination is kept, without forms lying apart; it is not called meaningless.

@p
@greek καὶ οὐκ ἂν τὸ δύσφραστον
And then sharing would not have been called the thing hardest to tell and most perplexing, but it would have been said most readily, being well known from its patterns. But even if we sometimes say illumination, we shall not mean it as we speak of illuminations of a perceptible thing into a perceptible; but since the things in matter are images, and the forms have the rank of archetypes, and illumination is such as to have what is illuminated apart, we say it so.
!flag This participation cannot be thought of as elusive or very perplexing ; on the contrary, it is obvious, accessible in many examples. | The Greek is unreal: if the forms lay apart, sharing "would not have been" called the hardest thing to tell and most perplexing, but would have been said readily, known from examples (παραδείγμασιν). It was called so, and it is hard: MacKenna has turned it into the claim that it is obvious.
!note Plato's Timaeus (50c) says the things that come into the receptacle are stamped from the beings "in a way hard to tell and wonderful" (τρόπον τινὰ δύσφραστον καὶ θαυμαστόν), and that it shares in the intelligible "in a most perplexing way" (ἀπορώτατά πῃ, 51a-b). The "patterns" (παραδείγματα) here are the examples one would have pointed to.

@p
@greek δεῖ δὲ νῦν ἀκριβέστερον
But now, speaking more exactly, we must not lay it down that the form is apart in place and then the idea is seen in matter as in water; but that matter, touching the idea from every side and again not touching it, has from the form, in every part of itself, by its nearness, as much as it can take, with nothing between, the idea not going through all of it and running over it, but staying in itself.
!flag the Idea itself not penetrating, not approaching, the Matter | The Greek says the idea is "not going through all of it and running over it" (οὐ ... διεξελθούσης καὶ ἐπιδραμούσης); "not approaching" is MacKenna's, and matter takes what it can "by its nearness" (τῷ πλησιασμῷ).
!note The image in water is the one that VI.4.10 weighed; matter as a mirror, in which the forms appear without being in it: III.6.7, III.6.13.

@p
@greek εἰ γὰρ μὴ ἐν τῇ ὕλῃ ἐστὶν οἷον
For if the idea of fire, say, is not in matter (let the argument take the matter that underlies the elements), fire itself, not coming to be in matter, will give the shape of fire through all the matter that has been set on fire. Let the first fire in matter be supposed to have come to be a great mass. The same argument will fit the other so-called elements too.
!flag The Ideal Fire, then, remaining apart | The Greek says "fire itself, not coming to be in the matter" (αὐτὸ δὴ πῦρ οὐκ ἐγγενόμενον αὐτὸ τῇ ὕλῃ); "remaining apart" is what the chapter denies, since the form is not apart in place.
!note Fire itself, and whether there is a form of fire: Plato's Timaeus (51b-e). The "so-called elements" (τὰ λεγόμενα στοιχεῖα): the Timaeus (48b-c) says fire and the rest are not even syllables, let alone letters.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν τὸ ἓν ἐκεῖνο πῦρ
If, then, that one fire is seen in all, giving an image of itself, and is not apart in place, it will not give it as the illumination we see does: for then all this fire in perception would be somewhere, if all of it were many of itself, while the idea itself stays in what has no place, having itself begotten places out of itself; since what is the same, become many, would have had to flee from itself, so as to be many in this way and share many times in the same.
!flag supposing that it were a whole of parts (as the analogy would necessitate) | The parenthesis is MacKenna's; the Greek says only "if all of it were many of itself" (εἰ πᾶν αὐτὸ πολλὰ εἴη ἑαυτοῦ).
!note The illumination we see is sunlight, which goes from a source in one place to things in other places; the form of fire has no place to send from.

@p
@greek καὶ οὐκ ἔδωκε μὲν ἑαυτῆς
And the idea, being unscattered, gave nothing of itself to matter; yet it was not unable, being one, to shape what is not one with its oneness, and to be present to all of it in such a way as not to shape this with one part of itself and that with another, but each and all with all of itself. For it would be absurd to bring in many ideas of fire, so that each fire should be shaped by another idea: so the ideas would be unlimited. Then, how will you divide the fires that come to be, fire being continuous and one? And if we added another fire to this matter, making it greater, we must say that the same idea has done the same things in that part of matter too; for surely not another.
!flag The Idea, impartible, gives nothing of itself to the Matter | The Greek has "unscattered" (ἀσκέδαστος): the idea is not dispersed over matter; "impartible" is MacKenna's.
!flag bringing it to pattern not by acting part upon part | The Greek has "to shape" (μορφῶσαι) "each and all with all of itself" (παντὶ ἕκαστον καὶ πᾶν): it shapes each with the whole of itself.
!note That one form is enough, and two would call for a third behind them: Plato's Republic X (597c) on the one bed, and the Parmenides' regress (132a-b).

@ch VI.5.9 | One maker of the sphere, one life, one soul
If the elements are brought in thought into one sphere, it is not made by many, each cutting off a part, but by one cause without parts, the sphere hung from it. One life holds it, and all souls are one, and unlimited. Some called soul a number, some a self-increasing number, because it fails nothing; but the increase is its never failing to be everywhere. The true one is neither composed nor bounded; it has multitude in its power from itself, is held in by one forming principle that it is itself, and stays in its own seat, which the things in place rest on.

@p
And so, if someone were to bring in thought all the elements, once they have come to be, into one spherical shape, one must not say that many make the sphere part by part, each cutting off a part for himself to make, but that the cause of the making is one, making with the whole of itself, not with one part of it making one thing and another another: for so there would again be many, unless you brought the making back to one without parts, or rather unless what makes the sphere were one without parts, not itself poured out into the sphere, but the whole sphere hung from what makes it. And so one life, the same, holds the sphere, the sphere in turn set in one life; and all the things in the sphere go back into one life; and all the souls, then, are one, but one in such a way as to be unlimited too.
!flag or, more precisely, the making principle must be a partless unity not permeating the sphere | The Greek says what makes the sphere is "not poured out into the sphere" (οὐκ αὐτοῦ χυθέντος εἰς τὴν σφαῖραν), but the sphere is "hung from" it (ἀνηρτημένης): it is not spread through it.
!note The world as one sphere made by one maker, with one soul set in its middle and stretched through it: Plato's Timaeus (33b, 34b). That all souls are one: IV.9.

@p
@greek διὸ καὶ οἱ μὲν ἀριθμὸν ἔλεγον
That is why some called it a number, and others said its nature was a number that increases itself, imagining this perhaps, that it fails nothing but reaches to all, staying what it is, and that if the world were larger, its power would not fail to reach all of it too, or rather the world would be in all of it. We must take the "increasing", then, not as the word says, but in that, being one, it does not fail to be everywhere: for its oneness is such as not to be of the kind that is measured by how much; that belongs to another nature, which falsely claims the one, and appears one by sharing.
!flag while others think of it as in its nature a selfincreasing number | The Greek says others called its nature "a number increasing itself" (αὑτὸν αὔξοντα): Xenocrates' "number that moves itself", with "increasing" for "moving", which the next sentences say is not to be taken as the word says.
!flag the virtue of soul would still compass it | The Greek has "power" (δύναμις), not virtue; MacKenna's "virtue" is the older English sense of power.
!note Xenocrates defined soul as a number that moves itself (ἀριθμὸς αὑτὸν κινῶν): Aristotle, On the soul I.2 (404b27-30) and I.4 (408b32-409a3). Plotinus reads the self-moving as self-increasing, and so as never failing.

@p
@greek τὸ δ’ ἀληθείας ἐχόμενον ἓν
But the one that holds to truth is such as neither to be composed of many, lest, if something were taken from it, that whole one should have perished, nor to be marked off by limits, lest, when the other things are fitted to it, it should either be made less, if they are greater, or be torn apart, wishing to go to all; and be present not whole to all, but by parts of itself to parts of them, and, as the saying goes, not know where on earth it is, unable to go to any one completion, being torn apart from itself.
!flag dismembered, it no longer performs any one single function | The Greek says it would be "unable to go to any one completion" (εἰς μίαν τινὰ συντέλειαν), one whole brought together, not a function.
!note "Not to know where on earth it is" (ἀγνοεῖν ὅπου γῆς ἐστιν) is a proverb for being utterly lost; Plato's Theaetetus (174b) has the philosopher who does not know what his neighbour is doing, nor whether he is a man.

@p
@greek εἴπερ οὖν ἀληθεύσει τὸ ἓν τοῦτο
If, then, this one is to be truly one, this of which one can predicate one as its substance, it must appear in a way to have the nature contrary to itself, that of multitude, in its power; and by having this multitude not from outside but from itself and out of itself, by this it is really one, and in the one it has being unlimited and multitude. And being such, it appears whole everywhere, having one forming principle that holds itself in, and being itself what holds it in, nowhere standing away from itself, but being in itself everywhere.
!flag this, as encircled by a single self-embracing Reason-Principle | The Greek says it has "one forming principle (λόγον) holding itself in" and is "itself what holds it in" (τὸν περιέχοντα αὐτὸν εἶναι): it is not encircled by something else. "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's for λόγος.
!flag but over all the universe remaining what it must be | The Greek says "being in itself everywhere" (ἐν αὑτῷ πανταχοῦ ὄντα); "the universe" is MacKenna's.
!note The one being that has multitude in it, the one of the Parmenides' second hypothesis (142b-145a), which is many by its parts and unlimited in number.

@p
@greek οὐ δή ἐστιν αὐτὸ οὕτως ἄλλου
It is not, then, parted in this way by the place of another: for it was before all things in place, and needed none of them, but they needed it, to be founded. And once they were founded, it did not stand away from its own seat in itself: for if that were moved, they would perish, their base and what supports them perishing; nor again was it so senseless as to leave itself and be torn apart, and, though kept safe in itself, to give itself to place, which cannot be trusted and needs it to be kept safe.
