!flag The unity is in this way saved from the local division of the things in which it appears | The Greek says only "it is not, then, parted in this way by the place of another" (ἄλλου τόπῳ διειλημμένον).
!note Being as the seat (ἕδρα) and base of what is in place: VI.4.2, where the world rests on the true All.

@ch VI.5.10 | Love at the door; one wisdom, one good
Being stays in itself, in its right mind; the other things hang from it, like Love who sleeps at the door, content to share as he can. Its many lovers have it whole, and it suffices for all because it stays. Wisdom too is common and whole to all, as an assembly finds wisdom by coming together; we touch the same good, not streams from it, for the giving there is not by sending. There is one world there, else there would be two perceptible worlds; and nothing crowds it, as the sciences do not crowd the soul.

@p
It stays, then, in itself, self-controlled, in its right mind, and could not come to be in another; but those other things hang from it, as if they had found by longing where it is. And this is Love who sleeps out at the door, present always from outside, aiming at the beautiful and always content to share in it in this way, as far as he can. For the lover here too is like this, not taking the beauty in, but lying beside it. But it stays by itself.
!flag It remains, then, poised in wisdom within itself | The Greek has "self-controlled" (σωφρονοῦν), in its right mind, against the senseless (ἀνόητον) of the last sentence; "wisdom" is the φρονεῖν of the next lines.
!flag happy when to the utmost of its power it attains | The Greek says Love is "always content" (ἀγαπῶν ἀεί) to share "as far as he can"; nothing is said of attaining.
!note Love "sleeping in doorways and on roads", always in need: Plato's Symposium (203c-d), where θυραυλῶν, "living out at the door", is said of him. In III.5.9 Plotinus reads him as soul's desire.

@p
@greek καὶ οἱ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἐρασταὶ
And the many lovers of the one, loving it whole, have it whole in this way, when they have it; for it was the whole that was loved. How, then, would it not suffice for all, staying as it is? Indeed it suffices for this reason, that it stays, and it is beautiful because it is whole to all. For wisdom too is whole to all: which is why wisdom is common, not some here and some there; for it would be absurd if wisdom were to need place. And wisdom is not like the white, for wisdom is not of a body; but if we really share in wisdom, it must be one, all of it together with itself in the same. And so from there, not taking portions of it, nor I a whole and you a whole, each torn from the other.
!flag because it is thus entire for all it can be The Good to all | The Greek says "and beautiful, because it is whole to all" (καὶ καλόν, ὅτι πᾶσιν ὅλον): it is the beautiful, not the Good.
!flag So must it be in our participation in the One | The Greek says only "and so from there" (καὶ οὕτως ἐκεῖθεν): the One is not named.
!note "Wisdom is common" (ξυνὸν τὸ φρονεῖν): Heraclitus, "thinking is common to all" (ξυνόν ἐστι πᾶσι τὸ φρονέειν, fragment B113).

@p
@greek μιμοῦνται δὲ καὶ ἐκκλησίαι
Assemblies and every gathering imitate this, as men who go to one in wisdom: each apart is weak in wisdom, but each, putting it together into one, has begotten and found wisdom in the gathering and in true understanding. For what will hold intellect apart, so that it is not in the same, one from one man and another from another? But being together, they seem to us not to be together: as if someone, touching the same thing with many fingers, were to think he touched one thing and another, or struck the same string without seeing it. And yet we ought to have kept in mind how we touch the good with our souls too.
!flag the road to sense is the road to unity | MacKenna's; the Greek says only that assemblies imitate it, "as men who go to one in wisdom" (ὡς εἰς ἓν τῷ φρονεῖν ἰόντων).
!flag as they begin to grow together, each, in that true growth, generates wisdom while he recognises it | The Greek says each, "putting it together into one" (συμβάλλων δὲ εἰς ἕν), in "the gathering and the true understanding" (τῇ συνόδῳ καὶ τῇ ὡς ἀληθῶς συνέσει), has begotten and found wisdom: the word plays on coming together (σύνοδος) and understanding (σύνεσις), and there is no growth.
!note That the many, coming together, may judge better than the few best: Aristotle, Politics III.11 (1281a42-b10). One string struck with many fingers: the same is touched, though the touches are many.

@p
@greek οὐ γὰρ ἄλλου μὲν ἐγώ
For it is not that I touch one thing and you another, but the same; nor is it the same, with one stream from there coming to me and another to you, so that it is somewhere above and what comes from it here. And the giver gives to those who take, so that they really take; and the giver gives not to strangers, but to its own. For the giving of intellect is not by sending. Since even with bodies set apart from one another in place, the giving of one to another is to its kin, and the giving and the making go to the same; and the bodily part of the All acts and is acted on in itself, and nothing comes into it from outside. If, then, with body, which by nature, as it were, flees from itself, nothing is from outside, how could anything be from outside with a thing that has no extension?
!flag in any real receiving of good, giver is in contact with taker | The Greek says "the giver gives to those who take, so that they really take" (ἵνα ὄντως λαμβάνωσι); nothing is said of contact.
!flag Now if in body, whose very nature is partition | The Greek says body by nature "as it were flees from itself" (οἷον φεύγοντος ἑαυτό), its parts outside one another.
!note That the All acts on itself and is acted on by itself, nothing coming from outside: Plato's Timaeus (33c-d). Sympathy among the parts of the All: IV.4.32.

@p
@greek ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ἄρα ὄντες
Being in the same, then, we see the good and touch it, being together with our own intelligibles. And there is one world there, far more so; or else there will be two perceptible worlds, divided into like parts, and the intelligible sphere, if it is one in the way this one is, will differ in nothing; or it will be more absurd, if this one's bulk is reasonable, being by necessity, while that one, needing nothing, will stretch itself out and stand outside itself. And what hinders it from being one? The one surely does not push the other out by not giving it room; just as we see every lesson and theorem, and all the sciences in general, in the soul, not crowded. But someone will say this is not possible with substances. It would not have been possible, if the true substances were bulks.
!flag It is therefore by identification that we see the good | The Greek says "being in the same" (ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ ὄντες) we see the good and touch it.
!flag brought to it by becoming identical with what is of the Intellectual within ourselves | The Greek says "being together with our own intelligibles" (ὁμοῦ ὄντες τοῖς ἡμετέροις νοητοῖς); the modern version keeps "intelligible".
!flag except, indeed, that it will be less worthy of respect | The Greek has "more absurd" (γελοιοτέρα): an extended intelligible sphere would be laughable, not less respected.
!note The sciences many in one soul, without crowding: IV.9.5 and VI.4.4.

@ch VI.5.11 | Time beside eternity
How does what has no extension reach over all body? It is not like a stone, a great cube measured to its bulk and power, but a first nature, unmeasured, all power. So it is outside time: eternity stays and is greater than time, which is like a line that seems to go to infinity but is hung from a point and circles about it. Over against this unlimited power runs a nature hung from it, which shares in it as far as it can. It is present everywhere as the immaterial triangle, not as the triangles in matter, though not all matter takes all form.

@p
But how does what has no extension reach over beside every body, which has so great a size? And how is it not torn apart, being one and the same? This has often been raised as a difficulty, the argument wishing in its eagerness to stop the mind's perplexity about these things. Now it has already been shown in many ways that it is so; but some encouragements are needed too. And yet the strongest help to persuasion, not the least, was to be taught what that nature is: that it is not like a stone, a great cube, say, lying where it lies, taking up as much room as it is, unable to step beyond its own bounds, measured to so much both in its bulk and in the stone's power, which is bounded together with it in it; but, being a first nature, not measured nor marked off as to how great it must be, for so it would be measured by another, it is all power, nowhere of such a size.
!flag The fact stands abundantly evident but there is still the need of intellectual satisfaction | The Greek says "it has been shown in many ways that it is so; but some encouragements (παραμυθιῶν) are needed": consolations to persuade, not an intellectual satisfaction.
!flag It is a First Principle, measureless | The Greek has "a first nature" (πρώτη φύσις), not measured.
!note The encouragement (παραμυθία) that persuades where proof has been given: Plato's Phaedo (70b, 115d), where Socrates' arguments are called a consolation.

@p
@greek διὸ οὐδ’ ἐν χρόνῳ
So it is not in time either, but outside all time; time scatters itself always toward extension, while eternity stays in the same, holds the mastery, and is greater, by an everlasting power, than time, which seems to go over many things: like a line that seems to go to infinity, hung from a point and running about it, the point appearing in it wherever it runs, the point not running, but the line circling about it.
!flag Time is like a radial line running out apparently to infinity | The Greek says time is like a line that seems to go to infinity, "hung from a point and running about it" (περὶ αὐτὸ θεούσης) and "circling about it" (κυκλουμένης): a circle round a centre, not a radius running out.
!flag as it goes it tells of that centre | The Greek says the point "appears in it" (ἐμφανταζομένου) wherever it runs.
!note Time a moving image of eternity, which stays in one: Plato's Timaeus (37d). Plotinus' own treatise on eternity and time is III.7, where time is the life of soul spread out (III.7.11).

@p
@greek εἰ τοίνυν χρόνος πρὸς τὸ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ
If, then, time has its analogy toward what stays in the same in substance, and that nature is unlimited not only by being always but also in power, one must set over against this unlimitedness of power a nature that runs beside it, hanging opposite it and depending from it; this nature runs, as it were, equal to time, toward the power that stays, which is greater in making; and that power is present to as much as this nature has been stretched out. What, then, is this nature that shares in that nature as far as it can, that nature being present whole, but not seen whole in all, by the weakness of the underlying thing?
!flag This secondary of Power, participating as far as it may in that higher, must be identified. | The Greek asks a question, "what, then, is this nature that shares...?" (τίς οὖν αὕτη ἐστὶν ἡ μεταλαμβάνουσα), which the next sentence answers with what is in matter.
!note The nature that runs beside the unlimited power, as time beside eternity, is the extended world of body; its weakness to receive is the matter that underlies it.

@p
@greek πάρεστι δὲ ταὐτὸν πάντη
It is present the same everywhere, not as the triangle in matter, which is more than one in number in many things, though the same, but as the immaterial triangle itself, from which the ones in matter come too. Why, then, is there not a triangle in matter everywhere, if the immaterial is everywhere? Because not all matter has shared in it, but one matter has one thing, another another, and not all is fit for all; since not even the first matter, all of it, is fit for all, but for the first of the kinds, and then for others after these; yet it was present to all.
!flag though these, too, are omnipresent | The Greek says "yet it was present to all" (παρῆν μέντοι παντί): the immaterial is present to all matter, whatever it takes; it is not that the kinds are everywhere.
!note The first of the kinds and their triangles: the bodies of the four elements built from two triangles in Plato's Timaeus (53c-55c); matter takes the elements first and then the things made of them.

@ch VI.5.12 | Let go of the "so much"
It is present as one life, everywhere in the living thing: a power not of some quantity, unlimited from the depths, boiling over with life. You will not find it in one place or halt where it fails; you will run with it, or give up and fall, looking elsewhere. You came to the All by letting go of "I am so much": you were always all, but became less by an addition from non-being. It did not come; you went away, and turned to the contrary. So the gods appear to one among many; and the cities, earth and heaven turn to that one.

@p
How, then, is it present? As one life: for life in a living thing does not go only so far and then cannot reach to all of it; it is everywhere. And if someone asks again how, let him remember the power: that it is not of some quantity, but, though you divide it in thought to infinity, it always has the same power, unlimited from the depths; for it has no matter in it, so that it should fail along with the size of the bulk, coming to something small.
!flag To return : How is that Power present to the universe ? | The Greek says only "How, then, is it present?" (πάρεστιν οὖν πῶς;): "to return" and "the universe" are MacKenna's.
!flag we appeal to the character of this power | The Greek says "let him remember the power" (ἀναμνησθήτω τῆς δυνάμεως), what has been said of it in chapter 11.
!note "From the depths" (βυσσόθεν) is a poet's word; life whole in each part of the living body: VI.4.1 and IV.2.1.

@p
@greek ἐὰν οὖν λάβῃς ἀέναον
If, then, you grasp an ever-flowing unlimitedness in it, a nature untiring and unwearied and in no way falling short, boiling over, as it were, with life in itself, then, whether you fix on some place or gaze at some thing, you will not find it there; the contrary would happen to you. For you will not go past it and beyond, nor again halt at something small, as if it had nothing more to give by failing little by little; but either, able to run with it, or rather coming to be in the All, you will seek nothing more; or, giving up, you will turn aside to something else and fall, not seeing what is present because you look to something else.
!flag The contrary is your only way | The Greek says "the contrary would happen to you" (τοὐναντίον δ' ἄν σοι γένοιτο): instead of finding it in one place, you would find it everywhere; MacKenna makes it a way to take.
!flag denying it, you have strayed away to something of another order and you fall | The Greek has "giving up" (ἀπειπών), growing weary of the chase, and turning aside "to something else" (εἰς ἄλλο).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ οὐδὲν ἔτι ζητήσεις
But if you seek nothing more, how will you ever be persuaded of this? Because you went to all, and did not stay in a part of it, nor did you say, "I am so much"; letting go of the "so much", you have become all, though you were all before too. But because something else was added to you after the all, you became less by the addition: for the addition was not from being (you will add nothing to that), but from non-being. And one who has come to be also from non-being is not all, except when he lets go of non-being.
!flag how do you experience it | The Greek asks "how will you be persuaded of this?" (πῶς ποτε τοῦτο πείσῃ;): the question is of conviction, not of experience.
!flag you cease to think of yourself as under limit | The Greek says you did not say "I am so much" (τοσοῦτός εἰμι), and let go of "the so much" (τὸ τοσοῦτον).
!note The addition (προσθήκη) that makes us less is the second man of VI.4.14, who added himself to the man we were there.

@p
@greek αὔξεις τοίνυν σεαυτὸν
You increase yourself, then, by letting go of the other things, and the All is present to you once you have let go; but to you as you are with other things it does not appear. Nor did it come so as to be present; it is you who went away, when it is not present. And if you went away, it was not from it, for it is present, nor did you go anywhere; but, being present, you turned to the contrary.
!flag By the lessening of the alien in you, you increase | The Greek says "you increase yourself by letting go of the other things" (ἀφεὶς τὰ ἄλλα): the increase is the self-increasing number of chapter 9, and "the alien" is MacKenna's.
!note "Let go of everything" (ἄφελε πάντα) is the last word of V.3.17; and the soul that "goes away" without going anywhere: VI.9.7.

@p
@greek οὕτω γὰρ καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι
So too the other gods, though many are present, often appear to one alone, because that one alone can see. But these are the gods who, "taking all kinds of shapes, go about the cities"; but to that one the cities turn, and all the earth and all the heaven, staying everywhere on him and in him, and having from him their being and the things that really are, down to soul and life, hanging from him and going to one that is unlimited by having no magnitude.
!flag It is so with the lesser gods | The Greek has "the other gods" (οἱ ἄλλοι θεοί); "lesser" is MacKenna's.
!flag everywhere with God and in Him | The Greek says "on him and in him" (ἐπ' αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ), "that one" (ἐκεῖνον); the name "God" is MacKenna's.
!note "The gods, like strangers from abroad, taking all kinds of shapes, go about the cities": Homer, Odyssey XVII (485-487), quoted in Plato's Republic II (381d). A god seen by one alone: Athena, seen by Achilles only (Iliad I 197-198), as in chapter 7.

# VI.6 (milestone E29): MacKenna's own English (vol. V, 1930, pp. 138-162).

@treatise VI.6 | On numbers
The thirty-fourth treatise in the order of writing, one of those Plotinus wrote in the six years Porphyry was with him (Life 5). It begins by asking whether multitude is a standing away from the one, and the unlimited a complete standing away, and so an evil: each thing is most itself when it is one, and the All is great and beautiful only because it is held by one and by beauty. There is no unlimited number in the things or in counting; the unlimited itself flees limit and is caught from outside, neither moving nor at rest (chapters 1 to 3). Then the numbers in the intelligible: are they seen upon the forms, or are they before them? Plato's days and nights seem to make number the soul's counting, but his "true number" gives it a being of its own. The forms are not made by intellect's thinking them; justice is a statue in intellect; being, intellect and the complete living being come in that order, and number is before the living being and before intellect (chapters 4 to 8). Number divided being and made it in travail with multitude: being is number united, the beings number unrolled, intellect number moving in itself, the living being number that holds; this is the substantial number, and the number of units is its image. The beings are as many as they are by purpose, not by chance, and whatever is predicated of a thing came from another or is its activity (chapters 9 and 10). Against those who say the one and the decad are nothing, an affection of the soul or a relation, Plotinus argues that the one must be bare before each thing is called one, that thought finds it and does not make it, that without it nothing can be thought or said, and that a thing is one by the presence of the one and two by the dyad, as the Phaedo says (chapters 11 to 14). Number is before the living being, in intellect as its activities and virtues are, and in being as the principle and spring of the beings; the numbers in us are of two kinds, the number of our substance, and the counting number; man is two, living and rational, and virtue four (chapters 15 and 16). Last, the "unlimited number" is unlimited only for us who count; the line itself, the first figures and the sphere are there, in intellect and the living being; and number there is bounded by itself, all measures and so all beautiful, in the life of the first living being, whose substance stays in eternity, so that Parmenides was right to call being one, and being is sufficient to itself (chapters 17 and 18).
@ch VI.6.1 | Multitude, a standing away from the one
Is multitude a standing away from the one, and the unlimited a complete standing away, multitude without number, and so an evil? A thing becomes many when it cannot stay in itself and pours out, and magnitude when the pouring stays. Each thing seeks itself, not another: it is most itself when it is its own, inclined toward itself. The All is great and beautiful only because it was held by one and by beauty; magnitude is the matter of beauty, and the greater, the more without order.

@p
Is multitude a standing away from the one, and the unlimited a complete standing away, in being a multitude without number; and is the unlimited therefore an evil, and we evil, when we are multitude? For each thing becomes many when, unable to stay toward itself, it pours out and stretches, scattering. And when it is deprived of the one altogether in the pouring, it becomes multitude, since there is nothing to unite one part of it to another; but if something comes to be that stays while it is always pouring, it becomes magnitude. But what is terrible about magnitude? If it perceived, it would be terrible: for it would perceive that it had come out of itself and stood away into the distance. For each thing seeks not another but itself, and the journey outward is vain or forced. Each thing is more, not when it becomes many or great, but when it is its own; and it is its own when it is inclined toward itself. The longing for what is great in this way belongs to one who does not know what is really great, and who hastens not where he should, but toward the outside; but what is toward itself was what is within.
!flag It is suggested that multiplicity is a falling away from The Unity | The Greek asks a question (Ἆρ’ ἐστὶ ... ;), "Is multitude a standing away (ἀπόστασις) from the one?", which the treatise goes on to answer; "it is suggested" is MacKenna's.
!flag Given consciousness, there will be, since the thing must feel its exile | The Greek says "if it perceived, it would be" (εἰ ᾐσθάνετο, ἦν ἄν), terrible: a condition contrary to fact. Magnitude does not perceive, so nothing is lost by it; MacKenna's "there will be" makes the grief real.
!flag in that outward moving there is frustration or compulsion | The Greek says the journey outward is "vain or forced" (μάταιος ἢ ἀναγκαία): idle, or under necessity, as the soul's going into body may be.
!note Multitude as a falling away and the unlimited as evil look back to the Pythagorean table of opposites, with limit, one and good on one side and unlimited, many and bad on the other (Aristotle, Metaphysics A.5, 986a22-26), and to Plato's Philebus (16c-17a, 23c-26d) on limit and the unlimited.
!note "Inclined toward itself" (πρὸς αὑτὸ νενευκός): the soul's inclining (νεῦσις) downward and its turning back are the theme of IV.8 and I.1.12.

@p
@greek μαρτύριον δὲ τὸ γενόμενον
A witness is what has come to be in magnitude: if it is broken apart, so that each of its parts is, then each of them is those parts, but not the thing it was from the beginning; and if it is to be itself, all the parts must be toward one: so that it is itself when it is in some way one, not great. It is through magnitude, then, and as far as magnitude goes, that it is lost to itself; but in so far as it has one, it has itself.
!flag in other words, a thing is itself not by being extended but by remaining, in its degree, a unity | The Greek says it is itself "when it is in some way one, not great" (ὅταν ἀμηγέπη ἕν, μὴ μέγα, ᾖ); "remaining, in its degree" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek καὶ μὴν τὸ πᾶν μέγα
And yet the All is great and beautiful. Rather, it is so because it was not let go to flee into the unlimited, but was taken round by one; and it is beautiful not by being great, but by the beautiful; and it needed the beautiful because it had become great. For, bare of this, the greater it was, the uglier it would have shown itself; and so the great is the matter of the beautiful, because what needs ordering is many. So the great is rather without order and rather ugly.
!flag it needed Beauty to parry that magnitude | The Greek says it "needed the beautiful because it had become great" (ἐδεήθη τοῦ καλοῦ, ὅτι ἐγένετο μέγα): beauty is needed, not to parry magnitude, but to order it.
!flag in the degree of its extension it was void of beauty and to that degree ugly | The Greek is a condition: bare of beauty, the greater it was, "the uglier it would have shown itself" (ἂν κατεφάνη αἰσχρόν). The All is not ugly, since it has beauty.
!flag The greater the expansion, the greater the disorder and ugliness | The Greek says only that the great as such is "rather without order and rather ugly" (μᾶλλον ἄκοσμον ... καὶ μᾶλλον αἰσχρόν); "the greater ... the greater" is MacKenna's.
!note "Ordering" (κόσμος) is also the word for the world: what is many needs a cosmos. Beauty as the form that masters matter: I.6.2.

@ch VI.6.2 | Number and the unlimited
How can there be a number of the unlimited? Perceptible things are not unlimited, and whoever counts, doubling and multiplying, bounds what he counts. In the intelligible, number is bounded, as many as the beings; we, as we make man many by applying him again and again, make images of number together with the images of things, and count the years with numbers that stay in us.

@p
What, then, of the so-called number of the unlimited? But first, how is it a number, if it is unlimited? For perceptible things are not unlimited, so neither is the number of them; nor does one who counts count the unlimited: even if he makes doubles or multiples, he bounds them, and if he takes them toward the future or the past, or both together, he bounds them.
!flag Nor is an enumerator able to number to infinity | The Greek says one who counts does not count "the unlimited" (τὴν ἀπειρίαν), the unlimitedness itself, as an object: whatever he counts, he bounds.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἄπειρος
Is it, then, not unlimited simply, but in such a way that one can always take more? Or rather, the begetting of it is not in the power of the one who counts; it is already bounded and stands. In the intelligible, as the beings are, so number too is bounded, as many as the beings are; but we, as we make man many by applying him many times, and the beautiful too, and the rest, so together with the image of each thing we beget an image of number too; and as we multiply a town that does not exist, so in the same way we make the numbers multiple too. And if we count times, we bring to the times numbers from those we have, while those numbers stay in us.
!flag Are we then to dismiss absolute limitlessness and think merely that there is always something beyond ? | The Greek asks whether number is "not unlimited simply, but so that one can always take more" (ὥστε ἀεὶ ἐξεῖναι λαμβάνειν): an unlimited only in this sense, which the answer then denies.
!flag we multiply a non-existent in and so produce multiple numbers | The Greek has "as we multiply a town (ἄστυ) that does not exist": a city repeated in thought, as the man and the beautiful are; MacKenna leaves out the town.
!note Number "as many as the beings" in the intelligible, and the unlimited only in our counting, is the answer of chapter 18. The potential unlimited of counting, which never is all at once: Aristotle, Physics III.6 (206a14-b16).

@ch VI.6.3 | The unlimited, caught from outside
How does the unlimited exist, if what exists is already bounded by number? Multitude in the beings is not evil, being one multitude, but less than the one. The unlimited flees the form of limit and is caught from outside; it has no place, and so neither moves nor stands. Thought, taking away the form, thinks it as contraries at once: come near, and it slips like a net's catch; take it as one and it looks many. Its slipping from intellect is its motion, its being held round from outside its rest.

@p
But this unlimited, how does it exist, being unlimited? For what exists and is has already been taken hold of by number. But first, if there is really multitude among the beings, how is multitude evil? Because the multitude is united, and prevented from being multitude altogether, being one multitude; and it is less than the one for this reason, that it has multitude, and is worse in so far as it is set against the one. Not having the nature of that one, but having gone out from it, it is lessened; but by the one it has from that one it has its dignity, and the multitude turned back to one and stayed.
!flag it is evil in comparison with unity pure | The Greek says it is "worse" (χεῖρον) in so far as it is compared with the one; it does not say "evil". The answer to the question is that multitude among the beings is not evil.
!flag multiplicity has value in so far as it tends to return to unity | The Greek says the multitude "turned back to one and stayed" (ἀνέστρεψε ... εἰς ἓν καὶ ἔμεινεν): a turning that has happened and holds, not a tendency.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ἡ ἀπειρία πῶς
But how is the unlimited? For the unlimited that is among the beings is already bounded; or, if it is not bounded, it is not among the beings, but perhaps among the things that come to be, as in time too. Or, even if it is bounded, it is unlimited by this very fact: for it is not the limit but the unlimited that is bounded; for there is nothing else between limit and unlimited that receives the nature of the bound. This unlimited flees, of itself, the form of limit, but is caught when it is taken round from outside. It does not flee from one place to another, for it has no place at all; but when it is caught, place came to be. So neither must its so-called motion be laid down as motion in place, nor any other of the motions said to belong to it of itself; so it would not move. Nor again does it stand: for where, when the "where" comes to be later? Its motion seems to be spoken of in this way, because it does not stay.
!flag To be brought to limit it must be unlimited | The Greek says that even when it is bounded "it is unlimited by this very fact" (τούτῳ γε ἄπειρος), because only the unlimited can be bounded; MacKenna makes it a condition.
!flag the recoil, of course, is not from one place to another | The Greek has "it flees" (φεύγει): the unlimited runs from the form of limit as a quarry runs from the hunter; "recoil" is MacKenna's.
!flag Hence what is known as the flux of the unlimited | The Greek has "its so-called motion" (τὴν λεγομένην κίνησιν αὐτῆς); "flux" is MacKenna's.
!note The unlimited "flees" and is "caught" (ἁλίσκεται), the hunter's words. That the unlimited is what is bounded, and receives the limit, is Plato's Philebus (24a-25b), where the more and less are the unlimited until number and measure come in.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν οὕτως ἔχει
Is it, then, so as to be suspended in the same place, or to swing to and fro there and here? Not at all: both are judged by the same place, both what is suspended and does not lean aside and what leans aside. How, then, would one think of it? By separating the form in thought. What, then, will one think? Contraries at once, and not the contraries: one will think it great and small, for it becomes both; and standing and moving, for it becomes these too. But before it becomes them, plainly it is neither in a bounded way; otherwise you have bounded it.
!flag could be known only by place (which Matter precedes) | The Greek says both are "judged by the same place" (πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν τόπον κρίνεται); "which Matter precedes" is MacKenna's, who speaks of matter where Plotinus speaks of the unlimited.
!flag We must fasten on the bare notion and take what that gives us | The Greek says one thinks of it "by separating the form in thought" (χωρίσας τὸ εἶδος τῇ διανοίᾳ): taking the form away, as with matter in II.4.10, not fastening on a notion.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν ἄπειρος καὶ ταῦτα
If, then, it is unlimited, and these in an unlimited and indefinite way, it would appear as either of them. And if you come near without throwing some limit on it like a net, you will have it slipping away from under you, and you will find nothing one, for then you would have bounded it; but if you come to something as one, it will appear many, and if you say "many", you will be wrong again, for when each is not one, all together are not many either. And this nature of it is motion, according to the one of its appearances, and, according to the one where the imagination came near, rest. And its not being able to see itself through itself is a motion away from intellect, and a slipping off; but its having no way of running away, but being shut in from outside and round about, and not being allowed to go forward, would be rest: so that one may not say that it only moves.
!flag And there is movement in its lack of consciousness | The Greek says "its not being able to see itself through itself" (τὸ μὴ δύνασθαι δι’ αὑτῆς αὐτὴν ἰδεῖν) is motion away from intellect; "lack of consciousness" is MacKenna's.
!flag Thus it is not true to speak of Matter as being solely in flux | The Greek says only "so that one may not say that it only moves" (μὴ μόνον ... κινεῖσθαι): its subject is the unlimited (ἡ ἀπειρία) of the whole chapter; "Matter" is MacKenna's.
!note The unlimited known by a kind of bastard reasoning, neither thought nor perceived, is the Timaeus' receptacle (52b), and matter in II.4.10, known by taking away form; but here Plotinus keeps to the word "unlimited", which he does not quite make matter.
@ch VI.6.4 | Is number in the intelligible before the beings, or after?
How are the numbers in the intelligible: as coming upon the other forms, or always following them, a monad for being, three when motion and rest come from it; or is number thought by itself, and then before the others or after? Plato, saying that men came to the notion of number by the alternation of days and nights, seems to make number the soul's passing from one thing to another; but when he speaks of substance in true number, he gives number an existence of its own, only stirred up in the soul by the changes of perceptible things.

@p
How the numbers are in the intelligible must be examined: whether as coming upon the other forms, or also always following them. For example, since being is such as to be first, we thought of a monad; then, since motion and rest come from it, there are three already; and so with each of the others, one for each. Or it is not so, but one monad was begotten together with each; or a monad for the first being, and for what comes after it, if there is an order, a dyad, or as great as the multitude of each, so that if there are ten, a decad. Or it is not so, but number was thought by itself: and if so, whether before the others, or after.
!flag Are they Ideas added to the other Ideas? | The Greek asks whether the numbers are "coming upon" (ἐπιγινομένων) the other forms, coming to them from outside and after, or "always following" them; MacKenna's "added" weakens the first, and "Ideas" is his word for the forms (εἴδεσιν).
!flag Number is a direct production of the Intellectual-Principle (an Idea in itself) | The Greek says only that number "was thought by itself" (αὐτὸς ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ... ἐνοήθη): intellect is not named, nor said to produce it.
!note Being, motion and rest, and then sameness and otherness, are the five greatest kinds of Plato's Sophist (254d-255e), which VI.2.7-8 sets in the intelligible. The decad, the number the Pythagoreans held to be complete: Aristotle, Metaphysics A.5 (986a8-12).

@p
@greek ὁ μὲν οὖν Πλάτων
Plato, then, saying that men came to the notion of number by the alternation of days and nights, giving the thought of it to the otherness of things, might perhaps be saying that the things counted first make number through otherness, and that number exists in the passing over of the soul as it goes through one thing after another, and comes to be when soul counts: that is, when it goes through them and says to itself "this one, and that one", whereas, as long as it thinks something the same and not another after it, it says "one". But when he speaks of substance in true number, and of number in substance, he would be saying again that number has an existence of its own, by itself, and does not exist in the soul that counts, but that the notion of number is stirred up in it by the alternation that concerns perceptible things.
!flag thus making the concept depend upon variation among things | The Greek says Plato gives the thought of number "to the otherness (ἑτερότητι) of things", one of the greatest kinds; the modern version keeps "otherness", and "variation" is MacKenna's.
!flag observing pure identity unbroken by difference, it says One | The Greek says "as long as it thinks something the same (ταὐτόν) and not another after it", the soul says one; the modern version keeps "the same", and "pure identity" is MacKenna's.
!flag the veritable Number has Being, is a Being | The Greek says Plato speaks of "substance in true number, and number in substance" (ἐν τῷ ἀληθινῷ ἀριθμῷ οὐσίαν καὶ τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἐν οὐσίᾳ); the modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία.
!note Men came to number through days and nights: Plato's Epinomis (978b-979a), where the god Heaven teaches number by turning night and day, and Timaeus (47a), where the sight of day and night, months and years, "has made number". "True number" (ἀληθινὸς ἀριθμός) is in Republic VII (529d).
!note Number as the soul's counting, a passing from one thing to another, is close to Aristotle's time, "the number of motion" counted by soul (Physics IV.14, 223a21-29); "stirred up" (ἀνακινεῖσθαι) is the language of recollection.
@ch VI.6.5 | Is number only seen upon things?
Is number something that follows each substance and is seen upon it, one man, one being, and all number with all things? Then how are two and three gathered into one? Number seen upon things might still exist, as white and motion do; but motion is something, and so one is seen upon it; and number made an accident would not be substance, though even an accident must be something first. So the one is before man and every other thing, before motion and being; not the one beyond being, but the one said of each form. The decad itself is before what it is said of; it must first be by itself.

@p
What, then, is its nature? Is it something that follows, and as it were is seen in addition upon, each substance: man, and one man; being, and one being; and all the intelligibles, each of them, and all number? But how are there a dyad and a triad, and how are all things one by one, and how would such a number be gathered into one? For so there will be a multitude of units, but none gathered into one except the simple one; unless someone were to say that the dyad is that thing, or rather what is seen upon the thing, which has two powers taken together, as a compound into one; or numbers such as the Pythagoreans spoke of, who seemed to speak of numbers from proportion, justice as a tetrad, for example, and other numbers in other ways. But in that way it would rather be that the number, so much one, like a decad, is yoked to the multitude of the thing, which is nevertheless one thing. And yet we do not speak of the ten so, but say "ten" bringing together things that stand apart. Or we say "ten" in that way, but when one comes to be out of many, "decad", as it is there too.
!flag Is it an accompaniment upon each substance | The Greek has "something that follows" (παρακολούθημα), and "as it were is seen in addition upon" (ἐπιθεωρούμενον) each substance: number would be what we see upon things over and above them. The modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία.
!flag in their symbolic system in which Justice, for example, is a Tetrad | The Greek says the Pythagoreans "seemed to speak of numbers from proportion" (ἐκ τοῦ ἀνὰ λόγον), by analogy; "symbolic system" is MacKenna's.
!flag This would apply in the Intellectual as in the sensible | The Greek says only "as it is there too" (ὡς κἀκεῖ οὕτως): the intelligible counts in the same way; "the sensible" is MacKenna's.
!note Justice as four, the first square number, "equal times equal": Aristotle, Metaphysics A.5 (985b29-30) and M.4 (1078b21-23), and Magna Moralia I.1 (1182a11-14). "Ten" said of things apart, and the decad as one: the difference between counting things and number as a unity is Aristotle's too (Metaphysics M.7, 1082b16-19).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ οὕτως, ἆῤ ἔτι ὑπόστασις
But if so, will there still be an existence of number, if it is seen upon things? But what is to prevent it, someone might say, since white too is seen upon things, and there is an existence of white in the things? For motion too is seen upon being, and there was an existence of motion, being in being. But number is not as motion is: it is because motion is something that one was seen upon it, so it is said. Then too such an existence takes number away from being a substance, and rather makes it an accident. And yet it is not an accident at all: for the accident must be something before it belongs, and even if it is inseparable, it must still be something by itself, a certain nature, as the white is, and already be what will be predicated, when it is predicated of another.
!flag But how then can number, observed upon: things, rank among Real Beings ? | The Greek asks whether there will still be "an existence" (ὑπόστασις) of number, if it is seen upon things; "rank among Real Beings" is MacKenna's.
!flag Besides, the kind of real existence thus implied annuls the reality of number | The Greek says such an existence "takes number away from being a substance" (ἀφίστησι τὸν ἀριθμὸν τοῦ οὐσίαν εἶναι) and makes it an accident; it does not annul its reality.
!note Motion among the beings is one of the Sophist's greatest kinds (254d), set in the intelligible in VI.2.7. Accident (συμβεβηκός) and what is predicated of another: Aristotle, Categories 2 (1a20-b9).

@p
@greek ὥστε, εἰ περὶ ἕκαστον τὸ ἓν
So, if the one is about each thing, and "one man" is not the same as "man", but the one is other than the man, and the one is common, and over each of the others too, the one would be before man and each of the others, so that man and each of the others may get, each, its being one. And so it is before motion too, if motion too is one, and before being, so that being too may get its being one. I mean not that one which we say is beyond being, but this one which is predicated of each of the forms. And so there is a decad too before that of which decad is predicated, and this will be the decad itself; for that thing upon which the decad is seen will not be the decad itself.
!flag the oneness being different from the manness and common to all things | The Greek says "the one is other (ἕτερον) than the man", and the one is common; "manness" is MacKenna's coinage.
!note "One man" is not the same as "man": Aristotle argues the contrary, that "one man" and "man" are the same (Metaphysics Γ.2, 1003b26-32). The one beyond being: Plato's Republic VI (509b) and Parmenides (141e); the one said of each form is the one that is, of the Parmenides' second hypothesis (142b-c).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ἆρα συνεγένετο
But was it born with the beings and did it come to exist with them? But if it was begotten with them as an accident, as health is with man, it must also be by itself; and if the one is as an element of a compound, there must first be one and the one itself, so that it may be with another; and then, mixed with another, which came to be through it, it will make that thing falsely one, making it two. And what of the decad? For what need has that thing of the decad, which will be a decad by so great a power? But if it is to give it form as if it were matter, and it will be ten and a decad by the presence of the decad, the decad must first be by itself, being nothing else than only decad.
!flag moreover if it were compounded with an object brought into being by its agency | The Greek says the one, mixed with another "that came to be through it" (τῷ γενομένῳ δι’ αὐτὸ), would make it falsely one; the compound is not brought into being by the one's agency, but the other comes to be through the one.
!flag The need may be like that of Form to Matter | The Greek says "if it is to give it form (εἰδοποιήσει) as if it were matter": a condition, which the decad meets only if it is first by itself; nothing is said of a need.
!note Form given to matter by presence (παρουσία): the language of Plato's Phaedo (100d), where the beautiful is beautiful by the presence of beauty, and the two two by sharing in the dyad (101c).

@ch VI.6.6 | The forms are not made by thinking them
If the one itself and the decad itself are without the things, what is their nature, and how did they come to be? Their generation must be taken in thought, not in time. The forms are not made by intellect's thinking them: justice did not come to be because intellect thought what justice is. Where there is no matter, the thing is not its knowledge; the thing itself is intelligible and thought, intellect and true knowledge. So motion itself made the thought of motion; and justice is a disposition or activity of intellect, whose face is lovelier than the evening and the morning star, a statue in intellect.

@p
But if the one itself and the decad itself are without the things, and then the intelligible things, after being what they are, will be some of them units, and some dyads and triads, what would their nature be, and how would it have come together? We must think that their generation is made in thought.
!flag Henads, Dyads, Triads | The Greek has "units" (ἑνάδες), "dyads and triads"; "Henads" is MacKenna's transliteration, and the modern version keeps "units".
!flag We cannot but think that some reason accounts for their origin | The Greek says "we must think that their generation is made in thought" (λόγῳ ... τὴν γένεσιν αὐτῶν ποιεῖσθαι): in the account, not in time, since there is no time there; it is not that some reason accounts for them.

@p
@greek πρῶτον τοίνυν δεῖ λαβεῖν
First, then, we must take the substance of the forms in general: that it is not that the one who thinks thought each, and then by the thinking itself gave them their existence. For it is not because he thought what justice is that justice came to be, nor because he thought what motion is that motion came to exist; for so this thought would have had to be later than the thing itself that was thought, the thought of justice itself later than justice, and again the thought earlier than what came to exist out of the thought, if it came to exist by being thought. And if justice is the same as such a thought, first it is absurd that justice should be nothing but its definition, as it were: for what is it to have thought justice or motion, but to grasp what they are? And this is the same as to grasp the account of a thing that does not exist; which is impossible.
!flag It is not that the thinking principle thought of each Idea | The Greek has "the one who thinks" (τοῦ νενοηκότος), who has thought each; "thinking principle" is MacKenna's, and the modern version keeps "forms" for the εἴδη he calls "Ideas".
!note Plotinus sets himself against a view in which the forms are intellect's thoughts and made by them; in V.9.7 too intellect does not think the forms into being, and V.5 holds that the intelligibles are not outside intellect.

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις λέγοι, ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν ἄνευ ὕλης
And if someone says that with things without matter the knowledge is the same as the thing, we must take what is said in this way: that he does not say that the knowledge is the thing, nor that the account which contemplates the thing is the thing itself, but, the other way round, that the thing itself, being without matter, is intelligible and thought; not such as to be an account of the thing, nor an applying of the mind to it, but the thing itself, being in the intelligible, is nothing other than intellect and knowledge. For it is not knowledge turned to itself, but the thing there made the knowledge, which does not stay as the knowledge of a thing in matter does, other: that is, true knowledge; that is, not an image of the thing, but the thing itself.
!flag but we must not misapply that statement | The Greek says "we must take what is said in this way" (ἐκείνως χρὴ νοεῖν τὸ λεγόμενον): it is read rightly, not guarded against misuse.
!flag it is that the thing in the Intellectual transmutes the knowledge | The Greek says "the thing there made the knowledge ... other" (ἑτέραν ἐποίησεν εἶναι) than the knowledge of things in matter, which does not stay; "transmutes" is MacKenna's, and the modern version keeps "intelligible".
!note "In things without matter the knowledge is the same as the thing": Aristotle, On the soul III.4 (430a2-5) and III.7 (431a1-2), and Metaphysics Λ.9 (1075a1-5). Plotinus turns it around: the thing is knowledge, not the knowledge the thing. "Applying of the mind" (ἐπιβολή) is the Epicureans' word for the grasp of an impression.

@p
@greek ἡ νόησις τοίνυν τῆς κινήσεως
The thought of motion, then, has not made motion itself, but motion itself has made the thought, so that it is itself motion and thought of itself. For the motion there is also the thought of that one, and itself motion because it is first, for there is no other before it; and it is real motion, because it does not belong as an accident to another, but is the activity of what moves, which is in activity: so it is substance too; but the notion of being is other.
!flag for movement as it exists There, bound up with Being, is a concept | The Greek says "the motion there is also the thought of that one" (κἀκείνου νόησις), of being; "bound up with Being" and "a concept" are MacKenna's.
!flag Thus it is a real existent though the notion of Being is different | The Greek says "so it is substance too" (ὥστε αὖ καὶ οὐσία); the modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία.
!note That motion in the intelligible is intellect's activity, and so a substance, not an accident of being: VI.2.7-8.

@p
@greek καὶ δικαιοσύνη δὲ οὐ νόησις
And justice too is not the thought of justice, but as it were a disposition of intellect, or rather an activity of such a kind, whose face is truly beautiful, and neither the evening star nor the morning star is so beautiful, nor anything at all of the perceptible things, but it is like a statue in intellect, as if standing out of itself and shown forth in itself, or rather being in itself.
!flag an Intellectual manifestation self-rising, self-seen | The Greek has "like a statue (ἄγαλμα) in intellect, as if standing out of itself and shown forth in itself" (οἷον ἐξ αὑτοῦ ἑστηκὸς καὶ προφανὲν ἐν αὑτῷ); MacKenna leaves out the statue.
!note "Neither the evening nor the morning star is so wonderful" is said of justice by Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.1 (1129b28-29), after Euripides' Melanippe; Plotinus uses it again in I.6.4. The statues (ἀγάλματα) in the intelligible: V.8.5 and VI.9.11.
@ch VI.6.7 | All things together in one nature
The things there must be thought of in one nature that holds them all, not each apart as in the perceptible, the sun in one place and something else in another, but all together in one: this is the nature of intellect, which soul and nature imitate. Yet all being together, each is apart, and intellect sees them by having them. Its greatness and beauty are shown by the soul's love for it; and the complete living being, which holds all living beings in itself, must be of a beauty wonderful and beyond telling.

@p
For in general we must think of the things as in one nature, and of one nature having all of them and as it were taking them round; not as in the perceptible things, each apart, the sun in one place and another thing elsewhere, but all together in one: for this is the nature of intellect. For soul too imitates it so, and so does what is called nature, by which and under which each of the things is begotten, one in one place and another in another, while it is together with itself.
!flag This is the very nature of the Intellectual-Principle as we may know from soul which reproduces it | The Greek says "this is the nature of intellect, for soul too imitates it so" (οὕτω μιμεῖται); "as we may know" is MacKenna's, and the modern version keeps "intellect" for νοῦς.
!flag while that Nature itself remains indissolubly one | The Greek says nature is "together with itself" (ὁμοῦ ἑαυτῇ οὔσης), while what it begets is one thing here and another there; "indissolubly" is MacKenna's.
!note Nature, the lowest part of the soul of the world, which makes while it contemplates: III.8.2-4. "Everything together" (ὁμοῦ πάντα) is Anaxagoras' phrase (fragment B1), which Plotinus uses for intellect (V.3.15, V.9.6).

@p
@greek ὁμοῦ δὲ πάντων ὄντων
But all being together, each is again apart; and the intellect that has them sees within itself the things in intellect and in substance, not looking upon them, but having them, nor separating each: for each has always been separated already in it.
!flag the all-embracing Intellect sees what is in it, what is within Being | The Greek says intellect sees what is "in intellect and in substance" (ἐν τῷ νῷ καὶ τῇ οὐσίᾳ); the modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία, and "all-embracing" is MacKenna's for "that has them".

@p
@greek πιστούμεθα δὲ πρὸς τοὺς
We find assurance, for those who wonder at it, from the things that have shared in it: its greatness and beauty from the soul's love for it; and the love of the other things for soul because of such a nature, and because by having it in some way it has been made like it. For it is absurd that there should be some living being that is beautiful, while the living being itself is not of a beauty wonderful and beyond telling. The complete living being, then, is made of all living beings, or rather holds all living beings in itself, and is one, as great as all of them, as this All too is one and holds all that is in the visible, all that is visible.
!flag Against doubters we cite the fact of participation | The Greek says "we find assurance, for those who wonder (τεθαυμακότας), from the things that have shared": they wonder at it, not doubt it; and "the fact of participation" is MacKenna's.
!flag the longing of the rest towards soul is set up by its likeness to its higher | The Greek says the others love soul "because of such a nature", and because, by having it in some way, soul "has been made like" (ὡμοίωται) it: soul is like intellect, and the things below love it for that.
!flag It is surely inconceivable that any living thing be beautiful | The Greek says "it is absurd" (ἄτοπον) that a living being be beautiful while the living being itself is not; "inconceivable" is MacKenna's.
!note The complete living being (παντελὲς ζῷον) that holds all living beings in itself, as this visible world holds the visible ones: Plato's Timaeus (30c-31b, 39e). Love for soul and for intellect, as the measure of their beauty: I.6.5-7 and VI.7.22.

@ch VI.6.8 | Being, intellect and the living being; number before them
Since there is the first living being, the living being itself, and intellect and real substance, and we say it holds all living beings, all number, justice itself and the beautiful, we must ask how each is. Leave perception behind, and see intellect with intellect: in us too life and intellect are not in bulk but in power without bulk, and true substance has stripped that off. Being comes first, then intellect, then the living being; number is not after the living being, for one and two were before it, nor after intellect, for substance before it was one and many.

@p
Since, then, there is a living being in the first way, and so the living being itself, and there is intellect and real substance, and we say that it has all living beings and all number and the just itself and the beautiful and the rest of such things (for we speak of man himself, and number itself, and the just itself, in another way), we must examine how each of these is, and what it is, as far as it is possible to find anything about them.
!flag there is Intellectual-Principle or Being, Authentic Being | The Greek says "there is intellect and real substance" (νοῦς ἐστι καὶ οὐσία ἡ ὄντως), both, not one as another name for the other; the modern version keeps "intellect" and "substance".
!flag for we ascribe an existence of their own to Absolute Man, Absolute Number, Absolute Justice | The Greek says we speak of man himself, number itself and the just itself "in another way" (ἄλλως): otherwise than of the many men and the many just things; "an existence of their own" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek πρῶτον τοίνυν ἀφετέον
First, then, we must let go of all perception, and contemplate intellect with intellect, and keep in mind that in us too life and intellect are not in bulk, but in power without bulk; and that true substance has stripped these off, and is a power standing by itself, not a feeble thing, but the most living and most intelligent of all, than which nothing is more living or more intelligent or more substantial; and what touches it has these according to the measure of the touching, what is near more nearly, what is far more distantly. If, then, being is desired, what most is is desired more, and what is most intellect, if thinking is desired at all; and with life in the same way.
!flag issue of Authentic Being which is power self-existing | The Greek says true substance "has stripped these off" (ἐκδεδυκέναι ταῦτα), bulk and magnitude, and is "a power standing by itself"; life and intellect in us are not called its issue.
!flag and producing its effect by contact and in the ratio of the contact | The Greek says "what touches it has these" (οὗ τὸ ἐφαψάμενον ἔχει ταῦτα), life and intellect, according to the measure of touching: it is the one who touches that has them, not substance that produces an effect.
!flag If Being is to be sought, then most to be sought is Being at its intensest | The Greek says "if being is desired (ἐφετόν), what most is is desired more"; "at its intensest" is MacKenna's.
!note "Not a feeble thing" (οὐκ ἀμενηνόν): Homer's "strengthless heads of the dead" (Odyssey X 521). Seeing intellect with intellect: V.3.4 and V.8.11. Being, life and intellect, the order of chapter 8, became the triad of the later Neoplatonists (Proclus, Elements of Theology 101-103).

@p
@greek εἰ δὴ τὸ ὂν πρῶτον δεῖ λαβεῖν
If, then, we must take being first, as first, then intellect, then the living being (for this already seems to hold all things), and intellect is second (for it is the activity of substance), then number would not be according to the living being, for one and two were already before it; nor according to intellect, for before it substance was, being one and many.
!flag Intellectual-Principle, as the Act of Real Being, is a second | The Greek says intellect is second because it is "the activity (ἐνέργεια) of substance"; the modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία.
!flag nor does it rise in the Intellectual-Principle since before that there existed Real Being which is both one and numerous | The Greek says number is not "according to intellect", for before it "substance was, being one and many" (ἡ οὐσία ἓν οὖσα καὶ πολλὰ ἦν); the modern version keeps "intellect" and "substance".
!note The order being, intellect, living being reverses Plato's Timaeus, where the maker (intellect) looks to the living being itself (30c-31a); Plotinus takes the living being as what holds the forms in their full multiplicity, after being and intellect.
@ch VI.6.9 | Number divided being: the substantial number
Did substance beget number by dividing itself, or did number divide substance? If two and three could be by themselves, without things counted, they could be before the beings. One who makes a man, a horse and a dog from what is in him must go to one, then to another, and make two; and the beings were not counted when they came to be, but how many was plain. So number was in being, not as the number of being, which was still one, but as a power that divided being and made it in travail with multitude: being is number united, the beings number unrolled, intellect number moving in itself, the living being number that holds. This is the substantial number; the number of units is its image.

@p
It remains, then, to consider whether substance begot number by its own dividing, or number divided substance; and indeed whether substance and motion and rest and sameness and otherness themselves begot number, or number these. The beginning of the inquiry: can number be by itself, or must two too be seen upon two things, and three likewise? And indeed the one that is in the numbers? For if it could be by itself, without the things counted, it could be before the beings. Before being too, then? Or we must leave this aside, and its being before number too, for the present, and grant that number comes to be from being. But if one is one being, and two are two beings, one will go before being, and number before the beings.
!flag whether Being by its distinction produced Number or Number produced that distinction | The Greek asks whether "substance (οὐσία) begot number by its own dividing, or number divided substance"; the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag It is certain that either Number was the cause of Being, movement, rest, identity and difference, or these the cause of Number | The Greek asks it, and does not say "it is certain": whether these "themselves (begot) number, or number these". The modern version keeps "sameness" and "otherness" for ταὐτόν and ἕτερον, where MacKenna has "identity and difference".
!flag For the present we must take it that Being precedes Number, is its source | The Greek says we must "leave this aside for the present" (ἐατέον ... ἐν τῷ παρόντι), whether number is before being, "and grant" that number comes to be from being; it is granted for the argument, not taken as true, and the next sentence overturns it.
!note Substance, motion, rest, sameness and otherness, the Sophist's five greatest kinds (254d-255e), are the kinds of VI.2.8. Whether number is a substance by itself or seen upon things is the question of Aristotle's Metaphysics M-N against the Platonists (M.1, 1076a19-32).

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν τῇ ἐπινοίᾳ
In notion, then, and in the applying of the mind? Or in existence too. Let us look at it in this way: when someone thinks of a man as being, and as one beautiful thing, he surely thinks the one later, upon each; and indeed when he thinks of a horse and a dog; and here plainly the two is later. But if he were to beget a man and beget a horse and a dog, or bring them forth when they were in himself, and neither beget nor bring them forth as it happened, will he not say: "I must go to one, and pass on to another one, and make two, and make another with me"? Indeed, the beings were not counted either, when they came to be; but how many had to come to be was plain, when they had to. All number, then, was before the beings themselves.
!flag that unity is certainly thought of as subsequent to a precedent duality | The Greek says one "surely thinks the one later, upon each" (ὕστερον δήπου τὸ ἓν νοεῖ ἐφ’ ἑκατέρῳ): the one is thought after the man and after the beautiful, not after a duality.
!flag with full intention from where they lie latent within itself | The Greek says "or bring them forth when they were in himself" (ἢ ἐν αὑτῷ ὄντας προφέροι), and "not as it happened" (μὴ κατὰ τὸ ἐπελθόν); "lie latent" is MacKenna's.
!flag counting myself there are three | The Greek has "and make another with me" (καὶ μετ’ ἐμοῦ καὶ ἄλλο ποιητέον): the maker goes on counting, with himself; "three" is MacKenna's reckoning.
!note The maker who brings forth from himself: the craftsman of Plato's Timaeus, who looks to the pattern (28a-29a). "How many had to come to be was plain": the number of the forms is fixed before them, as the number of the beings is bounded in chapter 2 and chapter 18.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ πρὸ τῶν ὄντων
But if it was before the beings, it was not beings. Or it was in being, not being the number of being, for being was still one; but the power of number, coming to exist, divided being, and made it as it were be in travail with the multitude. For either its substance or its activity will be number, and the living being itself and intellect will be number. Is being, then, number united, and the beings number unrolled, and intellect number moving in itself, and the living being number that holds? For since being came to be from the one, as that was one, so it must be number; and that is why they called the forms both units and numbers.
!flag for Being was still unparted | The Greek says "being was still one" (ἓν γὰρ ἦν ἔτι τὸ ὄν); "unparted" is MacKenna's.
!flag Clearly Being is to be thought of as Number Collective | The Greek asks it: "Is being, then, number united (ἡνωμένος)?" (ἆρ’ οὖν ...;); "clearly" is MacKenna's, and "united" is not "collective".
!flag while the Living-Form is Number container of the universe | The Greek says the living being is "number that holds" (ἀριθμὸς περιέχων); "of the universe" is MacKenna's.
!flag Hence it is that the Forms have been described as Henads and Numbers | The Greek says "they called the forms both units (ἑνάδας) and numbers"; the modern version keeps "units".
!note The forms as numbers: Aristotle reports it of Plato (Metaphysics A.6, 987b18-25, and M.8, 1084a7-10), and of the units Plato's Philebus speaks (15a-b, ἑνάδες, μονάδες). Being "in travail" (ὠδίνειν) is the Symposium's word (206e) and the Theaetetus' (148e).

@p
@greek καὶ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ οὐσιώδης
And this is the substantial number; the other, called the number of units, is its image. The substantial is, on the one hand, what is seen upon the forms and begets them together with them; and in the first way it is the number in being, with being and before the beings. The beings have in it their base and spring and root and principle. For to being the one is principle, and being is upon it, for else it would be scattered; but the one is not upon being, for then it would already be one before it had the one, and what has the decad would already be a decad before it had the decad.
!flag This is the authentic Number; the other, the ‘‘ monadic ” is its image | The Greek calls it "the substantial number" (ὁ οὐσιώδης ἀριθμός), and the other the number "of units" (ὁ μοναδικός), the number we count with; "authentic" is MacKenna's.
!flag serving to them as root, fount, first principle | The Greek says the beings have in it "their base and spring and root and principle" (βάσιν ... καὶ πηγὴν καὶ ῥίζαν καὶ ἀρχήν): MacKenna leaves out the base.
!note The substantial number and the number of units (μοναδικός, "monadic", made of units alike, that can be added) are Aristotle's terms for the Platonists' two kinds of number (Metaphysics M.6, 1080a15-b14). The one as root and spring: the Pythagorean oath by the tetractys, "spring and root of ever-flowing nature" (Golden Verses 47-48), and VI.9.9.
@ch VI.6.10 | Number laid down before the beings
Being standing in multitude is number, a preparation for the beings, units that give a place for what will be set on them. Here too a man says "I want so much gold": he would make gold into number, not number into gold. If the beings came before number, how many they are would be by chance; so number is cause, and what came to be shared in it. One who says ten thousand is not told it by the things, as their colours are, but his thought says it. As with good, so with number: either the things are a decad, or there is a decad by itself before them. What is predicated of a thing either came to it from another or is its activity; and the one and number are before.

@p
Being, then, standing in multitude, is number, when it was roused to be much; and it was as it were a preparation for the beings, and a first sketch, and as it were units holding a place for what was to be set on them. For even now someone says, "I want so great a multitude of gold", or "of houses". And the gold is one, but he wishes not to make the number gold, but the gold number; and, having the number already, he seeks to set it on the gold, so that it may happen to the gold to become so much.
!flag When it takes lot with multiplicity, Being becomes Number by the fact of awakening to manifoldness | The Greek says being "standing in multitude is number, when it was roused to be much" (ὅτε πολὺ μὲν ἠγείρετο): number is being as it stands in multitude, and "takes lot with" is MacKenna's.
!flag a total of henads offering a stay for what was to be based upon them | The Greek has "units holding a place" (ἑνάδες τόπον ἔχουσαι) for what was to be set on them; the modern version keeps "units", and "a stay" is MacKenna's.
!note "A first sketch" (προτύπωσις) is a painter's or sculptor's word, the outline drawn first. The number in the soul before the gold: Plato's Theaetetus (198a-199b), where the counter has numbers in his soul like birds in an aviary.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ τὰ ὄντα μὲν ἐγίνετο
But if the beings came to be before number, and number was seen upon them when the nature that counts was moved to as many as the things counted, they would be so many by chance, and not so many as they are by purpose. If, then, they are not so many at random, number is the cause of their being so many, being before them. That is, number being there already, the things that came to be shared in being so many, and each shared in the one, so that it might be one. It is being from being, since being too is being from itself; and one from the one. And each is one, if the one upon them was many together, as a triad is one and all the beings are so one: not as the one that goes with the monad, but as the ten thousand is one, or some other number.
!flag Number then preexists and is the cause by which produced things participate in quantity | The Greek says the things that came to be shared in "being so many" (τοῦ τοσαῦτα), not in quantity in general; "quantity" is MacKenna's.
!flag a unity is a unity in virtue of Being | The Greek says each is "one from the one" (ἓν δὲ παρ’ αὐτοῦ ἕν), as it is being from being; MacKenna makes unity come from being.
!note "Not by chance but by purpose" (οὐ κατὰ πρόθεσιν): the number of the forms is not that of a random heap. "The ten thousand is one" (μυριάς) is the largest single number name of the Greeks.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ λέγων ἤδη πράγματα
For one who says that ten thousand things have come to be already, if the one who counts said "ten thousand", does not say that the ten thousand are called out by the things themselves, showing it as they show their colours, but by his thought saying "so many": for if it did not say it, he would not know how great the multitude is. How, then, will it say it? As one who knows how to count; and this, if it knew number; and it would know it if there were number. And for that nature not to know how great its multitude is, is absurd, or rather impossible.
!flag it is he that produces the number | The Greek says the ten thousand are not called out by the things but by "his thought saying so many" (τῆς διανοίας λεγούσης τοσαῦτα); he does not produce the number, but says it, as one who knows how to count.
!flag that that Principle should not know its own total content is absurd, impossible | The Greek has "that nature" (τὴν φύσιν ἐκείνην), the intelligible, not knowing "how great its multitude is"; "Principle" and "total content" are MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ὥσπερ τοίνυν εἰ λέγοι τις ἀγαθά
So, just as when someone calls things good, either he calls them such of themselves, or he predicates the good of them as an accident: and if he speaks of the first things, he speaks of the first existence; but if of those to which the good belongs as an accident, there must be a nature of good, so that it may belong to others too, or the cause that made it also in another, either the good itself or what begot the good in its own nature: so too with the beings, one who speaks of a number, a decad for example, would either be speaking of a decad that exists itself, or, speaking of things to which the decad belongs as an accident, would be compelled to set down a decad by itself, which is nothing other than decad. So, if he calls the beings a decad, necessarily either they themselves are a decad, or before them there is another decad, which is nothing other than this very thing, decad.
!flag the goodness we have in mind is that First Hypostasis | The Greek says "if he speaks of the first things, he speaks of the first existence" (ὑπόστασιν ... τὴν πρώτην): the good of the first things is their first existence, not a hypostasis set over them; the capitals are MacKenna's.
!note The good, as a nature of its own and as what belongs to others: Plato's Phaedo (100c-e), the beautiful itself by whose presence the others are beautiful, and Aristotle's objection that the good is said in as many ways as being (Nicomachean Ethics I.6, 1096a23-29).

@p
@greek καθόλου τοίνυν δεικτέον
In general, then, it must be shown that everything whatever that is predicated of another either has come into it from another, or is its activity. And if it is such as not to be present at one time and not present at another, but to be always with it, then, if that thing is a substance, it too is a substance, and that thing is no more substance than it; and if one will not grant it substance, at any rate it is among the beings, and is a being. And if that thing could be thought without its activity, the activity would still be at the same time with it, but would be ranked later by us in notion; but if it cannot be thought of without it, as man cannot be thought without the one, either it is not later than it, but exists with it, or it is before it, so that the thing may exist through it. And we say that the one and number are before.
!flag the characteristic Act of that subject | The Greek says it "is its activity" (ἐνέργειά ἐστιν ἐκείνου); "characteristic" is MacKenna's.
!flag then, if the subject is a Real Being so also is the accidental in an equal degree | The Greek says "if that thing is a substance (οὐσία), it too is a substance, and that thing is no more substance than it"; the modern version keeps "substance", and Plotinus does not call it an accident here.
!note Activity always present with what it belongs to, and so substance with it: the motion of chapter 6, which is substance and not accident. "We say that the one and number are before" answers the question with which chapter 9 began.
@ch VI.6.11 | The unit, bare, before each thing is called one
If someone says the decad is nothing but so many units, why grant one unit and not ten? The one is common to all, a nature predicated of many, and so it must be by itself first. If only the first unit existed, joined to what most is or what is most one, the others would be units in name only, or what is most one would need no unit. So there must be a bare one before each is called one; and nature, begetting in order and not stopping at each, would beget the smaller numbers by halting early, the greater by moving further, and fit each multitude to its number, knowing that what is not fitted would be without number and without forming principle.

@p
But if someone were to say that the decad is nothing, or so many units: if he grants that the unit is, why will he grant that one unit is, but not the ten? For as the one has existence, why not the others too? For surely the one unit need not be yoked to some one of the beings; for so each of the others would no longer be one. But if each of the others too must be one, the one is common. And this is one nature predicated of many, which we said must exist by itself even before it is seen in many.
!flag We are certainly not compelled to attach that one henad te some one thing | The Greek says the one unit "need not be yoked (συνεζεῦχθαι) to some one of the beings"; the modern version keeps "units" for ἑνάδες, where MacKenna has "henads".
!flag the principle whose existence within itself we affirmed to be presupposed by its manifestation outside | The Greek says this one nature "must exist by itself even before it is seen in many" (πρὸ τοῦ ἐν πολλοῖς θεωρεῖσθαι), as chapter 5 said; "manifestation outside" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek οὔσης δὲ ἑνάδος ἐν τούτῳ
And if there is a unit in this thing, and it is seen again in another, then, if that one too exists, not one unit only will have existence, and so there will be a multitude of units; but if only that first one, it will be either with what most is, or with what is most one in every way. But if with what most is, the other units would be units in name only, and will not be ranked with the first; or number will be of unlike monads, and there will be differences of the monads in so far as they are monads; and if with what is most one, why would what is most one need this monad, in order to be one? If, then, these are impossible, there must be a one that is nothing else but bare one, left bare of being by its own substance, before each thing is called and thought one.
!flag or else Number becomes a collection of unlike monads and there are differences among monads (an impossibility) | The Greek says number would be "of unlike monads" and there would be "differences of the monads in so far as they are monads" (καθ’ ὅσον μονάδες); "(an impossibility)" is MacKenna's, though the next sentence counts it among the impossible things.
!flag there must exist a unity bare, unrelated by very essence | The Greek says the one is "bare" (ψιλόν), "left bare (ἀπηρημωμένον) of being by its own substance": a one that is nothing but one; "unrelated" is MacKenna's.
!note Units "in name only" (ὁμωνύμως), and number of unlike, incomparable monads: the Platonists' view, as Aristotle argues against it in Metaphysics M.7 (1080a18-b4, 1081a5-17).

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν τὸ ἓν ἄνευ τοῦ πράγματος
If, then, the one without the thing called one will be there too, why will not another one also exist? And, each apart, there are many monads, which are also many ones. But if nature were to beget in order, as it were, or rather had begotten, not stopping at each one of the things it begot, as if making a continuous one, then, by drawing a line round and stopping sooner in its going forth, it would beget the smaller numbers, and, moved further, not upon other things but in its motions themselves, it would bring the greater numbers into existence; and so it would fit each multitude to each number, and each of the beings, knowing that, if each were not fitted to each number, either it would not be at all, or it would be something else, gone astray, become without number and without forming principle.
!flag Each particular, considered in itself, would be a manifold of monads, totalling to a collective unity | The Greek says only "each apart (χωρὶς), there are many monads, which are also many ones"; "totalling to a collective unity" is MacKenna's.
!flag something outside, at once, of both Number and Reason | The Greek says it would be "without number and without forming principle" (ἀνάριθμον καὶ ἄλογον); the modern version keeps "forming principle" for λόγος, and "Reason" is MacKenna's.
