!note Nature "drawing a line round" (περιγράψασα) each number as it goes forth: the numbers are the stopping places of one motion. "Without number and without forming principle" recalls the Timaeus' chaos before the god brought it to order "with forms and numbers" (53a-b).

@ch VI.6.12 | Is the one only an affection of the soul?
Someone may say that the one and the monad have no existence, but are an affection of the soul toward each thing. Then being too would be an affection, and nothing would be; if being strikes the soul and gives an impression of being, so does the one. When we say "not one", we do not get the one from the thing; we have it in the soul. To those who say that it comes to us later from the things, like "this", "something", a crowd, a feast, an army, a multitude, or right and above, which are nothing apart from the things, the answer is that each of these has some existence, though not the same in all; each must be met by itself.

@p
But if someone were to say that the one and the monad have no existence (for nothing is one that is not some one thing), but that it is an affection of the soul toward each of the beings, first, what is to prevent him, when he says "being", from saying that it is an affection of the soul, and that nothing is being? And if he says it is because being pricks and strikes the soul and makes an impression of being, we see the soul pricked and taking an impression about the one too. Next, is the affection and the thought of the soul one, or a multitude? But when we say "not one", we do not get the one from the thing itself, for we say that the one is not in it: so we have the one, and it is in the soul without its being some one thing.
!flag so that all comes to an attitude of the mind towards things considered singly | The Greek says the one is "an affection of the soul" (πάθημα ... τῆς ψυχῆς) toward each of the beings: something the soul undergoes, and the modern version keeps "soul" for ψυχή, where MacKenna has "mind".
!flag something latent in our minds independently of any concrete one thing | The Greek says the one "is in the soul (ἐν ψυχῇ) without its being some one thing"; "latent" and "minds" are MacKenna's.
!note Impressions that "prick" (νύττει) and "strike" (πλήττει) the soul are the Stoics' words for perception; Plotinus answers them in their own language, as in IV.6.1-3.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ἔχομεν τὸ ἓν ἐκ τῶν ἔξωθεν
"But we have the one by taking from the things outside a certain thought and a certain imprint, as a concept from the thing." Those who set the kind of the numbers and of the one among what they call concepts would be setting them up as existences of that kind, if any such thing is in existence, and to them one might speak about it at the right time; but not if they were to say that it is such as to have come to be in us later from the things, as an affection or a thought, like "this" and "something", and indeed "crowd" and "feast" and "army" and "multitude". For as multitude is nothing apart from the many things so called, nor the feast apart from those gathered and making merry at the sacred rites, so neither do we think of the one alone, something by itself and left bare of the others, when we say "one".
!flag [An objector speaks :—] | The Greek gives the objection without naming a speaker; the brackets are MacKenna's, and the modern version marks it only with quotation marks.
!flag Those that take the notion of numbers and of unity to be but one species of the notions held to be inherent in the mind | The Greek speaks of "what they call concepts" (τῶν λεγομένων παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἐννοημάτων), the Stoics' word; "inherent in the mind" is MacKenna's, and the Stoics held that concepts are not in the mind from birth.
!note The concepts (ἐννοήματα) of the Stoics are "neither somethings nor qualities, but as it were somethings" (Stobaeus I.12.3, SVF I.65); the "something" (τί) is their highest kind, which VI.1.25 attacks.

@p
@greek πολλὰ δὲ καὶ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα εἶναι
"And there are many other such things, right, for example, and above, and their opposites. For what would there be toward existence in the case of the right, except that one stands or sits here and another there? And with above too in the same way: one thing has such a position, and is more in this part of the All, which we call above, and another in what is called below." To such things this must first be said: that there is some existence of what has been spoken of in each of them; not, however, the same in all of them, either of them toward one another or toward the one of them all. Each of the things that have been said must be met by itself.
!flag and have no significance outside of this sphere | The Greek says one thing is in that part "of the All" (τοῦ παντός) we call above, and another in what is called below; "no significance outside of this sphere" is MacKenna's.
!flag there does exist an actuality implicit in each one of the relations cited | The Greek says there is "some existence" (ὑπόστασίς τις) of each of the things spoken of; "actuality" is MacKenna's, and "relations" is his word for them.
!note Right and left, above and below as relations that have some existence, against the Stoics who made relative things nothing: VI.1.7-9. Aristotle's place has its up and down by nature (Physics IV.1, 208b12-22).
@ch VI.6.13 | The one is not taken from the things
How could the thought of the one come from the thing perceived, a man or a stone, when what appears is one thing and the one another? Thought, seeing something, says "one", as it says "here" seeing a position; the one is before "alone", before "other" and "different", and both the speaker and what he speaks of are one first. An army, a house, the continuous are one more and less, and the more and less is only among the beings: the one is a nature that exists, intelligible, seen in perceptible things by sharing. Without the one nothing can be thought or said; so it is before substance and begets it. "This" too is not empty, but points to a thing that is there.

@p
How, then, would it be reasonable that the thought of the one should come from the underlying thing, from the man in perception, or any other living being, or even a stone, when what appeared is one thing, and the one is another, and not the same? For then thought would not predicate the one of what is not a man as well. Next, just as with the right and such things it is not moved idly, but, seeing a different position, said "here", so here too it sees something when it says "one": for it does not say "one" as an empty affection and upon nothing. For it is not because it is alone and not another: for in "and not another" it says another one. Then the other and the different are later: for if thought has not leaned on one, it will say neither other nor different; and when it says "alone", it says "one alone": so that it says "one" before "alone".
!flag a presentation of that order is something very different from unity (which must be a thing of the Intellectual) | The Greek says only that "what appeared is one thing, and the one is another" (ἄλλου μὲν ὄντος τοῦ φανέντος, ἄλλου δὲ ... τοῦ ἕν); the bracketed words are MacKenna's.
!flag the mind does not affirm in some caprice but from observation of contrasted position | The Greek says thought "is not moved idly" (οὐ μάτην κινουμένη), but, "seeing a different position", says "here"; "caprice" is MacKenna's.
!flag Besides Otherness and Difference are later | The Greek has "the other and the different" (τὸ ἄλλο καὶ τὸ ἕτερον), the words just used, "another" and "not another"; "otherness" belongs to ἑτερότης, the kind, and the capitals are MacKenna's.
!note "Moved idly" (μάτην) answers the objection of chapter 12 that the one is an empty affection of the soul. That the other and the different are later than one: Plato's Parmenides (143b-c), where one and being, and the different, make two.

@p
@greek ἔπειτα τὸ λέγον
Next, what speaks is one before it says "one" about another, and what it speaks of is one before anyone says or thinks anything about it. For it is either one, or more than one and many; and if many, one must exist before. For when it says "multitude", it says more than one; and when it says "army", it thinks of many under arms and ranked together into one; and if thought does not let it be a multitude, though it is one, plainly here too it does this either by giving the one that the multitude does not have, or by quickly seeing the one that comes from the ordering, and gathering the nature of the many into one. For not even here is the one false, just as with a house the one is from many stones, though with a house the one is more.
!flag the object is a unity before any outside affirmation or conception | The Greek says what it speaks of "is one before anyone says or thinks anything about it" (πρὶν εἰπεῖν ἢ νοῆσαί τινα περὶ αὐτοῦ); "outside" is MacKenna's.
!flag In refusing to allow the manifold to remain manifold, the mind makes the truth clear | The Greek says "if thought does not let it be a multitude, though it is (one), plainly here too it does" one of two things: it gives the one, or sees it in the order; the clearness is in the argument, not truth made clear by the mind.
!note The army and the house as one from many: Aristotle's kinds of one, by order and by continuity (Metaphysics Δ.6, 1016a1-17, and I.1, 1052a19-25). In VI.9.1 Plotinus begins with the same examples: an army, a chorus, a flock, a house, a ship.

@p
@greek εἰ οὖν μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τοῦ συνεχοῦς
If, then, the one is more with what is continuous, and more with what is not divisible, plainly it is because the one is a nature that is and exists. For the more cannot be among what is not; but just as, predicating substance of each perceptible thing, and predicating it also of the intelligibles, we make the predication more properly of the intelligibles, setting the more and the more proper among the beings, and being is more in substance, even perceptible substance, than in the other kinds, so too, seeing the one more and more properly, differing by the more among the perceptible things themselves and among the intelligibles, we must say that it is in all the ways, but in reference to one.
!flag something which is a Nature or Principle of Unity | The Greek says the one is "a nature that is and exists" (ὄντος τινὸς φύσεως τοῦ ἑνὸς καὶ ὑφεστώσης); "Principle of Unity" is MacKenna's.
!flag we must similarly admit that Unity exists under all forms though still by reference, only, to that primal Unity | The Greek says the one is "in all the ways" (κατὰ πάντας τοὺς τρόπους), but "in reference to one" (εἰς ἀναφορὰν ... ἑνός); "that primal Unity" is MacKenna's.
!note "In reference to one" (πρὸς ἕν, here εἰς ἀναφορὰν ἑνός) is Aristotle's way of saying how being is said in many ways (Metaphysics Γ.2, 1003a33-b10); Plotinus uses it of the one. Substance said of perceptible and intelligible things, but more properly of the intelligible: VI.1.2-3 and VI.3.1.

@p
@greek ὥσπερ δὲ ἡ οὐσία καὶ τὸ εἶναι
And as substance and being are intelligible and not perceptible, even if the perceptible shares in them, so too the one might be seen about the perceptible by sharing, but thought takes it as intelligible, and in an intelligible way: so that from one thing it thinks another, which it does not see; so it knew it before. And if it knew it before, being this thing here, the same as being; and when it says "some one thing", it says "one" again: as when it says "some two" and "some many".
!flag The mind, from a thing present to it, comes to knowledge of something else | The Greek says thought "from one thing thinks another, which it does not see" (ἀπ’ ἄλλου ἄλλο νοεῖ, ὃ οὐχ ὁρᾷ); "comes to knowledge" is MacKenna's.
!note "It knew it before" (προῄδει): Plato's recollection, where seeing equal sticks and stones we think of the equal itself, which we must have known before (Phaedo 74a-75a).

@p
@greek εἰ τοίνυν μήτε τι νοῆσαι
If, then, it is not possible either to think or to say anything without one, or two, or some number, how can that not be, without which it is not possible to think or say anything? For to say that that is not, without whose being nothing whatever can be thought or said, is impossible; but what is needed everywhere for the coming to be of every thought or speech must exist before both speech and thought, for so it could be taken up for their coming to be. And if it is needed also for the existence of each substance (for nothing is a being that is not one), it would be before substance, and begetting substance. That is why it is "one being", but not being and then one: for in "being and one" there would be many, but in "one" there is no being, unless it were to make it, inclining to its begetting.
!flag Unity must precede Reality and be its author | The Greek says it would be "before substance, and begetting substance" (πρὸ οὐσίας ... καὶ γεννῶν τὴν οὐσίαν); the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag It is, therefore, an existent Unity, not an existent that develops Unity | The Greek says "it is one being, but not being and then one" (ἓν ὄν, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ὄν, εἶτα ἕν): the one comes first in the name; "develops" is MacKenna's.
!note "One being" (ἓν ὄν) is the one of the Parmenides' second hypothesis (142b-143a), in which being and one at once make many. The one that makes being "inclining" (προσνεῦσαν) to its begetting is said carefully: elsewhere the One makes without inclining (V.1.6).

@p
@greek καὶ τὸ τοῦτο δὲ οὐ κενόν
And "this" too is not empty: for it speaks of an existence that is pointed to, in place of its name, and of a certain presence, a substance or some other of the beings; so that "this" would mean something not empty, nor is it an affection of thought upon nothing that is, but there is a thing underlying, as if one were to speak its own name.
!flag the This shows a thing present, as much as if we used the strict name of the object | The Greek says "there is a thing underlying" (ἔστι πρᾶγμα ὑποκείμενον), as if one spoke "its own name" (τὸ ἴδιον αὐτοῦ ... ὄνομα); "strict" is MacKenna's.
!note "This" (τόδε τι, τοῦτο), Aristotle's mark of substance (Categories 5, 3b10-13); the Stoics made "something" (τί) their highest kind, to which chapter 12's objection belonged.
@ch VI.6.14 | Number is not a relation
Against the view that the one is a relation: the one does not lose its nature when something else is affected and it is not; to go out of one it must be divided. A bulk divided into two did not perish as bulk, so the one was present in it besides the underlying thing; what is now present and now absent is among the beings. One added to one does not become two; two is predicated of both. Two comes both by joining and by splitting, so it is not a relation. One is one by the presence of the one, two by the dyad, as white by white and just by the just; and quantity, both the continuous and the discrete, is among the beings. How things share in number is the question of all sharing; in the intelligible the truest numbers are by themselves, the decad itself.

@p
To what was said about relation one might reasonably say that the one is not such that, when another is affected and it is affected in nothing, it has lost its own nature; but, if it is to go out of the one, it must have undergone the privation of the one, divided into two or more. If, then, the same bulk, divided, becomes two, without perishing as bulk, plainly the one was present in it besides the underlying thing, and it threw the one away when the division destroyed it. And what is present to the same thing at one time and gone from it at another, how shall we not rank it among the beings, wherever it is? And we must say it belongs to these things as an accident, but is by itself, both when it appears in the perceptible and in the intelligible: an accident in the later things, but by itself in the intelligible, in the first, when it is one, and then being.
!flag The Unity is not of a nature to lose its own manner of being only because something else stands in a state which it does not itself share | The Greek says the one does not lose its nature "when another is affected (ἄλλου παθόντος) and it is affected in nothing"; to go out of one it must itself undergo "the privation of the one" (τὴν τοῦ ἑνὸς στέρησιν). The modern version keeps "privation".
!flag must be classed among Real-Beings, regardless of position | The Greek asks "how shall we not rank it among the beings, wherever it is?" (ὅπου ἂν ᾖ); "regardless of position" is MacKenna's.
!flag especially in the First in its aspect of Unity developing into Being | The Greek says it is by itself in the intelligible "in the first, when it is one, and then being" (τῷ πρώτῳ, ὅταν ἕν, εἶτα ὄν): the first of the intelligibles, which is one before it is being; "developing" is MacKenna's.
!note This answers the objection of chapter 12, that the one is a relation like right and above. That one is relative (πρός τι), changing when its correlative changes though it is not affected itself, is the Stoics' account of relatives "in a certain disposition" (VI.1.7-8).

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις λέγοι, ὡς καὶ τὸ ἓν
But if someone says that the one too, affected in nothing, will be no longer one but two when another comes to it, he will not speak rightly. For the one did not become two, neither what it was added to nor what was added; but each stays one, as it was; and two is predicated of both, while one is predicated of each apart, as it stays. So two and the dyad are not by nature in a relation. If it were by the coming together, and being in a coming together were the same as making two, perhaps such a relation would be two and the dyad; but as it is, a dyad is seen again in the contrary happening too: for when some one thing is split, it becomes two. So two is neither a coming together nor a splitting, so that it would be a relation. The same account holds for every number. For when it is a relation that begets something, the contrary relation cannot beget the same thing, so that this thing would be the relation.
!flag If one configuration produces a certain thing it is impossible that the opposite should produce the same | The Greek has "when it is a relation (σχέσις) that begets something, the contrary relation cannot beget the same"; "configuration" is MacKenna's.
!note Two by joining and two by splitting, neither the cause: Plato's Phaedo (96e-97b, 101b-c), where Socrates cannot see how one added to one, or one split, should make two, and says that two is two only by sharing in the dyad.

@p
@greek τί οὖν τὸ κύριον αἴτιον
What, then, is the cause in the proper sense? That a thing is one by the presence of the one, and two by the presence of the dyad, as also white by white, and beautiful by the beautiful, and just by the just. Or we must not lay it down that these are either, but they are relations, and the cause in these too must be found so: that a thing is just because of such a relation to such things, and beautiful because we are disposed so, though there is nothing in the underlying thing itself such as to dispose us, nor anything brought in that comes to what appears beautiful.
!flag Unity is due to the presence of Unity ; duality to that of Duality | The Greek says a thing is "one by the presence (παρουσίᾳ) of the one, and two by the dyad": the language of the Phaedo; the capitals are MacKenna's.
!flag Beauty from a certain pattern of the person | The Greek says a thing would be beautiful "because we are disposed so" (ὅτι οὕτω διατιθέμεθα): the beauty would be in our being affected, not in a pattern of the person.
!note "By the presence" (παρουσίᾳ): Plato's Phaedo (100d), where the beautiful is beautiful by the presence or sharing of the beautiful itself. Beauty as our being disposed, not in the thing, is the view I.6.1 rejects.

@p
@greek ὅταν τοίνυν ἴδῃς τι ἓν
When, then, you see something that you call one, it is surely great too in every case, and beautiful, and one could say ten thousand things about it. As, then, the great and magnitude are in it, and sweet and bitter and other qualities, why not the one too? For surely it will not be that every quality whatever exists, but quantity will not be among the beings; nor that the continuous is quantity, but the discrete will not be, though the continuous uses the discrete as its measure. So, as a thing is great by the presence of magnitude, so it is one by the presence of the one, and two by the dyad, and the rest in the same way.
!flag that thing possesses also size, form, and a host of other characteristics | The Greek says it is "great too, and beautiful" (καὶ μέγα καὶ καλόν), and ten thousand things could be said of it; "form" is MacKenna's.
!flag quantity (Number) has not | The Greek has only "quantity" (ποσότης); the bracketed "(Number)" is MacKenna's gloss, though the argument is about the discrete quantity, which is number.
!note Continuous and discrete quantity, and number as the discrete: Aristotle, Categories 6 (4b20-25). That the continuous is measured by the discrete, by number of units: Metaphysics I.1 (1052b20-24) and VI.3.13.

@p
@greek τὸ δὲ ζητεῖν πῶς μεταλαμβάνει
And to ask how it shares in it is common to the sharing in all the forms. But we must say that the decad present is seen in one way in things that are divided, and in another in the continuous, and in another in the many powers, so many, brought into one; and that in the intelligibles it has already gone up, and there, no longer seen in others, but being themselves by themselves, the truest numbers are: the decad itself, not a decad of some intelligibles.
!flag in the looser totals is different from its presence in the continuous | The Greek has "in things that are divided" (ἐν ... τοῖς διῃρημένοις), things apart from one another; "looser totals" is MacKenna's.
!flag Dekad-Absolute not Dekad of some particular Intellectual group | The Greek has "the decad itself (αὐτοδεκάδα), not a decad of some intelligibles"; the modern version keeps "intelligible".
!note How things share in the forms is the old difficulty of the Parmenides (130e-131e), which VI.4 and VI.5 answered for being.

@ch VI.6.15 | Number before the living being; intellect, being, and the true number
To say it again: the whole true being is being and intellect and the complete living being, and this All imitates its one as it could. It must be all number; if any number were missing it would not be complete; so number is before the living being. In intellect the intellects are parts, and their number too; intellect's acts, its justice, self-control, virtues and knowledge, are in it in the first way, since there the knower, the known and the knowledge are the same; in soul they are accidents. Then being, and number in it: being begets the beings moving by number, divided by the powers of number into as many as it wished. So number is principle and spring of existence to the beings, and here too things come to be with numbers. The first numbers are numbered; those in other things also number.

@p
For let us say again from the beginning, though this has been said already, that the whole true being there is being and intellect and the complete living being, and all living beings together; whose one this living being too, the All, has imitated with one, as far as it could: for the nature of the perceptible fled the one there, if it was to be perceptible. It must, then, be all number: for if it were not complete, it would fall short by some number; and if all the number of living beings were not in it, it would not be a complete living being. So number is before every living being and before the complete living being.
!flag for the sense-nature as such cannot compass that transcendental unity | The Greek says "the nature of the perceptible fled (ἔφυγε) the one there, if it was to be perceptible": the perceptible had to escape the one to be perceptible at all; "transcendental" is MacKenna's.
!flag thus that Living-All is inevitably Number-Entire | The Greek says "it", the whole true being of the first sentence, "must be all number" (ἀριθμὸν δὴ δεῖ αὐτὸ εἶναι σύμπαντα), not the living All, this world, which only imitates it.
!note "This All imitates" the complete living being: Plato's Timaeus (30c-31b, 39e), where the world is made like the living being that holds all intelligible living beings, "one and alone", so that it may be like it in being alone.

@p
@greek ʽ??ʼ μὲν δὴ ἄνθρωπος
Man, then, is in the intelligible, and the other living beings, in so far as it is, and in so far as that is a complete living being: for the man here too, in so far as the All is a living being, is a part of it; and each, in so far as it is a living being, is there in the living being. And in intellect, in so far as it is intellect, all the intellects are, each, as parts: and there is a number of these too. So number is not in intellect in the first way either; but it is in intellect as are all the activities of intellect, and as intellect's justice and self-control and the other virtues, and knowledge, and all that intellect has and is really intellect by having.
!flag and man is There also, in the Intellectual, in so far as he is intellect | The Greek says "in intellect, in so far as it is intellect, all the intellects are, each, as parts" (ὡς μὲν μέρη οἱ νοῖ πάντες καθέκαστον); it is the many intellects that are in intellect, not man as intellect.
!flag its presence There is the reckoning of the Acts of Intellectual-Principle | The Greek says number is in intellect "as are all the activities of intellect" (ὅσα νοῦ ἐνέργειαι), among them, not as their reckoning.
!flag its moral wisdom, its virtues, its knowledge | The Greek has σωφροσύνη, "self-control", and "the other virtues" (αἱ ἄλλαι ἀρεταί); "moral wisdom" is MacKenna's.
!note The Greek text as First1KGreek gives it has a damaged word at the start of this paragraph, shown as question marks; the sense, "man, then, is in the intelligible", is plain. The many intellects as parts of intellect: VI.2.20-22 and IV.8.3.

@p
@greek πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἐν ἄλλῳ ἡ ἐπιστήμη
How, then, is knowledge not in another? Because the knower, the known and the knowledge are the same and together, and the rest likewise. That is why each is there in the first way, and justice is not an accident; but to soul, in so far as it is soul, it is an accident: for in soul these are rather potentially, and actually when it turns toward intellect and is with it.
!flag where these virtues are mainly potential becoming actual by the intention towards Intellectual-Principle | The Greek says they are actual "when it turns toward intellect and is with it" (ὅταν πρὸς νοῦν καὶ συνῇ); "intention" is MacKenna's, and the modern version keeps "virtues" and "intellect".
!note The knower, the known and the knowledge the same: Aristotle, On the soul III.4 (430a3-5), as in chapter 6. The soul's virtues potential until it turns to intellect: I.2.4-6.

@p
@greek μετὰ δὲ τοῦτο ἤδη τὸ ὂν
After this, then, being, and in it number, with which it begets the beings, moving according to number, having set the numbers before their existence, as its own one too joins being itself to the first; but the numbers no longer join the other things to the first, for it is enough that being is joined; and being, having become number, joins the beings to itself. For it is split, not in so far as it is one, but its one stays; and split, according to its own nature, into as many as it wished, it saw into how many, and begot the number, then, which was in it: for it was split by the powers of number, and begot as many as the number was. The first and true number, then, is principle and spring of existence to the beings.
!flag Next we come to Being, fully realised, and this is the seat of Number | The Greek says "after this, then, being, and in it number" (μετὰ δὲ τοῦτο ἤδη τὸ ὂν καὶ ἐν τούτῳ ὁ ἀριθμός); "fully realised" is MacKenna's.
!flag its movement is planned to Number | The Greek says being begets the beings "moving according to number" (κινούμενον κατ’ ἀριθμόν); "planned" is MacKenna's.
!note After intellect "being": here Plotinus goes up from the living being through intellect to being, the reverse of the order in which chapter 8 came down. Number as "principle and spring" (ἀρχὴ ... καὶ πηγή) of existence: chapter 9.

@p
@greek διὸ καὶ ἐνταῦθα μετ’ ἀριθμῶν
That is why here too the coming to be of each thing is with numbers; and if something takes another number, it either begets another thing or comes to be nothing. And these are the first numbers, as numbered; but those in the other things have both already: in so far as they come from these, they are numbered; in so far as they are according to these, they measure the other things, counting both the numbers and the things numbered. For by what would they say "ten" but by the numbers they have in themselves?
!flag to suppose another number than the actual is to suppose the production of something else or of nothing | The Greek says that if something "takes another number" (ἄλλον ἀριθμὸν λάβῃ), it begets another thing or comes to be nothing: a thing, not a supposition, takes the number.
!flag These then are the primal numbers; they are numerable | The Greek says they are the first numbers "as numbered" (ὡς ἀριθμητοί): numbers that are counted, the things numbered, not numbers that count; the others both count and are counted.
!note The numbers that are counted and the numbers we count with: Aristotle, Physics IV.11 (219b5-9), where number is both what is numbered and that by which we number.
@ch VI.6.16 | Where the true numbers belong: two numbers in us
In what kind of being are the first and true numbers? Number seems to be in quantity, and the one in perceptible things a principle of quantity. A dog and a man, or ten men, counted are purely quantity, not substance. But man by himself as two, living and rational, is a number of another kind, substantial, holding the thing's nature together; ten men counted have no unit, as a chorus or an army has, and are ten only in you who count. The number in us before counting is the number of our substance, by which the soul shares in number and harmony; the number we make by counting is an activity of it. A triad in the living being there is substantial; virtue as four is a tetrad that is.

@p
These, then, which we call first and true numbers, where would you place them, someone might say, and in what kind of the beings? For with everyone they seem to be in quantity; and you made mention of quantity earlier, when you thought it right to set the discrete among the beings like the continuous. And again you say that these numbers belong to the first beings, and again you say that there are other numbers besides them, which count. How, then, do you arrange these? Tell us: for it is very puzzling. And then, the one in perceptible things, is it some quantity? Or is the one many times quantity, but itself only a principle of quantity, and not quantity? And, being a principle, is it akin, or something else? It is only just that you make all this clear to us.
!flag but you go on to say that there are the numbers belonging to the Firsts and then talk of other numbers quite distinct, those of reckoning | The Greek says these numbers "belong to the first beings" (πρώτων ὄντων), and there are other numbers "which count" (ἀριθμοῦντας); "reckoning" is MacKenna's, and "the Firsts" with a capital makes them the gods of VI.5.
!flag or is quantity here just so many units brought together | The Greek asks whether "the one is many times quantity" (πολλάκις μὲν τὸ ἓν ποσόν): the one taken many times makes quantity, while the one itself is only its principle; "brought together" is MacKenna's.
!note Number in the category of quantity, and the one as the principle of number and not a number: Aristotle, Categories 6 (4b22-31) and Metaphysics Δ.6 (1016b17-21), N.1 (1088a4-8). Plotinus set the discrete among the beings in chapter 14, and quantity among the kinds of the perceptible in VI.3.11-15.

@p
@greek λεκτέον οὖν ἀρξαμένοις
We must speak, then, beginning from here: when (but we must first make the account for the perceptible things), when, then, taking one thing with another you say "two", a dog and a man, for example, or two men or more, saying "ten" and "a decad of men", this number is not a substance, not even as there is substance in perceptible things, but is purely quantity; and dividing it one by one, and making the ones parts of this decad, you make and set down the one as principle of quantity: for one of the ten is not one by itself.
!flag the number affirmed is not a Reality, even as Reality goes in the sphere of sense | The Greek says this number is "not a substance (οὐσία), not even as (there is) in perceptible things"; the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag since the single individual is not a unity absolute | The Greek says "one of the ten is not one by itself" (οὐχ ἓν καθ’ αὑτό); "individual" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ὅταν δὲ τὸν ἄνθρωπον αὐτὸν
But when you speak of man himself, by himself, as a number, a dyad, for example, living being and rational, the way is no longer one here: but in so far as you go through it and count, you make a quantity; and in so far as the underlying things are two, and each is one, if each one fills up the substance, and the oneness is in each, you speak of another number, substantial. And this dyad is not later, nor does it only say how much from outside the thing, but it is what is in the substance and holds the nature of the thing together. For you do not make number here, going through things in your going through that are by themselves, and do not come together in being counted. For what would come to be toward substance for one man counted with another?
!flag in that he is at once living and reasoning | The Greek has "living being and rational" (ζῷον καὶ λογικόν), the two parts of the old definition of man, not two things he does.
!flag even the duality so formed is no posterior | The Greek says this dyad is "not later" (οὐχ ὕστερον) than the thing, and does not "only say how much from outside the thing"; it is not formed by our counting, as "so formed" suggests.
!note "Man, a rational living being" (ζῷον λογικόν) is the definition of the schools after Aristotle; its two parts fill up the substance, as genus and difference do (Metaphysics Z.12, 1037b8-1038a35).

@p
@greek οὐδὲ γάρ τις ἑνάς, ὥσπερ ἐν χορῷ
For there is no unit, as there is in a chorus; but this decad of men would have its existence in you who count, and in the ten that you count, not ranked together into one, it would not even be called a decad; but you make ten by counting, and this ten is of quantity; but in the chorus and in the army there is also something outside. But how is it in you? The number lying in you before you count is in another way; but the number that comes from the appearing of things outside toward the number in you is an activity, either of those numbers or according to them, as you count and at the same time beget number, and in the activity make a quantity exist, as in walking too you make some motion exist.
!flag in the ten of your reckoning there cannot be a dekad without a unitary basis | The Greek says in the ten you count, "not ranked together into one" (μὴ συντεταγμένοις εἰς ἕν), "it would not even be called a decad"; "unitary basis" is MacKenna's.
!flag is either an Act of these inherent numbers or an Act in accordance with them | The Greek says it is "an activity (ἐνέργεια), either of those numbers or according to them": the modern version keeps "activity".
!note The chorus and the army as one by order: chapter 13, and Aristotle, Politics III.3 (1276b4-6), where the chorus stays one while its members change.

@p
@greek πῶς οὖν ἄλλως ὁ ἐν ἡμῖν
How, then, is the number in us in another way? It is the number of our substance: "sharing", he says, "in number and harmony", and again number and harmony; for "it is neither body", someone says, "nor magnitude": so the soul is number, if it is substance. The number of the body is substance, as body; that of the soul substances, as souls. And in general with the intelligibles, if the living being there is itself more, a triad, for example, this triad is substantial, the one in the living being. But the triad that is not yet of a living being, but simply a triad in being, is a principle of substance.
!flag It is the Number of our essence | The Greek says "the number of our substance" (ὁ τῆς οὐσίας ἡμῶν); the modern version keeps "substance", where MacKenna has "essence".
!flag soul, then, is Number since it is essence | The Greek says "so the soul is number, if (εἴπερ) it is substance": a condition, and "substance" again.
!note "Sharing in number and harmony": the soul of Plato's Timaeus (36e-37a), which "shares in reasoning and harmony" (λογισμοῦ ... μετέχουσα καὶ ἁρμονίας), made of number and proportion (35b-36b). The soul "a self-moving number" was Xenocrates' definition (Aristotle, On the soul I.2, 404b27-30), as VI.5.9 recalled. "Neither body nor magnitude": that the soul is no body is argued in IV.7.1-8.

@p
@greek εἰ δ’ ἀριθμοῖς ζῷον καὶ καλόν
But if you count living being and beautiful, each is one, and you beget a number in you and put into act a quantity, and a dyad. If, however, you were to call virtue four, it is also a tetrad, as its parts are into one; and you call the underlying thing a unit-tetrad, and you fit to it the tetrad in you.
!flag But when you declare virtue to be a Tetrad, you are affirming a Tetrad which does actually exist | The Greek says "it is also some tetrad" (καὶ τετράς ἐστί τις), as its parts are into one: the virtue is four in its substance, as man is two; the modern version keeps "virtue" for ἀρετή.
!note Virtue four: the four virtues of Plato's Republic IV (427e-434d), wisdom, courage, self-control and justice, which Plotinus treats in I.2; and the Pythagoreans' justice as four (chapter 5).
@ch VI.6.17 | The unlimited number, the line itself and the first figures
What of the so-called unlimited number? The unlimited is at war with number; we call it unlimited as we call a line unlimited, because we can always think of a greater, doubling it in thought. Is there an unlimited line in the intelligible? It would be unlimited not as what cannot be gone through, but because the account of the line itself has no limit in it. The line there is later than number, and is a thing, though intelligible; the figures are there before bodies, without shape, first figures, the pyramid for the fire there. They are in intellect first, and in the living being: intellect has the bare sphere, the living being the sphere of a living being.

@p
What, then, of the so-called unlimited number? For these arguments give it a limit. And rightly, if it is to be number: for the unlimited is at war with number. Why, then, do we say "number is unlimited"? Is it as we call a line unlimited? We call a line unlimited, not because there is such a line, but because it is possible, at the greatest, the line of the All, for example, to think of a greater. So too with number: when it is known how great it is, it is possible to make it double in thought, not joining it to that: for how could you fasten to the beings the thought and imagination that is in you alone?
!flag does not all this reasoning set it under limit ? | The Greek says "these arguments give it a limit" (πέρας ... διδόασιν), as a statement, not a question.
!flag that of the (path of the) universe | The Greek has only "the line of the All" (τοῦ παντός), the greatest line there is, its diameter; "(path of the)" is MacKenna's.
!flag though not of course to produce the doubled quantity | The Greek says one doubles it in thought "not joining it to that" (οὐκ ἐκείνῳ συνάψαντα), the number known: the double is not added to the things.
!note "The unlimited is at war with number": the unlimited only potential, by adding, and no actual unlimited number: Aristotle, Physics III.5-7 (204b7-10, 206b3-207b15). The unlimited in number, as many as there are, is chapter 18's answer.

@p
@greek ἢ φήσομεν ἄπειρον ἐν τοῖς νοητοῖς
Or shall we say that there is an unlimited line in the intelligibles? For the line there would be of some quantity. But if it is not of some quantity, it would be unlimited in number. Or the unlimited is in another way, not as what cannot be gone through. But how unlimited? Because in the account of the line itself there is no limit thought in with it. What, then, is the line there, and where? For it is later than number, since the one is seen in it: for it is from one point and toward one dimension; and it does not have quantity, the measure of the dimension. But where is this? Only in a thought that defines, as it were? Or it is a thing too, though intelligible. For all things there are so, both intelligible and in a way the thing.
!flag It is our view that there does exist an infinite line, among the Intellectual Beings | The Greek asks it, "or shall we say (ἢ φήσομεν) that there is an unlimited line in the intelligibles?", and at once objects; it is not given as Plotinus' view.
!flag for There a line would not be quantitative | The Greek says the contrary: "the line there would be of some quantity" (ποσὴ γὰρ ἂν εἴη ἡ ἐκεῖ γραμμή), which is the objection; then "if it is not of some quantity", it would be unlimited in number. MacKenna reverses the first clause.
!flag In that the conception of the Absolute Line does not include the conception of limit | The Greek says "in the account (λόγῳ) of the line itself there is no limit thought in with it": the definition of a line, "length without breadth", sets no bound on its length.
!note "What cannot be gone through" (ἀδιεξίτητον) is Aristotle's first sense of the unlimited (Physics III.4, 204a3-7). The line "length without breadth", from a point: Euclid, Elements I, definitions 2-3; Aristotle reports that Plato called the point "the beginning of a line" (Metaphysics A.9, 992a20-22).

@p
@greek καὶ δὴ καὶ περὶ ἐπιπέδου
And so too with the plane and the solid and all the figures, where and how they are: for it is not we who think up the figures. A witness is the figure of the All, before us, and the other natural figures in the things that are by nature, which must be there before the bodies, without shape, and first figures. For they are not shapes in other things, but, being their own, they did not need to be stretched out: for what is stretched out belongs to others. In being, then, the figure is always one, and it was divided either in the living being or before the living being. I say "divided" not because it was made great, but because each was parted out to each, as the living being is, and given to the bodies there, the pyramid there, if you like, to the fire there. That is why this fire too wishes to imitate it, though it cannot, because of matter; and the others in proportion, as is said about the things here.
!flag There is a position, as well as a manner of being, for all configurations | The Greek asks "where and how" (ποῦ καὶ ὅπως) the figures are, the question of the line put again; "position" is MacKenna's.
!flag the configurations of the universe are obviously antecedent to ourselves | The Greek has "the figure of the All" (τὸ τοῦ παντὸς σχῆμα), one figure, the sphere, as a witness that the figures are not our making.
!flag and so of all the rest as we read in the account of the realm of sense | The Greek says "and the others in proportion (ἀνὰ λόγον), as is said about the things here": the other elements have their figures as fire has its pyramid.
!note The pyramid is the figure of fire, the cube of earth, the octahedron of air and the icosahedron of water: Plato's Timaeus (55d-56b); the figure of the All is the sphere (Timaeus 33b). Fire "cannot, because of matter" imitate its figure: the receptacle's shaking (52d-53a).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ οὖν ἐν τῷ ζῴῳ
But are they in the living being, in so far as it is a living being? They are in intellect first. For they are in the living being; if, then, the living being held intellect, they would be in the living being in the first way; but if intellect is before in order, they are in intellect before. But if there are souls too in the complete living being, intellect is before. But he says "intellect sees all that are in the complete living being": if, then, it sees, it is later. Or it is possible that "sees" is said in this way, that the existence comes to be in the seeing: for it is not other, but all are one, and thinking has the bare sphere, but the living being the sphere of a living being.
!flag But does the Life-Form contain the configurations by the mere fact of its life ? | The Greek asks whether they are in the living being "in so far as it is a living being" (καθ’ ὃ ζῷον); "by the mere fact of its life" is MacKenna's.
!flag the Act of the Intellectual-Principle possesses itself of bare sphere | The Greek says "thinking (ἡ νόησις) has the bare sphere": the modern version keeps "thinking", and "the Act of the Intellectual-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!note "Intellect sees the forms that are in the living being that is, how many and what": Plato's Timaeus (39e), the passage Plotinus reads as making intellect later, and answers. The order being, intellect, living being: chapter 8.
@ch VI.6.18 | Number there is bounded; being suffices to itself
Number there is bounded: it is we who think of more than what is set out, and so count the unlimited. It might be called unlimited there because it is not measured: by what? It is all, one, together and whole, bounded by no limit but by itself; the things there are measures, and so all beautiful. The living being there has the best life, with no death in it, the first light by which the souls there live; the wisdom of all and the whole intellect colour it with good. Here we look mostly at the lifeless; there all are wholly living, and one who sees the substance going through them will laugh at the lower nature's claim to substance. From it life and intellect stay, and the beings stand in eternity; Parmenides was right to say being is one. It gives for ever, and all things hang from it and love its trace; to us being comes before the good; being is sufficient to itself.

@p
But number there is bounded; we shall think of more than what was set before us, and so the unlimited belongs to us who count. There it is not possible to think of more than what has been thought: for it is already; nor was any number left out, nor will one be, so that one might be added to it. It might be unlimited there too, because it has not been measured: for by what? But what it is, it is all, being one and together and whole, and not taken round by some limit, but being by itself what it is. For none of the beings at all is in a limit; but the limited and measured is what was hindered from running into the unlimited, and needs a measure; and those things are all measures, which is why they are all beautiful.
!flag no number has been or could be omitted to make addition possible | The Greek says no number "was left out (ἐλήφθη) nor will be" so that one might be added: none was taken out, as one takes from a heap.
!flag its manner of being is settled for it by itself alone | The Greek says it is "by itself what it is" (ἑαυτῷ ὢν ὃς ἔστι), bounded by itself and not by a limit; "settled" is MacKenna's.
!flag There every being is Measure | The Greek says "those things are all measures" (ἐκεῖνα δὲ πάντα μέτρα), many measures, not one capitalized Measure.
!note Measure and beauty: Plato's Philebus (64d-65a), "measure and proportion everywhere turn out to be beauty and virtue", and the limited as what the limit has stopped from running into the unlimited (24a-25b), as in chapter 3.

@p
@greek καὶ γάρ, ᾗ ζῷον, καλόν
For in so far as it is a living being, it is beautiful, having the best life, falling short in no life, nor again having its life mixed with death: for nothing there is mortal or dies. Nor again is the life of the living being itself feeble; it is the first life, the clearest, having the distinctness of living, like the first light, from which the souls both live there and bring it with them when they come here. And it knows for the sake of what it lives, and toward what it lives, from which it also lives: for that from which it lives is also that into which it lives. And the wisdom of all, and the whole intellect, being upon it and with it and together with it, colouring it with more good and mixing wisdom into it, makes its beauty more majestic. For here too a wise life is what is majestic and beautiful in truth, though it is seen dimly; but there it is seen purely. For it gives the one who sees sight, and power to live more, and, living with more strength, to see and to become what he sees.
!flag a life not tainted towards death | The Greek says its life is not "mixed with death" (πρὸς θάνατον συμμιγῆ); "tainted" is MacKenna's.
!flag Nor is the life of that Absolute Living-Form some feeble flickering | The Greek has "not feeble" (ἀμενηνή), as in chapter 8; "flickering" is MacKenna's.
!flag and close above it stands the wisdom of all, the collective Intellectual-Principle | The Greek says the wisdom of all and the whole intellect are "upon it and with it and together with it" (ἐπὼν καὶ συνὼν καὶ ὁμοῦ ὤν); the modern version keeps "wisdom" for φρόνησις and "intellect" for νοῦς, and the dots before these words in MacKenna's text are his.
!note The souls bringing the light with them when they come here: Plato's Phaedrus (248a-c, 250b-c), the souls that saw the beings before they fell. "To become what he sees" is the end of the ascent in VI.9.10-11 and V.8.11.

@p
@greek ἐνταῦθα μὲν γὰρ ἡ ποσβολὴ
For here our striking upon things is mostly toward the lifeless, and when it is toward living beings, what is not living in them is put forward, and the life within is mixed. But there all are living beings, and wholly living and pure; and even if you take one as not a living being, at once it has flashed out its life to you. And seeing the substance that has gone through them, giving them life unmoved to change, and their wisdom, and the wisdom and knowledge in them, you will laugh at all the nature below for its pretence to substance.
!flag Here attention is set for the most part upon the unliving | The Greek has "our striking upon things" (ἡ προσβολή), the impression things make on us; "attention" is MacKenna's.
!flag once you have known the Essence that pervades them | The Greek has "the substance (οὐσία) that has gone through them"; the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag you can but smile at all the lower nature with its pretention to Reality | The Greek says "you will laugh" (γελάσει) at its pretence "to substance" (εἰς οὐσίαν); the modern version keeps "substance".
!note The Greek names two wisdoms here, φρόνησις and σοφία, and the modern version gives both as "wisdom", as the fixed renderings ask. Laughing at the pretence of what is below: the bodies "that are thought to be most real" of V.5.11 and III.6.6.

@p
@greek παρὰ γὰρ ταύτης μένει μὲν ζωή
For from it life stays, intellect stays, and the beings stand in eternity; and nothing drives it out of itself, or turns it, or moves it aside: for there is no being after it that will touch it. And if there were something, it would be by this; and if there were something contrary, this would be unaffected by the contrary itself. But being itself, the contrary would not have made this being; but something else, common, before it, and that would be being: so in this way Parmenides was right to say that being is one. And it is unaffected not because it is bare of another, but because it is being. For to this alone it belongs to be from itself.
!flag In virtue of this Essence it is that life endures | The Greek says "from it (παρὰ ... ταύτης) life stays", from substance; "Essence" is MacKenna's.
!flag nothing, indeed, is in being beside it to touch it | The Greek says "there is no being after it" (μετ’ αὐτό) that will touch it; "beside" is MacKenna's.
!flag Being itself could not make such an opposite into Being | The Greek says the contrary, if it were a being, "would not have made this being" (οὐκ ἂν τοῦτο ἐποίησεν ὄν), but something common before both would be being: it is the contrary, not being, that would fail to make.
!flag Being is thus beyond contact not because it stands alone but because it is Being | The Greek says "unaffected" (ἀπαθές), as before; "beyond contact" is MacKenna's.
!note Parmenides' being one, unmoved, whole and unchanging: his fragment B8 (lines 5-6, 22-25), which V.1.8 also quotes. "In eternity" (ἐν αἰῶνι): III.7.3-4, where eternity is the life of being that stays in one.

@p
@greek πῶς ἂν οὖν τις τὸ ὂν
How, then, could anyone take away from it being, or anything else, all that is really in activity and all that comes from it? For as long as it is, it supplies; and it is always; so these are too. It is so great in power and beauty that it charms, and all things hang from it, and, having a trace of it from it, love it, and after this seek the good. For being is before that, as it seems to us; and this whole world too wishes to live and be wise, so that it may be; and every soul and every intellect wishes to be what it is; but being is sufficient to itself.
!flag As long as it exists it produces | The Greek says "as long as it is, it supplies" (χορηγεῖ), the word for the leader who pays for a chorus; "produces" is MacKenna's.
!flag and rejoicing to hold their trace of it and through that to seek their good | The Greek says they love it, "and after this seek the good" (μετὰ τοῦτο τἀγαθὸν ζητεῖν): being is loved first, the good sought after; "through that" is MacKenna's.
!flag all this world desires life and wisdom in order to Being | The Greek says this world wishes to live "and be wise" (φρονεῖν) so that it may be; the modern version keeps "wise".
!note "Being is before the good, as it seems to us": in the order of our desire, not in the order of things; the Good is beyond being (Republic VI 509b), and the One beyond being in VI.9.3 and V.5.6. MacKenna's chapter 18 runs past his p. 161 onto the top of p. 162, before VI.7, and ends with these words.
@treatise VI.7 | How the many forms came to be, and on the Good
The thirty-eighth treatise in the order of writing, one of those Plotinus wrote in the six years Porphyry was with him (Life 5), and one of the longest. It begins with the senses that God, or some god, gave the souls when he sent them into becoming, and asks from what he foresaw their need. There is no reasoning or foresight in the intelligible: Plato speaks of a reasoning god only to show that all is as a wise man would have reasoned it; there all is present at once, the what and the why are one, and each form holds its cause in itself (chapters 1 to 3). Then the man there: the man here is a forming principle in a soul, an image of a better man of a more divine soul, who is an image of the man in intellect; each of us is the man by which he is active; the perceptibles there are perceived as they are there, so that the perceptions here are dim thoughts, and the thoughts there bright perceptions (chapters 4 to 7). Why are horses and the irrational living beings in intellect? What comes after the altogether one must be many, a complete living being; the irrational there is intellect of a kind, and horns and claws are for completeness; the All there has its heaven, earth, sea and air, plants and fire, all living and flowing from one spring; and intellect wanders in itself through the plain of truth, one many, divided always inward, the true friendship of which this world's is an imitation (chapters 8 to 14). From there the treatise rises to the Good: intellect's life and its many forms are a trace of the Good, which gives what it does not have, and the forms are desired because the Good colours them, as beauty is loved only when the light from the Good comes upon it (chapters 15 to 23). The Good is not pleasure, nor the mixture of the Philebus, but that to which each thing turns; the soul that sees it loves a beauty without shape, and leaves all to be alone with it (chapters 24 to 36). Last, against those who make the first think, the Good does not think, nor need to know itself: it is beyond intellect (chapters 37 to 42).
@ch VI.7.1 | Why the senses were given
When God, or some god, sent the souls into becoming, he gave them eyes and the other senses, foreseeing that the living being would be kept safe so. But from what did he foresee it? Reasoning needs starting points, and they are either perception, which there was not yet, or intellect, whose conclusion is knowledge, not the perceptible. There is no reasoning there: it is spoken of to show that all is as a wise man would have reasoned it. In god all is present at once, the future as already there, so that later one can say "this because of this".

@p
When God, or some god, sent the souls into becoming, he set light-bearing eyes about the face, and gave the other organs to each of the senses, foreseeing that the living being would be kept safe in this way: if it saw ahead and heard ahead, and, by touching, fled one thing and pursued another. But from what did he foresee these things? For it was not that other living beings came to be first, and then, when they perished for want of senses, he gave afterwards what men and the other animals would have to guard themselves from suffering.
!flag placed eyes in the face to catch the light | The Greek has "light-bearing eyes" (φωσφόρα ... ὄμματα), the Timaeus' word: eyes that bring light out, not eyes that catch it.
!flag providing thus for the safety which comes by seeing and hearing in time | The Greek has "if it saw ahead and heard ahead" (εἰ προορῷτο καὶ προακούοι), the same prefix as the god's foreseeing (προορώμενος): the senses are the living being's own foresight.
!flag But what led to this provision ? | The Greek asks "from what (πόθεν) did he foresee these things?": the source of the foresight, which the chapter goes on to seek, not what led to the provision.
!note "Light-bearing eyes" (φωσφόρα ὄμματα) are the first organs the young gods make in Plato's Timaeus (45b); the souls sent into becoming are those sown by the Demiurge in the Timaeus (41d-42e). The senses given for the living being's safety: Aristotle, On the soul III.12 (434b9-29).

@p
@greek ἢ εἴποι ἄν τις, ᾔδει
Or someone might say: he knew that the living being would be among hot and cold things and the other affections of bodies, and knowing this, so that the bodies of the living beings should not easily be destroyed, he gave them perceiving, and the organs through which the senses would be active. But either he gave the organs to souls that had the powers already, or he gave both. But if he gave the senses too, they were not perceptive before, though they were souls; and if they had them when they came to be souls, and came to be so that they might go into becoming, then going into becoming is inborn in them. Then it is against their nature to be away from becoming and in the intelligible; and they have been made to belong to another and to be in evil; and providence is this, that they should be kept safe in evil; and this is god's reasoning, and reasoning altogether.
!flag it is of their very nature to belong to process | The Greek says "going into becoming is inborn (σύμφυτον) in them": a going, not a belonging; and "process" is MacKenna's for γένεσις, "becoming".
!flag unnatural to them to be outside of process and within the Intellectual | The Greek has "in the intelligible" (ἐν τῷ νοητῷ); the modern version keeps "intelligible", and "the Intellectual" is MacKenna's.
!flag the divine provision would consist in holding them to their disaster | The Greek says providence is "so that they might be kept safe in evil" (ἵνα σώζοιντο ἐν τῷ κακῷ): the providence saves them in it, as the senses do, and does not hold them to it.
!flag this is God’s reasoned purpose, this the plan entire | The Greek says "this is god's reasoning, and reasoning altogether" (ὁ λογισμὸς ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ οὗτος καὶ ὅλως λογισμός): the objection ends by making god reason, which the chapter will deny; "purpose" and "plan" are MacKenna's.
!note That the soul's going into body is a fall, and yet in the order of the All, is the question of IV.8 (On the descent of the soul into bodies), where Plotinus sets the Phaedo's prison against the Timaeus' sowing.

@p
@greek ἀρχαὶ δὲ λογισμῶν
But what are the starting points of reasonings? For even if they come from other reasonings, one must surely go back to something, or some things, before reasoning. What, then, are the starting points? Either perception or intellect. But there was not yet perception: intellect, then. But if the premises are intellect, the conclusion is knowledge: about nothing perceptible, then. For how can what has its starting point from the intelligible, and comes at its end to the intelligible, arrive at this state, at a thought of the perceptible? So neither the providence of a living being, nor that of this whole All, came from reasoning.
!flag But sense-perception it cannot in this case be | The Greek says "there was not yet (οὔπω) perception": the senses had not yet been given, which is the point; "it cannot be" is MacKenna's.
!flag whether over living beings or over any part of the universe | The Greek says "nor that of this All altogether" (οὔθ’ ὅλως τοῦδε τοῦ παντός): the providence of the whole All, not of any part of it.
!note Every reasoning goes back to starting points that are not reasoned, perception or intellect: Aristotle, Posterior Analytics I.3 (72b18-25) and II.19 (100b5-17), where intellect (νοῦς) grasps the first principles and knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) is from them.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ ὅλως λογισμὸς ἐκεῖ
For there is no reasoning there at all; but it is called reasoning to show that all things are so as a wise man would have them from reasoning, in the things that come later; and foresight, because they are so as a wise man would foresee them in the things that come after. For in the things that did not come to be before reasoning, reasoning is useful, for lack of the power that is before reasoning; and foresight, because the one who foresees did not have a power by which he would have had no need of foresight. For foresight is so that this, and not that, may be, and it is as it were afraid of what is not such; but where there is only this, there is no foresight. And reasoning is "this instead of that". But if there is only one of the two, what does it even reason about? How, then, does what is alone and one and simple hold, unfolded, "this, so that not that"? Or "that would have been, if not this"? Or "this appeared useful, and this, once it came to be, saving"?
!flag we speak of reasoned purpose in the world of things only to convey that the universe is of the character which in the later order would point to a wise purposing | The Greek says all is "as a wise man (σοφός) would have it from reasoning in the things that come later": the reasoner is a wise man, and "the universe" and "purposing" are MacKenna's.
!flag Providence implies that things are as in the later order a competent foreplanning would produce them | The Greek has προόρασις, "foresight", not πρόνοια, "providence"; and it says again "as a wise man would foresee", where MacKenna has "a competent foreplanning would produce".
!flag The alone and one and utterly simplex cannot involve | The Greek asks how what is alone and one "holds, unfolded" (ἔχει ἀναπτυσσόμενον) "this, so that not that": the unfolding, which the chapter's end takes up again, is not in MacKenna.
!flag the serviceable thing appeared and at once approved itself so | The Greek has "this appeared useful, and this, once it came to be, saving" (σωτήριον): the safety of the chapter's first sentence; MacKenna leaves out the saving.
!note The reasoning god is the Timaeus' Demiurge, who "reasoned" (λογισάμενος, 30b) and "took thought beforehand" (34a-b). Plotinus reads it, here and in III.2.14 and V.8.7, as a way of showing the order of the All, not as deliberation in the god.

@p
@greek προείδετο ἄρα καὶ
So he did foresee, then, and did reason beforehand. And so what was said just now at the beginning holds: he gave the senses and the powers for this reason, however much at a loss one is about the giving, and how it was.
!flag But surely this is foreseeing, deliberating | The Greek is an objector's conclusion, not a question: "he foresaw, then, and reasoned beforehand" (προείδετο ἄρα καὶ προελογίσατο ἄρα).

@p
@greek οὐ μὴν ἀλλ’ εἰ δεῖ
Yet if each activity must not be incomplete, and if it is not right to think that anything whatever of god's is other than whole and all, then all things must be present in anything of his. So it must belong to what always is, and the future must be there as already present. There is nothing later in that one; what is already present there comes to be later in another. If, then, the future is already present, it must be present as having been thought out beforehand for what is later: that is, so as to need nothing then; and that is, so as to lack nothing. All things, then, already were, and always were, and were so that one could say later "this is because of this". For when it is stretched out and, as it were, unfolded, it can show "this after this"; but being all together, it is all "this": that is, it holds in itself its cause too.
!flag No: all turns on the necessary completeness of Act | The Greek says "if each activity (ἑκάστην ἐνέργειαν) must not be incomplete": each activity, not Act in general; and "No" is MacKenna's, where the Greek has "yet" (οὐ μὴν ἀλλ’).
!flag the All, in its extension and so to speak unfolding, is able to present succession while yet it is simultaneous | The Greek names no subject: what is stretched out and unfolded is what is in god, the all things; "the All" is MacKenna's.
!flag this is because it contains the cause of all as inherent to itself | The Greek says "it holds in itself its cause too" (ἔχον ἐν ἑαυτῷ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν): each thing its own cause, the theme of chapter 2; "the cause of all" is MacKenna's.
!note "All together" (ὁμοῦ πᾶν) is Parmenides' being (fragment B8, 5) and, in III.7.3 and III.7.11, the mark of eternity, where time is life stretched out (διάστασις). The future present "as already present": compare V.8.7, where the All's order was thought out before it, but not by reasoning.
@ch VI.7.2 | The what and the why are one there
Here we see that a thing is, but not why, or the why apart; there, all is in one, and the thing and its why are the same, as with an eclipse here. Each form, unfolded, holds its why: being intellect's, it lacks nothing, and comes to be together with its cause. As in this All all things are strung together, much more there each is toward the whole and toward itself, and holds its cause causelessly. The why is in the existence: the man there is whole from the beginning, and the man who comes to be is a thing come to be.

@p
This is why one could learn the nature of intellect from here no less, intellect which, though we see more of it than of the others, even so we do not see how great a thing intellect is. For we grant that it has the "that", but no longer the "why"; or, if we grant it, apart. And we see a man, or an eye, if it happens, as a statue, or a statue's part; but what is there is man and why man, if indeed the man there must himself be intellectual, and the eye, and why it is: or it would not be there at all, if not the why. But here, as each of the parts is apart, so too is the why. There, all things are in one, so that the thing and the why of the thing are the same.
!flag We know that it exists but its cause we do not see | The Greek says "we grant that it has the that (ὅτι), but no longer the why (διότι)": what we grant intellect holds, the that and the why of things, not our knowing that intellect exists.
!flag but this is an image or part of an image | The Greek says "as a statue (ἄγαλμα) or a statue's part": the word for an image of a god set up to be seen; "image" is MacKenna's.
!flag In the Intellectual all is at one | The Greek says "there" (ἐκεῖ); "the Intellectual" is MacKenna's.
!note The "that" (τὸ ὅτι) and the "why" (τὸ διότι) are Aristotle's pair, Posterior Analytics I.13 (78a22-b34) and II.1 (89b23-35).

@p
@greek πολλαχοῦ δὲ καὶ ἐνταῦθα
In many cases here too the thing and the why are the same, as with what an eclipse is. What, then, prevents each thing from being its why in the other cases too, and this from being the substance of each? Rather, it must be so; and for those who try in this way, it turns out that they grasp the "what it was to be" rightly. For what each thing is, it is because of this. I mean, not that the form is the cause of each thing's being — that is true — but that, if you unfold each form itself toward itself, you will find the why in it.
!flag and this cause being the essence of the thing | The Greek has "the substance (οὐσίαν) of each"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "essence" is MacKenna's.
!flag by this search after the cause the thing’s essence is reached | The Greek has "the what it was to be" (τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι), Aristotle's phrase, grasped rightly by those who try in this way.
!flag I am not here saying that the informing Idea is the cause of the thing | The Greek has "the form" (τὸ εἶδος); "the informing Idea" is MacKenna's.
!note The eclipse, whose what and why are one (the earth's coming between), is Aristotle's example, Posterior Analytics II.2 (90a14-23) and II.8 (93a29-b7); "the what it was to be" (τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι) is his phrase for the essence (Metaphysics Z.4). The form as the cause of being: Plato's Phaedo (100c-e).

@p
@greek ἀργὸν μὲν γὰρ ὂν
For if it were idle, even having life, it would not altogether have the why; but being a form, and intellect's, from where would it get the why? And if someone said "from intellect", it is not apart from it, if indeed it is intellect itself. If, then, intellect must have these lacking in nothing, they must not lack the why either. Intellect has the why of each of the things in it in this way: the things in it are each of them it itself, so that none needs, besides, the why of its having come to be; but it came to be together with it, and holds in itself the cause of its existence. And having come to be not at random, it would have nothing of the why left out, but having all, it has together with it the "well" of its cause. And so it gives to the things that share in it in such a way that they have the why.
!flag A thing of inactivity, even though alive, cannot include its own cause | The Greek says that if it were idle (ἀργόν) it would "not altogether" (οὐ πάντως) have the why; "cannot" is MacKenna's.
!flag where could a Forming-Idea, a member of the Intellectual-Principle, turn in quest of its cause? | The Greek has "being a form (εἶδος), and intellect's (νοῦ)"; the modern version keeps "form" and "intellect", and "Forming-Idea" and "Intellectual-Principle" are MacKenna's.
!flag it is an integral and so includes the excellence bound up with the cause | The Greek says it has "the well (τὸ καλῶς) of its cause": that it is as it should be, which the cause gives with it; "excellence" is MacKenna's.
!note Things here "share" (μεταλαμβάνουσιν) in the form: Plato's Phaedo (100c-102b) and Parmenides (130e-131a).

@p
@greek καὶ μήν, ὥσπερ ἐν τῷδε
And indeed, as in this All, which stands together out of many, all things are strung together with one another, and in all things' being there is also the why of each, as in each thing too the part is seen to hold toward the whole, not this coming to be, and then that after this, but the cause and the caused standing together toward one another at once: so, much more, must all things there be each toward the whole, and each toward itself. If, then, the existing-together of all is at once, and not at random, and they must not hang apart, the caused would have their causes in themselves, and each would be such as to have its cause causelessly. If, then, they have no cause of their being, but are self-sufficient and alone, apart from a cause, they would hold their cause in themselves, with themselves. And again, if nothing there is in vain, and the many in each thing are all that it has, you could say why each is.
!flag must all the singles exist for the whole and each for itself | The Greek has "toward" (πρὸς τὸ ὅλον ... πρὸς αὑτό): a holding toward the whole and toward itself, not existing for them as for a purpose.
!flag uncaused, independent and standing apart from cause, they must be self-contained, cause and all | The Greek is a condition: "if, then, they have no cause of their being" (εἰ οὖν μὴ ἔχει αἰτίαν τοῦ εἶναι), they would hold the cause in themselves; MacKenna makes it an assertion.
!note The All "strung together" (συνείρεται) and the part held toward the whole: the sympathy of the All in IV.4.32 and IV.4.40. Each thing's cause "causelessly" (ἀναιτίως): there is no cause before it, since it is its own why.

@p
@greek προῆν ἄρα καὶ συνῆν
The why, then, was there before and with it, not being a why but a that; or rather, both are one. For what would it have beyond intellect, as if it were a thought of intellect that was not such, a begotten thing not complete? If, then, it is complete, one cannot say in what it falls short, nor why this is not present. Being present, then, you could say why it is present: the why, then, is in the existence. In each thought and activity, then, as with man: the whole man appeared at once, bringing himself together with himself, and, having from the beginning all that he has together, he is ready, whole. Then, if he is not whole, but something must be added to him, he belongs to what is begotten. But he always is: so he is whole. But the man who comes to be is a thing come to be.
!flag not a cause but a fact of the being | The Greek says "not being a why (διότι), but a that (ὅτι)": the pair the chapter began with, now one.
!flag Take for example the Idea of Man; Man entire is found to contribute to it | The Greek says the whole man "appeared at once, bringing himself together with himself" (συμφέρων ἑαυτὸν αὐτῷ): he brings himself, and does not contribute to an Idea; "the Idea of Man" is MacKenna's.
!flag the man born is the derivative | The Greek says "the man who comes to be is a thing come to be" (γενητός): generated, as opposed to the man who always is; "derivative" is MacKenna's.
@ch VI.7.3 | Reasoning only on a supposition
Taking counsel beforehand about man is spoken of only because the account supposed things coming to be; saying that they always come to be takes it away, for there is no reasoning in the eternal. Things are beautiful with their cause: eyes and eyebrows are so that the thing may be all, and the cause is part of the substance. But if being perceptive is set in the form by everlasting necessity, how is intellect not leaning toward the things here, and how is it not absurd that the power there is fulfilled here only when the soul becomes worse?

@p
What, then, prevents his having taken counsel beforehand about him? Or he is in keeping with that one, so that nothing must be taken away or added; but the taking counsel and the reasoning are because of the supposition: for it supposed things coming to be. And so there is counsel and reasoning; but by showing them always coming to be, it took away his reasoning too. For there is no reasoning in what is always: it would belong to one who had forgotten how it was before, too. Then, if things are better later, they were not beautiful before; but if they were beautiful, they keep the same.
!flag insist on the eternity of the process and planning falls to the ground | The Greek says the account itself, by showing things "always coming to be" (ἀεὶ γινόμενα), took away that he reasons: it is the Timaeus' own account that takes the reasoning away, not our insisting.
!flag things stood ill at first ; if they stood well, so they must remain | The Greek says "they were not beautiful (καλά) before; but if they were beautiful, they keep the same": the beautiful, which the next paragraph takes up; "ill" and "well" are MacKenna's.
!note "It supposed things coming to be": Plato's Timaeus (28a-29a) tells of the world as coming to be. That this is "for the sake of teaching", as a geometer draws a figure that always is, was Xenocrates' reading, which Aristotle reports (On the heavens I.10, 279b32-280a2) and Plotinus follows (compare III.2.1).

@p
@greek καλὰ δ’ ἐστὶ μετὰ τῆς αἰτίας
And they are beautiful with the cause: since even now a thing is beautiful because it is all. For this is form too, its being all, and its holding matter fast: and it holds it fast if it leaves nothing of it unshaped; and it leaves something, if some shape is lacking, an eye, say, or something else. So when you give the cause, you say the whole. Why, then, eyes? So that it may be all. And why eyebrows? So that it may be all. For even if you said "for safety", you speak of a guarding of the substance present in it, and say that this contributes. So the substance was before this too, and the cause, then, was part of the substance: and this is another thing, but what it is belongs to the substance. All things, then, are toward one another, and the whole and complete and entire substance, and its "well" with the cause and in the cause; and the substance and the what it was to be and the why are one.
!flag Only in conjunction with their causes are things good; even in this sphere a thing is good in virtue of being complete | The Greek has "beautiful" (καλά, καλόν τι) both times: things are beautiful with their cause, and beautiful because they are all; "good" is MacKenna's.
!flag you affirm an indwelling safeguard of the essence | The Greek has "of the substance (τῆς οὐσίας)"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "essence" is MacKenna's.
!flag the being, the essence, the cause, all are one | The Greek says "the substance (ἡ οὐσία) and the what it was to be (τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι) and the why (τὸ διότι) are one": Aristotle's essence is the second of the three, and MacKenna's "the being" stands for the first.
!note The eyebrows as a guard for the eyes, against the sweat from the head, are in Xenophon's Memorabilia (I.4.6) and Aristotle's Parts of animals (II.15, 658b14-19). Form that "holds matter fast" (κατέχει) and leaves nothing unshaped is beauty in I.6.2.

@p
@greek εἰ τοίνυν ἔγκειται
If, then, being perceptive, and perceptive in this way, is set in the form by an everlasting necessity and completeness, since intellect has the causes in itself, if indeed it is complete, so that we see later that it is rightly so (for there the cause is one and fills the thing out, and it is not that the man there was intellect only, and the perceptive was added when he was sent into becoming), how would that intellect not lean toward the things here? For what would the perceptive be but what apprehends perceptible things? And how is it not absurd that there should be the perceptive there from everlasting, but perceiving here, and the activity of the power there fulfilled here, when the soul becomes worse?
!flag sense-perception—even in its particular modes—is involved in the Idea | The Greek says "being perceptive, and perceptive in this way (οὕτως)", is set "in the form" (ἐν τῷ εἴδει); "even in its particular modes" and "the Idea" are MacKenna's.
!flag thus Man in the Intellectual was not purely intellect, sense-perception being an addition made upon his entry into birth | The Greek denies both together: "it is not that the man there was intellect only, and the perceptive was added (προσετέθη) when he was sent into becoming". MacKenna keeps the addition as a fact, which the Greek denies.
