!note "Lean" (ῥέποι): the soul's inclining (νεῦσις, ῥοπή) toward the things here, I.1.12 and IV.8.4. The answer, that perception there is of the perceptibles there, is given in chapters 6 and 7.
@ch VI.7.4 | What is the man here?
First the man here: is he a forming principle other than the soul that makes him, or that soul, or the soul using a body? A forming principle of the compound of soul and body would not be everlasting, nor show the what it was to be; one must take the forming principle that made him. Man is rational life; but life is soul's, so man is either an activity of soul, and not a substance, or the soul itself; and then why is the soul not a man when it goes into another living being?

@p
Again, then, to meet this difficulty, we must take up from above who the man there is. But perhaps first we must say who the man here is, lest, not knowing exactly even this one, we seek that one as though we had this one. To some it might seem that this one and that one are the same.

@p
@greek ἀρχὴ δὲ τῆς σκέψεως ἐντεῦθεν
Let the inquiry begin from here: is this man a forming principle other than the soul that makes this man and gives him living and reasoning? Or is the soul of this kind the man? Or the soul that uses a body of this kind? But if man is a rational living being, and a living being is what is made of soul and body, this forming principle would not be the same as the soul.
!flag whether man as here is a Reason-Principle different to that soul | The Greek has λόγος; the modern version keeps "forming principle", and "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag or, again, the (yet lower) soul using the human body | The Greek says only "the soul that uses a body of this kind" (ἡ τῷ σώματι τῷ τοιῷδε ψυχὴ προσχρωμένη); "(yet lower)" is MacKenna's.
!note "A rational living being" (ζῷον λογικόν) is the school definition of man (compare Aristotle, Metaphysics Z.12, 1037b11-14, where man is a two-footed living being); the soul that uses the body is the man of Plato's Alcibiades (129e-130c), which I.1.3 takes up.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ τὸ ἐκ ψυχῆς λογικῆς
But if the forming principle of man is what is made of rational soul and body, how would it be an everlasting existence, since this forming principle of this kind of man comes to be when body and soul come together? For this forming principle will show what is going to be, not of the kind we call man himself, but rather like a definition, and such as does not even show the what it was to be. For it is not of the form in matter, but shows the compound, which already is: and if so, the man has not yet been found: for he was the one according to the forming principle.
!flag since what is indicated is not the Idea that is to enter Matter but only that of the known thing, the conjoint | The Greek says it is "not of the form in matter" (εἴδους ... τοῦ ἐνύλου), the form already in matter, "but shows the compound, which already is"; "that is to enter" and "the known thing" are MacKenna's.
!note "Man himself" (αὐτοάνθρωπος), the Platonists' word for the form of man: Aristotle, Metaphysics B.2 (997b8-10) and Nicomachean Ethics I.6 (1096a35-b5). The definition of the compound and of the form: Metaphysics Z.10-11 (1035b27-1037a5).

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις λέγοι
And if someone should say that the forming principle of such things must be some compound, this in this, he does not think fit to say that according to which each thing is. But even if one must speak of the forming principles of the forms in matter, and with matter, as much as one can, one must still take the forming principle itself that made it, the man, say; and most of all those who think fit to define the what it was to be for each thing, when they define in the strict sense.
!flag This does not define the principle of either. | The Greek says he "does not think fit to say that according to which each thing is" (καθ’ ὅ ἐστιν ἕκαστον): he leaves out what makes each thing what it is; "either" is MacKenna's.
!flag a complete definition must cover the essential manner of being | The Greek has "those who think fit to define the what it was to be (τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι) for each thing, when they define in the strict sense (κυρίως)": Aristotle's school, named by its phrase.
!note "This in this" (τόδε ἐν τῷδε), form in matter, is Aristotle's way of speaking of the snub, nose and concavity together (Metaphysics Z.5, 1030b16-26; On the soul III.4, 429b13-14).

@p
@greek τί οὖν ἐστι τὸ εἶναι ἀνθρώπῳ
What, then, is being for man? That is: what is it that made this man, present in him, not separate? Is the forming principle itself a rational living being, or is that the compound, and the forming principle itself something that makes a rational living being? What is it, itself? Or "living being" in the forming principle stands for rational life. Man, then, is rational life. Is it, then, life without soul? For either the soul will supply the rational life, and man will be an activity of soul and not a substance, or the soul will be the man. But if the rational soul is to be the man, when the soul goes into another living being, how is it not a man?
!flag What, then, is this essential of Man? | The Greek has "being for man" (τὸ εἶναι ἀνθρώπῳ), Aristotle's phrase for the essence of a kind; MacKenna's "this essential" loses the phrase.
!flag and what is it apart from that act of making ? | The Greek asks only "what is it, itself?" (τίς ὢν αὐτός;); "apart from that act of making" is MacKenna's.
!flag and man therefore is not an essence but simply an activity of the soul | The Greek has "not a substance (οὐσία)"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "essence" is MacKenna's.
!note The soul going into other living beings: Plato's Phaedo (81e-82b), Republic X (620a-d) and Timaeus (91d-92c); Plotinus takes it up in III.4.2 and in chapter 6 below.
@ch VI.7.5 | Three men, one above another
Man is a forming principle other than soul, as the forming principles in seeds are neither without soul nor simply souls. The soul that has come into this matter shapes another image of man in the body, as a painter paints a still lesser man, with dim characters and senses; above it is the man of a more divine soul, Plato's man "using a body", who rides on the soul that uses it first, does not leave the intelligible, and makes this dim man bright.

@p
Man, then, must be a forming principle other than the soul. What, then, prevents man from being a compound, soul in a forming principle of this kind, the forming principle being as it were an activity of this kind, and the activity unable to be without what is active? For so too are the forming principles in seeds: they are neither without soul, nor simply souls. For the forming principles that make are not soulless, and it is no wonder that such substances are forming principles.
!flag Man, thus, must be some Reason-Principle other than soul. | The Greek has λόγος; the modern version keeps "forming principle", and "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag there is nothing surprising in such essences being Reason-Principles | The Greek has "such substances (οὐσίας)"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "essences" is MacKenna's.
!note The forming principles in seeds (οἱ ἐν τοῖς σπέρμασι λόγοι) are the Stoics' seminal principles (λόγοι σπερματικοί, SVF II.1027), which Plotinus takes into nature's making (III.8.2, IV.4.39, V.9.6).

@p
@greek οἱ οὖν μὴ ποιοῦντες ἄνθρωπον
Then the forming principles that make not man, but other things, are activities of what kind of soul? Of the growing soul? Or of the soul that makes a living being, a brighter soul, and for this very reason more full of life. But the soul of this kind, which has come into matter of this kind, since it is this, being as it were so disposed even without the body, is man; and in a body, having shaped it after itself, and made another image of man, as much as the body received, as a painter too will make of this one again a still lesser man, it has the shape, and the forming principles, or the characters, the dispositions, the powers, all dim, because this is not the first; and so it has forms of other senses too, other senses which seem to be bright, but are dimmer compared with those before them, and images. But the man above this is of a soul already more divine, which has a better man and brighter senses.
!flag just as an artist may make a reduced image of that again | The Greek has "a painter" (ζωγράφος), who will make of this man "a still lesser man": the image of an image.
!flag It is soul, then, that holds the pattern and Reason-Principles of Man | The Greek has "the shape" (τὴν μορφήν); the modern version keeps "pattern" for παράδειγμα, and "Reason-Principles" is MacKenna's for the forming principles.
!note The painter who makes an image of an image, third from the truth: Plato's Republic X (597e-598b). The growing soul (φυτική) is the lowest power of soul, which plants have: Aristotle, On the soul II.4 (415a23-b2).

@p
@greek καὶ εἴη ἂν ὁ Πλάτων
And it would be this one that Plato defined, adding "using a body", because it rides upon the soul that uses a body first, while it uses it second. For when what came to be was already perceptive, this soul followed, giving a clearer life; or rather it did not even follow, but as it were added itself: for it does not stand out of the intelligible, but, joined to it, holds the lower soul as if hanging from it, mingling itself, forming principle with forming principle. Hence this man too, being dim, became plain by the illumination.
!flag This must be the Man of Plato’s definition | The Greek says "it would be (εἴη ἂν) this one that Plato defined": a likely reading of Plato, not a certainty; and MacKenna's quotation "Man is Soul" is his own.
!flag the soul, poised above, which touches body only through that intermediary | The Greek says it "rides upon" (ἐποχεῖται) the soul that uses body first, as on a vehicle, and uses it "second" (δευτέρως); "poised above" is MacKenna's.
!flag the higher soul enters to bestow a brighter life | The Greek says this soul "followed" (ἐπηκολούθησεν), and then corrects it: it did not even follow, but added itself. "Enters" is MacKenna's.
!flag for soul does not leave the Intellectual | The Greek has "the intelligible" (τοῦ νοητοῦ); the modern version keeps "intelligible", and "the Intellectual" is MacKenna's.
!flag blending with it by the natural link of Reason-Principle to Reason-Principle | The Greek says "mingling itself, forming principle with forming principle" (λόγῳ πρὸς λόγον); "natural link" is MacKenna's.
!note "Soul using a body" (ψυχὴ σώματι χρωμένη) is the man of Plato's Alcibiades (129e-130c). The soul's riding as on a vehicle (ὄχημα): Timaeus (41e, 69c). The two souls, the one that uses the body and the one above it, are I.1.10-12's "we" and the living being.
@ch VI.7.6 | Perception there; souls in beasts; daemons
The better soul perceives the perceptibles there, as they are there: the perceptive man here fits this harmony to the harmony there, and fire to the fire there. The man in intellect shines on the second man and the second on the third; each of us is the man by which he is active, though each has all. A soul that was all is active now by one, now by another: pure, it wants man; it makes daemons too, and a daemon hangs on a god as a man on a man; when it chooses a beast's nature, it gives the forming principle of that beast.

@p
How, then, is the perceptive in the better soul? It is perceptive of the perceptibles there, and in the way the perceptibles are there. This is why it perceives the perceptible harmony too in this way, while the perceptive man receives it by perception, and fits it to the last degree to the harmony there, and fits fire to the fire there, of which that soul had a perception in proportion to the nature of the fire there.
!flag it is the source of the soul’s perception of the sense-realm in its correspondence with the Intellectual | The Greek says "this is why it perceives the perceptible harmony (ἁρμονίαν) too in this way": the harmony, which the perceptive man fits to the harmony there, is not in MacKenna.
!flag proceeding from the fire Intellectual to the fire here | The Greek says the perceptive man "fits fire to the fire there" (πῦρ ἐναρμόσαντος πρὸς τὸ ἐκεῖ πῦρ): from the fire here to the fire there, the other way.
!note The harmony heard here as an image of the harmony there: the musician of I.3.1 and the harmonies of I.6.3. Fire there: chapter 11 below.

@p
@greek εἰ γὰρ ἦν ἐκεῖ σώματα ταῦτα
For if these bodies were there, the soul would have perceptions and apprehensions of them; and the man there, the soul of this kind, would apprehend them; hence the later man too, the imitation, had the forming principles in imitation; and the man in intellect had the man before all men. This one shines on the second, and this on the third; and the last has all of them in a way, not becoming them, but lying beside them. One of us is active by the last, another has something from the one before it too, another has activity from the third as well; and each is the one by which he is active, though each has all, and again does not.
!flag not in the sense of actually living by them all but as standing in under-parallel to them | The Greek says the last man has them all "not becoming (γινόμενος) them, but lying beside (παρακείμενος) them"; "actually living by them" is MacKenna's.
!flag in yet another there is a blending of the third grade with the others | The Greek says another "has activity from the third as well" (παρὰ τοῦ τρίτου ἡ ἐνέργεια); there is no blending.
!note The three men, one shining on the next, answer the "we" of I.1.10 and the lives of III.4.2. "Each is the one by which he is active": compare III.4.3, where our daemon is the power above the one by which we are active.

@p
@greek τοῦ δὲ σώματος χωρισθείσης
When the third life and the third man is separated from the body, if the second follows along, and follows without being separated from the things above, where that one is, this one too is said to be. But when it takes on a beast's body, one wonders how, being the forming principle of a man, it does so: or it was all things, and is active at different times by different ones.
!flag No doubt it seems strange that a soul which has been the Reason-Principle of a man | The Greek has λόγος; the modern version keeps "forming principle", and "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag and will at different times be this and that | The Greek says it "is active (ἐνεργεῖ) at different times by different ones": it was all things, and is active by one or another; MacKenna's "be" loses the activity.

@p
@greek καθαρὰ μὲν οὖν οὖσα
Being pure, then, and before it has become evil, it wants man, and is man. For this is more beautiful, and it makes the more beautiful. It makes daemons too, which are before, of the same form as the soul that makes man; and the one before it is more daemonic, or rather a god; and a daemon is an imitation of a god, hanging on a god, as a man on a man. For that on which man hangs is not called a god. For it has the difference that souls have from one another, even if they are of the same rank. And by daemons one must mean the kind of daemons that Plato calls daemons.
!flag It produces also the still loftier beings, the Celestials (Daimons) | The Greek has "daemons" (δαίμονας); the modern version keeps "daemon", and "the Celestials" is MacKenna's.
!flag higher still stands that Man more entirely of the Celestial rank, almost a god | The Greek says "rather a god" (μᾶλλον δὲ θεός): more truly a god than a daemon, not almost one.
!flag For that Being into which man develops is not to be called a god | The Greek says "that on which (εἰς ὃν) man hangs is not called a god", answering the daemon "hanging on" (ἀνηρτημένος) a god; nothing develops into anything.
!note Daemons between gods and men: Plato's Symposium (202d-203a); the daemon each soul is given, Republic X (617e, 620d-e) and Timaeus (90a), the theme of III.4 On our allotted daemon.

@p
@greek ὅταν δὲ συνέπηται
And when the soul that was joined to the soul it was joined to when it was a man follows along, having chosen the nature of a beast, it gave the forming principle of that living being which was in it. For it has it, and this activity is worse.
!flag chooses animal nature and descends to that | The Greek says it "follows along" (συνέπηται), joined to the soul it was joined to as a man; "descends" is MacKenna's.
!note The souls choosing the lives of beasts in the myth of Er: Plato's Republic X (620a-d).
@ch VI.7.7 | Craftsmen and dancers; dim thoughts and bright perceptions
If the soul makes beasts by becoming worse, they are lesser, but not against nature: like craftsmen who know many forms, it makes what it can, or what it is ordered to, or what the matter wants. The soul of the All may sketch beforehand, with illuminations running ahead into matter, and each soul shapes itself to its part, like a dancer to his drama. Those things do not look toward these; these hang on those. The perceptibles there are bodiless and apprehended otherwise: the perceptions here are dim thoughts, and the thoughts there bright perceptions.

@p
But if it is by becoming evil and worse that it shapes a beast's nature, then what made an ox or a horse was not there from the beginning, and the forming principle of a horse, and the horse, are against nature. Or lesser, but not against nature; rather, that was in a way a horse or a dog from the beginning too; and if it has the means, it makes the more beautiful, and if not, what it can, since it has been ordered at least to make: like craftsmen who know how to make many forms, and then make this one, either what they were ordered to, or what the matter wants by its fitness.
!flag it is like a skilful craftsman competent to create all kinds of works of art but reduced to making what is ordered | The Greek says craftsmen (δημιουργοί) who know how to make many forms "then make this one, either what they were ordered to, or what the matter wants": "reduced" is MacKenna's, and the craftsmen are many.
!flag the reason-principle of the animal, and the animal itself, must lie outside of the natural plan ? | The Greek says they are "against nature" (παρὰ φύσιν), as the answer repeats ("not against nature"); "the natural plan" is MacKenna's.
!note The craftsman who makes what the matter allows: the Demiurge of the Timaeus works "as far as possible" (30a, 53b), as far as the nature of the matter allows.

@p
@greek τί γὰρ κωλύει τὴν μὲν δύναμιν
For what prevents the power of the soul of the All, since it is the whole forming principle, from sketching beforehand, even before the soul's powers come from it, and the sketch from being as it were illuminations running ahead into matter; and the soul that works things out, following such traces, from making them by articulating the traces part by part, and each soul becoming what it came to, shaping itself, as the one in a dance shapes himself to the drama given him?
!flag The power of the All-Soul, as Reason-Principle of the universe, may be considered as laying down a pattern | The Greek asks a question, "what prevents ... from sketching beforehand (προυπογράφειν)?": an outline drawn before the painting, not a pattern; and the soul of the All is "the whole forming principle" (λόγον πάντα οὖσαν).
!flag this plan would be something like a tentative illumining of Matter | The Greek has "illuminations running ahead" (προδρόμους ἐλλάμψεις) into matter, like runners going before; "tentative" is MacKenna's.
!flag the elaborating soul would give minute articulation to these representations of itself | The Greek says the soul follows "such traces" (ἴχνεσιν) and articulates "the traces part by part"; "representations of itself" is MacKenna's.
!note The dancer who shapes himself to the drama is the pantomime of III.2.17 and IV.4.33, where the parts of the All move as the dancer's limbs do. The outline sketched beforehand (ὑπογραφή) is the painter's first drawing, as in Plato's Republic VI (501a-c).

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐπισπώμενοι
But we have come to this drawn on by what follows. Our question was how the perceptive belongs to man, and how those things do not look toward becoming. And it appeared to us, and the argument showed, that those things do not look toward the things here, but these hang upon those and imitate those; and that this man, having his powers from that one, is toward those things; and that these perceptibles are yoked to this man, and those to that one.
!flag But this is to anticipate | The Greek says "drawn on (ἐπισπώμενοι) by what follows, we came to this": a digression the argument led to, not an anticipation.
!flag the Intellectual in him is linked to the Intellectual | The Greek says "these perceptibles are yoked (συνεζεῦχθαι) to this man, and those to that one": the two men and their two kinds of perceptibles; "the Intellectual" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἐκεῖνα γάρ τὰ αἰσθητά
For those perceptibles, as we have named them, are apprehended in another way, because they are bodiless; and this perception here is dimmer than the apprehension there, which we called perception because it was of bodies, and which is brighter. And for this reason this man too is perceptive, because he is less, and apprehends lesser images of those: so that these perceptions are dim thoughts, and the thoughts there bright perceptions.
!flag so distinguished as dealing with corporeal objects | MacKenna takes "because it was of bodies" (ὅτι σωμάτων ἦν) with the perception here; in the Greek it goes with the apprehension there, which "we called perception because it was of bodies", the bodies there.
!flag perceptions here are Intellections of the dimmer order | The Greek says "these perceptions are dim thoughts (ἀμυδρὰς νοήσεις)": dim, as the images in chapter 5 are dim, not of an order.
!note The perceptibles there, and the bodies there, are the heaven, earth, water and air of chapters 11 and 12. "Dim" (ἀμυδρός) and "bright" (ἐναργής) run through chapters 5 to 7, as the images grow fainter going down.
@ch VI.7.8 | Why the beasts are there: intellect is many
The horse there was not thought in order to make a horse here: it was before, and the things here followed of necessity, since nothing could stop a power that can both stay and go forth. Why, then, are so many irrational living beings in god? What comes after the altogether one must be many, falling short of it; not a dyad, since each of the two is again two; with motion and rest, intellect and life, it is all intellect and all the souls, a complete living being, not man alone.

@p
So much for the perceptive. But the whole horse, and each of the living beings there, how does it not want to look toward the things here? If it was so that a horse or some other living being might come to be here that it found out the thought of a horse — and yet how was it possible, wanting to make a horse, to think a horse? For it is already plain that there was a thought of a horse, if indeed it wanted to make a horse; so it is not possible to think it in order to make it, but the horse that did not come to be must be before the one that was to be afterwards. If, then, it was before the coming to be, and was not thought in order that it might come to be, the one who had the horse there did not have it with him by looking toward the things here, nor did he have this and the others in order to make the things here; but those were, and these followed those of necessity: for it was not possible to stop at the things there. For who could have stopped a power able both to stay and to go forth?
!flag the universal horse, must look deliberately towards this sphere | The Greek asks "how does it not want (ἐθέλει) to look toward the things here?" of "the whole horse" (ἵππος ὅλος): a question, not an assertion; "universal" and "deliberately" are MacKenna's.
!flag Yet what was that there to present the idea of the horse it was desired to produce? | The Greek asks "how was it possible, wanting to make a horse, to think a horse?": the thought of the horse must be there already, before any wanting.
!flag the reproduction followed of necessity since the total of things was not to halt at the Intellectual | The Greek says "it was not possible to stop (στῆναι) at the things there"; "the total of things" and "the Intellectual" are MacKenna's.
!flag a power capable at once of self-concentration and of outflow | The Greek says "able both to stay (μένειν) and to go forth (προιέναι)": the staying and the going forth of every principle, not concentration and outflow.
!note That a power cannot stand still and keep itself to itself: IV.8.6, where nothing would be hidden if the One stood alone, and V.4.1-2, where what stays makes what comes after it.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ διὰ τί ἐκεῖ ζῷα ταῦτα
But why are these living beings there? For what are these doing in god? The rational ones, let them be; but what dignity has so great a multitude of irrational ones? Why not the opposite? Now that this one must be many, being after what is altogether one, is plain: or it would not be after that, but that one. And being after that, it could not rise above it to be more one, but falls short of it; and since that was best, being one, this had to be more than one: for multitude is in falling short.
!flag But how come these animals of earth to be There ? | The Greek asks only "why are these living beings (ζῷα) there?"; "of earth" is MacKenna's.
!flag The answer is that obviously the unity of our universe must be that of a manifold | The Greek says "this one (τοῦτο τὸ ἕν) must be many", the one being of intellect, after what is altogether one; "our universe" is MacKenna's.
!note What dignity the lesser things have, and whether there are forms of them, is young Socrates' doubt about hair, mud and dirt in Plato's Parmenides (130c-d). The one being that is many is the Parmenides' second hypothesis (142d-145a), which V.1.8 reads as intellect.

@p
@greek τί οὖν κωλύει δυάδα
What, then, prevents it from being a dyad? Or each of the two in the dyad could not be altogether one, but would again be two at least, and so again with those. Then too there was motion in the first dyad, and rest; and there was intellect, and life was in it; and a complete intellect, and complete life. It was, then, not as one intellect, but all, holding all the particular intellects, and as many as all of them, and more; and it lived not as one soul, but as all, with more power to make the souls each; and it was a complete living being, not holding man alone in itself: for then man alone would be here.
!flag and so progressively (in an endless dualisation) | The parenthesis is MacKenna's; the Greek says only "and so again with those" (καὶ ἐκείνων αὖ ὡσαύτως).
!flag it must be Intellect agglomerate including all the particular intellects | The Greek says "not as one intellect, but all (πᾶς)", holding the particular intellects; "agglomerate" is MacKenna's.
!flag it would be the entire living universe containing much besides man | The Greek says "it was a complete living being" (ζῷον παντελὲς ἦν), the Timaeus' pattern of the world; MacKenna makes it a condition ("would be") and the living being "the universe".
!note Motion and rest, life and intellect in being: Plato's Sophist (248e-249a), where being cannot be without motion, life, soul and intellect. The complete living being (παντελὲς ζῷον), which holds all the intelligible living beings: Timaeus (31b, 39e).
@ch VI.7.9 | The irrational there is intellect too
The man and the living beings there are greater than here, and the rational is not there, but what is before reasoning. Lives and thoughts must differ, first, second and third: some thoughts are gods, some rational, some called irrational; but there the irrational is a forming principle, and the thought of a horse is intellect. Each part of intellect is all, but in act it ends, here in a horse; the powers, unrolling, let something go and add claws, teeth and horns, so that intellect finds in itself the healing of what is lacking.

@p
But let it be so, someone will say, for the honourable among the living beings: but how, again, were the cheap and the irrational there? The cheap plainly belongs to what is irrational, if the honourable belongs to the rational; and if the honourable belongs to what thinks, the opposite belongs to what does not think. And yet how is there anything unthinking or irrational, when that one is there in which each thing is, or from which it is?
!flag The mean is the unreasoning since value depends upon reason | The Greek is a condition: the cheap belongs to the irrational "if (εἰ) the honourable belongs to the rational"; "since" is MacKenna's.
!flag but how can the divine contain the mean, the unreasoning ? | The Greek asks "how were the cheap and the irrational there (ἦν)?"; "the divine" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek πρὸ δὴ τῶν περὶ ταῦτα
Before what is to be said about these things and in answer to them, let us take it that the man here is not such as that one, so that the other living beings too are not there as they are here, but one must take them in a greater way. Then, the rational is not there either: here, perhaps, he is rational, but there he is the one before reasoning. Why, then, does this one reason here, and the others not? Or, since thinking there is different in man and in the other living beings, reasoning too is different: for there are, in a way, many works of thought in the other living beings too.
!flag here the reasoning, There the pre-reasoning | The Greek says "here, perhaps (ἴσως), he is rational": the "perhaps" is left out.
!flag Degrees of reasoning here correspond to degrees of Intellection in that other sphere | The Greek says "since thinking (τοῦ νοεῖν) there is different (διαφόρου) in man and the others, reasoning too is different": a difference, not degrees.
!note Traces of thought in the other animals: Aristotle, History of animals VIII.1 (588a18-b3), where they have "likenesses of understanding".

@p
@greek διὰ τί οὖν οὐκ ἐπίσης λογικά
Why, then, are they not equally rational? And why are men not equally so with one another? One must consider that the many lives, being as it were motions, and the many thoughts, could not be the same, but must be different lives, and thoughts in the same way; and the differences, in a way, brighter and clearer; and, by nearness to the first, first and second and third. This is why some of the thoughts are gods, others a second kind, in which is what is here called rational, and next after these what was called irrational. But there what is called irrational was a forming principle, and the unintelligent was intellect, since the one who thinks a horse is intellect, and the thought of a horse was intellect.
!flag but what we know here as unreasoning was There a Reason-Principle | The Greek says what is called irrational (ἄλογον) "was a forming principle" (λόγος ἦν), and the unintelligent (ἄνουν) "was intellect" (νοῦς): a play on the words; the modern version keeps "forming principle", and "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag the Thinker of Horse was Intellect and the Thought, Horse, was an Intellect | The Greek says "the thought of a horse (ἡ νόησις ἵππου) was intellect": the thought of a horse, not the Thought named Horse.
!note The thoughts that are gods: the intelligible gods of V.8.3-5 and V.1.4, each an intellect. Life as motion, and many lives as many motions: Plato's Sophist (248e-249b) and Laws X (895c).

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν νόησις μόνον
But if it were only a thought, there would be nothing absurd in the thought itself, being a thought, being of something unthinking; but as it is, if the thought is the same as the thing, how is the thought a thought, and the thing unthinking? For so intellect would make itself unthinking. Or it is not unthinking, but intellect of a certain kind: for it is life of a certain kind. For as any life whatever is not released from being life, so neither is intellect of a certain kind released from being intellect: since neither is the intellect that is according to any living being released from being intellect of all things, of man too, say, if indeed each part, whatever you take, is all, but perhaps in another way.
!flag But (it will be objected) if this were a matter of mere thinking we might well admit | The parenthesis is MacKenna's; the Greek raises the question itself, without an objector.
!flag Intellectual-Principle adapted to some particular living being does not cease to be the Intellectual-Principle of all | The Greek has νοῦς; the modern version keeps "intellect", and "Intellectual-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag every manifestation is the whole, though in some special mode | The Greek says "each part, whatever you take, is all, but perhaps (ἴσως) in another way": a part, not a manifestation, and the "perhaps" is left out.
!note The thought the same as the thing thought, in what is without matter: Aristotle, On the soul III.4 (430a2-5) and Metaphysics Λ.9 (1075a1-5), and V.9.5 and V.3.5 in Plotinus.

@p
@greek ἐνεργείᾳ μὲν γὰρ ἐκεῖνο
For it is that in act, but it is able to be all; and we take, in each case, what is in act; and what is in act is the last, so that the last of this intellect is a horse, and where, going forth always to a lesser life, it stopped, there it is a horse, while another stopped lower down. For the powers, as they unroll, always leave something behind upward. They go forth letting something go, and in letting go they find out, because of the living being's need, which appeared from the falling short, one thing and another to add: as, since there is no longer enough for life, a nail appeared, and the hooked claw, or the jagged tooth, or the nature of a horn: so that, by the way intellect came down, by that way it might rise up again by the self-sufficiency of the nature, and find in itself the healing that lies there for what is lacking.
!flag Thus the Intellectual-Principle by its very descent is directed towards the perfect sufficiency of the natural constitution | The Greek says that "by the way intellect came down, by that way it might rise up again" (ἀνακύψαι), lifting its head as from water; the rising up again is not in MacKenna.
!flag the outgoing is by loss and by this loss the powers become one thing or another | The Greek says the powers "go forth letting something go (ἀφιεῖσαι)" and "find out" (ἐξευροῦσαι) something to add: they are not made by the loss, but find a remedy for it.
!note Claws, hooves and horns given to the animals for their safety: Epimetheus' gifts in Plato's Protagoras (320d-321c); horns for defence, and the hand that is all tools, Aristotle's Parts of animals (III.2, 662b23-663a18; IV.10, 687a23-b5).
@ch VI.7.10 | Horns there: complete as a living being
Horns there are for completeness: as a living being, as intellect and as life it must be complete, with one thing in place of another, so that from all of them comes the most complete living being, and each is complete as what it is. A whole from many must be one, from things other in form, each kept safe: the parts of a man's shape, better and worse, eye and finger, are of one; and virtue too is common and particular, and the whole is beautiful.

@p
But how did it fall short there? For what are horns for there, for defence? Or for the self-sufficiency and completeness of a living being. For as a living being it had to be complete, and as intellect complete, and as life complete: so that, if not this, then this. And the difference lies in one thing instead of another, so that from all of them there should be the most complete living being, and the complete intellect, and the most complete life, and each complete as what it is.
!flag Its characteristic difference is in this power of being now this, now that | The Greek says "the difference (ἡ διαφορά) lies in one thing instead of another" (τῷ ἄλλο ἀντὶ ἄλλου): different things in different places, not a power of being now this, now that.
!flag while yet, over all that multiplicity, unity reigns | The Greek ends with "each complete as what it is" (ἕκαστον δὲ ὡς ἕκαστον τέλειον); the unity over all is MacKenna's, from the next paragraph.

@p
@greek καὶ μήν, εἰ ἐκ πολλῶν
And indeed, if it is from many, it must again be one; or it is not possible to be from many, and those all the same: or it would be one, sufficient to itself. It must, then, be from things always other in form, as every composite is, and with each kept safe, as the shapes and the forming principles are. For the shapes, of a man, say, are from how many differences, and yet over all is one; and things better and worse than one another, eye and finger, but of one; and worse with respect to the whole, but better because it is so. And the forming principle is living being and something else, which is not the same as living being. And virtue too is the common and the particular, and the whole is beautiful, the common being undifferentiated.
!flag The Reason-Principle, too, is at once the living form and something else | The Greek has λόγος; the modern version keeps "forming principle", and "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag and the total is good because the universal is not differentiated | The Greek says "the whole is beautiful" (τὸ ὅλον καλόν); "good" is MacKenna's.
!note A part worse taken by itself, but better as it is in the whole: the statue's eyes in Plato's Republic IV (420c-d), and III.2.11 in Plotinus. Virtue common and particular: the virtues one and many, Plato's Protagoras (329c-330b) and Meno (72a-74a).
@ch VI.7.11 | Plants, earth, fire, water and air there
This All has all things, and so the All there has plants, earth, fire and water, and they live. The plant here is a forming principle set in life, from a first plant there that lives before it. Stones grow and mountains are shaped by an ensouled forming principle within, earth's form, as nature is a tree's; so there is earth itself there, living. Fire is not from rubbing, but from a soul that makes it; and water and air have soul, though they do not show it, being poured out, as blood has soul and gives no perception.

@p
It is said that not even the heaven, in which many things appear, disdained the nature of all the living beings: since this All too has all things. From where, then, does it have them? Do the things there, then, have all that are here? Or all that have been made by a forming principle and according to a form. But when it has fire, it has water too, and it surely has plants too. How, then, are the plants there? And how does fire live? And how earth? For either they live, or they will be there as dead, so that not everything there lives. And what at all are these too, there?
!flag The very heavens, patently multiple, cannot be thought to disdain any form of life | The Greek says "it is said" (λέγεται): a saying Plotinus takes up, which MacKenna leaves out.
!flag But, having fire (warmth) and water | The parenthesis "(warmth)" is MacKenna's; the Greek has "fire" (πῦρ).
!note The heaven that does not disdain the living beings: the Timaeus' world that holds all the kinds (30c-31b, 39e-40a), and Plato's Phaedrus (246b-c), where soul goes about the whole heaven.

@p
@greek τὰ μὲν οὖν φυτὰ
The plants, then, might fit with the forming principle: since the plant here too is a forming principle set in life. If, then, the forming principle in matter, the plant's, by which the plant is, is a life of a certain kind and a soul of a certain kind, and the forming principle is something one, either this is the first plant, or not, but before it is the first plant, from which this one too comes. For that one is one, and these are many, and of necessity from one. If so, that one must live much before, and be this very thing, plant, and these come from it secondarily and thirdly, and live by a trace of that one.
!flag Vegetal life we can well admit, for the plant is a Reason-Principle established in life | The Greek has λόγος; the modern version keeps "forming principle", and "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag since every Reason-Principle is a unity | The Greek says "the forming principle is something one" (ὁ λόγος ἕν τι): this one, the plant's; "every" is MacKenna's.
!flag that primal must have much the truer life | The Greek says that one must "live much before" (πολὺ πρότερον ἐκεῖνο ζῆν): earlier, prior, not truer.
!note The many from one: the one over many of Plato's Republic X (596a) and the one bed of the god (597c). Living "by a trace" (κατ’ ἴχνος) of the first: compare IV.4.18, where the body has a trace of soul.

@p
@greek γῆ δὲ πῶς
But earth, how? And what is being earth? And what is the earth there that has life? Or first, what is this one: that is, what is being for this one? There must be some shape and forming principle here too. There, then, in the case of the plant, its forming principle here too was living. Is it so, then, in this earth too? If we took the most earthy things begotten and shaped in it, we would find the nature of earth here too. The growths and shapings of stones, and the inward mouldings of mountains as they spring up, one must surely think come about by a forming principle with a soul in it, working as a craftsman from within and giving form; and that this is the form of earth, which makes, as in trees what is called nature, while what is called earth is analogous to the wood of the tree; and the stone cut out is as if something were cut from the tree, while the stone that has not suffered this, but is still attached, is like what is not cut from the living plant.
!flag this, we must take it, is the creative earth-principle corresponding to what we call the specific principle of a tree | The Greek says "as in trees what is called nature" (τὴν λεγομένην φύσιν); "specific principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag except of course that there is no hurt done, the stone remaining a member of the earth as the twig, uncut, of the tree | The Greek sets two stones side by side: the stone cut out is like a twig cut from the tree, and the stone that has not suffered this, still attached, is like the part not cut from the living plant. MacKenna makes the cut stone suffer no hurt.
!note That stones grow while they are in the earth and stop when they are cut out, so that the earth has soul: IV.4.27. Aristotle has stones and metals made in the earth from exhalations (Meteorology III.6, 378a15-b4).

@p
@greek τὴν δὴ δημιουργοῦσαν
Having found, then, that the nature seated in the earth, which works as a craftsman, is life in a forming principle, we would easily believe from this that the earth there lives much before, and is a life of earth with a forming principle, earth itself, and earth first, from which the earth here comes too.
!flag that it is a reasoned Earth-Livingness, the earth of Real-Being, earth primally | The Greek says "a life of earth with a forming principle (ζωὴν ἔλλογον γῆς), earth itself (αὐτογῆν) and earth first": earth itself, like man himself, and "the earth of Real-Being" is MacKenna's.
!note "Earth itself" (αὐτογῆ) is made like "man himself" (αὐτοάνθρωπος) of chapter 4. The true earth above, living and bright, is in Plato's Phaedo (109d-111c).

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ καὶ τὸ πῦρ λόγος
And if fire too is a forming principle in matter, and the other things of this kind, and fire does not come of its own accord — for from where? Not from rubbing, as one might think: for the rubbing happens when there is already fire in the All, and the bodies rubbed together have it; nor is matter potential in such a way that fire comes from it — if, then, what makes it must be according to a forming principle, as what gives it shape, what would it be? Or a soul able to make fire: and this is life and forming principle, both one and the same. This is why Plato says that there is soul in each of these, in no other way than as making this perceptible fire. So what makes fire here too is a fiery life, a truer fire. The fire beyond, then, being more fire, would be more in life: so fire itself lives too. And the same account holds of the others, water and air.
!flag Fire, similarly, with other such things, must be a Reason-Principle established in Matter | The Greek is a condition: "if (εἰ) fire too is a forming principle in matter"; MacKenna makes it an assertion, and "Reason-Principle" is his.
!flag It is with this in mind that Plato says there is soul in everything of this sphere | The Greek says "in each of these" (ἐν ἑκάστῳ τούτων), the elements; "everything of this sphere" is MacKenna's.
!note Where Plato says that there is soul in each element is not certain; the nearest is Laws X (898d-899b), where soul drives each of the stars and "all things are full of gods". Fire itself, which is not only this fire: Timaeus (51b-e). Fire from rubbing: Aristotle, On the heavens II.7 (289a19-28) and Meteorology I.3 (341a17-31).

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ διὰ τί οὐκ ἔμψυχα
But why are these not ensouled too, like the earth? That these too are in the living being of the All is surely plain, and that they are parts of a living being; but life does not show in them, just as it does not in the earth either: but there it could be inferred from what comes to be in it. But living beings come to be in fire too, and more plainly in water; and there are standings-together of living beings in air too. But each fire, coming to be and quickly quenched, passes by the soul in the whole, and has not come to a bulk that stays, so as to show the soul in it; and air and water in the same way: since, if they were somehow fixed by nature, they would show it; but because they had to be poured out, they do not show the soul they have. And it is perhaps like what happens with the fluids in us, blood, say: for the flesh seems to have soul, and whatever of the blood becomes flesh, but the blood, giving no perception, does not seem to have it. And yet it must be in it too: since nothing forced happens to it, but it is ready to stand apart from the soul that is in it, as one must think it is with the three elements too: since even the living beings made of air that has come together have the power of not perceiving, so as not to suffer. And as air passes by the light, which is unbending and stays, while the light stays itself, in this way it passes by the soul round about it too, and does not pass by: and so with the others.
!flag its nature obliges it to abstain from the soul which nonetheless is indwelling in it | The Greek says "nothing forced happens to it, but it is ready to stand apart (διεστάναι) from the soul that is in it": ready, not obliged.
!flag the living beings formed from the close conglomeration of air (the stars) are not susceptible to suffering | The parenthesis "(the stars)" is MacKenna's: the living beings of air, in the Epinomis and in Plotinus, are daemons; the stars are of fire.
!flag so too, by the effect of its circular movement, it eludes soul | The Greek has "round about" (κύκλῳ): the soul is round about the air as the light is; there is no circular movement.
!note Living beings in fire: the winged creature in the furnaces of Cyprus, Aristotle, History of animals V.19 (552b10-15). Living beings of air, daemons with bodies of air: Plato's Epinomis (984d-985b). The blood without perception when touched: Aristotle, History of animals III.19.
@ch VI.7.12 | The heaven there, full of life
Since this All is toward that one as toward a pattern, the All there is a living being: its heaven full of stars, its earth, sea and air full of living beings, as here. To ask where the living beings come from is to ask where the heaven there comes from, and life, and all soul, and the whole intellect: there is no poverty there, all is boiling with life, flowing from one spring, like one quality that holds all qualities, tastes, colours, and all that touch and hearing know.

@p
But let us say it again in this way: since we say that this All is toward that one as toward a pattern, the All must be a living being there first too, and, if its being is complete, it must be all things. And the heaven there must be a living being, and not bare of stars, then, those which are called the heaven here; and this is being heaven. And there is plainly earth there too, not bare, but much more full of life, and there are in it all the living beings that are called walking and land creatures here, and plants plainly set in living; and there is sea there too, and all water in a flowing and a life that stays, and all the living beings in water; and the nature of air is a share of the All there, and there are living beings of air in it, in proportion to the air itself.
!flag Since in our view this universe stands to that as copy to original | The Greek says this All is "toward that one as toward a pattern" (πρὸς οἷον παράδειγμα); the modern version keeps "pattern", and "copy to original" is MacKenna's.
!flag that is the realm of complete Being and everything must exist There | The Greek is a condition: "if its being is complete (παντελές), it must be all things": the All there, not the realm.
!flag with the movement of their unending life | The Greek has "in a flowing (ἐν ῥοῇ) and a life that stays (ζωῇ μενούσῃ)": a flowing that stays, not a movement.
!flag air too must be a member of that universe with the living things of air as here | The Greek says the living beings of air are "in proportion to the air itself" (ἀνὰ λόγον αὐτῷ τῷ ἀέρι); "as here" is MacKenna's.
!note The four kinds of living beings in the complete living being, the heavenly gods, the winged in air, those in water and those that walk on land: Plato's Timaeus (39e-40a). The earth there "much more full of life" recalls the true earth of the Phaedo (110b-111c).

@p
@greek τὰ γὰρ ἐν ζῶντι
For how would what is in something living not be living? Where even here they are. How, then, is not every living being there of necessity? For as each of the great parts is, so of necessity is the nature of the living beings in them. As, then, the heaven holds and is there, so all the living beings in the heaven hold and are there, and it is not possible that they should not be: or that heaven will not be either.
!flag if those lesser forms were not There, that heaven itself would not be | The Greek says "it is not possible that they should not be; or that one (ἐκεῖνος, the heaven) will not be either"; "lesser" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ὁ οὖν ζητῶν πόθεν ζῷα
So whoever asks from where the living beings come is asking from where the heaven there comes: and that is asking from where the living being comes, and this is the same as from where life comes, and all life, and all soul, and the whole intellect, since there is no poverty nor want there, but all things are filled with life and as it were boiling. They have their flowing, as it were, from one spring, not as of some one breath or one warmth, but as if there were one quality holding and keeping safe all the qualities in itself, sweetness with fragrance, and at once the quality of wine and the powers of all flavours, and the sights of colours, and all that touches know. And let there be too all that hearings hear, all melodies and every rhythm.
!flag whence the All-Life, whence the All-soul, whence collective Intellect | The Greek has "all life (ζωὴ πᾶσα) and all soul (ψυχὴ πᾶσα) and the whole intellect": all soul, every soul, not the soul of the All; "the All-soul" and "collective" are MacKenna's.
!flag There no indigence or impotence can exist | The Greek has "no poverty (πενίας) nor want (ἀπορίας)": the names of Love's mother, Poverty, and her want of resource in the Symposium.
!note Poverty (Πενία) and Resource (Πόρος), Love's mother and father: Plato's Symposium (203b-c), read in III.5.6-9. The one spring of all (πηγὴ μία): Plato's Phaedrus (245c), the soul the spring and beginning of motion, and III.8.10, the spring that gives itself to all the rivers.
@ch VI.7.13 | Intellect's wandering in the plain of truth
Neither intellect nor soul is simple: the first's activity is all activities. What is between its start and its end is not like a line, or a body of like parts, for without otherness it would not even be active. A simple thing that moved would make two, and from the same and the other a third, all same and all other, and so become other upon all. Intellect wanders in itself among the substances, in the plain of truth, a wandering that stays; and it is all things because each of them is other, and so contributes to the whole.

@p
For neither intellect is simple, nor the soul that comes from it, but all things are varied in so far as they are simple, that is, in so far as they are not composite, and in so far as they are principles, and in so far as they are activities. For the activity of the last, as it ends, is simple, but that of the first is all activities. And intellect, moving, moves in the same way and according to the same and alike always, yet not as the same and one thing in part, but as all: since what is in part, again, is not one either, but this too is unlimited, being divided.
!flag Intellectual-Principle is moved in a movement unfailingly true to one course | The Greek says it moves "in the same way, according to the same and alike always" (ὡσαύτως καὶ κατὰ ταὐτὰ καὶ ὅμοια ἀεί), Plato's words for the circle's motion; "one course" is MacKenna's.
!note "In the same way and according to the same", the motion of the circle and of intellect: Plato's Laws X (898a-b) and Timaeus (34a, 40a-b). Simple "in so far as they are principles": what is first holds all things in power, as in V.3.15.

@p
@greek ἀπὸ τίνος δὲ φαῖμεν
We would say it is from something, and surely toward something, as its last. But is all that is between like a line, or like some other body, of like parts and unvaried? But then what dignity would it have? For if it has no change, nor does any otherness wake it up into living, it would not even be activity: for such a state would differ in nothing from not being active. And even if there were a motion of this kind, life would not be in every way, but in one way only: but all things must live, and from every side, and nothing must not live. It must, then, move toward all, or rather have moved.
!flag if no differentiation woke it into life | The Greek has "otherness" (ἑτερότης), one of the greatest kinds; the modern version keeps "otherness", and "differentiation" is MacKenna's.
!flag it would not be a Force | The Greek says "it would not even be activity" (οὐδ’ ἂν ἐνέργεια εἴη), and such a state would differ in nothing from not being active (μὴ ἐνεργείας).

@p
@greek ἁπλοῦν δὲ εἰ κινοῖτο
But if something simple moved, it has that only; and either it is itself and has gone forth into nothing, or, if it has gone forth, another stays: so that there are two. And if this is the same as that, it stays one and has not gone forth; but if it is other, it went forth with otherness, and made a third one from something the same and something other. What has come to be from the same and the other has the nature of being the same and other; and other not as something, but all other: for its sameness too is all. And being all same and all other, there is nothing of the others that it leaves out. It has, then, the nature of becoming other upon all. If, then, all the others are before it, it would already be affected by them; but if they are not, this one begot all things, or rather was all things.
!flag or if there has been advance it still remains a simplex and at once there is a permanent duality | The Greek says "if it has gone forth, another stays (ἄλλο μένον): so that there are two": what goes forth and what stays; MacKenna has it remain a simplex.
!flag This production, based on Identity and Difference | The Greek has "the same and the other" (ταὐτοῦ καὶ ἑτέρου), the greatest kinds; the modern version keeps "the same", "sameness" and "otherness", and "Identity" and "Difference" are MacKenna's.
!note Soul made from the same, the other and being: Plato's Timaeus (35a-b); sameness and otherness among the greatest kinds: Sophist (254e-255e), set in the intelligible in VI.2.8.

@p
@greek οὐκ ἔστιν ἄρα τὰ ὄντα
The beings, then, cannot be unless intellect has been active, and active always in one thing after another, and as it were wandering every wandering, and wandering in itself, as the true intellect is by nature to wander in itself: and it is by nature to wander among substances, the substances running along with its wanderings. But it is everywhere itself: so it has a wandering that stays. And its wandering is in the plain of truth, from which it does not go out. It holds the whole, having taken it in, and having made it for itself as it were a place for moving, and the place is the same as that of which it is the place. And this plain is varied, so that it may also go through it: and if it were not varied throughout and always, then in so far as it is not varied, it stands still. And if it stands still, it does not think: so that, if it had stood still, it has not thought: and if so, it is not either.
!flag this wandering permitted to its nature is among real beings which keep pace with its movement | The Greek has "among substances (ἐν οὐσίαις), the substances running along with (συνθεουσῶν) its wanderings"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "real beings" is MacKenna's.
!flag a wandering within the Meadow of Truth from which it does not stray | The Greek has "the plain of truth" (τὸ τῆς ἀληθείας πεδίον), Plato's Phaedrus' plain; the meadow (λειμών) is the next word there, but not here.
!note The plain of truth (τὸ ἀληθείας πεδίον) and the meadow that grows the soul's pasture: Plato's Phaedrus (248b-c); I.3.4 uses it of dialectic. "Wandering" (πλάνη) is the word for the planets; intellect's wandering stays in itself.

@p
@greek ἔστιν οὖν νόησις
It is, then, thinking: and the motion is all, filling all substance, and all substance is all thinking, taking in all life, and always another after another; and, because what is the same in it is also other, to one who divides it the other always appears. All its journey is through life, and all through living beings, as to one who goes through earth all that he goes through is earth, even if the earth has differences. And there, the life through which it goes is the same, but because it is always other, it is not the same. And always holding the same passage through things not the same, because it does not change, but is present to the others as the same and in the same way: for if there is not, about the others, the same and in the same way, all is idle, and what is in act and the activity are nowhere.
!flag its movement is complete, filling Being complete | The Greek has "filling all substance (οὐσίαν πᾶσαν)"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "Being" is MacKenna's.
!flag all is dead, activity and actuality exist nowhere | The Greek says "all is idle" (ἀργεῖ πάντη): at rest, without work, not dead.
!note "To one who divides it the other always appears": the division of the forms in dialectic, Plato's Sophist (253d-e) and Philebus (16c-17a). Intellect's going through life and living beings: the complete living being of chapter 8.

@p
@greek ἔστι δὲ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα αὐτός
And it is the others too, so that it is all itself. And if it is itself, it is all; and if not, it is not itself. And if it is all itself, it is also all because it is all things, and there is nothing that does not contribute to all things, and there is nothing of it that is not other, so that, being other, this too may contribute. For if it were not other but the same, it would lessen its substance, not bringing its own nature to the completion of it.
!flag If it knew no otherness but was pure identity its essential Being would be the less | The Greek says "if it were not other but the same (ταὐτόν), it would lessen its substance (οὐσίαν)"; the modern version keeps "the same" and "substance", and "identity" and "essential Being" are MacKenna's.
@ch VI.7.14 | One many; the true friendship
A forming principle that was only one would make nothing but matter: a face has nostrils and eyes, and the nose has parts. So the unlimited in intellect is its being one many, a figure holding figures within, divided not in a straight line but always inward, down to the indivisible form. This division of things not poured together is the true friendship in the All, of which this world's friendship, made from things apart, is an imitation.

@p
One can know what intellect is by using intellectual patterns too: that it does not endure to be, as it were in the way of a monad, not other. For what forming principle will you take as a pattern, whether of a plant or of a living being? For if it were something one, and not this one varied, it would not be a forming principle, and what came to be would be matter, the forming principle not having become all, so as to fall into every part of matter and leave nothing of it to be the same. A face, for example, is not one bulk, but there are nostrils and eyes too; and the nose, not being one thing, but other, and another again of it, if it was to be a nose: for if it were simply one, it would be a bulk only.
!flag On the nature of the Intellectual-Principle we get light from its manifestations | The Greek says one can know what intellect is "by using intellectual patterns (παραδείγμασι νοεροῖς)": examples drawn from intellect, a plant's or a living being's forming principle; "manifestations" is MacKenna's.
!flag they show that it demands such diversity as is compatible with its being a monad | The Greek says it "does not endure to be, as it were in the way of a monad (κατὰ μονάδα), not other": intellect refuses to be a monad; MacKenna turns it the other way.
!note A face not one bulk, and beauty not only in symmetry: I.6.1.

@p
@greek καὶ τὸ ἄπειρον οὕτως ἐν νῷ
And the unlimited is in intellect in this way, that it is one many, not as one house, but as a forming principle, many in itself, holding in one figure of intellect, as in an outline, outlines within it, and figurings within again, and powers and thoughts, and the division not in a straight line, but always inward, as the natures of living beings are contained in the whole living being, and again others toward the smaller of the living beings and the lesser powers, where it will stop at an indivisible form.
!flag There is infinity in Intellectual-Principle | The Greek has "the unlimited" (τὸ ἄπειρον); the modern version keeps "the unlimited", as in VI.6, and "infinity" is MacKenna's.
!flag all the outlines, all the patterns | The Greek has "figurings" (σχηματισμούς) within the outlines; the modern version keeps "pattern" for παράδειγμα, as in this chapter's first sentence.
!flag the division is not determined by a boundary but goes ever inward | The Greek says the division is "not in a straight line" (μὴ κατ’ εὐθύ), as a line is cut into pieces side by side, but always inward.
!flag where there is a halt at the individual form | The Greek has "an indivisible form" (εἶδος ἄτομον), the last species that cannot be divided further, not an individual.
!note Division down to the indivisible form: Plato's Phaedrus (277b), Sophist (229d) and Philebus (16d-e); the last species (ἄτομον εἶδος) in Aristotle, Metaphysics Z.12 (1038a15-20) and Parts of animals I.4 (644a24-b7).

@p
@greek ἡ δὲ διαίρεσις ἔγκειται
And the division is there among things not poured together, though they are into one; but this is what is called the friendship in the All, not the one in this All: for this one imitates it, being friendship from things that stand apart; but the true friendship is that all should be one and never be separated. But he says that what is in this heaven is separated.
!flag this is what is known as the Universal Sympathy | The Greek has "the friendship (φιλία) in the All", Empedocles' word; "Sympathy" is MacKenna's.
!flag that authentic Sympathy consists in all being a unity and never discriminate | MacKenna ends here; the Greek goes on, "but he says that what is in this heaven is separated" (διακρίνεσθαι δέ φησι τὸ ἐν τῷδε τῷ οὐρανῷ): Empedocles, whose Strife separates in this world.
!note Love (Φιλότης, Φιλία) that brings all into one and Strife that separates: Empedocles, fragments B17 and B26, and the Sphere (B27-B29); Aristotle, Metaphysics A.4 (985a21-29). Empedocles' exiled soul is cited in IV.8.1.
# VI.7 chapters 15-28 (milestone E31): MacKenna's own English (vol. V, 1930, pp. 181-196).
@ch VI.7.15 | The many life, a trace of the Good
Who that sees the life there, many and one, would not long to be in it? The lives here are darkness, a trace of life and intellect; the archetype there is good-formed, since it has the good in the forms. Intellect had from the Good the power to generate, and was given what the Good does not have; unable to hold the one power, it broke it into many. So it is a varied good: a living sphere, a thing all faces, all the pure souls run together with intellect on their summit; but to see it so is to see it from outside: one must become it.

@p
Who, then, seeing this life, the many and all and first and one, does not long to be in it, and think little of all the other? For the other lives, those below, are darkness: small and dim and cheap, and not pure, and they stain the pure ones. And if you look at them, you no longer see the pure lives, nor live all those lives together, in which there is nothing that does not live, and live purely, with nothing evil in it.
!flag All other life is darkness, petty and dim and poor | The Greek says "the others, those below (αἱ κάτω)": the lives here below; MacKenna leaves out "below".
!flag this life which includes all living | The Greek says you no longer "live all those lives together" (ζῇς ἐκείνας τὰς πάσας ὁμοῦ): the lives there, many and all at once, not one life that includes them.

@p
@greek τὰ γὰρ κακὰ ἐνταῦθα
For the evils are here, because here there is a trace of life and a trace of intellect; but there is the archetype, which he calls "good-formed", because it has the good in the forms. For that one is the Good, while this one, intellect, is good by having its life in contemplating; and what it contemplates is good-formed too, things it acquired when it was contemplating the nature of the Good. But they came into it not as they were there, but as it held them itself. For that one is the principle, and it is from that one that they are in this, and this is what made them, from that one. For it was not lawful that, looking to that one, it should think nothing, nor again that it should think what is in that one: for then it would not itself have generated. It had from that one, then, the power to generate, and to be filled with its own offspring, that one giving what it did not have itself.
!flag There is the archetype, that which is good in the very Idea—we read—as holding The Good in the pure Idea | The Greek says "he calls" (φησιν) the archetype "good-formed" (ἀγαθοειδές), Plato's word, "because it has the good in the forms" (ἐν τοῖς εἴδεσι): in the forms, plural; "the pure Idea" is MacKenna's.
!flag it sees also as good the objects of its contemplation because it holds them in its act of contemplating the Principle of Good | The Greek says it acquired (ἐκτήσατο) them "when it was contemplating" (ὅτε ἐθεώρει) the nature of the Good: a past acquiring, not a holding now.
!flag for it is their source | The Greek says "that one (ἐκεῖνος) is the principle": the Good is the principle, and the forms come from it into intellect; MacKenna makes intellect their source.
!flag In the very law | The Greek says "it was not lawful" (οὐ ... ἦν θέμις): a thing forbidden, not a law it follows.
!flag never, on the other hand, could it produce what is There | The Greek says it was not lawful for it to think "what is in that one" (τὰ ἐν ἐκείνῳ): had it thought what is in the Good, it would not have generated; "produce" is MacKenna's.
!note "Good-formed" (ἀγαθοειδῆ): Plato's Republic VI (509a), where knowledge and truth are good-formed, but neither is the Good. The Good giving what it does not have: V.3.15 and chapter 17 below.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἑνὸς αὐτοῦ πολλὰ τούτῳ
But from it, being one, came many to this one: for the power it was bringing away, unable to hold it, it broke apart, and made the one many, so that it could carry it so, part by part. What it generated, then, was from the power of the Good, and was good-formed, and it is itself good, from good-formed things: a varied good.
!flag it could not sustain the power poured upon it and therefore broke it up | The Greek says the power "it was bringing away" (ἐκομίζετο), carrying it for itself, and that "it broke it apart" (συνέθραυε); "poured upon it" is MacKenna's.
!flag it is good, itself, since it is constituted by these things of good | The Greek says it is good "from good-formed things" (ἐξ ἀγαθοειδῶν): made of things in the form of the good.
!note The one broken into many by intellect's weakness: III.8.8, where intellect, wishing to have the One, became many, and V.3.11, where intellect, trying to see the One, sees it as many.

@p
@greek διὸ καὶ εἴ τις αὐτὸν ἀπεικάζοι
So if someone likened it to a living, varied sphere, or imagined it as a thing all faces, shining with living faces, or as all the pure souls run together into the same place, not lacking, but having all that is theirs, and the whole intellect set on their summit, so that the place is lit by an intellectual light: imagining it so, he would see it from outside, as one thing sees another. But one must become that, and make oneself the sight.
!flag to a unity of souls, all the pure souls, not the faulty but the perfect | The Greek has the pure souls "run together into the same (εἰς τὸ αὐτὸ συνδραμούσας), not lacking (οὐκ ἐνδεεῖς), but having all that is theirs": not lacking, where MacKenna has "not the faulty but the perfect".
!flag with Intellect enthroned over all | The Greek says the whole intellect is "set on their summits" (ἐπ’ ἄκραις αὐταῖς ἱδρυμένον): at the top of the souls themselves, not over all.
!flag the true way is to become Intellectual-Principle and be, our very selves, what we are to see | The Greek says "one must become that and make oneself the sight" (τὴν θέαν ἑαυτὸν ποιήσασθαι): the seer becomes the sight; "Intellectual-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!note The shining sphere pictured and then given up: V.8.9, where one is told to picture the world as a transparent sphere and take away its bulk. Becoming the sight, and no longer seeing from outside: V.8.10-11 and VI.9.10-11.
@ch VI.7.16 | Intellect filled by the Good
One must not stay in the many beauty but rise and ask who generated it. Each form has its own stamp, but, being good-formed, has something common running over all. Did intellect, looking to the Good, think it as many? It was not yet intellect then, but lived toward it and turned to it; the movement, filled, made it intellect, seeing by the light of the giver. So the Good is cause of substance and of its being seen, as the sun is of things seen and of sight, being neither.

@p
But one must not stay always in this many beauty, but go on still, darting upward and letting this go, not from this heaven but from that one, marvelling who it is that generated it, and how. Each form, then, is each, its own, as a stamp; but, being good-formed, it has a common thing running over all of them. It has being over all, and each has the living being too, since life is common over all, and perhaps other things too. But in so far as they are goods, and because they are goods, what would that be?
!flag we must make haste yet higher, above this heaven of ours and even that | The Greek says "darting up (ἀίξαντα) and letting this go, not from this heaven but from that one": one goes up from the heaven there, not above it.
!flag Everything There is a single Idea in an individual impression | The Greek says "each form is each, and its own (ἴδιος), as a stamp": each form its own, not a single Idea.
!flag possesses also the total Living-Form in virtue of that transcendent life | The Greek says each has "the living being" (τὸ ζῷον), life being common "over all" (ἐπὶ πᾶσιν); "transcendent" is MacKenna's.
!flag But what is the Nature of this Transcendent in view of which and by way of which the Ideas are good ? | The Greek asks what would be common to them "in so far as they are goods, and because they are goods": what in them makes them good, not the nature of something transcendent.

@p
@greek πρὸς δὴ τὴν τοιαύτην σκέψιν
For such an inquiry it might be useful to begin from here. When intellect looked toward the Good, did it think that one as many, and, being one itself, think it as many, dividing it in itself because it could not think it whole at once? But it was not yet intellect when it looked at that one; it looked without thinking. Or one must say that it never even saw it, but lived toward it, and hung from it, and was turned toward it; and this movement, filled by moving there and around that one, filled it, and was no longer only movement, but movement sated and full. And next it became all things, and knew this in its awareness of itself, and was intellect at once, filled so as to have what it would see, and seeing them with light from the giver, and bringing this along too.
!flag applied its Act by breaking into parts what it was too feeble to know as a whole | The Greek has it "dividing (μερίζων) it in itself" because it "could not" (μὴ ... δύνασθαι) think it whole at once; "too feeble" is MacKenna's.
!flag No: that would not be Intellection looking upon the Good; it would be a looking void of Intellection | The Greek says "it was not yet (οὔπω) intellect when it looked at that one, but looked without thinking": a stage before intellect, not a hypothesis set aside.
!flag all the tendance taking place There and upon That must be a movement teeming with life | The Greek says "this movement, filled by moving there and around (περί) that one, filled it": a movement around the Good; "teeming with life" is MacKenna's.
!flag there is no longer bare Act, there is a filling to saturation | The Greek says it "was no longer only movement (κίνησις), but movement sated (διακορής) and full": movement, not Act.
!flag knows that fact in virtue of its self-knowing | The Greek has "in its awareness of itself" (ἐν συναισθήσει αὑτοῦ): a joint perception of itself, not knowing.
!flag seeing all by the light from the Giver and bearing that Giver with it | The Greek says it sees them with light from the giver, "bringing this (τοῦτο) along too": it carries the light, not the giver.
!note Intellect's coming to be in two moments, an unbounded looking and then a filling and bounding: V.4.2 and V.1.7, and chapter 17 below. "Sated" (διακορής): the play on κόρος, fullness, and Kronos, intellect, is in V.1.7 and III.8.11; Plato's Cratylus (396b) has Kronos from κόρος.

@p
@greek διὰ τοῦτο οὐ μόνον λέγεται τῆς οὐσίας
This is why that one is said to be the cause not only of substance but also of its being seen. And as the sun, being the cause to the perceptibles of their being seen and of their coming to be, is somehow the cause of sight too, and so is neither the sight nor the things that come to be, so the nature of the Good, being the cause of substance and intellect, and a light, by analogy, to the things seen there and to the one who sees, is neither the beings nor intellect, but their cause, and grants that they are thought, by its own light shed on the beings and on intellect.
!flag the Supreme may be understood to be the cause at once of essential reality and of the knowing of reality | The Greek says that one "is said" (λέγεται) to be cause of substance (οὐσίας) "and of its being seen", Plato's words; the modern version keeps "substance", and "essential reality" is MacKenna's.
!flag cause of Being and Intellectual-Principle | The Greek has "cause of substance (οὐσίας) and intellect"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "Being" is MacKenna's.
!note The Good the cause of knowledge and of being, as the sun is of sight and of becoming, and itself beyond substance: Plato's Republic VI (508a-509b).

@p
@greek πληρούμενος μὲν οὖν ἐγίνετο
While it was being filled, then, it was coming to be; when it was filled, it was; and at once it was completed and saw. Its principle was that, what it was before it was filled; and the other principle, as if from outside, was the one that filled it, from which, being filled, it was as it were stamped.
!flag This filling procures the existence ; after the filling the being | The Greek says "while being filled it was coming to be (ἐγίνετο), when filled it was (ἦν)": becoming, then being; "procures the existence" is MacKenna's.
!flag gave shape to the filled | The Greek says that, being filled, it was "as it were stamped" (οἷον ἐτυποῦτο): the stamp (τύπος) of the chapter's first sentences.
@ch VI.7.17 | The giver greater than the gift; life bounded is intellect
How are the forms in intellect, when they were not in what filled it? The giver need not have what it gives: it is greater than the gift, beyond activity and so beyond life. Life was a trace of the Good, unbounded as it looked and bounded once it had looked; life bounded is intellect, many intellects in one, each differing by being wholly one. Intellect seats the forms and is a light to soul; the Good is without shape or form, for so it makes form: were it a form, intellect would be a forming principle.

@p
But how are these in intellect, and how is intellect, when they were not there in what filled it, nor again in what was being filled? For when it was not yet filled, it did not have them. Or it is not necessary that one have what one gives; but in such things one must think the giver greater, and the given less than the giver: for such is coming to be among the beings. For what is in act must be first, and the things after must be in potency what is before them; and the first is beyond the second things, and the giver was beyond the given, for it is better. If, then, there is something before activity, it is beyond activity, and so beyond life too. If, then, there is life in this one, the giver gave life, but is more beautiful and more honourable than life. Intellect had life, then, and had no need of a varied giver; and the life was a trace of that one, not that one's life.
!flag But in what mode are these secondaries, and Intellectual-Principle itself, within the First ? | The Greek asks how these are "in it" (ἐν αὐτῷ), in intellect, when they were not in the one that filled it: not how they are within the First.
!flag Our sphere containing life, there is a Giver of Life | The Greek says "if, then, there is life in this one (ἐν τούτῳ)", in intellect: the life is intellect's, not our sphere's.
!flag this possessed Life and had no need to look for it to any giver in possession of Life’s variety | The Greek says intellect "had life, and had no need of a varied (ποικίλου) giver": it is intellect that had life, and the giver needed no variety.
!note The giver greater than the gift, not having what it gives: V.3.15 and chapter 32 below. Act before potency: Aristotle, Metaphysics Θ.8 (1049b4-1050a3).

@p
@greek πρὸς ἐκεῖνο μὲν οὖν βλέπουσα
Looking toward that one, then, it was unbounded, and having looked there it was bounded, though that one has no bound. For at once, looking toward one thing, it is bounded by it, and holds in itself bound and limit and form; and the form is in what was shaped, but what shaped it was shapeless. And the bound was not from outside, as if set around a magnitude, but it was the bound of all that life, which is many and unlimited, as shining out from such a nature; and it was not the life of this one thing, for then it would already have been bounded as an individual.
