But it was bounded, all the same: bounded, then, as the life of one thing that is many. And each of the many was bounded, bounded as many by the manyness of the life, and as one again by the bound.
!flag Life looks to unity and is determined by it, taking bound, limit, form | The Greek says "looking toward one thing (πρὸς ἕν τι)" it is bounded at once: toward something one; "unity" is MacKenna's.
!flag limitless itself as radiated from its great Prior | The Greek says the life is "many and unlimited (ἀπείρου)", "as shining out (ἐκλαμψάσης) from such a nature"; the modern version keeps "the unlimited", and "its great Prior" is MacKenna's.
!note The unbounded and the bound in intellect: the indefinite dyad bounded by the One (V.4.2) and the intelligible matter (II.4.5); the limit and the unlimited of Plato's Philebus (23c-25b).

@p
@greek τί οὖν τὸ ἓν ὡρίσθη
As what, then, was the one bounded? As intellect: for life bounded is intellect. And as what the many? As many intellects. All are intellects, then: the whole is intellect, and each is an intellect. But does the whole intellect, holding each, hold each as the same? Then it would hold one. If, then, there are many, there must be difference. How, again, did each have its difference? In becoming wholly one, it had its difference: for the whole is not the same as any intellect at all.
!flag all its multiplicity resolves itself into Intellectual-Principles | The Greek says "all, then, are intellects (νόες), and the whole (πᾶς) is intellect, and each (ἕκαστοι) is an intellect"; "collective" and "particular" are MacKenna's.
!flag It takes its characteristic difference by becoming entirely a unity within the collective whose totality could not be identical with any particular | The Greek says it had its difference "in becoming wholly one" (εἷς ὅλως γενέσθαι), for "the whole is not the same as any intellect at all"; "within the collective" is MacKenna's.
!note Many intellects in one, each the whole in its own way, as each theorem holds the whole science: V.9.8, IV.9.5 and VI.2.20.

@p
@greek ἦν οὖν ἡ μὲν ζωὴ δύναμις πᾶσα
Life, then, was all power, and the sight from there was the power of all things, and intellect, when it came to be, appeared as all these things. It sits upon them, not to be seated, but to seat them, having seen the form of the firsts, which is itself without form. And intellect becomes a light to soul in the same way as that one is to intellect; and when it too bounds the soul, it makes it rational, giving it a trace of what it had.
!flag Thus the Life in the Supreme was the collectivity of power | The Greek says "life was all power (δύναμις πᾶσα)": the life of intellect, the trace, not a life in the Supreme.
!flag Intellectual-Principle, thus arising, is manifested as this universe of Being | The Greek says intellect "appeared as all these things" (αὐτὰ ... τὰ πάντα), the all things of the sight; "this universe of Being" is MacKenna's.
!flag that it may serve as base to the Form of the Firsts, the Formless Form | The Greek says it sits upon them to seat them, "having seen the form of the firsts, which is itself formless (ἀνείδεον)": the formless one is the first, the Good, not a "Formless Form".
!flag it shapes it into Reasoning Soul | The Greek has "rational" (λογικήν): a soul given a forming principle; "Reasoning Soul" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἴχνος οὖν καὶ νοῦς ἐκείνου
Intellect too, then, is a trace of that one. But since intellect is form, and in extension and multitude, that one is shapeless and formless: for this is how it makes form. If that one were a form, intellect would be a forming principle. But the first had to be in no way many: for its manyness would hang from another again, before it.
!flag if the Prior were a Form, the Intellectual-Principle itself could be only a Reason-Principle | The Greek says intellect "would be a forming principle" (λόγος); the modern version keeps "forming principle" for λόγος, and "Reason-Principle" and "only" are MacKenna's.
!note The One without shape and form because it makes form: V.5.6 and VI.9.3, and chapters 32-33 below. What is first must be simple, or it would need another before it: V.4.1.
@ch VI.7.18 | What makes the forms good-formed
In what are the things in intellect good-formed? All that comes from the Good bears its trace, as heat from fire; but coming from it is not enough: there must be something common in them. Life is good not bare, but as true and from the Good; so intellect is good, and each form. Is the good in their substance, or is each whole good? The first activity, what is bounded on it, and both together are good, each in its way. Here order and rhythm make things good; there the things themselves; but why, the argument still asks.

@p
But in respect of what are the things in intellect good-formed? Is it as each is a form, or as they are beautiful, or as what? If, then, all that comes from the Good has a trace and stamp of it, or from it, as what comes from fire is a trace of fire, and what comes from sweet a trace of sweet; and life comes into intellect from that one, for it came to be from the activity from that one; and intellect is through that one, and the beauty of the forms is from there: then all would be good-formed, life and intellect and idea. But what is the common thing?
!flag as anything going back to warmth or sweetness carries the memory of those originals | The Greek says "what comes from fire is a trace of fire, and what comes from sweet a trace of sweet": fire and sweet, and a trace, not a memory.
!flag must inevitably have goodness | The Greek says all "would be good-formed" (ἀγαθοειδῆ ἂν εἴη): a conclusion under a condition, and good-formed, not "having goodness".
!note What comes from fire as a trace of fire: the two activities of a thing, its own and the one that goes out from it, V.4.2 and V.1.6.

@p
@greek οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἀρκεῖ
For it is surely not enough, for being the same, that they come from that one: the common thing must be in them. For what is not the same might come from the same, or what is given in the same way might become other in those who receive it: since what goes into the first activity is one thing, and what is given by the first activity another, and what comes after these is other again. Or nothing prevents each from being good-formed, yet one more so by another thing. In respect of what, then, most?
!flag there is difference, again, in the effect here | The Greek says "what comes after these (τὸ ἐπὶ τούτοις) is other again": what comes next, not "the effect here".
!flag Nonetheless every item may be good in a degree of its own | The Greek says nothing prevents each from being good-formed, "yet more so (μᾶλλον) by another": the question is which is most, not a degree of its own.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ πρότερον ἐκεῖνο
But first it is necessary to see this: is life good in so far as it is just this, life, seen bare and stripped? Or is it the life that is from it, and what is from it is something other, of this kind? Again, then, what is such a life? The Good's. But it was not its, but from it. But if in that life there is something from that one, and it is the life that really is, and nothing from that one may be called of no worth, and it is good in so far as it is life, then of the true intellect too, that first one, one must say that it is good; and it is clear that each form too is good and good-formed. Either, then, it has something good, either common, or one more than another, or one first and another next, in the second place.
!flag very different from the Life known here | The Greek asks whether life is good "seen bare and stripped" (ψιλὴ ... ἀπογεγυμνωμένη), or the life from it, "and what is from it is something other, of this kind"; "very different from the Life known here" is MacKenna's.
!flag so too we must admit in the case of Authentic Intellectual-Principle that its Life because good derives from that First | The Greek says of "the true intellect, that first one" (τοῦ πρώτου ἐκείνου), "that it is good": intellect is good, not its life derived.
!flag as a common property or as a distinct attribution or as held in some distinct measure | The Greek says "either common, or one more than another, or one first and another next and second" (πρώτως ... δευτέρως): an order of first and second.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ γὰρ εἰλήφαμεν ἕκαστον
For since we have taken each as already having something good in its substance, and as good because of this — for life was good not simply, but because it was called true and because it was from that one, and so was intellect, the one that really is — something of the same must be seen in them. For when things are different and the same is said of them, nothing prevents this from being present in their substance, yet one can take it apart in its account, as living being in man and horse, and the hot in water and fire, the first as a genus, the second as first in one and second in the other; or else each of the two, or each, would be called good by a mere sharing of the name.
!flag for Life we found to be good not in the bare being but in its derivation from the Authentic | The Greek says life was good "because it was called true (ἀληθινή) and because it was from that one": true life, not "derivation from the Authentic".
!flag thus life in man or horse yields the notion of animal | The Greek has "living being (τὸ ζῷον) in man and horse": the genus itself, not life.
!flag the first case is a definition of Kind, the other two cite qualities, primary and secondary respectively | The Greek has two cases: the living being said "as a genus", and the hot said "first in one and second in the other" (fire first, water second).
!flag Both or one part of Intellect, then, would be called by the one term good | The Greek says "or each of the two, or each, would be called good homonymously (ὁμωνύμως)": by name only, the alternative to be avoided; "part of Intellect" is MacKenna's.
!note The same said of different things as a genus, or first and second (πρώτως, δευτέρως), or only by name (ὁμωνύμως): Aristotle, Categories 1 (1a1-12) and Metaphysics Γ.2 (1003a33-b10); fire hottest, the cause of heat in others: Metaphysics α.1 (993b24-26). The account (λόγος) here is the definition, as in Aristotle, not the forming principle.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν ἐνυπάρχει
Is the good, then, present in their substance? Or is each, whole, good, not good by one thing in it? How, then? As parts? But the Good is without parts. Or it is one itself, but this is good in this way, and that in that: for the first activity is good, and what was bounded on it is good, and both together; the first because it came to be by that one, the second because it is an order from it, the third because it is both. They are from it, then, and none the same, as if from the same man came speech and walking and something else, all done rightly.
!flag Each of them is good but the goodness is not that of the Unity-Good | The Greek says "each whole is good, not good by one thing" (οὐ καθ’ ἕν): the whole thing good, not by one part in it; "the Unity-Good" is MacKenna's.
!flag By the mode of parts | The Greek asks it ("as parts?"), and answers at once: "but the Good is without parts".
!flag but here it has become particularised | The Greek says "it is one itself, but this is good in this way, that in that" (οὑτωσὶ δὲ τόδε): each in its own way; "particularised" is MacKenna's.
!flag the good that is an ordered system derived from that earlier, and the good that is in the actualisation (in the thing participant) | The Greek has three: the first activity, good as coming to be by that one; what was bounded on it, good as an order (κόσμος) from it; and both together (συνάμφω), good as both. "In the actualisation (in the thing participant)" is MacKenna's.
!flag like the speech and walk and other characteristics of one man, each playing its due part | The Greek says "all done rightly" (κατορθούμενα): from the same man, all right actions; "characteristics" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἢ ἐνταῦθα, ὅτι τάξις
Or here they are good because of order and rhythm; but there, what? But someone might say that here the being well is wholly from outside, since the things about which the order is are different, but there the things themselves are good. But why are they themselves good? For we must not let it go because we trust that they are from that one: we must grant that, being from that one, they are honourable, but the argument longs to grasp in respect of what their good is.
!flag We might answer that in the case of the sense-order, too, the good is imposed | The Greek says "here (ἐνταῦθα) the being well (τὸ καλῶς) is wholly from outside": no "too", and "sense-order" is MacKenna's.
!flag we do not deny that things deriving Thence are good | The Greek says "honourable" (τίμια), of worth: their goodness is what is asked.
!flag our subject demands that we discover the mode by which they come to possess that goodness | The Greek says "the argument (ὁ λόγος) longs (ποθεῖ) to grasp" in respect of what their good is: λόγος here is the argument, not the forming principle, and it longs.
@ch VI.7.19 | Desire is no test of the good
Shall we leave the judgment to desire and to the soul, and call good what it desires without asking why? That would be absurd: the good would be something relative, the desirers are many and desire different things, and we would not know the better without knowing the good. To judge by each thing's virtue leads up, rightly, to form and forming principle; but there, where nothing is evil, we are at a loss how they are good, since there the that is the why. Still, one must not give up.

@p
Shall we, then, give the judgment over to desire and to the soul, and, trusting its affection, say that what it desires is good, and not inquire why it desires it? And shall we bring demonstrations about what each thing is, and give the good over to desire? But many absurdities appear to us. First, that the good too will be one of the things said in relation to something; next, that the things that desire are many, and desire different things: how, then, shall we judge by what desires whether it is better? But perhaps we shall not even know the better while we do not know the good.
!flag Are we to rest all on pursuit and on the soul? | The Greek has "desire" (ἔφεσις) and "the judgment" (τὴν κρίσιν): whether to give the judgment over to desire; "pursuit" is MacKenna's.
!flag is the good to be dismissed as choice ? | The Greek asks whether we shall "give (δώσομεν) the good over to desire": hand it over to desire to judge, not dismiss it.
!flag The good becomes a mere attribute of things | The Greek says "the good will be one of the things relative (τῶν πέρι)": said in relation to something; "a mere attribute" is MacKenna's.
!flag objects of pursuit are many and different | The Greek says "the things that desire (τὰ ἐφιέμενα) are many, and desire different things": the desirers, not the objects.
!note Every soul pursues the good and does all for its sake, but divines it and is at a loss what it is: Plato's Republic VI (505d-e); all that knows the good hunts it: Philebus (20d).

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ ἆρα τὸ ἀγαθὸν ὁριούμεθα
But shall we define the good by each thing's virtue? But so we shall lead it up to form and forming principle, going rightly; but when we come there, what shall we say, when we are asking just this, how these are good? For in the worse things, it seems, we could know such a nature, though it does not have it purely, by setting it beside what is worse; but there, where nothing is evil, and the better things are by themselves, we shall be at a loss.
!flag Are we to determine the good by the respective values of things ? | The Greek says "by each thing's virtue (ἀρετήν)", its excellence; the modern version keeps "virtue", and "values" is MacKenna's.
!flag This is to make Idea and Reason-Principle the test : all very well | The Greek says "we shall lead it up (ἀνάξομεν) to form and forming principle (λόγον), going rightly"; the modern version keeps "forming principle" for λόγος, and "Reason-Principle" is MacKenna's.
!flag we are without a standard There where no evil exists, the Bests holding the field, alone | The Greek says "we shall be at a loss" (ἀπορήσομεν) there, where the better things are "by themselves"; "the Bests holding the field" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἆῤ οὖν, ἐπειδὴ ὁ λόγος
Is it, then, that since the argument seeks the why, and these are good of themselves, it is at a loss for the why because the that is the why? For even if we name another cause, the difficulty is likewise the same, since the argument does not reach there. Yet we must not stand off, in case something should appear to us going by another road.
!flag Reason demands to know what constitutes goodness | The Greek says "the argument (ὁ λόγος) seeks the why (τὸ διότι)": the cause, the why of the demonstrations; and it is asked as a question, "is it that ...?".
!flag the doubt still remains until our reason claims its rights There | The Greek says the difficulty is the same "since the argument does not reach (μὴ φθάνοντος) there": it does not get there at all; "claims its rights" is MacKenna's.
!note The that and the why one in the intelligible: chapter 2 of this treatise, and Aristotle, Posterior Analytics II.2 (90a14-23), where the what and the why are the same.
@ch VI.7.20 | Not intellect, but the Good, is what all desire
Turn then to the judgments and the opposites: order and disorder, symmetry, health, form, substance, being put together; the first of each pair is in the form of the good, and so are their makers: virtue, intellect, life, the wise soul. Why not stop at intellect and call it the Good? Because not all things desire intellect, and those that have it do not stop, but seek the good again; intellect is sought from reasoning, the good before reason; and life and being are desired as good.

@p
Since, then, for the present we do not trust the desires for laying down what the good is, or of what kind, must we go to the judgments and the oppositions of things, as order and disorder, the symmetrical and the unsymmetrical, health and disease, form and shapelessness, substance and destruction, and, in a word, being put together and vanishing? Who would dispute that the first of these, in each pair, are in the form of the good? And if so, their makers too must be set in the good's portion. And virtue and intellect and life and soul, the wise one at least, are in the form of the good; and so, then, is what a wise life desires.
!flag form, shapelessness; real-being, decay | The Greek has "substance (οὐσίαν) and destruction (φθοράν)"; the modern version keeps "substance", and "real-being" is MacKenna's.
!flag reasoning soul, at least | The Greek has "the wise one (ἔμφρων) at least": a soul with wisdom in it, not reasoning.
!flag so therefore does all that a reasoned life aims at | The Greek says "what a wise life (ἔμφρων ζωή) desires": wise, not reasoned.

@p
@greek τί οὖν οὐ στησόμεθα
Why, then, someone will say, shall we not stop at intellect and set this down as the Good? For soul and life are traces of intellect, and soul desires it. And so it judges and desires intellect: judging justice better than injustice, and each form of virtue before the form of vice; and what it prefers is what it chooses.
!flag that principle is the Term of Soul which on judgement sets itself towards Intellectual-Principle | The Greek says "soul desires (ἐφίεται) this", and judges and desires intellect; "the Term" is MacKenna's.
!flag pronouncing right preferable to wrong | The Greek has "justice (δικαιοσύνην) better than injustice"; the modern version keeps "justice".
!flag and thus ranking by its choosing | The Greek says "what it prefers is what it chooses (αἵρεσις)": preferring and choosing are of the same things.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν νοῦ μόνον ἐφίεται
But if it desired intellect only, perhaps more argument would be needed, to show that intellect is not the last, and that not all things are of intellect, but all are of the good. And of those that do not have intellect, not all seek to acquire intellect, and those that have intellect do not stop there, but seek the good again; and they seek intellect from reasoning, but the good even before reason. And if they desire life too, and always being and being active, what is desired would not be so as intellect, but as good, and from good, and toward good: since life is so too.
!flag The soul aiming only at that Principle would need a further lessoning | The Greek says "if it desired intellect only, perhaps more argument (λόγου) would be needed": more argument for us, to show that intellect is not the last; not a lesson for the soul.
!flag life itself is desirable only in view of good | The Greek says "since life is so too" (ἐπεὶ καὶ ἡ ζωὴ οὕτως): life too is from good and toward good; "only" is MacKenna's.
!note All things desire the good, not all intellect: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.1 (1094a2-3), "the good is that at which all things aim"; Plato's Philebus (20d); Plotinus I.7.1 and V.5.12.
@ch VI.7.21 | The light from above on intellect and life
What one thing in all these makes each good? Let it be dared: intellect and that life are good-formed, life the activity from the Good, intellect that activity bounded, and they are desired in so far as they are good-formed. Full of splendour, they are pursued by soul as akin; but the akin, if not good, is fled. The strong love comes not when they are what they are, but when they take something more from there: as bodies with light mixed in still need another light for their own to show.

@p
What, then, being one in all these, makes each good? Let it be dared thus: intellect and that life are good-formed, and they too are desired in so far as they are good-formed; and I call them good-formed in that life is the activity of the Good, or rather the activity from the Good, and intellect is that activity already bounded. And they are full of splendour, and pursued by soul as from there, and as leading back there: as akin, then, but not as goods; yet, being good-formed, not to be thrown away for this either. For the akin, if it is not good, is akin, but one flees it: since other things too, far off and below, might move one.
!flag Intellectual-Principle and that life are of the order of good | The Greek says they are "good-formed" (ἀγαθοειδῆ), the word of chapters 15 to 18: in the form of the good, not "of the order".
!flag because Life is an Activity in The Good | The Greek says life is "the activity of the Good (τἀγαθοῦ), or rather from the Good": of, not in.
!flag while Intellectual-Principle is an Activity already defined Therein | The Greek says intellect is "that activity already bounded" (ἤδη ὁρισθεῖσαν); "Therein" is MacKenna's.
!flag the related if not good is shunned in spite of that relationship | The Greek says "the akin (τὸ οἰκεῖον), if it is not good, is akin, but one flees it": the akin, the word of chapters 24 and 27.

@p
@greek γίνεται δὲ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἔρως
The intense love for them comes not when they are what they are, but when, being already what they are, they take on something else from there. For as with bodies, though light is mixed in them, there is need of another light, that the light in them may appear, so with the things there, though they have much light, there is need of another, better light, so that they too may be seen, both by themselves and by another.
!flag is due not to what they are but to the consideration of their nature as something apart, received from above themselves | The Greek says the love comes "when, being already what they are, they take on (προσλάβῃ) something else from there": something added, not "the consideration of their nature".
!flag or even they would not be visible to themselves and beyond | The Greek says "so that they may be seen both by themselves and by another (ὑπ’ ἄλλου)": by another, not "beyond".
!note Sight and colour need a third thing, light: Plato's Republic VI (507d-508a). Love for what the light from the Good comes upon: chapter 22 and V.5.12.
@ch VI.7.22 | Beauty is the light on the symmetry
Seeing this light one is moved toward them and delights in the light running over them, as love here is for the beauty that shows on bodies. Each is what it is by itself, and becomes desired when the Good colours it. The soul that takes in the flow from there is roused and becomes love; before that it lies idle even before intellect, as before a beautiful face without grace. So beauty is the light that shines on symmetry, not symmetry: the living face is more beautiful than the dead, the living ugly than the beautiful statue.

@p
When, then, one sees this light, then indeed one is moved toward them, and, longing for the light that runs over them, rejoices: as here too love is not for the bodies that underlie, but for the beauty that appears on them. For each is what it is by itself; but it becomes desirable when the Good colours it, as if giving graces to them, and loves to those who desire them. And so soul, taking into itself the flow from there, is moved and roused to Bacchic frenzy, and filled with goads, and becomes love.
!flag Every one of those Beings exists for itself | The Greek says "each is what it is by itself" (ἐφ’ αὑτοῦ): by itself, not for itself.
!flag The soul taking that outflow from the divine is stirred | The Greek has "the flow from there" (τὴν ἐκεῖθεν ἀπορροήν), from the Good; "the divine" is MacKenna's.
!flag goaded by these goads | The Greek says "filled with goads" (οἴστρων πίμπλαται), the gadfly's stings of the Phaedrus.
!note The flow (ἀπορροή) of beauty that the soul takes in, its warmth, the stings and the growing of its wings: Plato's Phaedrus (251a-252b); the Bacchic frenzy of philosophy: Symposium (218b).

@p
@greek πρὸ τοῦ δὲ οὐδὲ πρὸς τὸν νοῦν
Before this it is not moved even toward intellect, though intellect is beautiful: for its beauty is idle until it takes the light of the Good, and the soul lies on its back of itself, idle toward everything, and, though intellect is present, sluggish toward it. But when there comes into it as it were a warmth from there, it gains strength and wakes up and really grows wings, and, though excited by what lies by it and near, it is lifted all the same, as by memory, toward another, greater thing. And so long as there is something higher than what is present, it rises by nature, lifted up by the giver of the love. And it rises above intellect, but cannot run above the Good, because there is nothing that lies above it.
!flag for that beauty is dead until it take the light of The Good | The Greek says the beauty is "idle" (ἀργόν), without work, as in chapter 13: idle, not dead.
!flag spreads true wings | The Greek says it "really grows wings" (ὄντως πτεροῦται), the Phaedrus' feathering of the soul: the wings grow, they are not spread.
!flag speeds its buoyant way elsewhere, to something greater to its memory | The Greek says it "is lifted (κουφίζεται) toward another, greater, as by memory (οἷον τῇ μνήμῃ)"; "speeds its buoyant way" is MacKenna's.
!note The soul's wings grown by the warmth of beauty, and its lifting by memory of what it saw: Plato's Phaedrus (249c-d, 251b-c).

@p
@greek ἐὰν δὲ μένῃ ἐν νῷ
But if it stays in intellect, it sees beautiful and solemn things, but does not yet have altogether what it seeks. For it is as if it came near a face that is beautiful, but cannot yet move the sight, because no grace running over the beauty shines on it. So here too one must say that beauty is rather what shines on the symmetry than the symmetry, and that this is what is lovable.
!flag but not of power to hold its gaze | The Greek says the face "cannot yet move (κινεῖν) the sight": it does not stir the seer, not hold the gaze.
!note Beauty not symmetry alone: I.6.1, against the Stoic definition of bodily beauty as a fitting shape of the limbs with a pleasant colour (Cicero, Tusculan Disputations IV.31).

@p
@greek διὰ τί γὰρ ἐπὶ μὲν ζῶντος
For why is the splendour of beauty more on a living face, and only a trace of it on a dead one, though the face is not yet wasted in its flesh and its symmetries? And of statues, are not the more lifelike more beautiful, though the others may be more symmetrical; and is not a living man who is uglier more beautiful than the beauty in a statue? Because this is more desired; and this because it has soul; and this because it is more good-formed; and this because it is somehow coloured by the light of the Good, and, coloured, it is woken and lifted up, and lifts up what it has, and, as far as it can, makes it good and wakes it.
!flag though the face yet retains all its fulness and symmetry | The Greek says "not yet wasted (μεμαρασμένου) in its flesh and symmetries": not yet decayed; "all its fulness" is MacKenna's.
!flag Why are the most living portraits the most beautiful | The Greek has "statues" (ἀγαλμάτων), the more lifelike (ζωτικώτερα) of them: statues, not portraits.
!flag because there is more of the Idea of The Good | The Greek says "because it is more good-formed (ἀγαθοειδέστερον)": the word of chapters 15 to 21; "the Idea of The Good" is MacKenna's.
!flag so that the whole man is won over to goodness, and in the fullest measure stirred to life | The Greek says it "makes good (ἀγαθοποιεῖ) and wakes, as far as it can (ὡς οἷόν τε), what it has": the body it has, as far as it can; "the whole man" and "the fullest measure" are MacKenna's.
@ch VI.7.23 | The Good, best of all, and what it makes
No wonder that what the soul pursues has such power, drawing it back from all wandering to rest: what all things come from is better than all, most self-sufficient, and was before there was vice. Evil, the last, is its contrary with nothing between, so either there is no good, or this is it; the other goods look to it, and it to nothing. It made intellect, life, souls and all that shares in a forming principle; and now too it keeps them, breathing in intellect and life, and, where life cannot be, being.

@p
That, then, which soul pursues, and which gives light to intellect, and, falling on it, moves its trace: one should not marvel if it has such power, drawing to itself and calling back from all wandering, so that one may rest beside it. For if all things are from it, nothing is better than it, and all are less. How, then, is the best of beings not the Good? And indeed, if the nature of the Good must be most self-sufficient to itself, and without need of anything else at all, what other could one find it to be than this? It was what it was before the others, when there was not yet even vice.
!flag leaving its mark wherever it falls | The Greek says "falling (ἐμπεσόν) on it, moves its trace (ἴχνος)": it moves its own trace in intellect; "wherever it falls" is MacKenna's.
!flag From it came all and so there is nothing mightier | The Greek says "nothing is better (κρεῖττον) than it, and all are less": better, not mightier.
!flag when evil had yet no place in things | The Greek has "vice" (κακία): before there was even vice; evils come in the next sentence.
!note All things about the king of all, and for his sake: Plato's Letter II (312e). The good self-sufficient (ἱκανόν) and complete: Philebus (20d, 60c).

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ τὰ κακὰ ὕστερον
And if evils are later, in the things that have not shared in this even in one respect, and in the last things, and there is nothing beyond evils toward the worse, then evils would be contrary to it, having nothing between them for the contrariety. This, then, would be the Good: for either there is no good at all, or, if there must be, it would be this and no other. And if someone said there is none, there would be no evil either: then things would be indifferent by nature for choosing; and this is impossible. The other things that are called goods look to this, but it to nothing.
!flag there found where there is no trace of This | The Greek says evils are "in the things that have not shared (μετειληφόσι) in this even in one respect": in what has no share, not "no trace".
!flag there can then be no difference in objects coming up for choice | The Greek says things would be "indifferent (ἀδιάφορα) by nature for choosing": the Stoics' word for what is neither good nor evil.
!note Evil the last, with nothing beyond it, contrary to the Good: I.8.6-7. The indifferents (ἀδιάφορα), neither good nor evil: the Stoics in Diogenes Laertius VII.102-104.

@p
@greek τί οὖν ποιεῖ τοιοῦτον ὄν
What, then, does it make, being such? It made intellect, it made life, souls from this, and the other things, as many as share in a forming principle or intellect or life. And what is the spring and principle of these, who could say how good it is, and how great? But what does it make now? Now too it keeps those things safe, and makes the thinking things think and the living things live, breathing in intellect, breathing in life, and, if something cannot live, being.
!flag the souls which Intellectual-Principle sends forth | The Greek says "souls from this" (ἐκ τούτου); "which Intellectual-Principle sends forth" is MacKenna's.
!flag everything else that partakes of Reason, of Intellectual-Principle or of Life | The Greek has λόγου: what shares in a forming principle, as plants do; the modern version keeps "forming principle" for λόγος, and "Reason" is MacKenna's.
!note The spring and principle of all: III.8.10, the spring that gives itself to all the rivers and is not used up; the soul the "spring and principle of motion" in Plato's Phaedrus (245c).
@ch VI.7.24 | Is the good only a name for the pleasant?
And what does it do for us? Putting off the light for later, ask first: is the Good good because it is desired, by some or by all? Desire is a witness, but the desired must have such a nature. Do the desirers seek to receive something, or to delight in it? Is the good another's, or good to itself? And a hard man will object: why give grand names to life and intellect as good, when you say the Good is beyond them? Without pleasure they are not goods, and our being matters only by love of ourselves and fear of perishing.

@p
And what does it make in us? Or let us speak again about the light, what the light is by which intellect is lit and in which soul shares: or, putting this off for later, as is fitting, let us first raise these difficulties. Is the Good good, and called good, because it is desired by another, and being desired by some it is good to them, and being desired by all we call it the Good? Or one could make this a witness that it is good, but the desired itself must have such a nature that it would justly get such a name.
!flag We may recall what we have said of the nature of the light shining from it into Intellectual-Principle and so by participation into the soul | The Greek says "or let us speak again about the light, what the light is (τί τὸ φῶς)": to ask what it is, which is then put off.
!flag No doubt this universal questing would make the goodness evident | The Greek says "one could make this a witness (μαρτύριον)" that it is good; "universal questing" is MacKenna's.
!note Desired because good, or good because desired: Aristotle, Metaphysics Λ.7 (1072a29), "we desire it because it seems good, rather than it seems good because we desire it"; and the holy loved because it is holy, Plato's Euthyphro (10a-e).

@p
@greek καὶ πότερα τῷ τι δέχεσθαι
And do the things that desire desire by receiving something, or by delighting in it? And if they receive something, what is it? And if by delighting, why in this, and not in something else? In which there is also the question whether the good is in what is akin, or in something else; and indeed whether the good is wholly another's, or the good is good to itself too. Or whatever is good is not good to itself, but of necessity to another. And to what nature is it good? But there is a nature to which nothing is good.
!flag Further, is the questing determined by the hope of some acquisition or by sheer delight ? | The Greek asks whether they desire "by receiving something (τι δέχεσθαι)" or by delighting: receiving, not the hope of acquiring.
!flag Is goodness in the appropriate or in something apart | The Greek has "the akin" (τῷ οἰκείῳ), the word of chapters 21 and 27: what belongs to one.
!flag Any good is such, necessarily, not for itself but for something outside | The Greek puts it as one side of the question ("or whatever is good ..."), and it is answered at once by "a nature to which nothing is good".
!note A nature to which nothing is good: the One, good to others and not to itself, VI.9.6, and chapter 41 of this treatise.

@p
@greek κἀκεῖνο δὲ οὐκ ἀφετέον
And we must not let go what a hard-to-please man might say: "You there, why do you put on airs with names, up and down, calling life good and intellect good, though you put the Good beyond these? For why would intellect be good? Or what good would one who thinks the forms themselves have, contemplating each one itself? If he were deceived and taking pleasure in them, he might perhaps call it good, and life too, since it is pleasant; but if he stood in being without pleasure, why would he say they are goods? Is it his own being? For what fruit would he reap from being? Or what difference would there be in being or not being at all, unless one made his love of himself the cause of these? So it is because of this deception, which is natural, and the fear of perishing, that goods came to be laid down."
!flag you scatter praises here, there and everywhere | The Greek says "why do you put on airs with names (ἀποσεμνύνετε τοῖς ὀνόμασιν), up and down": exalting by grand names, not scattering praise.
!flag Or what do we gain by seeing the Ideas themselves if we see only a particular Idea and nothing else | The Greek asks "what good would one who thinks the forms themselves have, contemplating each one itself (αὐτὸ ἕκαστον)": each form in itself; "only a particular Idea and nothing else" is MacKenna's.
!flag If we are happy here we may be deceived into thinking life a good when it is merely pleasant | The Greek says "if he were deceived and pleased (ἡδόμενος) by these": pleased by the forms, not "happy here".
!flag but suppose our lot unhappy | The Greek says "if he stood in being without pleasure (ἀνήδονος)": without pleasure, not unhappy.
!note Love of oneself and the fear of perishing as the first things: the Stoic first impulse of a living being, to keep itself (Diogenes Laertius VII.85); Plotinus answers in chapter 27 that a thing loves itself because it has a portion of the good.
@ch VI.7.25 | The Philebus' mixture; each thing's good the one above it
Plato in the Philebus mixed pleasure with the end, perhaps aware of this difficulty, since he would not make the good the pleasant, nor intellect, without pleasure, the good; or because he held the good must give joy. But he sought our good, not the first. The good must be desired, yet it is desired because it is good. Each thing's good is the one above it: form for matter, soul for body, virtue for soul, then intellect, and the first nature above that, each giving something to those below.

@p
Plato, then, mixing pleasure with the end, and setting the good down not as simple nor in intellect alone, as is written in the Philebus, perhaps, aware of this difficulty, did not turn to set the good altogether in the pleasant, rightly, nor did he think he should set down intellect, being without pleasure, as the good, since he did not see what moves in it. Or perhaps not for this, but because he held that the good, having such a nature in itself, must of necessity be a thing of joy, and that the desired must surely bring joy to the one who gains it, so that what has no joy is not good, and so that, if joy belongs to the one desiring, it does not belong to the first: so that neither does the good.
!flag makes pleasure an element in the Term | The Greek says "mixing (μιγνύς) pleasure with the end (τῷ τέλει)": the mixed life of the Philebus; "the Term" is MacKenna's.
!flag since he sees no attractive power in it | The Greek says "not seeing what moves (τὸ κινοῦν) in it": what moves the soul, the stirring of chapter 22.
!note Plato's Philebus: the good life is the mixed life of pleasure and wisdom (20e-22e, 60a-61b), the good being neither pleasure nor intellect alone; intellect is akin to the cause of the mixture (30d-31a).

@p
@greek καὶ οὐκ ἄτοπον τοῦτο
And this is not absurd: for he was not seeking the first good, but ours; and, in general, for a being that is other, its good is other than itself, since it falls short and is perhaps composite. This is why what is solitary and alone has no good, but is good in another way, and greater.
!flag it is a mingled thing | The Greek says the being whose good it is "falls short and is perhaps composite (συνθέτου)": the being is composite, not the good.
!flag we are to understand that good does not hold place in the One and Alone whose being is too great and different for that | The Greek says "what is solitary and alone (τὸ ἔρημον καὶ μόνον) has no good, but is otherwise and greater": it has no good because it is good in another way; "the One" is MacKenna's.
!note "The alone": VI.9.11, the flight of the alone to the alone. The Good has no good of its own: VI.9.6.

@p
@greek ἐφετὸν μὲν οὖν δεῖ
The good, then, must be desired, yet it is not by being desired that it becomes good, but by being good that it becomes desired. Is it, then, that for the last among beings its good is what is before it, and the ascent always gives what is above each to be the good of what is below it, if the ascent does not depart from proportion, but always goes on to the greater? And then it will stop at a last, after which there is nothing further to take upward, and this will be the first, and what really is good, and most properly, and the cause for the others too.
!flag The solution, it would seem, lies in priority | The Greek has no such sentence: it goes straight on to the question of the ascent (ἀνάβασις), "for the last among beings, what is before it".
!flag so long as the movement does not tend awry but advances continuously towards the superior | The Greek says "if the ascent does not depart from proportion (τοῦ ἀνὰ λόγον)": it keeps its proportion, step by step; "tend awry" is MacKenna's.
!flag the supremely sovran | The Greek has "most properly (μάλιστα κυρίως)": good in the most proper sense; "sovran" is MacKenna's.
!note The ladder of goods, each the good of what is below it: I.7.2 and I.8.2; the ascent by steps: Plato's Symposium (210a-211c).

@p
@greek τῇ μὲν γὰρ ὕλῃ τὸ εἶδος
For to matter, form is its good — for if it got perception, it would welcome it; to the body, soul — for without it, it would not even be, nor be kept safe; and to soul, virtue. And higher still is intellect, and above this what we call the first nature. And each of these makes something for those whose goods they are: some order and adornment, others life already, others being wise and living well; and to intellect, the Good, which we say comes into it too, both because it is an activity from it, and because it now too gives what is called light: what that is, later.
!flag Matter would have Forming-Idea for its good | The Greek has "form" (τὸ εἶδος); "Forming-Idea" is MacKenna's.
!flag some will confer order and place | The Greek has "order and adornment (κόσμον)": the ordering of a world, not place.
!flag Intellectual-Principle will draw upon the Authentic Good which we hold to be coterminous with it | The Greek says "to intellect, the Good, which we say comes (ἥκειν) into it too": the Good comes into intellect; "coterminous with it" is MacKenna's.
!flag as even now taking light from it | The Greek says the Good "now too gives (δίδωσι) what is called light": the Good gives, not intellect takes.
!note Matter desires form as the female the male: Aristotle, Physics I.9 (192a20-25). The body kept in being by soul: IV.7.2-3.
@ch VI.7.26 | The proof of the good: rest, not pleasure
What can perceive knows the good when it comes and says it has it. If it is deceived, there must be a likeness by which it is deceived, and its good is what it is deceived about, since when that comes it turns from the false. Desire and travail witness a good for each. One has gained it when one is better, without regret, filled, staying and seeking nothing else: so pleasure is not enough, for it does not love the same thing twice, and one who takes the feeling for the good goes empty.

@p
And what is by nature able to perceive it of itself knows the good, if it comes to it, and says it has it. What, then, if it is deceived? There must, then, be some likeness by which it is deceived. And if so, that from which it is deceived would be its good: since, when that comes, it stands away from what deceived it. And the desire of each, and its travail, witness that there is some good of each. For to the soulless things the gift of the good is from another, but in what has soul desire works the pursuit; as for bodies that have become dead the care and burial are from the living, but for the living their providence is from themselves.
!flag Any conscious being if the good come to him will know the good | The Greek has "what is by nature able to perceive (αἰσθάνεσθαι)": perceiving, not conscious.
!flag All the striving, all the pain, show that to everything something is a good | The Greek has "travail" (ὠδίς), the birth pangs of the Symposium's lover, not pain.
!flag the lifeless finds its share in something outside itself | The Greek says "for the soulless (ἀψύχοις) the gift (δόσις) of the good is from another": given, not found.
!flag the living plan for their own good | The Greek says "for the living their providence (πρόνοια) is from themselves": they care for themselves, as the dead are cared for by others.
!note Travail (ὠδίς) for the beautiful: Plato's Symposium (206d-e), and the soul's travail for the truth, Republic VI (490b).

@p
@greek ὅτι δ’ ἔτυχε, πιστοῦται
That it has gained it is confirmed when it becomes something better, and without regret, and it finds itself filled, and stays with that, and seeks nothing else. This is why pleasure is not self-sufficient: for it does not love the same; for it is not the same because it is pleasure again: what it takes pleasure in is always other. The good, then, which one chooses, must not be the affection at what one gets: this is why one who thinks this good stays empty, having only the affection, which one might have had from the good.
!flag The witness of attainment is betterment, cleaving to state, satisfaction, settlement, suspension of pursuit | The Greek says it is confirmed when one becomes better "and without regret (ἀμετανόητον)", filled, staying and seeking nothing else: the regret is left out, and "cleaving to state" is MacKenna's.
!flag The good, worthy of the name, can be no such tasting of the casual | The Greek says the good one chooses "must not be the affection (πάθος) at what one gets": the feeling, not "the casual".
!note Pleasure a coming to be that never fills: Plato's Philebus (53c-54d), and the leaking jar of the Gorgias (493e-494b).

@p
@greek διὸ οὐκ ἂν ἀνάσχοιτό τις
This is why no one would put up with the affection at what he does not have: as with a child, to be pleased that he is present when he is not; nor, I think, would those who set the good in being filled in body be pleased as if eating when they are not eating, or as if enjoying sex when not with the one they wanted, or, in general, when not doing anything.
@ch VI.7.27 | Each thing's good is its better, a portion of the Good
By the coming of what does each have what befits it? A form: form for matter, virtue for soul. Is it good as akin? No: the like is akin, yet not yet the good. The akin is judged by the better, toward which a thing is in potency; matter is the neediest, and the lowest form is next to it. The form is good to a thing because it is a portion of the good, which is why the pure are most at home with themselves. Desire does not make the good, but comes because it is good, and it is to be chosen even without pleasure.

@p
But by the coming of what does each have what befits it? We shall say, of some form: for form is matter's, and virtue is the soul's form. But is this form good to that one by being akin, and is desire toward the akin? Or no: for the like is akin, and even if a thing wishes it and delights in the like, it does not yet have the good. But shall we say it is not akin, when we say it is good? Or one must say that the akin must be judged by what is better and stronger than it, toward which it is in potency.
!flag to soul moral excellence is this Form | The Greek has "virtue (ἀρετή) is the soul's form"; the modern version keeps "virtue".
!flag No: the aptest would be the most resemblant to the thing itself | The Greek says "the like (τὸ ὅμοιον) is akin": the like, not "the aptest" or "the most resemblant".
!flag to be a good to another a thing must have something beyond aptness | The Greek asks "but shall we say it is not akin, when we say it is good?", and answers that the akin is judged by what is better; "something beyond aptness" is MacKenna's.
!note The like and the akin: Plato's Lysis (214a-215c, 221e-222b), where neither like nor unlike is the friend, and the akin (οἰκεῖον) is what one desires; Symposium (205e), love is of the half or the whole only if it is good.

@p
@greek ὂν γὰρ δυνάμει πρὸς ὃ ἔστιν
For, being in potency toward what it is, it lacks it, and what it lacks, being better, is good to it. And matter is the neediest of all, and the last form is next to it: for after it comes the way upward. And if something is good to itself too, much more would its perfection be good to it, and its form, and what is better than it, which is such by its own nature, and is good to it because it makes it good.
!flag A thing is potentially that to which its nature looks | The Greek says "being in potency toward what it is (πρὸς ὃ ἔστιν), it lacks it": "its nature looks" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ διὰ τί αὐτῷ ἀγαθὸν ἔσται
But why will it be good to it? Because it is most akin to it? Or no: but because it is a portion of the good. This is why the pure, and those that are more good, are more at home with themselves. It is absurd, then, to ask why what is good is good to itself, as if it had to stand outside its own nature toward itself and not love itself as good. But in the case of the simple one must consider whether, where there is no this and that at all, its being at home with itself is good to itself.
!flag This is why the least alloyed and nearest to the good are most at peace within themselves | The Greek has "at home with themselves" (οἰκείωσις πρὸς αὑτούς): a belonging to oneself, the akin of the chapter, not peace.
!flag so that it must strain outside its essential quality to the good which it effectually is | The Greek says "as if it had to stand outside (ἐξίστασθαι) its own nature toward itself, and not love (ἀγαπᾶν) itself as good": the love of self is what is left out.
!note Being at home with oneself (οἰκείωσις): the Stoics' word for a living being's first belonging to itself (Diogenes Laertius VII.85; Cicero, On ends III.16).

@p
@greek νῦν δέ, εἰ ταῦτα ὀρθῶς λέγεται
As it is, if this is said rightly, the ascent too has the good lying in some nature, and it is not desire that makes the good, but desire comes because it is good; and something comes to those who acquire it, and at the acquiring, something pleasant. But the good is to be chosen, and sought for itself, even if no pleasure should follow.
!flag the striving of the lower possesses itself of the good as of a thing resident in a certain Kind | The Greek says "the ascent (ἐπανάβασις) has the good lying in some nature (φύσει)": the ascent, not the striving of the lower, and a nature, not a Kind.
@ch VI.7.28 | Matter, form, and the formless Good
If the good is everywhere form, would matter, if it could wish, wish to be form only? Then it would wish to perish; perhaps it would wish to be, and let go its badness. The argument gave matter perception only as a supposition: form came to it as a good dream. Vice does not choose; what is made bad does. If the good is form, and the higher the more form, the good draws near to what puts matter off; the nature of the Good, never near matter, has fled up into the formless, from which the first form comes.

@p
Now we must see what follows from the argument. For if what comes as good is everywhere a form, and the good for matter too is form, would matter, if it could wish, have wished to become form only? But if so, it will wish to perish: and everything seeks the good for itself. But perhaps it will not seek to be matter, but to be, and, having this, will wish to let go of its badness. But how will what is evil have desire for the good?
!flag for the good seeks to subject everything to itself | The Greek says "everything seeks the good for itself (αὑτῷ πᾶν ζητεῖ)": each thing seeks its own good, which would not be its perishing; MacKenna turns the sentence round.
!flag would not wish to remain at its own level | The Greek says "it will not seek to be matter (ὕλη εἶναι), but to be": "at its own level" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἢ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕλην ἐν ἐφέσει
Or we did not set matter among the desiring at all, but the argument made a supposition, giving it perception, if indeed one could give it while keeping it matter; and it said that, when form came upon it, as a good dream, it came to be in a more beautiful order. If, then, matter is the evil, that has been said; but if it is something else, such as vice, then, if its being got perception, would what is akin toward the better still be the good? Or it was not the vice that chose, but what was made bad.
!flag and we asserted that the entry of Form, that dream of the Good, must raise it to a nobler order | The Greek says form came upon it "as a good dream (ὥσπερ ὀνείρατος ἀγαθοῦ)": a dream that is good, not a dream of the Good; and it "came to be" in a more beautiful order, not "must raise".
!flag a wrong thing, let us say | The Greek has "such as vice (κακία)", the soul's evil, set beside matter.
!flag But not what is evil in Matter would be the quester of good but that element in it (lowest Form) which in it is associated with evil | The Greek says "it was not the vice that chose, but what was made bad (τὸ κακούμενον)": the one made bad by vice, the soul; "in Matter" and "(lowest Form)" are MacKenna's.
!note Matter as the first evil: I.8.3-5 and II.4.16. Matter a phantom on which the forms appear as in a dream: III.6.7.

@p
@greek εἰ δὲ ταὐτὸν τὸ εἶναι καὶ τὸ κακόν
But if being and evil are the same, how will this choose the good? But if evil got perception of itself, would it love itself? And how will the unlovable be loved? For we did not set the good in the akin. So much for this.
!flag This question implies that if Evil were self-conscious it would admire itself | The Greek asks it: "if evil got perception of itself, would it love (ἀγαπήσει) itself?": a question, and love, not admiration.
!flag and did we not discover that the good must be apt to the nature ? | The Greek says the opposite: "we did not set (οὐ ... ἐθέμεθα) the good in the akin (τῷ οἰκείῳ)", as chapter 27 showed: the good is not what is akin.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ εἰ εἶδος τὸ ἀγαθὸν
But if the good is everywhere form, and as one goes up there is more form — for soul is more form than the body's form, and of soul one part is more form, another still more, and intellect more than soul — the good would draw near to what is opposite to matter, and is as it were purified and puts it off, to each according to its power, and most to what puts off all that is of matter. And so the nature of the Good, having fled all matter, or rather never having come near it anywhere in any way, would have fled up into the formless nature, from which the first form comes. But about this later.
!flag Soul more truly Form than body is | The Greek says soul is more form "than the body's form" (ἢ σώματος εἶδος): than the form in a body.
!flag Intellectual-Principle standing as Form to soul collectively | The Greek says intellect is more form "than soul" (ψυχῆς); "collectively" is MacKenna's.
!flag then the Good advances by the opposite of Matter and, therefore, by a cleansing and casting away to the utmost possible at each stage | The Greek says the good "would draw near (προσχωροῖ) to what is opposite to matter, and is as it were purified (καθαιρομένῳ)": the good comes near to what is purified and puts matter off; MacKenna has the good advance by a cleansing.
!flag must hold itself aloft with that Formless in which Primal Form takes its origin | The Greek says it "would have fled up into the formless nature (εἰς τὴν ἀνείδεον φύσιν), from which the first form comes": the Good is that formless nature, as in chapter 17, not with it.
!note The first form from the formless Good: chapter 17 above, chapters 32-33 to come, and V.5.6.

@ch VI.7.29 | Against the man who is not struck by the Good
If something came before pleasure and caused it, it would be welcome; one may know the good is present and not be moved, as the self-controlled, and the first has no pleasure, since acquisition pleases only the needy. Against the man who hears of the Good and is not struck: in scorning it he sets some good before himself, and may even divine what is beyond intellect; let him learn it from its opposites, for everyone chooses to think, and the senses wish to be knowings; who scorns being and life witnesses against himself.

@p
But if pleasure did not follow the good, and yet something came before pleasure, because of which pleasure too comes, why would it not be welcome? Or, in saying "welcome", we have already said pleasure. But what if it will be there, and yet, once it is there, it is possible for it not to be welcome? If so, then when the good is present, what has it, having perception, will not know that it has it. Or what prevents it from both knowing and not being moved in any other way along with having it? This would belong more to the more self-controlled, and more to one who is not in need. This is why it does not belong to the first either: not only because it is simple, but because acquisition is pleasant to one who has been in need. But this too will become clear, with all the rest that remains, once we have cleared the way further and pushed off that opposing argument.
!flag this is quite likely in the case of the wiser and least dependent | The Greek has "the more self-controlled" (σωφρονεστέρῳ), not the wiser; the modern version keeps "self-control", as for σωφροσύνη throughout.
!flag and indeed it is so with the First, immune not merely because simplex | The Greek says that being moved along with having the good "does not belong to the first either" (οὐδὲ τῷ πρώτῳ): the first has no pleasure in it; "immune" is MacKenna's.
!flag and the rebuttal of the argument brought up against us | The Greek has "that opposing (ἀντίτυπον) argument", pushed off once the way is cleared; it is not said to be brought against "us".

@p
@greek ἔστι δὲ οὗτος, ὃς ἀπορεῖ
This is the argument that asks what one who has intellect would reap toward a share of the good, if he is not struck at all when he hears these things, because he has no understanding of them, or hears only a name, or takes each of them for something else, or seeks something perceptible and sets the good in money or some such things. To him we must say that, when he holds these things in no honour, he agrees that he sets some good before himself, but is at a loss how these things fit the notion he has of it. For one cannot say "not this" while being wholly without experience of this and without a notion of it. And perhaps he even divines what is beyond intellect.
!flag What gain is there in the Good to one who, fully conscious, feels nothing | The Greek has "one who has intellect" (ὁ νοῦν ἔχων), the sensible man, who is "not struck at all" (οὐδὲν πληττόμενος) when he hears; "fully conscious" is MacKenna's.
!flag because he holds to false values | The Greek says he "takes each of them for something else" (ἄλλο τι ἕκαστον αὐτῶν ὑπολαμβάνων): a misreading of the words, not false values.
!flag there will generally have been, even, some inkling of the good beyond Intellection | The Greek says "perhaps" (τάχα), not "generally", and he divines "what is beyond intellect" (τὸ ὑπὲρ νοῦν).
!note "Not this": one who rejects a good must already have some notion (ἔννοια) of the good, as every soul divines the good without grasping it (Republic VI 505d-e, quoted in chapter 19).

@p
@greek ἔπειτα δέ, εἰ τῷ ἀγαθῷ
Next, if, coming upon the good or what is near it, he does not recognize it, let him come to a notion of it from its opposites. Or will he not even set down folly as an evil? And yet everyone chooses to think, and takes pride in thinking. The senses too bear witness, wishing to be knowings. If, then, intellect is precious and beautiful, and the first intellect most of all, what would one imagine, if one could, of its begetter and father? And one who holds being and life in no honour bears witness against himself and against all his own affections. But if someone is disgusted with the life with which death is mixed, he is disgusted with such a life, not with true life.
!flag otherwise he will not even hold ignorance an evil | The Greek has "folly" (ἄνοια), the want of intellect (νοῦς), set against the thinking everyone chooses; not ignorance.
!flag so that our very sensations seek to ripen into knowledge | The Greek says "the senses too bear witness, wishing to be knowings (εἰδήσεις)"; "ripen" is MacKenna's.
!flag what must be present to those of power to see the Author and Father of Intellect | The Greek asks "what would one imagine (φαντασθείη), if one could, of its begetter and father?": what one could picture of it, not what is present to those who see it.
!flag brings evidence against himself and all his state | The Greek says he witnesses against himself "and all his own affections (πάθεσι)": his own clinging to being and life speaks against his scorn of them.
!note The senses wishing to be knowings: Aristotle, Metaphysics A.1 (980a21-27), "all men by nature desire to know; a sign is the delight we take in the senses". "Begetter and father": the maker and father of this all (Timaeus 28c), and "the father of the leader and cause" (Letter VI 323d).

@ch VI.7.30 | Pleasure in the mixed life is a metaphor
Is the good mixed with pleasure? One opinion makes intellect the good and our joy a feeling at having it; another mixes pleasure with intellect into one thing, since what is alone could not be chosen as good. But neither bodily pleasure nor the soul's irrational joys can mix with intellect: what is called pleasure there is the brightness of an unhindered activity, named by metaphor, as the poets say "drunk on nectar". The truly welcome is there, and the cause is what coloured it; we have our share in the mixture, and in another way by leading ourselves up to the best in us.

@p
But if pleasure must be mixed with the good, and life is not complete for one who contemplates the divine things, and most of all their principle, then it is fitting for us, now that we are laying hold of the good, to look at this by all means. To think that the good is made of intellect as the substrate and of the soul's affection that comes from being wise is not to set the composite of both as the end, or as the good itself; rather, intellect would be the good, and we would be rejoicing in having the good. And this would be one opinion about the good.
!flag is a question not to be ignored in any enquiry into the nature of the good | The Greek says it is fitting "now", for those "laying hold of the good" (ἐφαπτομένους τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ), to look at it; the enquiry is theirs, not any enquiry.
!flag that state of soul or mind which springs from wisdom | The Greek has "the soul's affection (πάθος) that comes from being wise (φρονεῖν)": a feeling, the joy of it, not a state of soul or mind.
!note The two opinions are those of Plato's Philebus (20b-22e, 60a-61b): that the good is wisdom (φρόνησις), or a mixed life of wisdom and pleasure, which Socrates prefers to either alone.

@p
@greek ἑτέρα δὲ εἴη ἂν παρὰ ταύτην
But there would be another opinion beside this, which mixes pleasure with intellect and sets this, one thing made of both, as the substrate, so that we have the good by acquiring, or even by seeing, such an intellect: for what is bare and alone can neither come to be nor be chosen as a good. How, then, could intellect be mixed with pleasure into one completed nature? That one would not think the body's pleasure can be mixed with intellect is surely clear to everyone; nor any irrational joys of the soul.
!flag this theory would maintain that the isolated and unrelated could be the good, could be an object of desire | The Greek says the opposite: "what is bare and alone (τὸ ἔρημον καὶ μόνον) can neither come to be nor be chosen as a good", which is why this opinion mixes pleasure in.
!flag the unreasoning satisfactions of soul (or lower mind) | The Greek has "the irrational joys (χαραὶ ... ἄλογοι) of the soul"; "(or lower mind)" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ἀλλ’ ἐπειδὴ πάσῃ ἐνεργείᾳ
But every activity, and every disposition and life too, must be followed, and as it were accompanied, by what runs over it. By this, for one life, going according to nature, there is what hinders, and something of the opposite mixed in, which does not let the life be its own; for another the activity is pure and unmixed and the life in a bright disposition. Since this is so, they set down such a state of intellect as most welcome and most to be chosen, and say it is mixed with pleasure, at a loss for a proper name: as the poets do too, carrying over the other names of things we love here, "drunk on nectar", and "to the feast and banquet", and "the father smiled", and countless others of the kind.
!flag will be followed and as it were escorted by the overdwelling consciousness | The Greek has "what runs over it" (τὸ ἐπιθέον), the bloom that comes on an activity; there is no consciousness in the Greek.
!flag so that the life is the less self-guided | The Greek says the hindrance "does not let the life be its own (ἑαυτῆς)": a life not its own, not less self-guided.
!note What runs over the activity: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics X.4 (1174b31-33), pleasure completes the activity "as a supervening end, like the bloom on those in their prime". The poets: "drunk on nectar" is Resource in Plato's Symposium (203b), read again in chapter 35; "the father smiled" is Zeus in Homer's Iliad (V.426, XV.47).

@p
@greek ἔστι γὰρ καὶ τὸ ἄσμενον ὄντως ἐκεῖ
For the truly welcome is there, and the most loved and the most longed for, not coming to be, nor in motion; and its cause is what coloured these things, and shone on them, and made them bright. This is why he adds truth to the mixture, and makes the measure before it, and says that the symmetry and the beauty in the mixture have come into the beautiful from there: so that it is in this way that we would have a share in it too. But what is truly desirable for us is, in another way, ourselves to ourselves, when we lead ourselves up to the best of ourselves: this is the symmetrical and beautiful, a composite form, and a life clear and intellectual and beautiful.
!flag the very principle of all the colour and radiance and brightness found here | The Greek says "the cause is what coloured (ἐπιχρῶσαν) these things, and shone on them": the Good colours the welcome things there, as in chapters 21 and 22; "found here" is MacKenna's.
!flag this best is what is symmetry, beauty, collective Idea | The Greek has "a composite form" (εἶδος σύνθετον): a form made of parts, not a collective Idea.
!flag life clear, Intellective and good | The Greek has a life "clear and intellectual and beautiful (καλήν)": beautiful, not good.
!note Truth in the mixture, and the measure first: Plato's Philebus (64a-66a): without truth nothing could come to be; the measure and the symmetrical are ranked first, and the good has taken refuge in the beautiful.

@ch VI.7.31 | The soul loves the Good and is suspicious of beauty here
All things got light from what is before them, intellect its radiance and soul a power of life. Intellect stayed with it; the soul that turned took pleasure and was struck, and, having something of it in itself, came to longing, as lovers here shape themselves to the beloved. The soul that has its love ready to hand needs no reminder from beauty here, but is suspicious of it, seeing it in flesh and stained, and knows it has its beauty from elsewhere; it is carried there and, near, perceives what it has long sought.

@p
But since all things were made beautiful by that which is before them, and got light, intellect the radiance of its intellectual activity, by which it lit up its own nature, and soul a power for living, since more life came into it: intellect, then, was raised up there and stayed, content to be about that one. And the soul too that was able turned, and, as it knew and saw, took pleasure in the sight, and was struck with amazement, as far as it was able to see.
!flag which flashed Nature into being | The Greek says intellect "lit up its own nature (τὴν φύσιν ἐξέλαμψε)" by the radiance of its activity: its nature shone out; Nature was not flashed into being.
!flag Thence soul took power towards life, in virtue of that fuller life streaming into it | The Greek has "since more life came into it": "streaming" is MacKenna's.
!flag clung to what it saw | The Greek says the soul "turned" (ἐπιστραφεῖσα) and, as it knew and saw, "took pleasure in the sight" (ἥσθη τῇ θέᾳ); there is no clinging.

@p
@greek εἶδε δὲ οἷον πληγεῖσα
It saw, as though struck, and, having something of it in itself, it perceived it with itself, and, being so disposed, came to be in longing, as those who are moved by the image of the one they love wish to see the beloved himself.
!flag but having in itself something of that principle it felt its kinship | The Greek says it "perceived it with itself" (συνῄσθετο): it was aware of what it had in itself; "kinship" is MacKenna's.
!note The image of the beloved: Plato's Phaedrus (250d-251a), the lover who sees a godlike face or body, an image (εἴδωλον) of beauty, shudders and reveres the beloved as a god.

@p
@greek ὥσπερ δὲ ἐνταῦθα σχηματίζονται
And as here those who love shape themselves into likeness to the one they love, making their bodies more comely and leading their souls into likeness, so as not to fall short, as far as they can, of the beloved's self-control and the rest of his virtue (or they would be rejected by such beloveds; and these are the ones who are able to be with them), in this way the soul too loves that one, moved from the beginning by him to love.
!flag they are unwilling to fall short in moral quality or in other graces | The Greek has the beloved's "self-control (σωφροσύνῃ) and the rest of his virtue (ἀρετῇ)"; the modern version keeps self-control and virtue.
!flag and only among such can true love be | The Greek says "these are the ones who are able to be with (συνεῖναι) them": to be with the beloved, not true love.
!flag In the same way the soul loves the Supreme Good | The Greek says the soul "loves that one" (ἐρᾷ ἐκείνου), moved by him to love; "the Supreme Good" is MacKenna's name for him.
!note Lovers shaping themselves to the beloved: Plato's Phaedrus (252d-253c), where each lover follows his god and leads the beloved into the god's likeness.

@p
@greek καὶ ἡ πρόχειρον ἔχουσα τὸν ἔρωτα
And the soul that has its love ready to hand does not wait for a reminder from the beautiful things here; but, having the love, even if it does not know that it has it, it seeks always, and, wishing to be carried to that one, it looks down on the things here; and, seeing the beautiful things in this All, it is suspicious of them, because it sees them in flesh and bodies, stained by their present dwelling, divided by magnitudes, and not being the beautiful things themselves: for those, such as they are, would not dare to step into the mud of bodies and soil themselves and blot themselves out. And when it sees them flowing past as well, it knows at once and fully that they have from elsewhere what ran over them.
!flag The soul which has never strayed from this love | The Greek has the soul "that has its love ready to hand (πρόχειρον)", near and at hand, not one that has never strayed.
!flag with one glance at the beauty of the universe dismisses all | The Greek says, seeing the beautiful things in this All, "it is suspicious (ὑποψίαν ἔχει) of them": suspicion, not dismissal at a glance.
!flag for it sees that all is put together of flesh and Matter | The Greek says it sees them "in flesh and bodies (σώμασιν)": there is no matter here.
!flag By only noting the flux of things it knows at once | The Greek says "when it sees them flowing past (παραρρέοντα) as well": their flowing away is a further sign, not the only one.
!note A reminder (ὑπόμνησις) from beauty here: Plato's Phaedrus (249d-250b), beauty here stirs recollection of beauty there. The mud (βόρβορος): the uninitiated lie in mud in Hades (Phaedo 69c), and the eye of the soul is buried in a barbaric mud (Republic VII 533d); see I.6.5-6.

@p
@greek εἶτα ἐκεῖ φέρεται
Then it is carried there, clever at finding what it loves, and it would not stand off before it had taken it, unless someone took away its love itself. There it saw all things beautiful and true, and it was strengthened more, being filled with the life of being; and, having become truly being itself, and taken in an understanding of what truly is, it is near, and perceives what it has long been seeking.
!flag it enters by that neighbouring into conscious possession of what it has long been seeking | The Greek says "being near, it perceives (αἰσθάνεται)" what it has long sought: perception of what is near, not possession.

@ch VI.7.32 | The formless maker of beauty, beauty above beauty
Where is the maker of so much beauty and life, the begetter of substance? He must be none of the beautiful things, no shape or power, but above them all: the principle is the formless, from which all intellectual shape comes, none of the beings and all. It has no magnitude; its greatness is that nothing is more powerful or equal to it; it has neither measure nor measurelessness, nor figure. Of what has no shape the love is without measure: its beauty is beauty above beauty, the flower of beauty and its principle and limit; it makes beautiful, and what shares in beauty is shaped, not beauty.

@p
Where, then, is the one who made such great beauty and such great life, and begot substance? Do you see the beauty on all these forms, many-coloured as they are? It is beautiful to stay here; but, being in the beautiful, one must look to where these come from, and from where they are beautiful.
!flag the begetter of the veritable | The Greek says he "begot substance" (γεννήσας οὐσίαν); the modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία.
!flag You see the splendour over the things of the universe with all the variety begotten of the Ideas | The Greek asks "do you see the beauty on all these forms (εἴδεσι), many-coloured as they are?": the beauty on the forms there, not on the things of the universe, and nothing begotten of the Ideas.

@p
@greek δεῖ δ’ αὐτὸν εἶναι
But he must be none of these: for he would be some one of them, and a part. So he is not such a shape, nor some power, nor again all the powers that have come to be and are here, but he must be above all powers and above all shapes. The principle is the formless: not what needs shape, but that from which all intellectual shape comes. For what came to be, if it came to be, had to come to be something, and it had its own shape; but what no one made, who would make it something? So it is none of the beings, and all: none, because the beings are later; all, because they are from it.
!flag were it so, it too would be a thing of parts | The Greek says "it would be some one of them, and a part (μέρος)": itself a part of them, not a thing of parts.
!flag but what shape can that have which no one has shaped | The Greek asks "what no one made (ἐποίησε), who would make it?": made, not shaped; nothing made it something.
!note None of the beings and all: so of the One in V.2.1 ("the One is all things and not one of them") and III.8.9.

@p
@greek πάντα δὲ ποιεῖν δυνάμενον
But what can make all things, what magnitude would it have? Or it would be unlimited. But if unlimited, it would have no magnitude: for magnitude is among the last things; and, if it is to make this too, it must not have it itself. And the greatness of substance is not a quantity: something else after it would have magnitude. Its greatness is that nothing is more powerful than it, and nothing can be made equal to it: for to which of its things could anything come to be equal, having nothing the same? And "for ever" and "to all" give it neither measure nor, again, measurelessness: for how would it measure the other things? So it has no figure either.
!flag The greatness of the Authentic cannot be a greatness of quantity | The Greek has "the greatness of substance (τῆς οὐσίας)": the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag Its eternity and universal reach entail neither measure nor measurelessness | The Greek has "for ever and to all" (τὸ εἰς ἀεὶ καὶ εἰς πάντα), its power reaching always and to everything; "eternity" is MacKenna's.
!note Unlimited, not in magnitude but in power: V.5.10-11 and VI.9.6; magnitude belongs to the last things, the bodies.

@p
@greek καὶ μήν, ὅτου ἂν ποθεινοῦ ὄντος
And yet, of what is longed for, if you can grasp neither figure nor shape, it would be most longed for and most lovable, and the love would be without measure: for the love is not bounded here, because the beloved is not either, but the love of it would be unlimited; so that its beauty too is in another way, and beauty above beauty.
!flag granted beauty, the absence of shape or form to be grasped is but enhancement of desire and love | The Greek says "of what is longed for (ποθεινοῦ)": the longing is there already, not beauty granted.

@p
@greek οὐδὲν γὰρ ὂν τί κάλλος
For, being none of the things, what beauty is it? But, being lovable, what begets would be beauty. So, being the power of all that is beautiful, it is the flower of beauty, beauty-making: for it begets beauty and makes it more beautiful by the overflow of beauty from itself, so that it is the principle of beauty and the limit of beauty. And, being the principle of beauty, it makes beautiful that of which it is the principle, and makes it beautiful not in shape; but what has come to be is itself shapeless too, and in another way in shape: for what is called just this, shape, is in another, but by itself it is shapeless. So what shares in beauty is shaped, not beauty.
!flag it cannot be beauty since it is not a thing among things | The Greek asks "being none of the things, what beauty is it?" and answers that, being lovable, "what begets would be beauty": MacKenna makes the question a denial.
!flag it will be the ultimate of beauty | The Greek has "the flower (ἄνθος) of beauty", its bloom, not its ultimate.
!flag the source and height of beauty | The Greek has "the principle (ἀρχή) of beauty and the limit (πέρας) of beauty": its beginning and its end, not its height.
!note Beauty by itself, not in another: Plato's Symposium (211a-b), beauty itself "not in some other thing, but itself by itself with itself". Beauty above beauty: I.6.9 and V.8.8.

@ch VI.7.33 | The formless form; love that rises to the more shapeless
