When beauty is spoken of, flee from shape, even the shape in an account by which justice differs from self-control. Intellect, thinking each or all, has an intelligible shape, still in need; the soul reaches for what is above it without saying why, and the argument says it is the real, if the best is in what is wholly without form. What has shape is measured and mixed; the first beauty is formless. The lover loves only when he begets an impression in his soul, and would rise to the more shapeless; shape is the trace of the shapeless, and from matter to soul to intellect each is more form and more lovable.

@p
This is why, when beauty is spoken of, one must rather flee from such a shape, and not set it before the eyes, so as not to fall out of the beautiful into what is called beautiful by a dim sharing. But the shapeless form is beautiful, if indeed it is a form, and the more so the more you strip away all shape, even the shape in an account (λόγος), by which we say that one thing differs from another, as justice and self-control are other than each other, though they are beautiful.
!flag When therefore we name beauty, all such shape must be dismissed | The Greek says "one must rather flee (φευκτέον) from such a shape, and not set it before the eyes": a flight from shape, not its dismissal.
!flag even that given in thought to mark difference | The Greek has "the shape in an account (ἐν λόγῳ)", the shape of a definition, by which justice differs from self-control; not "given in thought".
!flag as for instance the difference between Justice and Sophrosyny | The Greek has "justice and self-control (σωφροσύνην)"; the modern version keeps "self-control".

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ δὲ ὁ νοῦς ἴδιόν τι νοεῖ
But since intellect thinks something of its own, it is lessened, even if it takes together all that is in the intelligible. If it takes each, it has one intelligible shape; if all together, a many-coloured one, as it were, still in need: as one must see what is above that all-beautiful one, many-coloured and not many-coloured, which the soul reaches for without saying why it longs for such a thing; but the argument says that this is the real one, if indeed the nature of the best and of the most lovable is in what is wholly without form.
!flag The Intellectual-Principle is the less for seeing things as distinct | The Greek says intellect is lessened "since it thinks something of its own (ἴδιόν τι)", a shape proper to it, even if it takes all together; seeing things as distinct is MacKenna's.
!flag reason, however, urging that This at last is the Authentic Term | The Greek says "the argument (ὁ λόγος) says that this is the real (τὸ ὄντως)"; "the Authentic Term" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek διὸ ὅ τι ἂν εἰς εἶδος
This is why, whatever you lead up to form and show to the soul, it seeks, beyond this, something else that gave it shape. The argument says that what has shape, and the shape, and the form, are all measured; and this is not all, nor self-sufficient, nor beautiful of itself, but this too is mixed. So these must be beautiful, but the real, or the beyond-beautiful, must not be measured; and, if so, must not be shaped, nor be a form. So what is primarily, and first, is without form, and the beauty there is the nature of the intelligible good.
!flag reason answers that while there exists the giver having shape to give | The Greek says "the argument says that what has shape, and the shape, and the form, are all measured (μεμετρημένον)": there is no giver of shape in the sentence.
!flag the beauty in it must be, simply, the Nature of the Intellectual Good | The Greek says "the beauty there (ἐκεῖ) is the nature of the intelligible good (νοητοῦ ἀγαθοῦ)": intelligible, not intellectual.

@p
@greek μαρτυρεῖ δὲ καὶ τὸ τῶν ἐραστῶν πάθος
The affection of lovers bears witness too: as long as one is with what has the perceptible impression, he does not yet love; but when from it he begets in himself an impression that is not perceptible, in his partless soul, then love grows. He seeks to see the beloved, so as to water that impression as it withers. But if he should understand that he must pass over to what is more shapeless, he would reach for that: for what he felt from the beginning was love of a great light from a dim gleam.
!flag so long as the attention is upon the visible form, love has not entered | The Greek says "as long as one is with (ἐν) what has the perceptible impression": with the perceptible one, not attending to a visible form.
!flag then the lover longs for the sight of the beloved to make that fading image live again | The Greek says he seeks to see the beloved "so as to water (ἐπάρδῃ)" the impression "as it withers": watering, as of a plant or of the wings.
!note Watering the withering: Plato's Phaedrus (251b-e, 255c-d), the stream of beauty from the beloved waters the lover's wings, which wither and close when he is away.

@p
@greek τὸ γὰρ ἴχνος τοῦ ἀμόρφου μορφή
For the trace of the shapeless is shape: this at least begets the shape, not the shape this, and it begets it when matter comes to it. And matter is of necessity farthest off, because it has of itself not even one of the last shapes. If, then, it is not matter that is lovable, but what has been formed by the form, and the form on matter is from soul, and soul is more form and more lovable, and intellect more form than soul and more lovable still, then one must set the first nature of the beautiful as without form.
!flag Shape is an impress from the unshaped | The Greek has "the trace (ἴχνος) of the shapeless is shape", the trace of chapters 17 and 18; MacKenna's "impress" is near, and the modern version keeps "trace".
!flag but to that which draws upon Form | The Greek has "what has been formed by the form (τὸ εἰδοποιηθὲν διὰ τὸ εἶδος)": the thing made a form, not something that draws upon form.
!note The ascent from matter to soul to intellect, each more form: chapter 28 above, and I.6.2-3, where the form on matter comes from soul.

@ch VI.7.34 | Alone with the alone
The soul that loves the Good puts off every shape, even the intelligible, to receive it alone. When it appears in her suddenly, there is nothing between and they are one, as lovers here wish to blend; she no longer perceives her body, nor calls herself man or being, and looks at it instead of herself. She would not exchange it for the whole heaven; there is no deceit there; she says "it is that one", in silence, and is not tickled but well. She looks down on offices, riches and sciences, fears nothing, and would let all about her perish to be with it alone.

@p
And we shall no longer wonder if what gives such terrible longings is wholly free even of intelligible shape: since the soul too, when it takes an intense love of it, puts off every shape it has, even whatever shape of the intelligible is in it. For it is not possible, having something else and being active about it, either to see it or to be fitted to it: but one must have nothing else ready to hand, neither evil nor good, so that the soul alone may receive it alone.
!flag even to the Intellectual shape that has informed it | The Greek says "whatever shape of the intelligible (νοητοῦ) is in it": intelligible, and nothing of its having informed the soul.
!flag There is no vision, no union, for those handling or acting by any thing other | The Greek says it is not possible "having something else and being active about it, either to see or to be fitted (ἐναρμοσθῆναι) to it": fitted, as a harmony, not union.
!note Alone to the alone: VI.9.11, "the flight of the alone to the alone", and I.6.7.

@p
@greek ὅταν δὲ τούτου εὐτυχήσῃ
When the soul has this good fortune, and it comes to her, or rather, being present, appears, when she has turned aside from the things present, and made herself ready to be as beautiful as possible, and come into likeness (the preparation and the adorning are clear, I think, to those who prepare themselves), and she sees it suddenly appearing in her (for there is nothing between, nor are they two any longer, but both are one: you could not tell them apart while it is present; lovers and beloveds here, wishing to blend into one, are an imitation of this), she no longer perceives her body, that she is in it, nor does she call herself anything else, not man, not living being, not being, nor all: for the sight of these is somehow uneven; and she has no leisure for them, nor wishes it, but, having sought it, she meets it when it is present, and looks at it instead of herself; and who she is that looks, she has no leisure even to see.
!flag by those preparings and adornings which come unbidden to those growing ready for the vision | The Greek says "the preparation and the adorning are clear (δήλη), I think, to those who prepare themselves": known to them, not coming unbidden.
!flag any observation of such things falls away | The Greek says "the sight of these is somehow uneven (ἀνώμαλος)": a sight out of keeping with the even one she has; not that it falls away.
!note "Suddenly" (ἐξαίφνης): Plato's Symposium (210e), the lover at the end "suddenly" sees beauty itself, and Letter VII (341c-d), the light kindled suddenly in the soul. Lovers wishing to blend into one: Aristophanes in the Symposium (192d-e).

@p
@greek ἔνθα δὴ οὐδὲν πάντων ἂν τούτου ἀλλάξαιτο
There she would not exchange this for anything at all, not even if someone gave her the whole heaven to rule, since there is nothing else better still, nor more good: for she runs no higher, and all the other things are on the way down, even if they are on high: so that then she has the power to judge well, and to know that this is what she longed for, and to set down that there is nothing stronger than it. For there is no deceit there: or where could she come upon what is truer than the true? What she says, then, is "it is that one", and she says it later, and says it in silence; and, being well, she is not deceived that she is well: nor does she say it because her body is tickled, but because she has become this, what she was long ago, when she was fortunate.
!flag she is of perfect judgement and knows that This was her quest | The Greek says "then she has the power to judge well (κρίνειν καλῶς)": a judging she has then, not a perfect judgement.
!flag and the truth she affirms, that she is, herself | The Greek says "what she says, then, is 'it is that one' (ἐκεῖνό ἐστι)": she says what it is, not that she is herself.
!flag for this is no affirmation of an excited body | The Greek has a body "tickled" (γαργαλιζομένου), the pleasure of scratching, not excitement.
!note Tickling and itching: the mixed pleasures of the body in Plato's Philebus (46a-47a), and the scratcher of the Gorgias (494c-e).

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα πάντα
And all the other things in which she took pleasure before, offices, or powers, or riches, or beauties, or sciences, she says she looks down on; and she would not say it if she had not met with things stronger than these. Nor does she fear that something may happen to her, while she is with that one, or even if she has only seen it at all; and if the other things about her should perish too, she even wishes it very much, so that she may be with this alone: to such a pitch of well-being she has come.
!flag linked to This she can fear no disaster nor even know it | The Greek says she does not fear "while she is with that one, or even if she has only seen it at all (οὐδ’ ὅλως ἰδοῦσα)": even the sight is enough; "nor even know it" is MacKenna's.

@ch VI.7.35 | The house and its master; intellect drunk with nectar
The soul then despises even thinking, a motion: as a man entering a beautiful house admires its ornaments until he sees the master, and then looks only at him and blends his sight with what he sees; better, if the master were a god filling the soul. Intellect has two powers, one to think what is in it, one to see what is beyond it by a direct touch: the sober intellect, and intellect loving, drunk on the nectar. The Good, running over both and making them one, lifts the soul beyond place, life and thinking, since she must be made like it.

@p
And she is so disposed then that she even despises thinking, which at other times she welcomed, because thinking was a kind of motion, and she does not wish to be moved: for she says that the one she sees is not moved either, although she herself, having become intellect, contemplates, as though made intellect and come to be in the intelligible place. But, having come to be in it, and having the intelligible about her, she thinks; but when she sees that one, she lets everything go at once: as if someone who came into a many-coloured house, and so beautiful, were contemplating each of the ornaments inside and admiring them, before he saw the master of the house; but, seeing him and delighting in him, not like the nature of the statues but worthy of the true sight, he would let those go and look only at him from then on; and then, looking and not taking his eye away, he would no longer see a sight, because of the continuance of the seeing, but would blend his sight with what is seen, so that in him what was seen before has now become sight, and he would forget all the other sights. And perhaps the image would keep the analogy, if it were not a man who came upon the one contemplating the things of the house, but some god, and he not appearing to the eye, but filling the soul of the one who contemplates.
!flag she has nothing to say of this very Intellectual-Principle by means of which she has attained the vision | The Greek says "she says that the one (ἐκεῖνον) she sees is not moved either": she speaks of what she sees, the Good, not of intellect.
!flag so as to be able to take stand in that Intellectual space | The Greek has "the intelligible place" (τῷ τόπῳ τῷ νοητῷ), Plato's phrase: intelligible, not intellectual.
!flag no thing of ornament but calling for the truest attention | The Greek says the master is "not like the nature of the statues (ἀγαλμάτων)" in the house, "but worthy of the true sight (θέας)": the statues, and a sight, not attention.
!note The intelligible place (τόπος νοητός): Plato's Republic VI (508c) and VII (517b).

@p
@greek καὶ τὸν νοῦν τοίνυν δεῖ
And intellect too, then, must have one power for thinking, by which it sees what is in itself, and another by which it sees what is beyond itself by a kind of direct touch and reception, by which it saw before, only seeing, and, seeing, later got intellect too and is one. And that is the sight of intellect in its senses, this is intellect loving. For when it goes out of its senses, drunk on the nectar, then it becomes loving, simplified into well-being by its fill: and it is better for it to be drunk than to be too solemn for such drunkenness.
!flag the first seeing is that of Intellect knowing | The Greek has the sight "of intellect in its senses (νοῦ ἔμφρονος)", the sober intellect, set against intellect "out of its senses" (ἄφρων); not knowing.
!flag by this excess it is made simplex and is happy | The Greek says it is "simplified into well-being by its fill (τῷ κόρῳ)": its fill, as in chapter 16, not an excess.
!flag whereby to know its transcendent | The Greek says it sees "what is beyond (ἐπέκεινα) itself by a kind of direct touch (ἐπιβολῇ) and reception": seeing by touch, not knowing.
!note Drunk on the nectar: Resource in the garden of Zeus (Plato's Symposium 203b), read in III.5.9; chapter 30 above said that "pleasure" in intellect is such a metaphor.

@p
@greek παρὰ μέρος δὲ ὁ νοῦς ἐκεῖνος
Does that intellect see some things at one time, others at another? Or no: the account, in teaching, makes them come to be, but intellect has thinking always, and has also not thinking, but seeing that one in another way. For in seeing that one it had offspring, and perceived them as they came to be and were in it: and in seeing these it is said to think, but that one by the power by which it was going to think. And the soul, as it were mingling and making vanish the intellect that stays in her, or rather her intellect sees first, and the sight comes into her too, and the two become one.
!flag reason unravelling gives process | The Greek says "the account (λόγος), in teaching, makes them come to be (γινόμενα)": it tells in order what is at once, as the myths do in III.5.9; "unravelling" is MacKenna's.
!flag In this seeing of the Supreme it becomes pregnant | The Greek says "in seeing that one it had offspring (γεννήματα)", already born, which it perceived as they came to be and were in it.
!flag in a later (lower) stage it is to become | The Greek says it sees that one "by the power by which it was going to think" (ᾗ δυνάμει ἔμελλε νοεῖν): the power from which its thinking came, not a later or lower stage.
!note The account that tells in time what is at once: III.5.9, "the myths, if they are to be myths, must divide in time what they tell", and the reasoning god of chapter 1 above.

@p
@greek ἐκταθὲν δὲ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς
And the Good, spread out over them and fitted to the joining of both, running over them and making the two one, is upon them, giving a blessed perception and sight, lifting them so high that they are neither in place nor in anything else in which one thing is by nature in another: for it is not anywhere itself; the intelligible place is in it, but it is not in another. This is why the soul is not moved then, because that one is not either: nor is she soul, then, because that one does not live, but is above living: nor intellect, because it does not think either: for she must be made like it; and she does not think that one, because it is not thought either.
!flag or in that realm of difference where everything is rooted in some other thing | The Greek says "nor in anything else in which one thing is by nature in another": there is no realm of difference.
!flag The Good spreading out above them and adapting itself to that union which it hastens to confirm | The Greek says the Good is "fitted to the joining (συστάσει) of both, running over them (ἐπιδραμὸν)": running over, as the bloom of chapter 30; "hastens to confirm" is MacKenna's.
!note Made like it: likeness to god (Theaetetus 176b), carried here past soul and intellect to the Good.

@ch VI.7.36 | The greatest study and the wave of intellect
The knowledge or touch of the Good is the greatest study, which Plato means as learning something about it first. Analogies, negations, knowledge of what comes from it and steps up teach it; purifications, virtues and settling in the intelligible bring one to it, until one is substance, intellect and complete living being, and it is next. Then, letting all study go, one is lifted by the wave of intellect and sees suddenly, not how: the light itself is the sight, for in it there is no seen and light, but a radiance that begets intellect and stays.

@p
For the rest is clear, and something has been said about this too. But all the same we must speak of it briefly now as well, starting from there, and going forward by reasonings. The knowledge of the good, or the touching of it, is the greatest thing, and he says that this is the greatest study, calling it a study not of looking at it, but of learning something about it first.
!flag We need not carry this matter further; we turn to a question already touched | The Greek says "the rest is clear, and something has been said about this too": the question is the same one, the Good, not a new one.
!flag this—we read—is the grand learning | The Greek says "he says" (φησι), Plato, that this is "the greatest study" (μέγιστον μάθημα), his word in the Republic.
!note The greatest study: Plato's Republic VI (505a), "the form of the good is the greatest study (μέγιστον μάθημα)", by which just things and the rest become useful.

@p
@greek διδάσκουσι μὲν οὖν ἀναλογίαι
We are taught by analogies, and negations, and knowings of what comes from it, and certain steps up; we are brought on our way to it by purifications, and virtues, and adornings, and footholds in the intelligible, and settlings upon it, and feastings on what is there, so that one becomes at once spectator and spectacle, himself of himself and of the others, and, having become substance and intellect and complete living being, no longer sees it from outside; and, having become this, he is near, and next is that one, and it is close now, shining over all the intelligible.
!flag We come to this learning by analogies, by abstractions | The Greek has "negations" (ἀφαιρέσεις), takings away of what it is not; "abstractions" is MacKenna's.
!flag Purification has The Good for goal | The Greek says "purifications (καθάρσεις) ... bring us on our way (πορεύουσι)" to it, with the virtues and the rest: they lead, they are not said to have it as goal.
!flag identical with Being and Intellectual-Principle and the entire living all | The Greek says "having become substance (οὐσία) and intellect and complete living being (ζῷον παντελές)": the modern version keeps "substance", and the complete living being is Plato's.
!flag radiant above the Intellectual | The Greek says it is "shining over all the intelligible (ἐπὶ παντὶ τῷ νοητῷ)": intelligible, not intellectual.
!note The ways of knowing the first: Alcinous, Didaskalikos 10 (165.14-34): by negation (ἀφαίρεσις), by analogy, and by ascent through beauty, as in the Symposium. The complete living being (παντελὲς ζῷον): Plato's Timaeus (31b).

@p
@greek ἔνθα δὴ ἐάσας τις πᾶν μάθημα
There one lets all study go; and, led as by a tutor up to this, and settled in the beautiful, he thinks, as far as that in which he is; but, carried out by the very wave of intellect, as it were, and lifted on high by it as it swells, he saw suddenly, not seeing how; but the sight, filling his eyes with light, did not make him see something else through it, but the light itself was the sight. For in that one there was not the seen on one side and its light on the other, nor intellect and what is thought, but a radiance begetting these for later, and letting them be beside it; and he himself is a radiance only, begetting intellect, not quenching itself in begetting, but staying itself, while that one came to be by this one's being. For if this were not such, that would not have come into being.
!flag and allowed them to occupy the quester’s mind | The Greek says the radiance let them "be beside it" (εἶναι παῤ αὐτῷ), beside the Good; there is no quester's mind.
!flag With This he himself becomes identical, with that radiance | The Greek says "he himself (αὐτὸς) is a radiance only, begetting intellect": he is the Good, which begets intellect; MacKenna makes him the quester, made one with it.
!flag disciplined to this pitch | The Greek has "led as by a tutor (παιδαγωγηθεὶς) up to this": the slave who leads a boy to school, not discipline.
!note Lifted on a wave: Odysseus, "lifted on a great wave", sees the land near (Homer, Odyssey V.392-393). Led up rightly, then "suddenly" seeing: Plato's Symposium (210a, 210e).

@ch VI.7.37 | Those who make the first think itself
Some gave the first thinking of itself, as if thinking made it more solemn; but if its honour is from thinking it is not honourable by itself, and if by itself, it is complete before thinking. If it is a substance always thinking, it is two; if it is thinking, it does not think, as motion is not moved. We give thinking to what comes from another and turns to its maker; what never came to be has no cause to think, and Plato rightly sets it beyond intellect. To call it mindless is to accuse by privation what has no work: it is enough for itself.

@p
Those, then, who gave it thinking did not give it thinking of the lesser things and of what comes from it; and yet, some say, this too is absurd, that it should not know the other things. But at any rate those, finding nothing more honourable than it, gave it the thinking of itself, as if it would be more solemn by thinking, and thinking were stronger than what it is in its own being, and not as if it made thinking solemn.
!flag Those ascribing Intellection to the First have not supposed him to know the lesser, the emanant | The Greek has "the lesser things and what comes from it (τῶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ)": there is no word of emanation.
!flag not something whose value derives from him | The Greek says "and not as if he made thinking solemn (σεμνύνοντος)": he would give it its dignity, not its value.
!note Thinking that thinks itself: Aristotle, Metaphysics Λ.9 (1074b15-35): the divine intellect must think the most excellent, so it thinks itself, and its thinking is a thinking of thinking; it would be absurd for it to think some things.

@p
@greek τίνι γὰρ τὸ τίμιον ἕξει
For by what will it have its honour, by its thinking or by itself? If by its thinking, it is not honourable by itself, or less so; if by itself, it is complete before thinking, and not completed by thinking. But if they say it must think because it is activity and not potency: if it is a substance always thinking, and they call it activity for this, they still speak of two, the substance and the thinking, and do not speak of a simple thing, but add something other to it, as seeing in activity is added to the eyes, even if they always see. But if they say "in activity" because it is activity and thinking, then, being thinking, it would not think, as motion would not be moved either.
!flag If in the Intellection, he has no worth or the less worth | The Greek says "it is not honourable by itself (αὑτῷ), or less so": its honour would be another's; "by itself" is what MacKenna leaves out.
!flag Now if this means that he is an essence eternally intellective | The Greek has "a substance (οὐσία) always thinking"; the modern version keeps "substance" for οὐσία.
!flag though the two are inseparable | The Greek says "even if they always see" (κἂν ἀεὶ βλέπωσιν): the seeing is still added to the eyes; "inseparable" is MacKenna's.
!note Activity, not potency: Aristotle, Metaphysics Λ.6 (1071b19-20), a principle whose substance is activity, and Λ.9 (1074b17-21). Motion that is not moved: Physics V.2 (225b15-16), there is no motion of motion.

@p
@greek τί οὖν; οὐ καὶ αὐτοὶ λέγετε
What then? Do you not say yourselves that those things there are substance and activity? But we agree that these are many, and these are other, while the first is simple; and we give thinking to what comes from another, and, as it were, seeks its own substance, and itself, and what made it, and, turned to it in the sight and knowing it, is intellect now by right. But what neither came to be nor has anything before it, but is always what it is, what cause of thinking will it have? This is why Plato rightly says it is beyond intellect.
!flag But do not we ourselves assert that the Beings There are essence and Act | The Greek has "substance (οὐσίαν) and activity"; the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag bent inward for this vision | The Greek says it is "turned (ἐπιστραφὲν) to it in the sight": turned toward what made it, not bent inward.
!note "Beyond intellect": Plato says the Good is "beyond substance" (Republic VI 509b); the words "beyond intellect" are in a fragment of Aristotle's On prayer, "god is either intellect or something even beyond intellect" (fr. 49 Rose). See V.1.8, V.3.13 and V.6.

@p
@greek νοῦς μὲν γὰρ μὴ νοῶν
For an intellect that does not think is mindless: for in what has thinking by nature, if it does not do this, it is mindless; but in what has no work, why would anyone bring a work to it and accuse it, by privation, of not doing it? As if one were to call it no physician. And it has no work because nothing falls to it to do: for it is enough by itself, and need seek nothing beside itself, being above all things: for it is enough for itself and for the others, by being itself what it is.
!flag why import one and declare a defect because it is not performed | The Greek says "accuse it by privation (κατὰ στέρησιν)": a privation is only of what is by nature able, so it does not apply here.
!note Privation: Aristotle, Metaphysics Δ.22 (1022b22-31), a thing is deprived of what it, or its kind, would by nature have; the first is not mindless, as a stone is not blind.

@ch VI.7.38 | Not even "is", nor "I am good"
It is not even "is": we say "the Good" not as predicating it, but because we cannot show it otherwise, without "is". Will it not know "I am"? It is not. Nor "I am good", which again predicates "is"; and if it thinks itself as good it must think "I am the good". If the thinking is the good, the good is the thinking; if other, the good is before it and does not need it. So nothing else is present to it, only a simple direct touch toward itself.

@p
But it is not even the "is": for it needs nothing, not even this: since not even "it is good" is said of it, but of that of which the "is" is said; and the "is" is said not as one thing of another, but as signifying what it is. And we say "the Good" about it, not saying it, nor predicating that it belongs to it, but that it is it: then, not thinking it right to say "is good", nor even to put the "the" before it, but not being able to show it if one took it away altogether, so that we do not make one thing and then another, so as not to need the "is" any longer, in this way we say "the Good".
!flag it is to state identity | The Greek says the "is" is said "as signifying what it is (σημαῖνον ὃ ἔστι)"; the sentence is about what the "is" signifies.
!flag it conveys an identification | The Greek says we say "the Good" about it "not predicating that it belongs to it, but that it is it (ὅτι αὐτό)".
!flag it is that sheer negation does not indicate | The Greek says "not being able to show it if one took it away altogether (εἰ ... ἀφέλοι)": if one took away the word, or the "the"; not negation.
!note Not "it is good": so in V.3.13 and VI.9.6, the Good is good not to itself; and in Plato's Parmenides (141e-142a), the one, if it is one, "is not even so as to be one".

@p
@greek ἀλλὰ τίς παραδέξεται φύσιν
But who will accept a nature that is without perception and knowledge of itself? What, then, will it not know "I am"? But it is not. Why, then, will it not say "I am good"? Or again it will predicate the "is" of itself. But will it say only "good", adding what? For one might think "good" without the "is", if one did not predicate it of another: but what thinks itself as good will by all means think "I am the good"; and if not, it will think "good", but the thinking that it is itself this will not be present to it. So the thinking must be "I am good".
!flag But he does not possess Being | The Greek says "but it is not" (ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔστι): it is not, not that it does not possess being.
!flag adding nothing : the goodness would be taken without the being and all duality avoided | The Greek asks "but will it say only 'good', adding what?": the question is what it would add; "all duality avoided" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek καὶ εἰ μὲν ἡ νόησις αὐτὴ τὸ ἀγαθόν
And if the thinking itself is the good, it will not be a thinking of itself, but of the good, and it will not itself be the good, but the thinking will. But if the thinking of the good is other than the good, the good is already before its thinking. And if the good is before the thinking, being self-sufficient to itself for good, it would need nothing of the thinking about itself: so that, as good, it does not think itself. But as what? Or nothing else is present to it, but there will be a simple direct touch of it toward itself.
!flag No such foreign matter is present to it | The Greek says "nothing else (οὐδὲν ἄλλο) is present to it": no other, not foreign matter.
!flag it can have only an immediate intuition self-directed | The Greek has "a simple direct touch (ἁπλῆ ἐπιβολή)", the word of chapter 35, not an intuition.
!note The direct touch (ἐπιβολή): the Epicureans' "application of the mind" (ἐπιβολὴ τῆς διανοίας, Diogenes Laertius X.50-51), and Plotinus' word for a grasp without discourse, as in chapter 35 above.

@ch VI.7.39 | The first stands in solemnity, beyond thinking
With no interval or difference in it, what touches itself is itself; otherness is where intellect and substance are, for intellect needs otherness and sameness to think. If it thought, it would think all, and become many; every thinking is many-coloured, and the simple has nothing intellectual. So it will know neither the others nor itself, but stand still in solemnity: their thinking would be acquired, and providence is enough in its being. Plato gave thinking to substance, and "standing in solemnity" to what is beyond thinking.

@p
But since there is no interval, as it were, nor difference toward itself, what would what touches itself be but itself? This is why otherness is rightly taken where there are intellect and substance. For intellect must always take otherness and sameness, if it is to think. For it will not distinguish itself from the intelligible by its relation to it as to another, and it will not contemplate all things, if no otherness has come to be so that they are all: for there would not even be two.
!flag at the point where Intellectual-Principle and Being are differentiated | The Greek says otherness is taken "where there are intellect and substance (οὐσία)": where they are, not where they are told apart; the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag must inevitably comport difference with identity | The Greek has "otherness and sameness" (ἑτερότητα καὶ ταυτότητα), two of Plato's greatest kinds.
!note Otherness and sameness: Plato's Sophist (254d-255e), the greatest kinds, being, motion, rest, same and other; and VI.2.8, where they are the kinds of intellect.

@p
@greek ἔπειτα, εἰ νοήσει
Next, if it is to think, it will surely not think itself only, if it thinks at all: for why not all things? Or will it be unable? And in general, in thinking itself, it does not stay simple, but the thinking about itself must be of another, if it could think itself at all. And we said that this is not thinking, unless it wished to see itself as another. And having thought, it becomes many itself: intelligible, thinking, moving, and all else that belongs to intellect. Besides this, one should see that too, which has been said already elsewhere, that every thinking, if it is to be thinking, must be something many-coloured, while the simple and wholly the same, like a movement, if it is such as a touching, has nothing intellectual.
!flag nothing could prevent it knowing all things; but this is impossible | The Greek asks "why not all things? Or will it be unable (ἀδυνατήσει)?": a question, not the assertion that knowing all is impossible.
!flag That act requires a manifold—agent, object, movement | The Greek says "having thought, it becomes many itself": intelligible, thinking, moving; it is the first that would become many, not the act that requires it.
!note Said elsewhere: V.3.10-13, where thinking needs otherness and many-coloured content, and the first, which is simple, does not think.

@p
@greek τί οὖν; οὔτε τὰ ἄλλα οὔτε αὑτὸν
What then? Will it know neither the other things nor itself, but stand still in solemnity? The other things are later than it, and it was what it was before them, and the thinking of them would be acquired, and not always the same, and not of things that stand; and, even if it thinks the things that stand, it is many. For it is not that the later things will have their substance together with their thinking, while its thoughts will be only empty contemplations. Providence is enough in its being itself, from which all things are. And how is it toward itself, if it does not think itself? But it will stand still in solemnity.
!flag but will hold an august repose | The Greek has "will stand still in solemnity" (σεμνὸν ἑστήξεται), Plato's words in the Sophist; "repose" is MacKenna's, and he says himself below that it is used for want of a fitter word.
!flag the dependent he cannot know when he has no knowledge of himself | The Greek asks "and how is it toward itself (πρὸς αὐτόν), if it does not think itself?": its relation to itself, not knowledge of the dependent.
!note Standing still in solemnity: Plato's Sophist (248e-249a), "shall we believe that what wholly is has no motion, life, soul or thought, but stands, solemn and holy, without intellect, unmoved?" Providence from the first's being: III.2.1 and VI.8.17.

@p
@greek ἔλεγε μὲν οὖν ὁ Πλάτων
Plato, then, speaking about substance, said that it would think, but not that it would stand still in solemnity: as if substance thinks, while what does not think will stand still in solemnity; "will stand still" because he could not have expressed it otherwise, but thinking that what is beyond thinking is more solemn, and truly solemn.
!flag Plato dealing with essential Being allows it intellection | The Greek has "speaking about substance (οὐσίας)": the modern version keeps "substance"; and it is Plato's Sophist that gives it thinking.
!flag That which transcends (the movement of) Intellection | The Greek has "what is beyond thinking (τὸ ὑπερβεβηκὸς τὸ νοεῖν)"; "(the movement of)" is MacKenna's.

@ch VI.7.40 | Thinking comes after the first
Those who have touched it know there is no thinking in it; but the argument must add necessity to persuasion. All thinking is from something and of something: either it completes its substrate, begetting nothing, or it is with substance and brings it into being, and is then not in its source; this first activity is an image of something so great that it became substance. Beyond this substance and thinking one comes to the wonderful, which has neither. Thinking is worse than the good and stands apart, leaving it pure; if one made the first think itself, another would be needed before it.

@p
That there must be no thinking about it, those who have touched such a thing would know; but one must bring some encouragements besides what has been said, if in some way it is possible to signify it in speech. And the persuasion must have necessity mixed with it.
!flag we need overwhelming persuasion | The Greek says "the persuasion must have necessity (ἀνάγκην) mixed with it": persuasion joined with proof, not overwhelming persuasion.
!flag but some further confirmation is desirable | The Greek has "some encouragements (παραμύθια)", words of comfort to bring to the argument, not confirmation.
!note Persuasion and necessity: in Plato's Timaeus (48a) intellect rules necessity by persuasion; here the argument would join them.

@p
@greek δεῖ τοίνυν γινώσκειν ἐπιστήσαντα
One must know, then, attending to it, that all thinking is from something and of something. And the one that is with what it is from has as its substrate that of which it is the thinking, and becomes as it were laid upon it, being its activity and filling what is in potency in it, while it begets nothing itself: for it is only, as it were, a completion of that of which it is.
!flag There is the intellection that remains within its place of origin | The Greek has "the one that is with (συνοῦσα) what it is from": being with it, as an activity is with its subject.
!note The two activities, one of a thing and one from it: V.4.2, the activity of the substance and the activity from the substance, as fire's own heat and the heat it gives off.

@p
@greek ἡ δὲ οὖσα νόησις μετ’ οὐσίας
But the thinking that is with substance and has brought substance into being could not be in that from which it came: for it would not have begotten anything if it were in that. But, being a power of begetting, it begot by itself, and its activity is substance, and it is with and in the substance; and the thinking and this substance are not other; and even if this nature thinks itself, the thought and the thinker are not other, except in account, being a multitude, as has been shown in many places.
!flag There is also the intellection inbound with Being—Being’s very author | The Greek has "the thinking that is with substance (μετ’ οὐσίας) and has brought substance into being"; the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag it produces therefore of its own motion and its act is Real-Being | The Greek says "it begot by itself (ἐφ’ ἑαυτῆς), and its activity is substance": "Real-Being" for οὐσία is MacKenna's.
!flag save the logical distinction of thinker and thought | The Greek says they are not other "except in account (λόγῳ)": in the account of them, not by a logical distinction.

@p
@greek καὶ ἔστιν αὕτη πρώτη ἐνέργεια
And this is the first activity, which begot a reality into substance, and, being an image of another, it is of something so great that it became substance. But if it were of that one and not from that one, it would not be anything other than that one's, and would not be a reality by itself.
!flag If instead of moving outward it remained with the First | The Greek says "if it were of that one and not from (ἀπ’) that one": belonging to it, not coming from it; "moving outward" is MacKenna's.
!flag it is an image, but of an original so great that the very copy stands a reality | The Greek says it is an image "of something so great that it became substance (ἐγένετο οὐσία)": substance, the word of the chapter.

@p
@greek πρώτη δὲ οὖσα αὕτη ἐνέργεια
And being the first activity and the first thinking, it would have neither activity nor thinking before itself. So one who passes over from this substance and thinking will come neither to substance nor to thinking, but will come beyond substance and thinking to something wonderful, which has in itself neither substance nor thinking, but is alone, by itself, needing nothing of what comes from it. For it did not first act and so beget activity (for then activity would have been before it came to be), nor did it think and beget thinking (for then it would have thought before thinking came to be).
!flag we come not to more being and more intellection but to what overpasses both | The Greek says one comes "neither to substance nor to thinking, but beyond substance (ἐπέκεινα οὐσίας) and thinking": Plato's "beyond substance".
!note Beyond substance: Plato's Republic VI (509b), the Good "beyond substance (ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας), surpassing it in seniority and power".

@p
@greek ὅλως γὰρ ἡ νόησις, εἰ μὲν ἀγαθοῦ
For in general thinking, if it is of the good, is worse than it: so it would not be the good's. I say "not the good's", not because it is not possible to think the good (let that be possible), but because in the good itself there would be no thinking: or else the good and what is less than it will be one together. And if it is worse, the thinking will be together with substance. But if the thinking is better, the intelligible, what is thought, will be worse. So the thinking is not in the good; but, being worse, and valued because of the good, it would be elsewhere than it, leaving it pure of itself, as of the other things. And, being pure of thinking, it is unmixedly what it is, not hindered by thinking present to it, so as not to be unmixed and one.
!flag all intellection, even of the Good, is beneath it | The Greek says "thinking, if it is of the good, is worse (χεῖρον) than it": the thinking of the good is worse than the good, not beneath the first beside all other thinking.
!flag leaving the Good unsoiled by it as by all else | The Greek says thinking leaves it "pure (καθαρὸν)" of itself, as of the other things: pure, not unsoiled.

@p
@greek εἰ δέ τις καὶ τοῦτο ἅμα νοοῦν
And if someone makes this too at once thinking and thought, and substance and thinking together with substance, and wishes in this way to make it think itself, it will need another too, before this: since the activity and the thinking, being either the completion of another substrate or coming into being together with it, also have another nature before themselves, to which the thinking fittingly belongs: for it has what it will think, because there is another before it; and when it thinks itself, it as it were learns what it got from the sight of another, in itself.
!flag Anyone making the Good at once Thinker and Thought identifies it with Being | The Greek says he makes it "substance (οὐσίαν) and thinking together with substance": substance, kept here for οὐσία.
!flag or it points, by that duality, to a prior principle having intellection as a characteristic | The Greek says thinking, as completion or as coming into being with another (συνυπόστασις), has another nature before it "to which thinking fittingly belongs (εἰκότως)"; "by that duality" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek ᾧ δὲ μήτε τι ἄλλο πρὸ αὐτοῦ
But what has neither anything else before it nor anything with it from another, what will it think, or how will it think itself? For what would it seek? Or what would it long for? Its power, how great it is, as if it were outside it, in so far as it thought? I mean, if its power that it learned were one, and that by which it learned another; but if they are one, what does it seek?
!flag To essay its power of knowing | The Greek asks whether it would seek "its power, how great it is (ὅση)": the extent of its power, not its power of knowing.

@ch VI.7.41 | Thinking is a help to the lesser; "know yourself"
Thinking was given as an eye to natures more divine but lesser: the light does not seek light, nor that radiance thinking. If it thought, it would be two, or three; if intellect, thinking and thought were one they would vanish, and if distinct it would not be the first; add anything and you lessen it. Thinking is fine for soul and intellect; "know yourself" is for those who are many and must count themselves. The first is not good to itself, nor sees itself; it has given all these to what comes after it, so there is no account, perception or knowledge of it.

@p
For thinking seems to have been given as a help to natures that are more divine but lesser, and as an eye to them, as if they were blind. But what need would the eye have to see what is, being light itself? But what needs light through the eye seeks light, having darkness in itself. If, then, thinking is light, and light does not seek light, that radiance, which does not seek light, would not seek to think, nor will it add thinking to itself.
!flag what must take the light through the eye needs the light because of its darkness | The Greek says what needs the eye "seeks light, having darkness in itself (σκότον ἔχον παῤ αὑτῷ)": it seeks the light, and the darkness is its own.
!note The eye and the light: Plato's Republic VI (507d-508b), and V.5.7, where the eye, turning from what it sees, sees the light itself.

@p
@greek τί γὰρ καὶ ποιήσει
For what will it do, or what will it add, when even intellect itself needs to add something in order to think? So it does not perceive itself, for it does not need to; nor is it two, or rather more: itself, the thinking (for the thinking is surely not itself), and there must be a third too, the intelligible, what is thought. But if intellect, thinking and thought are the same, becoming wholly one, they will make themselves vanish in themselves; and, distinguished by otherness, they will again not be that one. So the other things must be let go entirely, in the case of the best nature, which needs no help: for whatever you add, you have lessened by the addition the nature that needs nothing.
!flag What could even intellection need and add to itself for the purpose of its act | The Greek has "intellect itself (αὐτὸς ὁ νοῦς)" that needs to add, in order to think: intellect, not intellection.
!flag It is no duality but, rather, a manifold | The Greek says "nor is it two, or rather more" (οὐδ’ ἐστὶ δύο, μᾶλλον δὲ πλείω): it is neither two nor many; MacKenna makes it a manifold.
!flag but the distinction has existed | The Greek says that if they were one "they will make themselves vanish in themselves (ἀφανιεῖ)", and if distinguished by otherness they will not be the first; nothing of a distinction that has existed.

@p
@greek ἡμῖν μὲν γὰρ ἦν ἡ νόησις καλόν
For us thinking was a fine thing, because the soul needs to have intellect; and for intellect, because its being is the same as thinking, and thinking made it: so it must be with thinking, and always take in an understanding of itself, that this is this, that the two are one. But if it were one only, it would be enough for itself, and would not have needed to take it in.
!flag to the Intellectual-Principle it is appropriate as being one thing with the very essence | The Greek says "its being (τὸ εἶναι) is the same" as thinking: being, not essence.
!flag carrying the assurance of identity, of the unity of the two | The Greek says it takes in an understanding of itself "that this is this, that the two are one (ὅτι τὰ δύο ἕν)".
!note Intellect's being the same as its thinking: Parmenides' fragment B3, "for thinking and being are the same", quoted in V.1.8 and V.9.5.

@p
@greek ἐπεὶ καὶ τὸ γνῶθι σαυτὸν
For "know yourself" is said to those who, because of the multitude in them, have the task of counting themselves up and learning what and how many things they are, not knowing all of them, or none, nor what rules, nor in respect of what they are themselves. But if it is anything to itself, it is so in a greater way than by knowledge and thinking and joint perception of itself: since it is not even anything to itself. For it brings nothing into itself, but is enough for itself. So it is not good to itself either, but to the others: for they need it, but it would not need itself: for that would be laughable, for so it would also be in need of itself.
!flag The First on the contrary if it have content must exist in a way too great | The Greek says "if it is anything to itself (τί ἐστιν αὐτῷ), it is so in a greater way": anything to itself, not content.
!flag it would be absurd to suppose The Good standing in need of goodness | The Greek says "that would be laughable (γελοῖον): for so it would also be in need of itself": of itself, not of goodness.
!note "Know yourself": the Delphic saying, read in Plato's Alcibiades I (128e-130e), where what rules in us is the soul, and Phaedrus (229e-230a), whether I am a beast more many-folded than Typhon.

@p
@greek οὐδὲ βλέπει δὴ ἑαυτό
Nor does it see itself: for something must be, and come to be, for it from the seeing. For it has given up all these to what comes after it, and it seems that nothing of what belongs to the others is present to it, as substance is not either. So it does not think either, if substance is here, and the first thinking, in the proper sense, and being, are both together. This is why there is neither account nor perception nor knowledge of it, because there is nothing one can predicate of it as present.
!flag even Being cannot be There | The Greek has "as substance (οὐσία) is not either": the modern version keeps "substance".
!flag which is a thing of the lower sphere | The Greek says "if substance is here (ἐνταῦθα)", with intellect, where the first thinking and being are together: in the intelligible, not a lower sphere.
!flag Reason, perception, intelligence, none of these | The Greek has "neither account (λόγος) nor perception nor knowledge (ἐπιστήμη)": knowledge, not intelligence, and λόγος as the account, as in the Parmenides.
!note No account, perception or knowledge: Plato's Parmenides (142a), of the one "there is no name, nor account (λόγος), nor any knowledge, nor perception, nor opinion".

@ch VI.7.42 | All about the king of all
When at a loss where to put these powers, put away what you think solemn in the second things: set the second about the first and the third about the second, and let each be as it is, the later hanging from the earlier. So it is said, "about the king of all are all things, and for his sake": he is the cause of their being, other than all, and if intellect is among all, intellect is not his. He sets the beautiful in the forms, the second, and him above all beauty; this world hangs from soul, soul from intellect, intellect from the Good, all through intermediaries.

@p
But when you are at a loss in such a matter, and seek where these things must be put, setting out to them by reasoning, put away these things that you think solemn among the second things, and do not add the second things to the first, nor the third to the second, but set the second about the first, and the third about the second: for so you will leave each of them as it is, and you will hang the later things from the earlier, as running round them, while those are by themselves.
!flag Secondaries are to be ranged under the First, tertiaries under the secondaries | The Greek says set the second "about (περὶ) the first", and the third about the second: about, as in the Letter quoted next, not under.
!flag Faced by the difficulty of placing these powers | The Greek says "these things (ταῦτα)", the solemn things of chapter 41, thinking and knowing; "powers" is MacKenna's.

@p
@greek διὸ καὶ ὀρθῶς καὶ ταύτῃ λέγεται
This is why it is rightly said in this way too: "about the king of all are all things, and for his sake are all things": he calls all the beings "all things", and says "for his sake", since he is the cause of their being, and they reach for him, as it were, as being other than all things and having nothing that is present to them: or else they would no longer be all things, if anything of the others after him were present to him. If, then, intellect too is among all things, intellect is not his either.
!flag for certainly His very nature requires that nothing of the later be in Him | The Greek says "or else they would no longer be all things, if anything of the others after him were present to him": the argument is about the all, not his nature's requirement.
!flag and they reach to Him as to something differing from them all | The Greek says they reach for him "as it were" (οἷον), as other than all things; MacKenna leaves out the "as it were".
!note "About the king of all": Plato's Letter II (312e), "about the king of all are all things, and for his sake are all things, and he is the cause of all beautiful things; and second things about the second, and third things about the third", read as Plotinus' three, the Good, intellect and soul, in I.8.2 and V.1.8.

@greek αἴτιον δὲ λέγων πάντων καλῶν
And calling him the cause of all beautiful things, he seems to set the beautiful in the forms, and him above all this beautiful. Setting these as second, he says that the third, what came after these, hang from them; and setting things about the third, it is clear that he means the things that came from the third, this world, as hanging from soul. And, with soul hanging from intellect and intellect from the Good, so all things hang from that one through intermediaries, some near, some neighbours of those near, while the perceptibles, at the farthest remove, hang from soul.
!flag He being set above all that is beautiful here | The Greek says he is set "above all this beautiful (ὑπὲρ τὸ καλὸν πᾶν τοῦτο)", the beauty in the forms; "here" is MacKenna's.
!flag Where we read that He is the cause of all beauty we are clearly to understand that beauty depends upon the Forms | The Greek says "he seems (φαίνεται) to set the beautiful in the forms": Plato seems to, Plotinus reads; MacKenna makes it clear.
!note All things hanging from the Good through intermediaries: the ladder of chapter 33 above, from matter to soul to intellect, read downward; and V.5.3.
